The film also shows the press being easily manipulated by government sources, further highlighting the untrustworthiness of institutions.

title: Tess
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The church is portrayed as uncaring and unwilling to provide a Christian burial for Tess's child, highlighting the institution's failure to offer compassion. The legal system is also implicitly criticized, as Tess fears being hanged for her actions, suggesting a lack of faith in justice. The narrative shows characters circumventing societal norms and expectations, such as Tess's self-baptism of her child, further emphasizing the distrust in established institutions. The family's obsession with their noble lineage, which ultimately brings them no tangible benefit, underscores the emptiness and ineffectiveness of social structures.

title: The Howling
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police investigation into Eddie Quist seems initially competent, but quickly devolves into a half-assed operation where Karen is nearly killed. The news station, KDHB, exploits Karen's trauma for ratings, prioritizing sensationalism over her well-being. The Colony, presented as a therapeutic community, is revealed to be a haven for werewolves led by Dr. Waggner, who manipulates and controls them. The film suggests that these institutions, meant to protect and heal, are either ineffective or actively harmful, forcing Karen to take matters into her own hands.

title: Take This Job and Shove It
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a corporation (Ellison Group) acquiring a local brewery (Pickett's) with the intent of maximizing profit, disregarding the well-being of the employees and the quality of the beer. Frank, the protagonist, is tasked with implementing these changes, leading to layoffs and a decline in product quality. Dialogue such as "You can take your job and shove it!" and the workers' collective decision to start their own brewery highlight a deep distrust of corporate institutions and a desire to circumvent them. The climax involves sabotaging the brewery to expose the corporation's disregard for quality, further emphasizing the theme.

title: The Devil and Max Devlin
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. The narrative features a slum landlord (Joe Basuti) who is mentioned as someone the agents of hell would get anyway, suggesting a systemic problem. Max Devlin is a real estate agent who is portrayed as someone who doesn't care about the tenants, as he says, "Some landlords will allow a place to go to hell in a trash can, but not me." He also complains about the tenants, especially the children, and their "mangy little hands on your fresh paint." This recurring theme affects Max's choices as he tries to find souls to take his place, and the agents of hell are portrayed as corrupt and willing to lie to get what they want.

title: Taps
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative revolves around the impending closure of Bunker Hill Academy due to a decision by the board of trustees, who prioritize real estate potential over the school's tradition and the blood of its graduates. General Bache expresses his frustration, stating, "They didn't consult me...They just papered it and penciled it and they went ahead and did it because that's what the numbers said." This highlights a distrust in the institution's leadership and their motives. The cadets, led by Major Moreland, actively fight against this decision, viewing the institution as inherently corrupt and prioritizing profit over honor and tradition, culminating in an armed standoff.

title: Nighthawks
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The ATAC squad is formed due to a "serious lack of ruthlessness by the police." The training emphasizes that law enforcement is "poorly armed" and indoctrinated in "non-deadly force," which is "catastrophic with terrorists." DaSilva's rogue actions and distrust of the system are highlighted, culminating in his decision to disobey orders and confront Wulfgar directly. The film portrays the police as ineffective and bureaucratic, requiring vigilante-style action to combat terrorism, as evidenced by the instructor's statement: "To combat violence you need greater violence."

title: Atlantic City
justification: The film presents a world where institutions are unreliable and easily corrupted. The protagonist, Lou, is a former mobster navigating a decaying Atlantic City, where the promise of casino-driven revitalization is tainted by exploitation and crime. The police chief is portrayed as more concerned with maintaining a clean image than addressing the underlying issues. Sally is fired from her job due to her husband's criminal record, highlighting the arbitrary and unfair nature of institutional decisions. The narrative suggests that individuals must rely on their own wits and connections to survive, rather than trusting in formal systems.

title: Southern Comfort
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Louisiana National Guard is portrayed as incompetent and indifferent to the well-being of its members. Spencer predicts the command's delayed response to their disappearance: "At three they'll start checking the bars. By four they'll really get steamed. By five it'll occur to someone that maybe we got lost." This highlights a lack of faith in the institution's responsibility. Further, the narrative suggests the Guard is more concerned with maintaining social order through force ("beating up on college kids and tear gassing niggers") than actual military preparedness. The disastrous training exercise and the subsequent abandonment of the lost squad underscore the institution's failure to protect its members, forcing the protagonists to rely on their own rogue actions for survival.

title: An Officer and a Gentleman
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The Navy, as an institution, is portrayed as harsh, unforgiving, and even abusive. Drill Instructor Foley embodies this cynicism, using psychological manipulation and physical challenges to break down the officer candidates. Dialogue such as, "I will use every means necessary, fair and unfair, to trip you up," and his constant berating of the candidates, highlights the adversarial relationship between the individual and the institution. The Puget Sound debs are also presented as cynical, scheming to trap the officer candidates into marriage, further illustrating a distrust of genuine connection and a reliance on manipulation.

title: Porky's
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in "Porky's." The film depicts law enforcement as corrupt and complicit with criminal activity, specifically with Porky, the owner of an illegal establishment. This is evidenced by dialogue where it's revealed that the sheriff is Porky's brother, and the sheriff actively protects Porky's interests, even threatening the protagonists. The boys are extorted by the sheriff after being caught at Porky's, highlighting the abuse of power. The film also portrays the school administration as ineffective and easily manipulated, further reinforcing the theme of institutional failure.

title: Star Wars Ep. IV: A New Hope
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Imperial Senate is dissolved because it is seen as an obstacle to the Empire's control, with regional governors taking direct control. Tarkin expresses distrust in Leia's truthfulness, leading to the destruction of Alderaan. The narrative also highlights the Empire's disregard for diplomacy, as seen in their attack on Leia's consular ship, which they claim was carrying rebel spies. The dissolution of the Imperial Senate and the reliance on fear to maintain control demonstrate a deep-seated cynicism towards traditional institutions and governance.

title: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Starfleet is portrayed as bureaucratic and uncaring, exemplified by the Kobayashi Maru scenario, a 'no-win situation' designed as a 'test of character' rather than a practical exercise. Admiral Kirk is shown chafing under the constraints of his administrative role, longing for command. Carol Marcus expresses distrust of Starfleet's intentions regarding Project Genesis, fearing its weaponization. Khan's exile and the Reliant crew's orders to seize Genesis highlight Starfleet's potential for misuse of power and disregard for individual well-being, driving the plot forward.

title: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this narrative. The story revolves around the conflict between Sheriff Ed Earl Dodd, who tolerates the Chicken Ranch, and Melvin P. Thorpe, a consumer advocate who exposes it on television. The Governor's reluctance to take a clear stance, prioritizing public opinion polls over justice, exemplifies institutional failure. The town council's initial support for the Chicken Ranch due to its economic contributions, followed by their swift condemnation when public opinion shifts, highlights the corruptibility of local government. Ultimately, the Chicken Ranch is shut down due to public pressure and political maneuvering, demonstrating the power of media and public opinion over local tradition and the Sheriff's personal beliefs.

title: Annie
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Miss Hannigan's orphanage is depicted as a place of neglect and abuse, where the children are exploited for labor and affection is feigned ('I love you, Miss Hannigan'). The police are shown as unsympathetic and bureaucratic, initially dismissing Annie's claims about Sandy ('Yeah? Where's his licence? Where's his leash?'). While these instances highlight flaws within specific institutions, the narrative also presents Oliver Warbucks, a powerful figure, working with President Roosevelt to address societal problems, suggesting that institutions can be reformed and utilized for good. The New Deal is presented as a potential solution, albeit one debated, indicating a belief in the possibility of institutional improvement.

title: Firefox
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative revolves around the theft of a Soviet warplane, an act necessitated by the perceived threat the plane poses to global security. The American and British intelligence agencies are willing to engage in morally questionable activities, such as drug smuggling and sacrificing agents, to achieve their goals. The dialogue highlights a deep mistrust of the Soviet system, portraying it as oppressive and willing to sacrifice individuals for its own ends. The protagonist, Gant, must circumvent the KGB and other Soviet institutions to succeed, indicating a fundamental distrust in their ability to act justly or predictably.

title: First Blood
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts law enforcement, particularly Sheriff Teasle and his deputies, as abusing their power and acting unjustly. Rambo is arrested for vagrancy and resisting arrest, but the deputies escalate the situation through brutality and abuse, leading to Rambo's escape and a violent conflict. The dialogue highlights the deputies' disregard for Rambo's rights and their willingness to use excessive force. The arrival of Colonel Trautman underscores the incompetence of the local authorities in handling the situation, further emphasizing the failure of the institution to maintain order and justice.

title: Tootsie
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Michael's agent, George, embodies the failures of the agent-actor relationship, prioritizing money over talent and dismissing Michael's artistic integrity. George states, "This is gonna disgust you, but a lot of people are in this business to make money." He also tells Michael, "You've got one of the worst reputations in this town, Michael. Nobody will hire you." The soap opera world is portrayed as superficial and creatively stifling, with the director, Ron, being condescending and artistically shallow. The hospital setting in the soap is rife with unprofessional behavior and power imbalances, further highlighting the corruption and dysfunction within established systems.

title: Conan the Barbarian
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. King Osric's inability to deal with Thulsa Doom's snake cult, requiring him to hire thieves to retrieve his daughter, highlights institutional weakness. The line, "I've chafed for years at this demigod. Snakes in my beautiful city," shows the king's powerlessness. The film depicts formal authority as ineffective against the cult's pervasive influence, forcing characters to operate outside the law to achieve justice. The king's lament, "when the throne room becomes a prison," further emphasizes the limitations and disillusionment associated with institutional power.

title: The Toy
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Jack, encounters systemic barriers in his job search due to racial discrimination, as highlighted by the dialogue: "They're not hiring any blacks." and "I just want a job." The newspaper owner, U.S. Bates, embodies institutional corruption, using his wealth and influence to manipulate people and evade legal consequences. The legal system is also portrayed cynically, as Angela's activism against the KKK is met with resistance and the senator's involvement with the Klan is exposed. Jack's eventual employment at the newspaper is framed as a compromise, suggesting that even those who challenge the system may be co-opted.

title: The World According to Garp
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. While there are instances of characters behaving outside of societal norms (e.g., Jenny's unconventional approach to motherhood, Garp's violent outburst at the stop sign), these actions stem more from individual eccentricities or emotional responses than from a systemic critique of institutions. The school setting appears relatively benign, and while there's a mention of hate mail directed at Jenny, it doesn't indicate a fundamental failure of institutions to protect her. The narrative focuses more on personal relationships and individual struggles than on systemic corruption or ineffectiveness.

title: Blade Runner
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Deckard is a former "blade runner" who is pulled back into service by Captain Bryant, despite Deckard's desire to remain retired. Bryant's line, "If you're not cop, you're little people. No choice, huh? No choice, pal," highlights the coercive nature of the police force and the lack of individual agency. The Tyrell Corporation, a powerful entity, is shown to be manipulative and exploitative, creating replicants with limited lifespans and implanted memories to control them. The police are portrayed as brutal and willing to use lethal force, as seen in the deaths of Zhora and Pris. The ending, where Gaff implies Rachael's life is also limited, reinforces the idea that even those in positions of authority are complicit in a system that devalues life.

title: 48 Hrs.
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays law enforcement as flawed and sometimes corrupt. Jack Cates is portrayed as a 'hot dog' cop who bends the rules, and his superiors are concerned about the department appearing to be in the 'revenge business' after a cop killing. The dialogue includes instances of police brutality and racial slurs, suggesting a systemic problem within the force. The judicial system is also criticized when Reggie Hammond says, 'The judicial system ain't shit' after Luther, who shot at a cop, is released.

title: Things Are Tough All Over
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The characters repeatedly encounter institutions that fail them or are actively corrupt. The police are portrayed as prejudiced and ineffective, as seen when the woman reports a pervert and the officer is dismissive and makes prejudiced remarks. The Arabs' car wash business is a front for money laundering, and they resort to violence and illegal activities. The characters are cheated out of their money, highlighting a lack of trust in business dealings and the legal system to provide recourse. The final resolution involves exploiting the pornography industry to launder money, further emphasizing the corruption and moral bankruptcy of institutions.

title: Night Shift
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Chuck is forced onto the night shift because his supervisor's nephew wants his job, highlighting corruption within the workplace. The police are portrayed as easily bought off or manipulated, as seen when Bill uses a morgue vehicle for personal gain and later when they raid the health club. The legal system is also shown as flawed, with Belinda facing charges and the system seemingly favoring those with connections or money, culminating in the lawyer getting them their jobs back. The narrative emphasizes characters operating outside or against these flawed systems to achieve their goals, such as Chuck and Bill's pimping venture and their eventual confrontation with the police and mobsters.

title: Dead Men Don’t Wear Plaid
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts institutions, particularly law enforcement and government, as easily manipulated or bypassed. The protagonist, Reardon, frequently circumvents official channels, relying on his own methods and contacts like Marlowe. The entire plot revolves around a conspiracy that exploits a scientist and involves former Nazi officers, highlighting a deep-seated distrust in established systems. The dialogue reveals that even local law enforcement in Carlotta is corrupt or easily swayed, further emphasizing the systemic failure.

title: Pink Floyd: The Wall
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The lyrics depict schools as oppressive environments that stifle creativity and individuality, with teachers using "dark sarcasm" and thought control. The line "All in all it's just another brick in the wall" suggests a systemic problem within the education system. The legal system is also portrayed cynically, with the protagonist subjected to a show trial where the judge is biased and eager to impose the "full penalty of law." The line "The evidence before the court is incontrovertible" suggests a predetermined outcome, highlighting the system's lack of fairness.

title: Grease 2
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. Miss McGee and Mr. Spears are presented as figures of authority, but they are mostly played for comedic effect, with Mr. Spears' mental exhaustion being a recurring joke. There's a brief scene where Miss McGee confronts Nogerelli about motorcycles on the lawn, but it's ineffective. The school system is more of a backdrop for teenage romance and social dynamics than a target of critique. The most salient example is the farcical sex education class, but it's more about awkwardness than institutional failure.

title: Monsignor
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not the dominant engine. The narrative portrays institutions, particularly political ones, as flawed and often self-serving. For example, the Communist party leaders manipulate Peppone by promoting him to Senator to remove him from local politics: "Promoveatur ut amoveatur, remember." Similarly, the Church hierarchy sends Don Camillo away to Rome, ostensibly for a promotion, but really to neutralize his influence. The film also shows the local council prioritizing political gains over the needs of the people, as seen in their initial plan to build houses on consecrated ground. While the film ultimately resolves conflicts through cooperation, the initial distrust and manipulation within institutions are recurring and impactful.

title: Making Love
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. The main characters, Zack and Claire, are shown to have careers, Zack as a doctor and Claire in television, but the narrative does not focus on the institutions themselves as being corrupt or untrustworthy. Claire expresses frustration with her job, stating, "Every time I come up with an idea... that's fresh or unconventional, I just get shot down," but this is more about creative differences than systemic corruption. The medical institution is only shown through Zack's interactions with patients, and there is no indication of systemic issues. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but does not drive the plot.

title: Tex
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While there are no explicit statements condemning institutions, the narrative subtly reveals their shortcomings. The family's poverty and reliance on unstable income sources, like rodeo winnings, suggest a failure of social safety nets. The school system is portrayed as somewhat indifferent to Tex's individual needs, as seen in his teacher's dismissive attitude towards his book reports. Cole's influence and threats to involve the 'state welfare people' and 'County Juvenile Bureau' highlight the potential for institutions to be used as tools of control or intimidation, rather than support.

title: Class of 1984
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Mr. Norris, faces constant obstruction from the school administration and the police. The principal prioritizes the school's image over student safety, as evidenced by his reluctance to suspend Stegman after the assault, stating, "There will be no disciplinary measures taken on hand by one of my teachers." The police express their inability to effectively prosecute juvenile offenders, stating, "Nowadays, you wanna make a case against a juvenile... you gotta be holding his hand while he's robbing you." This systemic failure forces Mr. Norris to take matters into his own hands, culminating in a violent confrontation with Stegman and his gang to protect his pregnant wife and his students.

title: Bambi
justification: The provided subtitles offer minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The narrative primarily focuses on the life cycle of animals in the forest, their relationships, and the dangers they face. While 'Man' is presented as a threat, there's no indication of any formal institutions being corrupt, incompetent, or untrustworthy. The Great Prince of the Forest is respected, but this doesn't imply a systemic reliance on or disillusionment with any formal structure. The story is more about natural survival and personal growth than societal critique.

title: Megaforce
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in Megaforce. The film portrays SCUFF (Supreme Command United Free Forces), a clandestine organization representing the world's free nations, as duplicitous and self-serving. General Byrne-White betrays Megaforce, claiming their actions are a 'blatant act of war' and abandoning them to Guerera's forces. This betrayal highlights the untrustworthiness of formal institutions and their willingness to sacrifice individuals for political expediency. Hunter's line, 'It's all on the wheel. It all comes around,' suggests a cyclical nature of betrayal and disillusionment with established power structures.

title: The Concrete Jungle
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Elizabeth, is framed for drug trafficking by her boyfriend, highlighting a corrupt system. Once imprisoned, she encounters a prison environment rife with corruption, drug abuse, and violence, overseen by a Warden (Fletcher) who is complicit in the illicit activities. Elizabeth is forced to navigate this system, ultimately becoming an informant to expose the corruption, indicating a deep mistrust and active fight against the institution. The film concludes with the exposure of the corrupt system, reinforcing the idea that institutions are fundamentally flawed and require external intervention to achieve justice.

title: Vice Squad
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the police force as deeply flawed, with officers engaging in unethical and brutal behavior. Walsh manipulates Princess, highlighting the corrupt nature of the system. The dialogue reveals a pervasive sense of disillusionment, as characters like Walsh acknowledge the futility of their efforts to clean up the streets. The ending reinforces this cynicism, with Walsh's actions being questioned and the overall impact of his work deemed negligible, suggesting a system that is fundamentally resistant to positive change.

title: Tempest
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are references to strikes and labor problems affecting the construction of a casino, suggesting some frustration with labor unions or regulations. However, these issues are presented more as obstacles to business than as evidence of systemic corruption or failure. The doctor's comment about renewing his contract because of 'expensive fantasies' hints at a possible dissatisfaction with the medical system, but it's not a central theme. Overall, institutions are present but not portrayed as inherently untrustworthy or actively fought against.

title: Paradise
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative consistently portrays institutions, particularly those associated with Western civilization and religious authority, as untrustworthy or actively harmful. The British East India Company is presented as exploitative, with characters like Sheik Hab El-Aziz, enabled by the company's presence, engaging in slavery. The Reverend James McBride embodies religious hypocrisy and intolerance, leading to his family's demise. The protagonists must circumvent these flawed systems to survive, relying on their own resourcefulness and each other rather than external aid or established structures. The climax involves escaping capture and choosing to release the chimpanzees rather than subject them to captivity, highlighting a rejection of societal norms.

title: The Seduction
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police, represented by Max, are portrayed as largely ineffective and constrained by bureaucracy. Despite Jamie being stalked and terrorized, Max states, "as far as the law is concerned, the guy really hasn't committed a crime." He later admits, "There's no way you can stop these kinda people." and ultimately suggests Brandon "Get a gun." The police emergency line is shown to be useless, with Jamie only hearing a recording when she desperately needs help. This systemic failure forces Brandon to consider vigilantism and Max to unofficially use an ex-con for protection.

title: They Call Me Bruce
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts law enforcement as easily bribed and corrupt, as evidenced by the officers who accept a bribe to ignore the protagonist's illegal activities. The FBI is portrayed as needing to be bribed with 'cigars' (dynamite). The protagonist and his friend Freddy are manipulated by the mafia, who use them to deliver drugs across the country, highlighting the failure of the system to protect innocent individuals. The protagonist is ultimately saved by a federal agent, but only after he has been thoroughly exploited by criminal organizations, suggesting that the system is reactive rather than preventative.

title: Six Weeks
justification: The subtitles present a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While there are no explicit examples of corruption, the dialogue suggests a general dissatisfaction with the political process. The politician, Patrick Dalton, acknowledges that politicians often sound alike and that issues are complicated unnecessarily. Charlotte Dreyfus expresses a dislike for politicians, implying a degree of mistrust. However, these instances are not structurally central to the plot; they serve more as background context than driving forces behind the narrative. The story focuses more on personal relationships and individual struggles than on systemic failures.

title: Evil Under the Sun
justification: The subtitles contain a few instances that suggest a mild level of institutional cynicism. Poirot is hired by an insurance company to investigate a potential fraud, implying a reliance on external investigators rather than internal controls. There's also a brief mention of Tyranian doctors' limited skills, suggesting incompetence within the medical system. Daphne's comment about the King of Tyrania keeping her quiet with a summer palace also hints at corruption. However, these instances are isolated and do not form a central theme of the narrative, as the primary focus is on solving the murder mystery, not on systemic institutional failures.

title: Night Crossing
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative revolves around families attempting to escape East Germany, highlighting the oppressive nature of the regime and its control over its citizens' lives. The border, heavily guarded and equipped with automated weapons, symbolizes the institution's determination to prevent its people from leaving. Dialogue such as "It is designed not to keep enemies out, but to keep its own people in" and the constant surveillance by neighbors who "could be phoning the SSD right now" underscore the pervasive distrust and fear of the state. The lengths to which the families go to circumvent the system, including building a hot air balloon in secret, further emphasize the central role of institutional failure and the need for rogue actions to achieve freedom.

title: Star Wars Ep. VI: Return of the Jedi
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a dominant theme. The Empire is presented as an oppressive force, but the focus is more on the personal conflict between Luke and Vader than on systemic institutional failures. The Rebel Alliance, while fighting against the Empire, is not explicitly portrayed as distrustful of institutions in general. There are instances of characters circumventing or manipulating the Empire's systems, such as using a stolen shuttle with a secret code, but these actions are driven by necessity rather than a deep-seated cynicism towards institutions. The narrative primarily centers on individual heroism and familial conflict, with institutional critique playing a secondary role.

title: Flashdance
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal amount of institutional cynicism. The primary example is Alex's reluctance to date her boss, Nick, because it's "not a good idea to go out with the boss." This suggests a potential distrust of workplace dynamics and power structures. However, this is a minor element and doesn't drive the plot. The narrative focuses more on personal relationships and individual aspirations than on systemic issues or institutional failures.

title: Trading Places
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Duke brothers manipulate the system for their own gain, highlighting a deep mistrust in fairness. They explicitly discuss rigging the orange juice market using insider information obtained through bribery, stating, "If Mr. Beeks does what we paid him to do, we should have a very happy New Year." Winthorpe is framed and unjustly imprisoned, showcasing the ease with which the legal system can be corrupted. The police are easily manipulated, arresting Winthorpe based on planted evidence, further illustrating the system's vulnerability. The narrative structurally relies on the failure of institutions to deliver justice or fairness.

title: WarGames
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the military and government institutions as deeply flawed and prone to catastrophic errors. The WOPR computer system, designed to manage nuclear war, nearly initiates a global thermonuclear war due to a programming flaw, highlighting the danger of relying solely on technology and removing human judgment. The dialogue reveals a lack of trust in human decision-making within the military, with characters advocating for computers to take over critical decisions. The protagonist, David, must circumvent these institutions to prevent disaster, demonstrating their ineffectiveness and the need for rogue action.

title: Octopussy
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The plot revolves around General Orlov's rogue attempt to undermine disarmament talks by detonating a nuclear bomb on a US airbase, showcasing a deep mistrust of the Soviet government's policies. Bond actively works against Orlov and the Soviet military to prevent this disaster, highlighting the failure of institutional checks and balances. The British government is portrayed as somewhat naive, initially viewing the situation as a simple jewelry smuggling operation, further emphasizing the need for Bond to operate outside of established channels. The dialogue explicitly reveals Orlov's belief that the 'handful of old men in Moscow' are willing to 'bargain away our advantage in disarmament talks,' driving his treacherous actions.

title: Mr. Mom
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The primary example is Jack's experience with his company, where he and his colleagues are abruptly fired ('canned') despite their contributions. The dialogue highlights the company's focus on profits over people, as seen in Jinx's statement, 'If you can't sell cars, you can't pay people.' However, the narrative doesn't dwell extensively on systemic corruption or the impossibility of finding justice within the system. While Jack and his colleagues are initially bitter, they eventually find new opportunities, suggesting that the institutional failure is not absolute or insurmountable. The film also touches on the superficiality and competitiveness of the advertising industry, but this is more a critique of corporate culture than a deep-seated indictment of institutions.

title: Staying Alive
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The characters are primarily focused on their personal lives and careers as dancers. There are brief mentions of the difficulties of finding work and the competitive nature of the industry, such as Jackie's comment that the auditioners "make you feel like you're wasting your time." However, these instances are isolated and do not suggest a systemic distrust or failure of institutions. The director's behavior is harsh, but it is not clear that this is representative of the industry as a whole.

title: Risky Business
justification: The film exhibits a moderate degree of institutional cynicism. While not the central engine of the plot, mistrust and circumvention of institutions are relevant and recurring themes. Joel's parents' overbearing involvement in his college application process, including arranging an interview with Princeton, suggests a manipulation of the educational system. The school's disciplinary actions against Joel for his absence, while justified, are portrayed as overly harsh and potentially damaging to his future prospects. The police are depicted as aggressive and misinformed when they raid the house, highlighting a potential for institutional overreach. These instances contribute to a sense that institutions are not always helpful or just, influencing Joel's choices and actions.

title: National Lampoon's Vacation
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. The car dealership scene introduces the idea that businesses may not be trustworthy, as the protagonist is misled about his car order. Later, the police officer who pulls them over for the dog incident is initially aggressive and threatening, suggesting a potential for abuse of power. However, he eventually shows understanding and lets them go, mitigating the cynicism. The con artist at the motel and the exploitative Native American mechanic further contribute to a sense of societal untrustworthiness, but these instances are episodic and don't fundamentally challenge the institutions themselves.

title: Superman III
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. Gus Gorman's initial unemployment experience highlights the perceived ineffectiveness and uncaring nature of the unemployment system, where he is quickly dismissed and labeled as ineligible. Ross Webster, a powerful businessman, actively manipulates global markets and weather patterns for personal gain, showcasing a disregard for ethical and legal boundaries. The film also portrays the military-industrial complex in a negative light, with a general prioritizing chemical production over public safety. While Superman ultimately intervenes to restore order, the narrative emphasizes the systemic flaws and corruptibility of institutions, making it a recurring theme that affects major character choices and plot developments.

title: Never Say Never Again
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. M initially expresses reluctance to reactivate the Double-O agents, suggesting a preference for other methods. Q laments bureaucratic red tape and budget cuts hindering his work, stating, "Bureaucrats running the place, everything done by the book. Can't make a decision unless the computer gives you the go-ahead." Bond's superior, M, is shown to be ineffectual, requiring Bond to take matters into his own hands. The theft of nuclear warheads occurs due to a compromised American Air Force officer, highlighting a failure in security protocols and institutional oversight. The narrative relies on Bond's rogue actions and circumvention of formal channels to resolve the crisis, indicating a distrust in the ability of institutions to handle the situation effectively.

title: Gandhi
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Gandhi", though not the dominant engine. The film portrays the British Empire's legal and political systems in South Africa and India as inherently unjust and discriminatory towards Indians. Dialogue such as "There are no coloured attorneys in South Africa" and the imposition of pass laws demonstrate systemic oppression. Gandhi's resistance involves challenging these laws and circumventing the established order through nonviolent civil disobedience. While the film also shows some British officials grappling with their conscience, the overall narrative highlights the structural flaws and biases within the imperial system, making mistrust in institutions a recurring theme.

title: Jaws 3-D
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays institutions, particularly Sea World management, as prioritizing profit and public image over safety and ethical considerations. Calvin Bouchard's decisions, such as moving the shark against Dr. Morgan's advice to boost attendance, exemplify this. The film also shows a disregard for regulations, as seen when the shark gate is left open, leading to Overman's death and the shark's entry. The narrative highlights the characters' need to circumvent or challenge the institution to address the shark threat and save lives, indicating a significant level of institutional failure.

title: The Big Chill
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are no clear indications of characters actively fighting against or circumventing corrupt systems. The dialogue focuses primarily on interpersonal relationships, grief, and personal struggles following a friend's suicide. While characters express dissatisfaction with their lives and choices, this does not translate into a systemic critique of institutions. The only possible hint is a brief mention of a character leaving the public defender's office because his clients were too guilty, but this is a personal choice rather than a systemic indictment.

title: Terms of Endearment
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. While there are mentions of institutions like schools and hospitals, they are not portrayed as inherently corrupt or untrustworthy. For example, there are brief mentions of Flap's job at a college and Emma's visit to the doctor, but these institutions are not central to the plot. The characters' personal relationships and struggles are the primary focus, rather than any systemic issues within institutions. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but does not drive the narrative.

title: Blue Thunder
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays law enforcement and government as deeply corrupt. The protagonist, Murphy, uncovers a conspiracy involving a dangerous helicopter prototype ('Blue Thunder') and the murder of a councilwoman. His superiors actively cover up the truth, ordering his grounding and psychiatric reevaluation to silence him. The dialogue explicitly reveals the willingness of officials to assassinate those who threaten their project, as Fletcher says, "Just drop the hammer on him." Murphy is forced to operate outside the system, becoming a rogue agent to expose the truth, highlighting the institutional failure.

title: Sudden Impact
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Inspector Callahan, frequently clashes with the police bureaucracy and legal system. The opening scene shows a judge dismissing a case due to Callahan's illegal search, highlighting the system's focus on procedure over justice. Callahan's superiors often criticize his methods, calling him a "dinosaur" whose ideas "don't fit today," and suspend him for his aggressive tactics. He is sent away to another town to investigate a case, which is perceived as a way to get him out of the way, further illustrating the institutional mistrust and desire to control his actions.

title: Porky's II: The Next Day
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts formal institutions, such as the school board, the county commission, and the police, as easily manipulated by corrupt individuals and groups (e.g., Reverend Flavel, Commissioner Gebhardt). Dialogue reveals that the school principal is pressured to suspend the Shakespeare production due to the influence of the Righteous Flock. Commissioner Gebhardt admits to engaging in "old-fashioned horse trading" to influence the school board's decision. The police are shown to be easily swayed by money and influence, as seen in their willingness to arrest the drama club based on a dubious warrant. The film portrays institutions as obstacles to artistic expression and personal freedom, requiring the characters to actively fight against or circumvent the system.

title: Psycho II
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film opens with Norman Bates being released from psychiatric care, despite public outcry and the victims' families' protests, highlighting a perceived failure of the legal system to protect the innocent. Mrs. Loomis voices this directly: "our courts protect the criminals, not their victims." The sheriff's initial reluctance to investigate the new murders, requiring external pressure from Lila Loomis, further underscores institutional inertia. The hospital board's hiring of Toomey, who runs the motel as a drug den, also shows institutional incompetence.

title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal amount of institutional cynicism. The primary conflict stems from the Queen's personal jealousy and desire to remain the fairest in the land, not from any systemic failure. While the Huntsman is ordered to kill Snow White, he disobeys, suggesting a personal moral compass overrides institutional demands. The dwarfs' independent lifestyle and distrust of strangers could be interpreted as a mild form of cynicism, but it's more about self-preservation than a critique of broader societal structures.

title: Twilight Zone: The Movie
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. In one segment, a man named Bill is denied a promotion and blames it on Jews, blacks, and Orientals, suggesting a distrust of corporate or governmental institutions. Later, he is robbed and shot, and the people he encounters are violent and prejudiced, indicating a breakdown in societal order and justice. In another segment, the residents of Sunnyvale Rest Home circumvent the rules to recapture their youth, implying that the institution's regulations stifle their well-being. Finally, in the segment with John Valentine, the pilot and crew initially dismiss his concerns about a creature on the wing, potentially endangering the flight, which shows a lack of responsiveness from authority figures.

title: Easy Money
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. There are minor instances of characters circumventing or complaining about systems, such as Monty needing Nicky's truck to pick up the wedding cake, implying a difficulty in obtaining resources through normal channels. The mother's lawyer, Scrappleton, is mentioned, but his role is primarily related to the will and not necessarily indicative of institutional corruption. The most significant example is the horse race fix, which suggests distrust in the fairness of gambling institutions, but this is a relatively isolated incident. Overall, while there are glimpses of cynicism, institutions are not structurally central to the plot.

title: High Road to China
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While there isn't a dominant theme of corruption, there are instances where institutions are portrayed as flawed or unhelpful. For example, the RAF initially refuses to lend Eve an aircraft, highlighting bureaucratic hurdles. Additionally, Bentik influences a judge to declare Eve's father dead, showcasing potential corruption within the legal system. However, these instances don't entirely drive the plot, as the main focus is on Eve's personal journey to find her father, rather than a systemic critique of institutions.

title: The Outsiders
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not dominant. The dialogue reveals a clear distrust of the judicial system, particularly regarding the potential for Ponyboy and Soda to be placed in a boys' home if they get into trouble with the police ("Darry says the court will split us up for sure if I do"). Dally's repeated run-ins with the police and his eventual death by police shooting further highlight a sense of institutional mistrust. The narrative also suggests that institutions like schools are ineffective in preventing social divisions and violence, as Ponyboy and Cherry, despite attending the same school, exist in separate worlds due to their social class. The film does not portray institutions as inherently helpful or just, but rather as systems that can be manipulated or circumvented, contributing to a moderate level of cynicism.

title: Spring Break
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts institutions as corrupt and easily manipulated. Dalby, Nelson's stepfather, uses bribery and the Unsafe Buildings Commission to try and shut down the Breeze n' Seas Motel, showcasing the abuse of power. Ames, a member of the Unsafe Buildings Commission, is explicitly bribed to close the motel. The police are portrayed as easily swayed, as seen when Dalby attempts to use his connections to avoid arrest. The narrative ultimately resolves with the exposure of Dalby's corruption, highlighting the need to fight against the system.

title: Sophie's Choice
justification: The subtitles present a limited degree of institutional cynicism. Sophie's father, a law professor, is revealed to be an anti-Semite whose writings contributed to the persecution of Jews, suggesting a corruption within the academic and legal systems. However, this is presented as a personal failing rather than a systemic one. Additionally, Sophie recounts her experiences in Auschwitz, where the Nazi regime represents a complete failure of societal institutions, but this is largely presented as historical context rather than a driving force in the present-day narrative. The subtitles do not show characters actively fighting or circumventing institutions, but rather grappling with the aftermath of their failures.

title: My Tutor
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Bobby's father pressures him to attend Yale, highlighting a potential distrust in alternative paths or institutions. The whorehouse scene depicts a failed attempt to engage with a social institution for pleasure, though this is played more for comedic effect than a serious critique. The language agency and the French tutor could be seen as a commentary on the commodification of education, but it's not presented as inherently corrupt. Overall, while there are hints of dissatisfaction with certain institutions, they don't fundamentally drive the plot or character actions.

title: Scarface
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film opens with Tony being processed by immigration, where he lies and manipulates the system to gain entry. He later agrees to assassinate a political figure for a green card, highlighting the corruptibility of the system. Tony's distrust extends to law enforcement, as evidenced by his bribery of Detective Bernstein to avoid legal repercussions. The banking system is also portrayed negatively, with Tony lamenting the high rates charged for laundering his money and expressing distrust of bankers. The film culminates in Tony's downfall, partially due to his defiance of Sosa, a powerful figure with connections to corrupt government officials, further emphasizing the pervasive nature of institutional corruption.

title: Class
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The headmaster is portrayed as more concerned with the school's image than with the students' well-being, as evidenced by his initial handling of the suicide and the SAT cheating scandal. The investigation into SAT cheating, while ostensibly about fairness, is also used to pressure students and protect the school's reputation. Skip's father, a board member of AT&T, represents a corrupt system where connections and wealth matter more than merit. The dialogue highlights a sense of disillusionment with authority and a system that seems rigged in favor of the privileged.

title: The Dead Zone
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative features a sheriff, Bannerman, who, frustrated by conventional methods, seeks help from a psychic to solve a series of murders, indicating a lack of faith in traditional law enforcement. Furthermore, the political system is portrayed cynically through the character of Greg Stillson, a manipulative politician who gains power through deceit and exploitation. The film suggests that institutions are vulnerable to corruption and manipulation, requiring individuals to take matters into their own hands, as the protagonist ultimately attempts to assassinate Stillson to prevent a catastrophic future.

title: Breathless
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Jesse, is a criminal on the run for shooting a cop, immediately establishing a conflict with law enforcement. He actively evades the police throughout the film, highlighting a distrust of the justice system. The police are portrayed as aggressive and willing to bend the rules, as seen when they pressure Monica for information and threaten her with deportation. Jesse's attempts to cash a check from a 'slick job' and his reliance on shady characters like Tolmatchoff and Berrutti further emphasize a world where institutions are bypassed or corrupted.

title: Yentl
justification: The film presents a society where religious law and tradition, while not overtly corrupt, actively restrict women's access to education and intellectual pursuits. Yentl's desire to study Talmud is consistently thwarted by societal norms and interpretations of religious law, as seen in the bookseller's refusal to sell her sacred texts and the general disapproval of women engaging in scholarly activities. While not a central conflict, this institutional barrier motivates Yentl's deception and journey, highlighting a subtle critique of rigid social structures. The dialogue reveals a system where women are expected to prioritize domestic roles over intellectual development, contributing to a sense of institutional limitation.

title: Max Dugan Returns
justification: The film exhibits a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The protagonist, Nora, experiences firsthand the ineffectiveness of the police in recovering her stolen car, highlighting their bureaucratic processes and lack of genuine concern. Lieutenant Costello, while seemingly dedicated, is constrained by the system and ultimately unable to prevent further crimes. The dialogue reveals a general distrust of authority, with characters like Nora expressing anger at 'thieves' and questioning the value of formal institutions. However, the narrative doesn't solely focus on institutional failure; it also explores personal relationships and individual actions, preventing cynicism from becoming the dominant theme.

title: All the Right Moves
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. Coach Nickerson's actions, particularly blackballing Stefen from college opportunities due to a personal grudge, demonstrate a misuse of power within the high school football system. The dialogue reveals that Nickerson lied about Stefen's attitude to a college recruiter, actively sabotaging his chances. Additionally, the town's reliance on the failing steel mill and the limited opportunities for non-athletes, as expressed by Lisa, suggest a systemic failure to provide avenues for success beyond traditional roles. While the film doesn't focus solely on institutional corruption, these elements significantly impact the protagonist's journey and choices.

title: Valley Girl
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are no explicit critiques or distrust of institutions. The narrative focuses on interpersonal relationships and social dynamics within a high school setting. The only potential hint of cynicism is the casual disregard for rules, such as skipping cotillion ("Pass on cotillion just this once, okay?") or driving without permission, but these are presented as typical teenage rebellion rather than a systemic critique.

title: Krull
justification: The subtitles present a world where alliances between kingdoms are necessary to fight a common enemy, but these alliances are fraught with distrust and political maneuvering. King Turold expresses skepticism about the marriage alliance, stating, "I see no reason for an alliance with our ancient enemies." This suggests a pre-existing institutional distrust. However, the narrative focuses more on the external threat (the Beast and the Slayers) than on the internal failings or corruption of the kingdoms themselves. While there's a hint of cynicism, it doesn't become a central plot driver.

title: Spacehunter: Adventures in the Forbidden Zone
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Intergalactic Consortium offers a reward for rescuing survivors, but the planet Terra 11 is under quarantine due to a plague, suggesting institutional neglect or failure to address the crisis. The planet is ruled by 'Overdog McNabb,' a former member of a medical expedition who assumed dictatorship, indicating a breakdown of order and governance. The protagonist, Wolff, operates outside the law, collecting merilium scrap and ignoring parking tickets, suggesting a disregard for institutional rules. Sector Chief Washington, despite being a representative of authority, is portrayed as somewhat corrupt and self-serving, willing to bend the rules for personal gain, further reinforcing the theme of institutional cynicism.

title: A Christmas Story
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. The school system is portrayed neutrally, with Miss Shields being a somewhat eccentric but ultimately fair teacher. There's a brief mention of 'official justice' when Schwartz is punished, but it's not a central theme. The only hint of cynicism comes from Ralphie's disappointment with the Little Orphan Annie decoder pin, which turns out to be a commercial: 'Be sure to drink your Ovaltine.' Son of a bitch.' However, this is more about disillusionment than a systemic critique.

title: Richard Pryor Here and Now
justification: The provided subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. While Richard Pryor touches on societal issues, his commentary primarily revolves around personal experiences, observations on race, and humorous anecdotes. There are brief mentions of police encounters and the legal system, but these are presented more as comedic fodder than as indictments of systemic corruption or failure. For example, Pryor jokes about telling on people to avoid jail time, but this is framed as a personal survival tactic rather than a critique of the justice system's fairness. The absence of sustained or plot-relevant criticism of institutions suggests a low salience of institutional cynicism in this particular performance.

title: Still Smokin
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. The Amsterdam International Film Festival is portrayed as somewhat disorganized and financially unstable, as evidenced by the cancellation telegram and the promoter running off with the money. The characters exploit the confusion around Burt Reynolds's identity, suggesting a degree of opportunism and a willingness to circumvent established norms. However, the narrative doesn't heavily rely on institutional failure as a central plot driver; the characters' antics and drug use are more prominent. The police are briefly shown in a comedic sketch, but not in a way that highlights systemic corruption or incompetence.

title: Monty Python's The Meaning of Life
justification: Institutional cynicism is a recurring theme, though not the dominant engine of the narrative. The opening segment depicts the 'Permanent Assurance Company' as failing under 'oppressive new corporate management,' leading to violent rebellion. Later, the film satirizes the medical establishment, portraying doctors as detached and profit-driven, exemplified by the 'machine that goes 'ping'' and the administrator's focus on leasing agreements. The military is also mocked, with officers displaying incompetence and indifference to casualties ('Jolly good' after learning of significant losses). While these instances highlight institutional flaws and absurdities, they are presented satirically rather than as central plot drivers, suggesting a relevant but not dominant theme.

title: Two of a Kind
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Zack is pressured to testify against Debbie, and vice versa, despite lacking concrete evidence. The legal system is also presented as easily influenced, with the mention of a D.A. who is a 'friend' and willing to offer probation in exchange for testimony. The police prioritize closing the case over ensuring justice, highlighting a distrust in their ability to uphold the law fairly. The film culminates with the police failing to prevent the hostage situation, further emphasizing their ineffectiveness.

title: Private School
justification: The subtitles present a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Miss Dutchbok, the headmistress, is frequently mocked and referred to as "Douchebag," suggesting a lack of respect for her authority. The school's focus on outdated and awkward sex education, as well as the confinement imposed on the students for minor infractions, hints at a rigid and somewhat absurd system. However, the narrative doesn't heavily rely on institutional failure as a central plot driver; the characters' personal relationships and romantic entanglements take precedence over any systemic critique.

title: Uncommon Valor
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film revolves around Colonel Rhodes's deep mistrust of the government's efforts to find missing POWs, leading him to undertake a private, illegal mission. Dialogue such as "That's all I ever heard in Washington. Nobody could do anything. That's why I came here" and "The same politicians that never lost a single son in Vietnam, not one" highlights his belief that official channels are ineffective and uncaring. The need to circumvent government regulations and the CIA, as evidenced by the confiscation of weapons and the pursuit by government agents, further emphasizes the systemic failure and corruption that drives the plot. The film's narrative is structured around the protagonist's active fight against and circumvention of the system.

title: Christine
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Christine." While not the central engine, distrust in authority figures and institutions significantly impacts the narrative. Mr. Casey, the shop teacher, is initially presented as a figure of authority, but he fails to adequately address the bullying situation with Repperton, leading to further conflict. Detective Junkins represents law enforcement, but his methods are questionable, and he seems more interested in harassing Arnie than solving the murders. Arnie's parents also represent a form of institutional control, and he actively rebels against their attempts to control his life, particularly regarding his car. These instances contribute to a sense that institutions are either ineffective or actively working against the characters, influencing their choices and actions.

title: The Right Stuff
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative repeatedly highlights the flaws, limitations, and even potential dangers associated with formal institutions, particularly the military and NASA. For example, the initial breaking of the sound barrier is achieved outside of formal channels, with Yeager being paid under the table. Later, the Mercury program is portrayed as prioritizing public image and political goals over the expertise and desires of the test pilots, leading to conflicts over capsule design and control. The film also suggests a degree of distrust in the government's handling of information, particularly regarding the space race with Russia, and the downplaying of Grissom's capsule loss.

title: The Entity
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not dominant. Carla seeks help from a walk-in clinic and is seen by Dr. Sneiderman. While he attempts to help her, his methods are questioned by his superior, who dismisses Carla's experiences as hysteria and safe sex. The parapsychologists are also portrayed with some skepticism, as they are more interested in proving the existence of an entity than in Carla's well-being. This is exemplified when one of them says, "I want to get it so bad, I can taste it."

title: The Rescuers
justification: The film features an orphanage where Penny feels unloved and unwanted, highlighting a potential failure of the child welfare system. The police are mentioned as having given up looking for Penny, suggesting a lack of faith in law enforcement's ability to help. However, the Rescue Aid Society, an international organization, is portrayed positively, actively working to help those in need. While there are hints of institutional shortcomings, the narrative primarily focuses on the heroic actions of individuals and a benevolent organization, rather than systemic corruption or failure.

title: Stroker Ace
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Stroker Ace," though not dominant. The primary conflict arises from Stroker's contract with Clyde Torkle's Chicken Pit, which forces him to compromise his image and values. The legal system, represented by the lawyers, upholds this contract, trapping Stroker. While not overtly corrupt, the contract and its enforcement represent a system that prioritizes commercial interests over individual integrity. Stroker's eventual defiance and manipulation of the contract, along with Torkle's attempts to circumvent it, further highlight a distrust of formal agreements and a willingness to bend the rules.

title: Lone Wolf McQuade
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. The protagonist, Ranger McQuade, is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' who clashes with his superiors and federal agencies. Captain Tyler criticizes McQuade's 'brutal, uncooperative, obsolete and discriminatory nature,' highlighting a systemic perception of Rangers as problematic. McQuade is put on probation and faces a federal indictment, indicating a lack of trust and cooperation between different law enforcement bodies. Despite this, McQuade circumvents official channels to rescue his daughter, suggesting a distrust in the ability of institutions to provide justice effectively.

title: Zelig
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in "Zelig." The medical establishment is portrayed as initially baffled and then exploitative of Zelig's condition, with doctors offering conflicting diagnoses and ultimately failing to understand or help him. The legal system is shown as opportunistic, with lawyers exploiting Zelig's situation for personal gain and the courts unable to hold him accountable for actions committed while in his chameleon state. The film also touches on the media's sensationalism and the public's fickle fascination with Zelig, highlighting a general lack of genuine care or understanding. The protagonist actively circumvents the system, eventually escaping from the hospital and later fleeing the country to avoid legal consequences.

title: The Lords of Discipline
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the Carolina Military Institute as deeply flawed, with a corrupt secret society ("The Ten") operating within it. The protagonist, Will, actively fights against this system to protect a black cadet, Pearce, from being unjustly driven out. Dialogue such as "If 10 guys can go around in the dark, can change the rules any time they want, and get away with it, if that's the honor of this Institute, then that ring is a piece of crap" and the General's involvement in covering up the activities of The Ten highlight the systemic corruption and the need for rogue actions to achieve justice. The climax involves exposing the General and forcing the dissolution of The Ten, solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: The Smurfs and the Magic Flute
justification: The narrative contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not structurally central. The King is portrayed as somewhat foolish and easily manipulated, as seen when he readily believes Pirlouit's excuse for the merchant's departure and when he falls for Mortaille's trap. The army is briefly discredited when Pirlouit uses the flute to make them dance, but this is played for comedic effect rather than a serious critique. While the King's authority is undermined, the story primarily focuses on the magical flute and the characters' quest to retrieve it, rather than a systemic critique of the kingdom's institutions.

title: D.C. Cab
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in "D.C. Cab." The hack bureau is portrayed as ineffective and easily manipulated, as seen when Bravo is bribed and Harold openly disregards regulations. The police are shown as incompetent, failing to protect the community from crime and corruption, and are easily outsmarted by the cab drivers. The legal system is also depicted as flawed, with Myrna exploiting loopholes to steal the reward money and evade justice. The protagonist and his colleagues must circumvent these institutions to achieve their goals, highlighting the film's structural reliance on institutional failure.

title: Deal of the Century
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film portrays the arms industry as inherently corrupt, prioritizing profit over human life and global stability. Characters like Eddie Muntz explicitly acknowledge selling weapons to dictators and military juntas, highlighting the amorality of the business. The Peacemaker drone demonstration reveals institutional incompetence and a willingness to prioritize appearances over safety, culminating in a chaotic and destructive event. The film also shows how corporations exploit legal loopholes and engage in bribery to secure deals, further emphasizing the corruption within the system.

title: Doctor Detroit
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts formal institutions, particularly the police and the legal system, as easily manipulated and failing to deliver justice. Thelma's arrest and subsequent release due to a farcical courtroom scene highlights the system's vulnerability to theatrics and social connections. Additionally, the college is portrayed as being on the verge of collapse, dependent on a single donor, and more concerned with appearances than actual education. The protagonist, Clifford, must circumvent these failing systems by adopting the persona of "Doctor Detroit" to fight against the criminal underworld, indicating a lack of faith in traditional institutions to resolve the conflict.

title: The Man with Two Brains
justification: The subtitles present a world where medical professionals, while competent, are often eccentric and self-serving. Dr. Brandon expresses concern about Michael operating on a patient he personally injured, suggesting a potential conflict of interest, but this is quickly dismissed. The Austrian Institute of Craniology is portrayed as somewhat absurd, with stolen brains and a chaotic lecture. While these instances suggest flaws within institutions, they don't fundamentally drive the plot or portray institutions as inherently corrupt or untrustworthy. The narrative primarily focuses on individual eccentricities and romantic entanglements rather than systemic institutional failures.

title: Revenge of the Ninja
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police, represented by Lt. Dime, are portrayed as largely ineffective and reliant on Cho's expertise to understand the threat, highlighted by Dime's statement, "We're up against the wall in this case." The dialogue reveals a deep-seated mistrust of the police, particularly from Caifano, who states, "We don't need the police, we don't need you!" This sentiment, coupled with the police's inability to prevent or solve the crimes, underscores the failure of law enforcement and the necessity for Cho to take matters into his own hands, solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: The Year of Living Dangerously
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the Indonesian government under Sukarno as unstable and corrupt, with characters like Billy Kwan expressing disillusionment with Sukarno's leadership and the government's failure to address poverty. The military is depicted as exploitative, demanding money from local businesses. The political climate is so volatile that a coup attempt occurs, leading to widespread chaos and violence. The protagonist, Guy Hamilton, actively seeks to uncover the truth about an arms shipment, indicating a distrust of official narratives and a willingness to circumvent established channels to report the story.

title: Educating Rita
justification: The film portrays the academic institution as flawed and somewhat detached from the real world. Frank, the professor, is disillusioned and openly admits to being an "appalling teacher," suggesting a lack of faith in his role within the institution. He drinks heavily and expresses a desire to throw students out the window, indicating a deep dissatisfaction with his job and the academic environment. While not overtly corrupt, the institution is depicted as a place where Frank feels trapped and unfulfilled, and where students may not be getting the best education. The film also shows the institution as being more concerned with appearances than with the quality of education, as evidenced by the complaint about Frank being drunk in his tutorial.

title: Lovesick
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Dr. Benjamin faces scrutiny from "the society" (a psychoanalytic organization) for his unorthodox methods and relationships with patients. The society threatens suspension or termination, highlighting the rigid and potentially punitive nature of the institution. The dialogue reveals a system prioritizing conformity and reputation over individual patient needs, as seen in the pressure to abandon treating schizophrenics because "there's no percentage in treating them." The film also shows the social security office as a dehumanizing bureaucracy, further reinforcing the theme of institutional failure.

title: The Black Stallion Returns
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in the film. The Berber tribe's traditions and leadership are presented as being under threat from the Uruk tribe, who seek to disrupt the old ways and seize power. The Uruk's leader, Kurr, explicitly states his desire to destroy the traditions of the Berbers, indicating a distrust and disdain for the established social order. Additionally, the Berber tribe relies on vigilantism to protect their horse and traditions, suggesting a lack of faith in formal institutions to provide security. The protagonist, Alec, must navigate this conflict and ultimately participate in a race that determines the fate of the tribes' horses, further highlighting the importance of circumventing the system.

title: Without a Trace
justification: Institutional failure is a central theme. The police investigation is portrayed as initially incompetent, focusing on the father as a suspect despite the mother's insistence of his innocence. The detectives pursue leads based on psychics and ignore the mother's insights. The police are also shown to be heavy-handed in their questioning of children, causing distress. Ultimately, the mother's persistence and a tip lead to the discovery of her son, highlighting the limitations and potential failures of the official investigation.

title: Hercules
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the gods as manipulative and self-serving, using humans as pawns in their cosmic games. King Minos and his daughter Adriana are actively corrupting institutions for personal gain, such as stealing the sacred sword from the Temple of Hera to undermine the king of Thebes. The oracle's prophecy regarding Cassiopea is manipulated for political advantage. Hercules must circumvent these corrupt power structures and rely on his own strength and the help of morally ambiguous figures like Circe to achieve justice.

title: Bad Boys
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The juvenile correctional facility, Rainford, is portrayed as a brutal and corrupt environment where violence and exploitation are rampant. Staff members like Daniels and Wagner are either ineffective or complicit in the abuse. The justice system itself is criticized, as the judge laments the limitations of juvenile law, stating, "Your status as a juvenile prevents me from imposing the punishment you deserve." O'Brien's initial encounters with the police are dismissive, as he states, "They don't do shit...It's a joke."

title: The Sword in the Stone
justification: The film presents a medieval England in disarray after the king's death, described as a "dark age, without law and without order" where "men lived in fear of one another." This suggests a failure of the existing political and social structures to provide stability and justice. However, the narrative quickly shifts focus to the legend of the sword in the stone and Arthur's personal journey, rather than dwelling on the systemic issues. While the initial setting implies institutional weakness, it serves more as a backdrop for Arthur's rise to power than a central theme actively explored or challenged.

title: Brainstorm
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a research project, TRIAD, initially intended for communication breakthroughs, being co-opted by the military for brainwashing purposes ('They're using my invention for brainwashing people.'). The protagonist, Michael, expresses distrust and anger towards Alex, who he believes sold out their work ('Alex sold us out.'). The dialogue reveals a struggle against external forces seeking to control and weaponize their research, highlighting a deep mistrust of institutional motives and actions. The protagonist actively fights against this co-opting of the project.

title: Deathstalker
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Lord Munkar, a ruler, is portrayed as inherently corrupt and untrustworthy, using magic and manipulation to maintain power. The tournament itself, ostensibly a fair competition, is revealed to be a sham designed to eliminate potential threats to Munkar's rule. Deathstalker actively fights against Munkar's corrupt system, seeking to destroy the sources of his power rather than participate in his games. The dialogue highlights Munkar's willingness to kill the tournament winner, demonstrating the institution's fundamental brokenness.

title: Tender Mercies
justification: The subtitles present a world where institutions are largely absent or operate in the background. There's a brief mention of the army not knowing the exact circumstances of a soldier's death ("They couldn't tell me anything except that he'd been found dead."), suggesting a degree of bureaucratic indifference or incompetence. The protagonist's past run-ins with the law are alluded to ("Mama says you tried to kill her once."), but the legal system itself isn't a central focus. The narrative primarily revolves around personal relationships and individual struggles, with institutions playing a minimal role.

title: The House on Sorority Row
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the police as initially dismissive and ineffective, only arriving after significant damage has been done. Dr. Beck's experimental procedure and subsequent cover-up highlight the corruption and unethical behavior within the medical establishment. Mrs. Slater's confinement and the lack of proper care for her mental state further demonstrate the failure of institutions to protect vulnerable individuals. The characters are forced to take matters into their own hands, bypassing or actively fighting against these flawed systems to survive.

title: Silkwood
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The dialogue reveals a deep-seated mistrust of Kerr-McGee, the company employing the protagonists, and its safety protocols.
