The miners distrust the legal system, believing LaHood can manipulate it to his advantage, and the preacher's past suggests a deep-seated mistrust of formal justice, leading him to take matters into his own hands. The narrative emphasizes that the miners must fight or circumvent the system to protect their claims and lives.

title: Pee Wee's Big Adventure
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Pee-wee's bike is stolen, and the police explicitly state they "can't do anything" because they "don't have the resources." Pee-wee states, "I knew the police wouldn't help," indicating a pre-existing distrust. He then takes matters into his own hands, conducting his own investigation and even resorting to vigilante actions like confronting Francis. Mickey, the escaped convict, also expresses distrust in the legal system, stating he "tried to go through legal channels" but the cops "just gave me the runaround," leading him to "take the law into my own hands."

title: Brewster's Millions
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The film features a legal system that is easily manipulated by wealth and influence, as seen when J.B. Donaldo, representing anonymous parties, posts bail for Brewster and Nolan. The will itself, crafted by Rupert Horn, reflects a deep distrust of traditional values and a belief that money corrupts. The film also portrays the political system as corrupt, with Brewster running for mayor as a joke against two equally unappealing candidates, highlighting a lack of faith in the political process. While not the dominant engine, these elements recur and affect character choices.

title: Jagged Edge
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The District Attorney, Krasny, is portrayed as ambitious and willing to bend the rules to further his career, as evidenced by his withholding of exculpatory evidence in a previous case, leading to an innocent man's suicide. This past misconduct is a recurring point of contention, with the defense attorney, Teddy Barnes, directly accusing Krasny of similar behavior in the current case. The legal system itself is shown as susceptible to manipulation, with the prosecution relying on circumstantial evidence and potentially unreliable witnesses. The narrative also suggests that the media, represented by Forrester's own newspaper, can be influenced to shape public opinion, further eroding trust in institutions.

title: St. Elmo’s Fire
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme, though not dominant. The characters frequently encounter institutions that are unhelpful or actively detrimental. Wendy's father uses his wealth to try and influence legal outcomes after Billy's drunk driving arrest ('Miss Beamish won't press charges, so why not let it slide?'). Jules's welfare experience is dehumanizing ('Just give me my check.'). Kevin's writing career is stalled by the unfulfilling nature of his obituary work, highlighting the limitations of the media. While characters don't actively fight the system, they often express frustration and seek to circumvent it.

title: Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this narrative. Bartertown, the primary settlement, operates under a system of laws and customs that are frequently arbitrary and brutal, as evidenced by the 'Thunderdome' where disputes are settled through violent combat with 'no jury, no appeal, no parole.' Aunty Entity, the leader, manipulates these systems for her own gain, highlighting the corruption within the power structure. The 'Bust a deal, face the wheel' concept further illustrates the capricious nature of justice. The protagonist, Max, must navigate and ultimately challenge this system to achieve his goals, indicating that institutional failure is a driving force in the plot.

title: Commando
justification: The film exhibits a moderate degree of institutional cynicism. While not the central driving force, distrust in formal structures is a recurring element. The protagonist, Matrix, is betrayed by someone within his own military unit, leading to the kidnapping of his daughter. General Kirby's involvement and the need for Matrix to circumvent official channels to rescue his daughter suggest a system that is not entirely trustworthy. The dialogue hints at corruption and betrayal within the military, affecting Matrix's choices and actions, but it is not the sole focus of the narrative.

title: Silverado
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The sheriff in Turley is corrupt, allowing a black man to be abused and run out of town and later imprisoning Jake on flimsy charges. The legal system is portrayed as unjust, as Jake is sentenced to hang despite claiming self-defense. Paden and Emmett must circumvent the law to free Jake. Later, in Silverado, Sheriff Cobb is complicit in McKendrick's land-grabbing scheme, prioritizing his own interests over justice and allowing violence to occur.

title: The Killing Fields
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative highlights the US government's secret bombing of Cambodia and its misleading statements to the press, as evidenced by Major Reeves' evasiveness and Bob's admission of a cover-up regarding casualties. The film also portrays the ineffectiveness and eventual collapse of the Cambodian government, unable to protect its citizens from the Khmer Rouge. The American embassy's evacuation process is depicted as chaotic and prioritizing foreigners over locals, forcing the protagonist to make difficult choices to save his friend. The dialogue reveals a deep mistrust of official narratives and a sense that institutions are failing to protect the innocent.

title: Teen Wolf
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The coach's self-serving attitude and the vice principal's abuse of power contribute to this theme. The coach's advice is nonsensical and self-centered, as evidenced by lines like, "These were poor people. These were hungry people with real problems." and his admission that he didn't care about the kid who quit because "He was a third-stringer, I didn't need him." The vice principal's actions, such as threatening Scott and abusing his authority, further highlight the flaws within the school system. However, these instances are not the central driving force of the plot, which primarily focuses on Scott's personal journey and acceptance of his werewolf identity.

title: The Last Dragon
justification: The subtitles present a world where institutions are largely absent or ineffective, but this isn't a central driver of the plot. The police are never seen, and the legal system is only alluded to. Laura initially suggests calling the cops when J.J. is threatened, but dismisses the idea, saying, "My life is not filled with all that craziness." This implies a lack of faith in their ability to help. However, the narrative focuses more on individual actions and conflicts, such as Leroy's journey and the battles against Sho'nuff and Eddie Arkadian, rather than systemic issues or institutional failures.

title: White Nights
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays Soviet institutions, particularly the KGB, as manipulative and untrustworthy. Nikolai, a former Soviet dancer, is essentially imprisoned and forced to perform for propaganda purposes, highlighting the lack of individual freedom. The American embassy is also depicted as bureaucratic and slow to act, initially dismissing Anne's concerns about Nikolai's well-being. Raymond, an American defector, is shown to be disillusioned with both American and Soviet systems, indicating a broader cynicism towards political institutions. The climax involves a tense standoff where both Soviet and American authorities prioritize political maneuvering over individual safety, further emphasizing the theme.

title: Desperately Seeking Susan
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. The police are portrayed as somewhat ineffective and dismissive of Gary's concerns about his missing wife, Roberta. Leslie says, "What did the police say?" and Gary replies, "They seem to think she's having an affair!" This suggests a lack of faith in their ability to handle the situation seriously. However, the narrative primarily focuses on personal relationships and identity exploration, rather than a systemic critique of institutions. The police do eventually help Gary find Roberta, indicating a degree of functionality.

title: Prizzi's Honor
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative revolves around the Prizzi family, a criminal organization that operates outside the bounds of law and order. The dialogue reveals that institutions like banks and insurance companies are easily manipulated for the family's gain, as seen in the kidnapping plot. The police are portrayed as corruptible, with the family having 'done business with the Police commissioners squad for over 40 years.' The protagonist, Charley, is forced to choose between his loyalty to the family and his love for Irene, highlighting the inherent conflict between personal relationships and the demands of a corrupt system. The ending, where Charley is compelled to kill Irene to maintain his position within the family, underscores the dominance of institutional loyalty over individual morality.

title: Out of Africa
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Out of Africa," though not dominant. The subtitles reveal instances where characters express distrust or frustration with governmental or societal structures. For example, the protagonist encounters bureaucratic hurdles when trying to secure land for her Kikuyu tenants after losing her farm, highlighting the indifference of the colonial administration. The dialogue also reveals a general skepticism towards the British Empire and its motives, particularly during wartime, with characters questioning the value and purpose of the conflict. The protagonist's interactions with colonial officials and her struggle to navigate the social expectations of the British community in Kenya further underscore a sense of alienation from established institutions.

title: A Passage to India
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The dialogue reveals a deep mistrust of the British Raj's legal and social structures. Characters like Aziz are immediately suspected and unjustly treated by the legal system, as evidenced by McBryde's prejudiced investigation and the biased trial. The line, "We're out here to do justice and to keep the peace," is followed by a description of the 'entertainment' as an exercise in power, highlighting the hypocrisy of the civil service. The expulsion of Mrs. Moore and the manipulation of the trial further demonstrate the systemic corruption and the protagonist's fight against it.

title: Agnes of God
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the Church and legal system as prioritizing scandal avoidance over justice, exemplified by figures like Lyon pressuring Dr. Livingston for a quick diagnosis. The Church's desire to avoid a trial and the bishop's pressure highlight the institution's self-preservation. Dr. Livingston actively fights against this systemic pressure, seeking the truth despite institutional obstacles. The narrative also suggests a distrust of psychiatric institutions, with the line 'It's either prison or a nut house and the differences are pretty thin!'

title: Fright Night
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Charley's initial attempt to report the vampire to the police is met with disbelief and dismissal, highlighting the ineffectiveness of law enforcement in addressing supernatural threats. Lieutenant Lennox explicitly threatens Charley with jail if he returns to the station with his claims: "If I ever catch your ass at the station again, I'm throwing it in jail forever!" This failure of the police to take Charley seriously forces him to seek help elsewhere, specifically from Peter Vincent, a figure outside of traditional institutions. The narrative relies on the failure of formal institutions to protect Charley and his community, pushing him towards vigilantism.

title: Summer Rental
justification: The subtitles contain a few instances that suggest a mild level of institutional cynicism. The protagonist, Jack, encounters bureaucratic frustrations, such as the need for a pass at work despite being a long-term employee: "Why do they need these anyway? I've worked here 10 years. They know me by now." He also faces unfair treatment at a restaurant due to a reservation system that favors a local celebrity: "You don't take reservations... We don't, except for Mr. Pellet." These examples indicate some dissatisfaction with established systems, but they are not central to the overall plot, which focuses more on personal growth and family bonding.

title: The Emerald Forest
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in the film. The dialogue reveals a distrust of the dam project and its impact on the indigenous people and environment. The protagonist, Bill, is portrayed as someone who initially participates in the project but later questions its consequences. The film also touches on the exploitation of indigenous people and their land, suggesting a critique of larger systems at play. The dialogue about the 'log jam' and the potential for a flood, combined with the discussion of the dam's safety margin, hints at a potential institutional failure.

title: Santa Claus
justification: The film portrays a significant level of institutional cynicism, primarily directed towards the toy industry and, to a lesser extent, the established traditions of Christmas. B.Z. Toys, a major corporation, is depicted as prioritizing profit over the safety and well-being of children, manufacturing dangerous toys and exploiting the Christmas spirit for financial gain. This is exemplified by B.Z.'s willingness to produce and distribute exploding candy canes, despite knowing the risks. The film also shows a disregard for regulatory oversight, as B.Z. dismisses concerns raised by a senate subcommittee. Santa Claus himself expresses disillusionment with the commercialization of Christmas, suggesting a broader critique of societal values.

title: The Gods Must Be Crazy
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While the Bushmen live outside of any formal structure, the film contrasts their lifestyle with that of 'civilized man,' highlighting the absurdities and inefficiencies of modern life, such as the rigid schedules and pointless tasks in the workplace. The journalist's struggle to publish meaningful stories due to editorial constraints suggests a distrust of media institutions. Additionally, the Botswanan government's initial refusal to allow foreign forces to pursue Sam Boga, despite the severity of his crimes, indicates a degree of bureaucratic inflexibility. However, the film also shows institutions functioning, such as the police eventually capturing Sam Boga and the legal system processing Xi's case, albeit imperfectly.

title: The Care Bears Movie
justification: The film contains a minor element of institutional cynicism. Kim and Jason are orphans who have been hurt by their parents leaving, leading them to distrust others and institutions like orphanages. They state, "They always let you down, So we'd rather not have any friends." However, this distrust is primarily interpersonal rather than directed at formal institutions. The orphanage itself is not portrayed negatively, and the focus is on the children's emotional wounds rather than systemic failures. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but not a central driver of the plot.

title: Friday the 13th Part V: A New Beginning
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Pinehurst, the mental institution, is portrayed as somewhat ineffective, with patients easily escaping and staff being negligent. The local law enforcement, represented by the Sheriff, seems more concerned with appeasing angry locals like Ethel Hubbard than ensuring the safety of the institution's residents. The dialogue highlights this when the Sheriff confronts Matt about the patients trespassing and Ethel demands the institution be shut down. Furthermore, the paramedics, like Roy, are shown to be capable of extreme violence and deception, using their position to cover up personal vendettas, indicating a failure of institutional oversight and accountability.

title: The Black Cauldron
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. Dallben, a wizard, seems to be a figure of authority and wisdom, but he is not explicitly part of a larger institution. The Horned King represents a malevolent force, but his opposition is more about good versus evil than a critique of societal structures. King Eidellig of the Fairfolk appears benevolent and concerned, but his role is limited. The witches of Morva are self-serving but not representative of a formal institution. Therefore, while there are figures of authority, the narrative does not focus on the failure or corruption of institutions as a central theme.

title: A Nightmare On Elm Street Part 2: Freddy’s Revenge
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in the narrative. The police are present, but their effectiveness is questionable, as evidenced by the officer's flippant remark to Jesse's father: "I'd keep a short leash on him if I were you." The parents' attempts to seek help for Jesse are met with limited success; the mother suggests a psychiatrist, while the father dismisses it, highlighting a lack of faith in professional intervention. The school setting is also portrayed as somewhat ineffectual, with the teacher seemingly oblivious to Jesse's distress. The narrative suggests that the characters are largely on their own in confronting the supernatural threat, indicating a degree of institutional inadequacy.

title: Porky's Revenge
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the high school principal, Mr. Carter, as ineffectual and easily manipulated, shown by his inability to control the students or the situation with the stag film. The police are absent, and the legal system is bypassed as the students take matters into their own hands to protect Coach Goodenough from Porky's illegal gambling operation. The school system is portrayed as hypocritical, focusing on superficial decency while ignoring deeper issues. The students actively circumvent the rules and authority figures to achieve their goals, highlighting a distrust in the ability of institutions to provide justice or guidance.

title: 101 Dalmatians
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. While not the central engine, distrust in institutions, particularly law enforcement, is present. The police are portrayed as somewhat ineffective, with Roger questioning what they can do to find 15 puppies in a city this size. The inspector is sympathetic but offers little concrete help. Ultimately, the protagonists and the dogs themselves are responsible for resolving the situation, highlighting a reliance on individual action rather than institutional support. The film also shows the fashion industry as cutthroat and uncaring.

title: Code of Silence
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the police department as deeply flawed, with corruption, cover-ups, and internal conflicts hindering justice. Cragie, a fellow officer, plants a gun on a kid and gets away with it. The protagonist, Cusack, faces resistance and betrayal from within the department when he tries to expose the truth. The Citizens' Review Board is portrayed as ineffective, and the police force is shown to be more concerned with protecting its own than with upholding the law, as evidenced by the lack of backup Cusack receives when he needs it most.

title: Volunteers
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Peace Corps, a US institution, is portrayed as deeply flawed. Kent joins to 'expose the less-privileged of the world to self-styling adorn,' indicating a superficial understanding of global issues. Lawrence replaces Kent to escape debt, highlighting the institution's vulnerability to manipulation. John Reynolds, representing the 'American agriculture mission,' is revealed to be a CIA operative, using the Peace Corps' bridge project for covert operations ('Operation red-belly'), demonstrating institutional corruption and deceit. The narrative emphasizes the characters' need to circumvent or fight against the system to achieve their goals.

title: Year of the Dragon
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Captain Stanley White, encounters corruption and bureaucratic obstacles at every turn. He is stonewalled by his superiors (Lou and the Commissioner) who prioritize political relationships over justice, as evidenced by their attempts to shut down his investigation into Joey Tai. The dialogue highlights the deep-seated mistrust of law enforcement within the Chinatown community, stemming from historical experiences of corruption and ineffectiveness. This is exemplified by Uncle Harry's explanation that Chinese people don't go to the police because they'll get in trouble, and the restaurant owner's story of being stabbed after reporting a gang leader. White's frustration with the system's inability to address the criminal activity in Chinatown drives him to increasingly rogue actions, such as illegal wiretaps and aggressive tactics, further emphasizing the failure of formal institutions.

title: Ladyhawke
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Bishop of Aquila is portrayed as corrupt and abuses his power, cursing Navarre and Isabeau due to his unrequited love. The narrative revolves around breaking this curse, which was enacted through the Church's authority. Characters like Phillipe must circumvent the Bishop's guards and the Church's influence to aid Navarre and Isabeau. The dialogue emphasizes the Bishop's evil nature and the lengths he goes to maintain his power, highlighting the institutional corruption that drives the plot.

title: The Sure Thing
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The primary focus is on interpersonal relationships and personal growth, rather than systemic issues. There are minor instances of dissatisfaction with academic assignments and college life, such as the character Gib's complaints about rewriting assignments and the perceived superficiality of college girls. However, these are isolated complaints and do not drive the plot or suggest a broader distrust of institutions. The professor's unconventional teaching methods are presented as quirky rather than indicative of systemic failure.

title: Invasion U.S.A.
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts widespread violence and chaos across the nation, with authorities seemingly helpless to prevent it. The news reports state, "Authorities have thus far been helpless in their efforts to prevent it." Furthermore, the protagonist, Hunter, operates outside the law, taking vigilante action against terrorists, indicating a lack of faith in the ability of formal institutions to maintain order. The governors of all 50 states are gathering for an emergency meeting to create an effective plan to turn back the tide of terror, and to head off an impending suspension of constitutional rights and the imposition of total martial law in the land.

title: The Falcon and the Snowman
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Chris, discovers the CIA's covert actions, leading him to distrust the government. He states, "Details of covert action that have nothing to do with national security. Manipulations of foreign press, political parties, whole economies. I mean, it's incredible. I had no idea the extent of the lie. The level of deception." This disillusionment drives him to leak information to the Soviets. Daulton's experiences with law enforcement and the justice system further highlight institutional corruption and the characters' need to circumvent the system.

title: Young Sherlock Holmes
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. The police, represented by Mr. Lestrade, are portrayed as dismissive and incompetent, initially refusing to investigate the murders that Holmes brings to their attention. Lestrade explicitly states, "I don't have time for any more of your... playpen crimes." This dismissal forces Holmes to investigate independently. Furthermore, the school board unjustly expels Holmes based on circumstantial evidence, highlighting a lack of fairness and due process within the educational institution. The headmaster, while sympathetic, is ultimately bound by the board's decision, demonstrating the limitations and potential for injustice within the system.

title: To Live and Die in L.A.
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Chance, frequently expresses distrust and circumvents official channels. He disregards procedures, evidenced by his partner Vukovich's statement: "You violated section 302.5." Chance also plans a robbery, stating, "I was gonna get Masters and I didn't give a shit how I did it." The legal system is also portrayed cynically, with a lawyer stating, "Masters has been making a mockery out of you, me and this whole system." The film also shows a judge who is reluctant to sign a writ, suggesting corruption or bureaucratic obstruction. These instances demonstrate a narrative where institutions are flawed and actively bypassed.

title: Weird Science
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are brief mentions of school, but these are mostly in the context of social status and popularity, not the institution's inherent flaws. The police are mentioned when the father threatens to call them on Lisa, but this is more about parental control than distrust of law enforcement. The military school Chet attended is mentioned, but only as a place where he picked up violent habits, not as an institution that is inherently corrupt or failing. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but not structurally central.

title: Death Wish 3
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police are portrayed as ineffective and possibly corrupt, with the chief suggesting Kersey "work for me" and "do your thing" (vigilante justice) instead of arresting him, indicating a willingness to circumvent the law. The public defender expresses frustration with the system, asking Kersey, "You're just going to walk away?" after he is released without charges. Rodriguez states, "What about the cops? They do anything? Yeah. They enforce the parking laws," highlighting the perceived ineffectiveness of law enforcement. Bennett says, "They've cleaned up and are through with their investigation. Cops don't care."

title: King Solomon's Mines
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts formal institutions as corrupt and untrustworthy, particularly through the characters of Dogati and Colonel Bockner, who exploit and enslave people for profit and power. The German army's pursuit of King Solomon's mines, driven by greed and a desire for world domination, further exemplifies this corruption. Characters like Kassam are portrayed as opportunistic and willing to betray others for personal gain. The protagonist, Quatermain, actively fights against these corrupt figures and circumvents their authority, highlighting the failure of institutions to uphold justice.

title: Remo Williams: The Adventure Begins
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative explicitly states, "Our cops are corrupt, our judges are bought, our politicians are up for sale. Everywhere you look, slime is on the loose." This sets the stage for the protagonist, Remo, to become "the Eleventh Commandment," suggesting the formal system is inadequate. The organization that recruits Remo operates outside the law because "our legal system doesn't work the way it's supposed to." Furthermore, the film depicts a military cover-up regarding a defective weapon and a corrupt defense contractor who evades justice, reinforcing the idea that institutions are failing to uphold their responsibilities.

title: Baby: Secret of the Lost Legend
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts scientists Eric and Nigel, who are associated with a research institution, as prioritizing personal gain and scientific advancement over ethical considerations and the well-being of the creatures they study. They tranquilize and capture the dinosaurs, disregarding the potential harm. The local government, represented by the Colonel, is portrayed as corrupt and easily manipulated by Eric, prioritizing political gain over scientific integrity. The Red Cross is also implicated, with Dr. Dubois providing information that leads to the dinosaurs' capture. The protagonists, Susan and George, must actively circumvent these institutions to protect the dinosaurs and ultimately release the hatchling back into the wild.

title: The Return of the Living Dead
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative hinges on the failure of the military and government to contain a dangerous chemical, 245-Trioxin, leading to a zombie outbreak. Frank explicitly states the cover-up of the original incident at the VA hospital and the army's mishandling of the contaminated bodies. The dialogue reveals a systemic disregard for public safety, culminating in the military's decision to bomb the city to contain the outbreak, resulting in mass casualties and a complete breakdown of order. The final scene shows the military casually dismissing the civilian deaths and environmental damage, highlighting a deep-seated institutional indifference to human life.

title: Tomboy
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. Seville's repeated failures to secure funding through formal channels (investors, TV stations) highlight a distrust in established systems. Tommy expresses a general distrust of relying on others, stating, "The more you depend on other people, the more punishment you set up for yourself." Junior's exploitation of designers and Earl's acknowledgement of the Leeds family's history of "ripping off designers" further reinforces this theme. While not the dominant engine, the narrative does show characters needing to circumvent or fight against established systems to achieve their goals.

title: Sesame Street Presents Follow That Bird
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Miss Finch and the Feathered Friends organization are portrayed as misguided and overly rigid in their belief that Big Bird should only be with his 'own kind,' leading to his unhappiness and desire to return to Sesame Street. This suggests a critique of institutions that prioritize conformity over individual well-being. However, the narrative doesn't depict outright corruption or malevolence, and the focus is more on the characters' personal journeys and friendships than on systemic institutional failure. The other characters are not shown to distrust institutions, and the story is more about finding where you belong.

title: The Color Purple
justification: The subtitles present a world where formal institutions are largely absent or ineffective in protecting vulnerable individuals. The church is mentioned, but its influence is limited to social gatherings and doesn't offer tangible support to Celie or Nettie. The legal system is only alluded to in the context of violence against women ('His wife dead. She was killed by her boyfriend, coming home from church'), but there's no indication of justice being served. While these instances suggest a lack of institutional support, they don't form the central conflict or drive the plot significantly. The story primarily focuses on interpersonal relationships and individual struggles within a patriarchal society, rather than a direct confrontation with or subversion of formal institutions.

title: One Magic Christmas
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Jack, is fired from Continental Radio by Frank Crump, and his family is evicted from their company house. Ginnie is also fired from her job at Glen's Market due to Herbie's unreasonable demands. The city council refuses to provide free electricity for the town Christmas tree, highlighting bureaucratic stinginess. These events force the family to struggle financially, impacting their Christmas and overall well-being, and driving the plot forward.

title: Vision Quest
justification: The film contains a minimal amount of institutional cynicism. The coach initially refuses to let Louden drop weight classes, citing concerns for the team and Louden's scholarship prospects, but this is presented more as a protective measure than systemic corruption. The school paper publishes an article critical of Louden's choices, but this is framed as individual opinion rather than institutional opposition. The primary focus is on Louden's personal journey and relationships, with institutions playing a secondary role.

title: Real Genius
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the military and academic institutions as deeply flawed. The Crossbow project is developed in secret, bypassing ethical considerations, and is described as a 'peacetime weapon' implying nefarious uses. Dr. Hathaway is willing to threaten Chris's graduation and career to force him to complete the project, showcasing academic corruption. Kent is manipulated and exploited, highlighting the institution's disregard for individual well-being. The climax involves circumventing military security protocols, further emphasizing the distrust and need to bypass formal structures.

title: Perfect
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative revolves around a reporter, Adam, investigating Joseph McKenzie, who claims the government framed him for trying to sell computers to an Iron Curtain country. This claim, along with the government's aggressive pursuit of McKenzie and the reporter's subsequent imprisonment for protecting his source, highlights a deep mistrust of governmental institutions. The narrative also shows the press as untrustworthy, with the reporter being pressured to reveal his sources and having his story rewritten to fit a different narrative, further emphasizing the theme of institutional failure and manipulation.

title: Kiss of the Spider Woman
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts a corrupt prison system where the warden manipulates Molina for information, promising parole in exchange for betraying Valentin. The political surveillance department is shown to be ruthless, willing to use and discard individuals like Molina to achieve their goals. Valentin, a political prisoner, distrusts the system and is actively fighting against it. The film suggests that the institutions are not to be trusted and that individuals are often used and abused by them.

title: Lifeforce
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the government and military as struggling to contain a threat they don't understand, leading to drastic measures like martial law and the consideration of thermonuclear sterilization of London. The Prime Minister seems more concerned with appearances than the actual crisis, as evidenced by his initial meeting with Caine and Carlsen being interrupted by a trivial matter. The military's quarantine procedures are initially ineffective, and the government's attempts to control information (the "D" notice situation) highlight a distrust of the public's ability to handle the truth. The dialogue reveals a sense of institutional failure, with characters like Caine and Carlsen taking matters into their own hands to fight the alien threat, often circumventing or ignoring official protocols.

title: Just One of the Guys
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not dominant. The protagonist, Terry, faces gender bias when her journalism teacher, Mr. Raymaker, dismisses her article and suggests she become a model instead: "What do you give me straight A's for, my wardrobe?" and "Because a pretty girl can't possibly have a brain?" This suggests a system where merit is overlooked due to superficial judgments. Later, Terry disguises herself as a male student to resubmit her article, indicating a belief that the institution (the journalism competition) is biased. While Terry ultimately succeeds, the need to circumvent the system highlights a degree of institutional mistrust.

title: Clue
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The entire plot is driven by the characters' vulnerability to blackmail, stemming from secrets that would ruin them if exposed, particularly within their professional spheres. Mrs. White fears scandal, Professor Plum's medical license was revoked, and Colonel Mustard is a war profiteer. Mr. Green is an FBI plant, highlighting the government's involvement in the blackmail scheme. The characters' distrust in the system is evident as they attempt to solve the murders themselves, rather than involving the police, until Mr. Green reveals his true identity.

title: Krush Groove
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Krush Groove," though not dominant. The most salient example is Rick's difficulty securing a loan from a bank, despite having recording equipment he values at $50,000. The loan officer denies the request, stating, "I'm very sorry...there's no way I can offer you a loan at this time." This forces Rick to seek funds from a less reputable source, Jay B, leading to further complications. Additionally, the police are portrayed as antagonistic, harassing the main characters without clear justification: "Let me see some ID...Y'all just blew up overnight? Get out of here. Step outside, man." These instances suggest a distrust of formal institutions, but they are not the central driving force of the plot.

title: Silver Bullet
justification: The film exhibits a moderate degree of institutional cynicism. The town sheriff, Joe Haller, is portrayed as incompetent and ineffective, as highlighted by Andy Fairton's repeated criticisms and the community's decision to form a vigilante group due to the lack of progress in the investigation ("This investigation is as efficient as a submarine with screen doors."). The community's distrust in the sheriff's ability to protect them is further emphasized by Herb Kincaid's emotional outburst at Brady's funeral, where he dismisses Haller's talk of "private justice" after his son was "torn to pieces." While the narrative doesn't solely rely on institutional failure, it is a recurring theme that influences the characters' actions and decisions, particularly in their pursuit of justice outside the formal system.

title: Missing in Action 2: The Beginning
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the US government as having 'forgotten' the POWs, leaving them to suffer in a brutal prison camp. This is reinforced by dialogue such as 'Our country has forgotten about us' and 'nobody gives a damn about us.' The International Freedom House is revealed to be a sham, further highlighting the lack of reliable institutional support. Braddock's rogue actions and vigilantism are necessary because formal channels have failed, making institutional failure a key driver of the plot.

title: The Purple Rose of Cairo
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. The primary institution in question is the economic system during the Depression, which is portrayed as failing Monk, Cecilia's husband, leading to his unemployment and subsequent negative behavior. Cecilia's dissatisfaction with her life is partly fueled by the economic hardship and lack of opportunities. While the film doesn't explicitly depict widespread corruption or malevolence, the characters struggle within a system that offers little support or hope, as seen in Monk's inability to find work and Cecilia's low-paying job. The dialogue highlights the desperation and disillusionment caused by the economic climate, but it doesn't become the central conflict of the story.

title: Return to Oz
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this narrative. Dorothy is taken to a doctor who intends to use a dangerous electrical machine to cure her 'delusions' about Oz, highlighting a distrust of the medical institution. The clinic is portrayed as a place of confinement and questionable practices, as evidenced by Dorothy being tied down and subjected to experimental treatments against her will. The burning down of the clinic and the death of Dr. Worley, who prioritized his machines over safety, further reinforces the idea of institutions as flawed and potentially harmful. Dorothy ultimately escapes the institution and finds validation in Oz, suggesting that the real world's institutions are inadequate and even dangerous compared to the magical realm.

title: Compromising Positions
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. While there are mentions of hospitals being overwhelmed ("the hospitals back then were out of beds"), this is presented more as a logistical challenge due to external circumstances (the virus) rather than inherent institutional failure. The narrative focuses primarily on interpersonal relationships and personal struggles, with institutions playing a minor role. The characters' problems stem more from personal failings and circumstances than from systemic issues.

title: Moving Violations
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a corrupt system where a judge and a traffic school instructor, Halik, conspire to fail students and profit from selling their impounded cars. Halik is offered a proposition by the judge to fail the class and split the money from the car sales. This is confirmed by the line, "I'll order their cars sold. We'll give half the money to the county. The rest you split with me." The protagonists actively fight against this corruption, ultimately exposing the scheme to Chief Fromm, indicating a systemic failure that requires rogue actions to address.

title: American Ninja
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the military and law enforcement as deeply compromised. The colonel is complicit in illegal arms dealing, as evidenced by his relationship with Ortega and his willingness to overlook the sergeant's corruption. Joe is framed for crimes he didn't commit, and the investigation is a sham to protect the corrupt individuals. The dialogue highlights this, with the colonel dismissing concerns about the sergeant and prioritizing the operation over justice, indicating a systemic failure.

title: Better Off Dead...
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. While there isn't a dominant theme of corruption or systemic failure, there are instances where institutions are portrayed as flawed or unhelpful. For example, the ski team tryouts are judged solely by one person's 'vast expertise,' suggesting a potentially biased or arbitrary system. Additionally, the protagonist's family seems to operate outside of societal norms, such as the mother's bizarre cooking and the father's awkward attempts to involve him in dating, implying a slight disconnect from conventional institutions. However, these instances are not central to the plot's progression.

title: After Hours
justification: The subtitles contain some instances of characters encountering unhelpful or frustrating systems, but these are not central to the plot. For example, Paul is unable to get a subway token because the fare increased, and the clerk refuses to give him a break, stating, "l could lose my job." Later, Paul attempts to report a death to the police, but the officer on the phone is dismissive and unhelpful. However, these instances are more like obstacles the protagonist encounters rather than a systemic critique of institutions. The narrative focuses more on the protagonist's increasingly bizarre and dangerous night than on a deliberate failure of institutions.

title: Lost in America
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The protagonist, David, experiences a significant betrayal by his employer, Ross & McMahon, when he is denied a promotion he was promised. He is fired after expressing his anger, highlighting the company's lack of loyalty and ethical behavior. This event drives the narrative, leading David and his wife to abandon their conventional life and embark on a journey of self-discovery, indicating a rejection of corporate institutions. The film suggests that success within these institutions is often based on factors other than merit, fostering a sense of distrust in the system.

title: Once Bitten
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. There are no instances of characters actively fighting against or circumventing institutions. The only possible example is when Mark seeks help from a priest, but this is a personal matter and not a systemic critique. The priest's advice is somewhat unhelpful, but it doesn't suggest a broader institutional failure. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but does not drive the plot.

title: Explorers
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are no clear indications of characters actively fighting against or circumventing institutions. The narrative focuses on the characters' personal experiences and relationships, with institutions playing a negligible role. The only possible hint is the boy's truancy from school, but this is not structurally central to the plot.

title: A Chorus Line
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal amount of institutional cynicism. The characters are participating in an audition process, which is inherently hierarchical and potentially exploitative, as suggested by the line, "We’re being treated like worms." However, this sentiment is not structurally central to the narrative. The characters primarily express anxiety about the audition process itself and their personal chances of success, rather than systemic critiques of the theater industry or the audition process. The focus is on individual struggles and aspirations within the existing system, not on actively fighting or circumventing it.

title: Tuff Turf
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. The narrative includes instances of characters circumventing or distrusting formal structures. For example, Miss Wright allows Howard to skip biology class due to a 'sinus condition,' suggesting a lax enforcement of school rules. Morgan's past behavior at prep school and his initial attitude at Lawson High indicate a disregard for institutional norms. The film also depicts instances of vigilantism and characters taking the law into their own hands, such as Nick's violent actions and the final confrontation, implying a lack of faith in the justice system.

title: Sweet Dreams
justification: The lyrics suggest a world where people are looking to use, get used by, or abuse others. While this hints at a potential distrust of interpersonal relationships, it doesn't explicitly target formal institutions. The line "Who am I to disagree?" could be interpreted as a passive acceptance of a flawed system, but it's too vague to definitively indicate institutional cynicism. The lyrics focus more on individual interactions and desires rather than systemic issues. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present only in a minimal way.

title: Target
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Walter Lloyd, is revealed to be a former CIA agent operating under an assumed identity, indicating a deep mistrust of government institutions. The narrative reveals that Walter's past actions within the CIA have directly led to his present predicament, as his wife is kidnapped by a former adversary seeking revenge for actions taken during a covert operation. The CIA's involvement and potential betrayal are further highlighted by the presence of double agents and conflicting loyalties, suggesting that the organization itself is corrupt or untrustworthy. The protagonist and his son must navigate this treacherous landscape, relying on their own skills and instincts rather than trusting the institutions that are supposed to protect them.

title: Cat's Eye
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Quitters, Inc. organization operates outside the bounds of normal ethical or legal constraints, using threats of violence against family members to enforce compliance, as stated by Morrison: "First offense, your wife gets the juice...Second time, we bring your daughter Alicia here...The third offense, I'm afraid I have to send someone out to rape your wife." This demonstrates a complete disregard for the law and individual rights. Cressner's actions also highlight a system where wealth and power allow him to operate with impunity, manipulating the legal system to frame his wife's lover: "In 10 minutes, Albert will call the police and tell them a tale of heroin, 1970 mustangs...aging tennis pros with drug records."

title: Gotcha
justification: Institutional cynicism is central to the plot. The protagonist is pursued by both the CIA and KGB, neither of which are presented as trustworthy. The protagonist is initially dismissed by the FBI when he reports being followed. The CIA manipulates him, putting him in danger, and trashes his apartment. The film culminates in a confrontation where the protagonist must outsmart both agencies, highlighting their untrustworthiness and self-serving nature.

title: Mischief
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal degree of institutional cynicism. While there are some authority figures present, such as teachers and parents, their roles do not significantly drive the plot through corruption or failure. The school system is portrayed neutrally, with a teacher discussing the line of succession in government, and the police are shown briefly, but their actions do not indicate systemic issues. The primary conflicts arise from interpersonal relationships and individual actions, rather than a fundamental distrust or failure of institutions.

title: The River
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts a banking system that readily forecloses on farmers, exemplified by Tom Garvey's struggle to secure a loan and the subsequent auction of Dan Gaumer's possessions. Joe Wade, a powerful figure, manipulates the system to acquire land for a dam project, disregarding the livelihoods of the farmers in the valley. The legal system is also portrayed negatively, as the farmers are forced to take the law into their own hands to protect their land and livelihoods, culminating in a violent confrontation at the levee.

title: The Man With One Red Shoe
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The CIA is portrayed as deeply corrupt, engaging in drug smuggling and framing agents. The Senate inquiry is manipulated by those within the CIA to settle scores and maintain power. Dialogue such as "I haven't felt this good since I overthrew the government in Chile" and the constant surveillance and manipulation of innocent individuals highlight the agency's disregard for ethical boundaries. The protagonist, Richard Drew, is an innocent bystander caught in the crossfire of institutional power struggles, forced to navigate a system where truth and justice are secondary to political maneuvering.

title: Top Gun
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Top Gun." While the Navy is presented as a source of pride and skill, there's a recurring undercurrent of distrust in its rigid rules and bureaucracy. Maverick's reckless behavior and disregard for protocol are constant sources of conflict, highlighting a tension between individual talent and institutional control. The inquiry into Goose's death, while ultimately clearing Maverick, suggests a system that could potentially scapegoat individuals. Viper's classified revelation about Maverick's father further implies that institutions may conceal truths for political reasons, affecting character choices and plot progression.

title: Crocodile Dundee
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. While there are some minor instances of characters circumventing rules or expressing skepticism, these are not central to the plot. For example, Dundee is described as a "bloody croc poacher," suggesting he operates outside legal channels, but this is a minor detail. Sue's father, who owns the newspaper, is shown to have some influence, but this is more about familial relationships than institutional power. Overall, the narrative focuses on personal relationships and cultural clashes rather than systemic institutional failures.

title: The Karate Kid, Part II
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. While the Cobra Kai dojo, led by Sensei Kreese, promotes a philosophy of 'no mercy' and aggression, which could be seen as a critique of certain competitive institutions, the primary conflict is interpersonal. The tournament itself is presented as a legitimate competition with rules and referees, even if those rules are bent or broken. The film does not focus on systemic corruption or the failure of institutions to deliver justice, but rather on individual choices and rivalries. The police or other authority figures are not present in the film.

title: Back to School
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a dominant theme. While Thornton Melon initially bypasses the traditional admissions process through a large donation, this is portrayed more as comedic eccentricity than a systemic critique. Dr. Barbay's initial resistance to Melon's admission highlights ethical concerns within the academic institution, but this is largely resolved through Melon's eventual participation in the academic process. The film does not focus on widespread corruption or systemic failure, but rather on individual challenges and eccentric solutions within the existing framework.

title: Aliens
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Ripley faces disbelief and dismissal from the Interstellar Commerce Commission regarding the alien threat, leading to the suspension of her flight license. The company, represented by Burke, prioritizes profit over safety, sending colonists to a dangerous location without warning. This systemic disregard for human life and safety, coupled with the ineffectiveness of regulatory bodies, drives Ripley to take matters into her own hands, actively fighting against the corporation's agenda and the alien threat.

title: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Admiral Kirk and his crew are court-martialed for saving Spock, highlighting a conflict between Starfleet regulations and personal loyalty. The trial itself is portrayed as somewhat farcical, with Kirk pleading guilty on behalf of the crew to serious charges. The President acknowledges their heroism but still enforces a demotion, illustrating the inflexibility of the system. The crew's initial exile and subsequent assignment to a 'bucket of bolts' further underscore the system's perceived unfairness and bureaucratic nature.

title: Ruthless People
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Ruthless People," though not the dominant engine of the plot. The police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated, as evidenced by Sam Stone's initial success in convincing them his wife was kidnapped, despite his involvement. The police chief is later portrayed as potentially corrupt or easily swayed, as the blackmailer expresses disbelief that the police chief would not arrest Sam Stone. The blackmailer also expresses disbelief that the courts would release Sam Stone. However, the narrative also shows the police eventually uncovering the truth and arresting Sam, suggesting a degree of institutional functionality.

title: Ferris Bueller’s Day Off
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Dean Rooney's relentless pursuit of Ferris, driven by a desire to maintain control and punish perceived insubordination, highlights a distrust of the educational system. Rooney actively abuses his authority, exemplified by his attempts to manipulate Sloane's grandmother's death and his disregard for George Peterson's distress. The dialogue, such as Rooney's line, "You just produce a corpse, and I'll release Sloane," demonstrates the institution's willingness to exploit personal tragedy for bureaucratic ends. Furthermore, Jeanie's interactions with the police and her general frustration with authority figures reinforce the idea that institutions are often obstacles rather than sources of help.

title: Down and Out in Beverly Hills
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. The police are called multiple times, but their effectiveness is questionable, and one character, Orvis, complains about the slow response time and lack of resources when he reported a break-in. However, these instances are more anecdotal than structurally integral to the plot. The characters primarily deal with personal and familial issues, and while the police are present in a few scenes, their actions do not significantly drive the narrative forward or demonstrate a systemic failure of law enforcement.

title: The Golden Child
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The protagonist, Chandler, is shown to distrust the police and other authorities, preferring to operate outside of formal channels. This is evidenced by his reluctance to involve the police in Cheryl Mosely's case and his willingness to confront criminals directly. The dialogue also suggests a general lack of faith in the system, as characters often resort to vigilante actions or seek help from unconventional sources. While not the dominant engine, the narrative does show a recurring theme of mistrust in institutions, affecting major character choices and driving the plot forward.

title: Legal Eagles
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the District Attorney's office as politically motivated, prioritizing public image over justice, as seen in the Chief's willingness to suspend or fire Tom Logan based on public perception rather than the merits of the case. The police are portrayed as corrupt, with Detective Cavanaugh revealed to be a murderer who manipulated the system to frame others. The legal system is shown as easily manipulated, with evidence suppressed and witnesses intimidated, highlighting a deep-seated mistrust in the ability of institutions to deliver justice. The protagonist, Tom Logan, must operate outside the bounds of the system to uncover the truth, actively fighting against the corruption within the institutions he once trusted.

title: Cobra
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Cobra, frequently clashes with the police bureaucracy and legal system, believing they hinder effective crime-fighting. He expresses frustration with 'bullshit rules' that protect criminals, stating, 'as long as we play by these bullshit rules and the killer doesn't, we're gonna lose.' His superiors and colleagues criticize his violent methods and disregard for procedure. The film depicts internal affairs investigations and legal scrutiny following Cobra's actions, highlighting the conflict between his vigilante approach and institutional constraints. The ending reinforces this as Cobra rejects a transfer to an 'easier' role, choosing to remain outside the system.

title: Stand by Me
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Stand By Me," though not the dominant engine of the plot. The primary example is Chris Chambers's experience with the milk money theft, where he attempts to return the money but is still punished, suggesting a lack of faith in the school's justice system. He states, "No one asked me if I took the milk money. I just got a three-day vacation." This highlights a perceived unfairness and a belief that the system is biased against him due to his family's reputation. Additionally, the boys' decision to make an anonymous call about Ray Brower's body rather than directly involving the authorities indicates a degree of distrust in the official process.

title: The Color of Money
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are no explicit mentions of institutions, their failure, or characters actively fighting against them. The narrative focuses on personal relationships, hustling in pool, and the dynamics between characters. While there are mentions of the New Jersey Casino Control Commission ensuring fair play, this does not imply distrust or corruption, but rather the opposite. Therefore, institutional cynicism is not a structurally central theme in the provided subtitles.

title: Police Academy 3: Back in Training
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The governor's decision to close one of the police academies sets the stage for competition and sabotage, with Commandant Mauser actively working to undermine Commandant Lassard's academy. This is evident in Mauser's line, "We'll see who's got an academy when this is over," and his instructions to Proctor to ensure Lassard's cadets "screw up." The evaluation committee's presence and the cadets' fieldwork are manipulated for political gain, highlighting the corrupt nature of the system. The film also portrays the police force as flawed, with instances of incompetence and abuse of power, such as the cab driver's exorbitant fare and the cadets' disastrous performance in the field.

title: An American Tail
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The film portrays immigration officials as indifferent, renaming immigrants arbitrarily ('Smovolodny-Dhromovichsky' to 'Mr. Smith'). Gussie Mausheimer, a wealthy mouse, acknowledges the ineffectiveness of the system, stating, 'Those cats are killing everyone! They don't even know the difference between rich and poor.' The mice ultimately have to take matters into their own hands to fight the cats, highlighting the failure of existing institutions to protect them.

title: Poltergeist II: The Other Side
justification: The film exhibits a notable degree of institutional cynicism. The appearance of Reverend Kane, who claims to represent an organization concerned with families in crisis, is revealed to be a manipulative and dangerous figure, preying on the family's vulnerability. The film suggests that established institutions and figures of authority cannot be trusted and may even be malevolent. The family must rely on unconventional figures like Tangina and Taylor, who operate outside of traditional structures, to combat the supernatural threat, indicating a need to circumvent or fight against the system.

title: Short Circuit
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film portrays Nova Robotics and the military as prioritizing profit and weapon development over ethical considerations and safety. Dr. Marner is willing to lie and cover up the dangers of the robot, while Captain Skroeder is eager to destroy Number 5 despite potential harm to civilians. The dialogue highlights this disregard, such as when Marner instructs Skroeder to detain Number 5 "the best you can... and still avoid an incident," but then tells him, "Whatever it takes to put that stupid contraption out of commission, gentlemen, that's what you do." Crosby's initial reluctance to engage with the institution and Ben's cynicism about PR further underscore this theme.

title: Pretty in Pink
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The school setting is present, but the narrative doesn't focus on its failures or corruption. title: Peggy Sue Got Married
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. There are no instances of characters actively fighting against or circumventing institutions. justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. title: Running Scared
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonists, Hughes and Costanzo, are often at odds with their superiors and the established procedures of the police force. title: The Fly
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "The Fly," though not dominant. title: The Money Pit
justification: The subtitles present a moderate level of institutional cynicism. title: Gung Ho
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a failing American auto factory being taken over by a Japanese corporation, Assan Motors. The Japanese management is portrayed as exploitative and uncaring, prioritizing production over worker well-being, and ultimately breaking their promise to provide raises, leading to a factory shutdown. The protagonist actively fights against the system, ultimately leading the workers to take matters into their own hands.

title: Heartbreak Ridge
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant and recurring theme. Sergeant Highway frequently clashes with superiors like Major Powers, who represent the 'new Marine Corps' focused on procedure over practical combat readiness. Highway's insubordination and disregard for protocol, while framed as necessary for effective training, highlight a distrust of the modern military bureaucracy. Dialogue such as, "Marines are fighting men, sir, they shouldn't be sitting on their asses...filling out forms for equipment they should already have," exemplifies this cynicism. Furthermore, the film portrays the military's supply and logistics as inefficient and inadequate, requiring Highway to circumvent the system to properly equip his men.

title: Hannah and Her Sisters
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The doctor's initial misdiagnosis and the subsequent anxiety it causes Mickey could be interpreted as a minor institutional failing, but it is quickly resolved. Overall, the narrative focuses on interpersonal relationships and personal struggles, with institutions playing a negligible role. Therefore, institutional cynicism is not structurally central to the story.

title: Nothing in Common
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The advertising agency, Boile, Gargas, Lionel and Basner, is portrayed as a cutthroat environment where employees are easily fired ("Hear what happened to Clemens? He got terminated.") and personal relationships are often transactional ("Doris, did you miss me? Of course. Thanks for the quickie."). The protagonist, David Basner, navigates this environment by bending rules and prioritizing personal connections, suggesting a distrust in the system's fairness. While the film doesn't focus solely on institutional failure, the recurring themes of manipulation and self-interest within the agency contribute to a sense of cynicism.

title: Three Amigos
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The villagers of Santa Poco are being terrorized by El Guapo and seek help, but state, "They are no better than El Guapo. They will not help us. No one will help us." This demonstrates a lack of faith in any formal authority to provide justice or protection. The villagers are forced to hire outsiders (the Amigos) to solve their problem, highlighting the failure of existing institutions. The Amigos themselves are initially motivated by money, not a sense of justice, further emphasizing the ineffectiveness and corruption of the system.

title: Soul Man
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The narrative shows Mark facing significant hurdles in accessing financial aid and loans for law school, highlighting a system that favors the already wealthy. He is denied financial aid because his parents are rich, even though they refuse to pay for his tuition. The bank denies him a loan due to a poor credit history stemming from minor unpaid bills, despite his ability to pay. This forces him to circumvent the system by fraudulently obtaining a scholarship intended for black students. While the film does not explicitly portray institutions as corrupt, it does show them as inflexible and unresponsive to individual circumstances, leading the protagonist to take extreme measures.

title: Murphy's Romance
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. The protagonist, Murphy, encounters bureaucratic hurdles and unhelpful figures, such as the banker who denies her a loan because she is a woman with no collateral. This is evident in the dialogue: "You're not a good risk. There's no husband to cosign. There's no collateral. You're renting. I don't see any assets." and "If I wore a fly, not a zipper, I'd get the loan? You'd have a better chance." However, these instances don't dominate the narrative. While Murphy challenges the town council over parking meters, this is more about individual defiance than a systemic critique. Other institutions, like the fire department and local businesses, are portrayed positively or neutrally, suggesting a limited scope of institutional distrust.

title: Wildcats
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Molly, faces systemic obstacles in her pursuit of coaching football. She encounters gender discrimination from Dan, who initially refuses to consider her for the JV position, stating, "Molly, a girl can't coach boys' football. You know that." Later, she is offered a position at Central High, a school with no resources and apathetic administration, as a way to get rid of her. The principal, Edwards, admits, "No practice? I wouldn't even know how to round the guys up." The system actively works against her, forcing her to fight for her position and the success of her team.

title: Jumpin' Jack Flash
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts British Intelligence and the CIA as deeply compromised, with agents like Talbot revealed as a KGB mole. The protagonist, Terry, is forced to circumvent official channels, such as the British Consulate, because they are either unhelpful or actively hostile. Jack, a British agent, is betrayed by his own agency and must rely on Terry's rogue actions to survive. The film highlights the untrustworthiness of formal institutions and the necessity of operating outside the system to achieve justice, as evidenced by the dialogue: "British Intellig..." (referring to Jack's affiliation, cut short, implying danger) and Terry's repeated attempts to report the situation, only to be dismissed or endangered.

title: Heartburn
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. There are no instances of characters actively fighting against or circumventing institutions. It's the closest you ever get to a cure," which suggests a cynical view of the therapeutic profession. However, this is an isolated comment and does not drive the plot or affect major character choices. The narrative primarily focuses on interpersonal relationships and personal growth, not on systemic failures or corruption.

title: Iron Eagle
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the U.S. government and military bureaucracy as slow, ineffective, and more concerned with political maneuvering than with the life of a captured American pilot. Colonel Blackburn expresses frustration with the State Department's negotiation tactics, saying they are 'full of shit' and that the government is acting like they only have 'a pair of twos, waiting on a face card.' Doug's frustration with the lack of action leads him to take matters into his own hands, planning and executing a rogue rescue mission because 'nobody would lift a finger to help my dad.' The general's conditional release at the end further emphasizes the institution's self-preservation over justice.

title: Children of a Lesser God
justification: The subtitles suggest a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While the school for the deaf is presented as generally functional, there are hints of underlying issues. The dialogue also implies a degree of stagnation or resistance to change, as seen in the assistant superintendent's comment about 'nobody's trying to change the world here'. However, these elements are not central to the plot, and the institution is not portrayed as overtly corrupt or malicious, resulting in a moderate salience score.

title: Little Shop of Horrors
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. However, these instances are more about individual exploitation and societal neglect than a systemic critique of formal institutions. title: The Great Mouse Detective
justification: Based solely on the provided lyrics, there is minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The lyrics primarily focus on criminal activity and personal relationships. title: Tough Guys
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonists, Harry and Archie, are immediately confronted with a hostile parole officer who predicts their failure. title: Lady and the Tramp
justification: The film contains minimal institutional cynicism. title: F/X
justification: Institutional cynicism is a dominant structural engine in this film. However, Rollie soon discovers that the situation is far more complex and dangerous than he initially believed, as corrupt elements within the Justice Department are using him as bait. Rollie states, "Ellen, an hour ago two cops tried to kill me!" and later, "WHY YOU? BECAUSE THEY KNEW I'D FALL FOR IT. 'ROLLIE, YOU'RE THE BEST.' HA. I DROPPED MY PANTS AND BENT OVER." This leads to a series of betrayals and violent encounters, forcing Rollie to take matters into his own hands to survive and expose the corruption.

title: Friday the 13th Part VI: Jason Lives
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The sheriff actively dismisses Tommy's warnings about Jason, prioritizing the town's reputation over safety: "no one in Forest Green wants to be reminded of what that maniac did here." He arrests Tommy despite evidence, showcasing a clear distrust and obstruction of justice. The deputy is eager to use excessive force, highlighting a potential abuse of power. The sheriff's initial reluctance to investigate the missing counselors further emphasizes the institution's failure to protect its citizens.

title: House
justification: Institutional cynicism is central to the plot. The narrative reveals a mental hospital's failure to contain a dangerous patient, Robert Henkel, who escapes and terrorizes a sorority house. The police are initially absent and ineffective, arriving only after multiple deaths. Dr. Lindsey's frantic calls to Detective Gilbert highlight the urgency and the system's slow response. The characters are forced to rely on their own resourcefulness and courage to survive, indicating a significant distrust in the ability of institutions to protect them.

title: A Room with a View
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism.
