title: Flight of the Navigator
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. After David reappears, NASA immediately takes control of the situation, isolating him from his family under the guise of scientific study. Dr. Faraday promises David's parents that he will be returned in 48 hours, but this promise is broken, and David is kept longer. David expresses feeling trapped and used as a "guinea pig." Carolyn, an intern, also expresses awareness of the deception, indicating a systemic issue within the institution. This mistrust in NASA's motives and actions significantly impacts David's choices, leading him to escape and seek refuge elsewhere.

title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life is Calling
justification: The subtitles present a world where institutions are flawed and sometimes unhelpful, but not structurally central to the narrative. There are instances of characters encountering bureaucratic hurdles, such as Jo Jo's difficulty in securing a job at the club, despite having been promised one ("You said if I was ever in Cleveland, I could look you up and get a job. I'm all booked up."). The police are present, but their role seems more reactive than proactive, and there's no indication of systemic corruption. The hospital staff are shown trying to save Jo Jo's life, indicating a functional, if imperfect, system. While there are instances of characters circumventing the law (e.g., Sal's criminal activities), these are presented as individual actions rather than a systemic indictment.

title: The Delta Force
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the US government as prioritizing political considerations over the immediate safety of hostages, as evidenced by the President's initial reluctance to authorize the Delta Force's intervention in Algiers ("The President doesn't want to risk any lives. If he can release our people by negotiations, that's what he wants."). This hesitation directly endangers the hostages and necessitates rogue actions by Colonel Alexander and his team. Furthermore, the Lebanese government's initial denial of landing permission in Beirut highlights the unreliability and obstructionist nature of international political bodies in crisis situations, forcing the pilot to defy orders to save lives. The film also shows the US military's willingness to sacrifice soldiers for political gain, as seen in the opening scene where the Colonel prioritizes the squadron over saving Scott and Pete.

title: Howard the Duck
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Howard the Duck." While not the dominant engine, distrust and circumvention of institutions significantly affect the plot. The military/scientific establishment, represented by Dyna-Technics, is portrayed as reckless and irresponsible, causing Howard's initial displacement and later unleashing a Dark Overlord. The police are depicted as brutal and incompetent, leading to Howard's wrongful arrest and a chaotic chase scene. Howard's line, "If you got blasted millions of miles through space... and were given an I.Q. test by a janitor, you'd be pissed off too!" encapsulates the film's cynicism towards authority and expertise.

title: Raw Deal
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Mark, is a former bureau agent who was forced to resign due to political pressure after a controversial case. He expresses distrust towards the system, stating, "They gave me a chance to resign. If it would've gone to trial... I would've lost and they would've kicked me out." He is later recruited to work outside official channels to take down a mob boss because the bureau has a leak, highlighting the ineffectiveness and corruption within the institution. The narrative emphasizes the need for rogue actions and vigilantism to achieve justice, as Mark operates independently with limited official support.

title: Armed and Dangerous
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Frank Dooley, is a former cop framed for a crime he didn't commit, highlighting corruption within the police force and judicial system. The union is portrayed as corrupt, with leaders exploiting members' dues and colluding with criminals. The private security firm is depicted as exploitative and incompetent, offering minimal training and low wages. Dialogue such as "This court Looks upon corruption with great disdain" and "The world is a shithole, full of shitty little scumbags" underscores the pervasive distrust in formal institutions and the need for vigilante justice.

title: Legend
justification: The subtitles contain a moderate level of institutional cynicism. Lily's father's rules and expectations are presented as a constraint on her freedom and happiness, as she seeks magic outside the palace. Nell's proverbs suggest a distrust of the 'willful heart' and 'king's command,' implying that societal rules can lead to despair. However, these elements are not central to the plot's driving conflict, which primarily revolves around the Dark Lord and the unicorns, rather than systemic institutional failures.

title: Song of the South
justification: The film exhibits a low level of institutional cynicism. The primary conflict revolves around familial relationships and personal choices, rather than systemic failures. While the mother initially leaves her husband and moves to her mother's plantation, this is presented as a personal decision driven by marital discord, not a critique of societal structures. The grandmother's lament, "A grandmother doesn't count for much these days," hints at a potential shift in family dynamics, but it doesn't translate into a broader institutional critique. title: Youngblood
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not dominant. While these instances highlight flaws within the hockey system, the narrative doesn't solely focus on these failures, but rather on the protagonist's personal journey and growth within the sport.

title: Crimes of the Heart
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The character Chick expresses a belief that Babe will be imprisoned and 'left to rot,' indicating a distrust of the justice system's fairness. While the legal proceedings are central to the plot, the narrative also focuses on family dynamics and personal struggles, preventing institutional cynicism from becoming the dominant theme.

title: Psycho III
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The sheriff is portrayed as somewhat lazy and dismissive, initially reluctant to investigate Emma Spool's disappearance, despite her employer's concerns: "Still beats the hell out of me. Just doesn't show up for work one day." He also seems more concerned with keeping the peace and protecting Norman Bates than with thoroughly investigating potential crimes. The mental health system is also questioned, as Norman Bates is deemed sane by the state after 22 years of incarceration, yet he clearly struggles with his mental state. The dialogue highlights societal skepticism towards rehabilitation: "Many people think they can't be rehabilitated and there shouldn't be an insanity defense."

title: Sweet Liberty
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film portrays the making of a historical movie, and the protagonist, a historian, is constantly battling against the director and screenwriter's inaccurate and sensationalized portrayal of history. The director explicitly states that the movie audience is 80% kids and that they want to see authority defied and property destroyed. The protagonist's attempts to maintain historical accuracy are consistently undermined, highlighting a distrust in the film industry's ability to handle historical narratives responsibly. The protagonist's frustration culminates in a confrontation where he calls the director an "asshole" for prioritizing entertainment over accuracy.

title: One Crazy Summer
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. For example, the bank is unsympathetic to Cassandra's plight, ultimately selling her grandfather's mortgage to the antagonist, Beckerstead, despite her efforts to raise the money. This action highlights a perceived lack of compassion or flexibility within the banking system. Additionally, the legal system is bypassed when the community decides to resolve their conflict with Beckerstead through a sailing race rather than legal means. These instances suggest a degree of distrust or disillusionment with formal institutions, though it doesn't become the central driving force of the plot.

title: Extremities
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Marjorie reports a rape attempt to the police, but the officer's insensitive questioning and the bureaucratic process are immediately apparent. The officer's wording of the report is insensitive, and she is told that without a description, it will be her word against his, and he'll "get off." When she asks for protection, the officer simply says, "You call and we'll be there." This perceived lack of institutional support directly leads to Marjorie and Terry taking matters into their own hands, deciding to kidnap and potentially murder the attacker rather than rely on the police.

title: Critters
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film opens with a blatant disregard for protocol and life by prison transport officers who kill Crite prisoners to conserve food. Later, local law enforcement, represented by Jeff, is portrayed as incompetent and dismissive of Charlie's warnings about the alien threat, prioritizing donuts and coffee over his duties. Harv, another law enforcement officer, is initially skeptical and slow to respond, highlighting a systemic failure to take the threat seriously. The dialogue, such as Jeff's dismissive attitude towards UFO reports and Harv's delayed response, underscores the ineffectiveness and unreliability of these institutions in protecting the community.

title: April Fool's Day
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The constable is eventually contacted and arrives, suggesting the police force is functional, even if slow to respond. title: Labyrinth
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Goblin King, Jareth, represents a corrupt authority figure who manipulates the labyrinth to prevent Sarah from rescuing her brother. He actively deceives and threatens characters like Hoggle, forcing them to betray Sarah. The labyrinth itself is a system designed to trap and discourage, reflecting a distrust in any straightforward path to justice or resolution. Sarah must actively fight against Jareth's power and the labyrinth's obstacles, highlighting the failure of any conventional system to aid her.

title: Club Paradise
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The governor is portrayed as jaded and cynical about the island's future, suggesting a lack of faith in the system. Jack and Ernest actively fight against the corrupt system, highlighting the ineffectiveness of formal institutions in protecting their interests. The dialogue explicitly mentions "corruption, injustice," and the constitution being "written in pencil," underscoring the systemic issues.

title: Firewalker
justification: The narrative features a general who is corrupt and seeks to kill the protagonists for personal gain, showcasing a clear distrust of authority. The protagonists actively circumvent the law and engage in illegal activities, such as impersonating priests to cross borders, indicating a lack of faith in legal systems. The dialogue includes instances where characters express skepticism towards institutions, such as when Max states, "The government isn't letting anyone in without official clearance," suggesting that official channels are obstructive. These elements contribute to a recurring theme of institutional failure and the need for characters to operate outside the system, making institutional cynicism a relevant theme.

title: Big Trouble in Little China

This forces the protagonists to operate outside the bounds of conventional institutions to address the threat posed by Lo Pan and rescue Miao Yin. title: Under the Cherry Moon

title: SpaceCamp

title: Platoon
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The dialogue reveals a deep mistrust of authority and the military hierarchy. title: Bustin' Loose

The legal system is shown as flawed, with Braxton attempting to return to prison to escape his parole officer, highlighting a distrust in the justice system's ability to protect him. The town mayor ultimately intervenes, showcasing a local authority stepping in where larger institutions have failed.

title: Reds

The narrative also hints at corruption and manipulation within institutions, such as the government's alleged collusion with capitalists and the suppression of dissent. title: Sharky's Machine
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Sharky is transferred to Vice after a civilian is shot during a drug bust, indicating a lack of faith in his methods by superiors. The Vice unit itself is portrayed as a dumping ground for cops who "don't make waves," and Friscoe expresses cynicism about the Department's willingness to pursue powerful figures like Hotchkins. The fact that the Department allows all but one wiretap, the one connected to Dominoe, further highlights the corruption. Sharky actively circumvents the system, using personal connections to get the Dominoe wiretap and ultimately taking matters into his own hands to pursue Scarelli, indicating a deep mistrust of institutional justice.

title: The Survivors
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Donald, is fired by a parrot due to 'reorganization,' highlighting corporate absurdity. Paluso's struggle to get unemployment benefits reveals bureaucratic incompetence and indifference ('An owner cannot be unemployed'). The police are portrayed as inept, failing to recognize a known criminal and prioritizing procedure over justice ('Drop the gun, scumbag'). The media is also criticized for sensationalism and trivializing serious events ('Hotshots with dumb luck have no business handling crime'). These instances collectively demonstrate a systemic distrust and failure of institutions, driving the narrative and character actions.

title: Gorky Park
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The dialogue reveals a deep-seated mistrust of the KGB and other state institutions. Renko is warned multiple times to drop the case, with the implication that the KGB is involved and will retaliate. The Chief Prosecutor Iamskoy is revealed to be corrupt and in league with Osborne. Renko actively circumvents the system, stealing files and working outside official channels, indicating a belief that justice cannot be achieved through normal procedures. The General's primary concern is appearances and quick resolution, not necessarily justice.

title: The Osterman Weekend
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts the CIA as deeply corrupt, engaging in murder and manipulation. Fassett's actions, sanctioned by higher-ups, highlight the agency's willingness to sacrifice innocent lives for political gain. Dialogue such as "Accidents happen, sir. There are no accidents in war. You were screwing your wife in a foxhole and a mortar shell fell on it" and "Omega is as real as we need it to be" demonstrates a callous disregard for human life and truth. The climax involves a live television broadcast where the CIA director is exposed as a murderer, further solidifying the theme of institutional corruption.

title: Beverly Hills Cop
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Axel Foley, consistently disregards police procedure and authority, highlighting a distrust in the system's ability to deliver justice effectively. He goes undercover without authorization, leading to reprimands from his superiors. Dialogue such as "I think the issue should be my blatant disregard for proper procedure" and the constant conflict with Beverly Hills police officers Taggart and Rosewood, who are initially portrayed as rule-bound and ineffective, demonstrate a systemic critique. The narrative emphasizes Foley's rogue actions as necessary to solve the case, suggesting that the formal institutions are inadequate.

title: Footloose
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not the dominant engine. The town's council, led by Reverend Moore, enforces strict rules against dancing and certain types of music, reflecting a distrust of outside influences and a desire to control the community's morality. This is evident in the dialogue where characters discuss the town's history of banning dancing after a tragic accident and the council's resistance to Ren's efforts to organize a dance. The police also represent this institutional control, as seen when they ticket Ren for playing loud music. While Ren challenges these restrictions, the narrative also explores the Reverend's internal conflict and eventual change of heart, suggesting that institutions can evolve, but initially, they are presented as obstacles to individual expression.

title: Romancing the Stone
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not the dominant engine. The subtitles reveal a distrust of law enforcement and government, particularly in Colombia. Characters frequently circumvent or operate outside the law, suggesting a lack of faith in its ability to provide justice or safety. For example, Jack's bird smuggling and Juan's drug dealing are both illegal activities. Additionally, the Colombian police are portrayed as corrupt and easily manipulated by Zolo, further highlighting the ineffectiveness of formal institutions. The American consulate is mentioned as a place to seek help, but Jack advises Joan not to mention his name, indicating a lack of trust in even foreign institutions.

title: Tightrope
justification: The narrative demonstrates a significant level of institutional cynicism. The police, while ostensibly investigating crimes, are portrayed as flawed and potentially corrupt. The protagonist, Detective Block, faces resistance and skepticism from his superiors and the mayor, who are more concerned with public image than solving the murders. The rape center worker, Beryl, expresses distrust in the police's handling of the case, highlighting a systemic issue. Additionally, the killer himself was a former cop who went to prison for rape, indicating a deep-seated corruption within the institution.

title: Teachers
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the school administration as prioritizing the institution's reputation and financial stability over the students' education and well-being. This is evident in the superintendent's concern about publicity and the bond issue, as well as the pressure on teachers to conform and avoid rocking the boat. The teachers are shown as disillusioned and struggling within a system that seems to fail many students, as exemplified by the John Calvin case and Eddie Pilikian's situation. The protagonist, Alex Jurel, ultimately chooses to fight against the system, highlighting the structural importance of institutional failure and the need for individual action.

title: City Heat
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Mike Murphy, is a former cop who turned in his badge and now operates outside the system. Lieutenant Speer, a current police officer, is portrayed as both antagonistic and ineffectual, often resorting to violence and intimidation rather than legitimate investigation. The dialogue highlights a deep mistrust of the police and the legal system, with characters like Murphy frequently circumventing or outright defying law enforcement. The prevalence of corruption, as seen with Primo Pitt and Leon Coll, further underscores the systemic failure of institutions to uphold justice, forcing Murphy to take matters into his own hands.

title: The Woman in Red
justification: The film contains some instances of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. The protagonist's workplace is portrayed as somewhat demanding and bureaucratic, with the boss assigning tasks at the last minute and expecting employees to work late. This is evident in the dialogue where the protagonist complains about being asked to "Clean this up for tomorrow morning," feeling like a "cleaning man." Additionally, there's a brief mention of air conditioning being "on the blink again" at the office, suggesting a minor level of institutional neglect. However, these instances are relatively isolated and do not significantly drive the plot or character decisions, indicating a low level of salience.

title: The Morning After
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Alex, is framed for murder, and the police are portrayed as potentially biased and easily manipulated by wealth and influence. Turner, an ex-cop, expresses distrust in the justice system, suggesting Alex turn herself in but also acknowledging the system's potential for unfairness. The dialogue reveals a system where wealth and social standing can influence outcomes, as seen with Isabel Harding's potential escape from justice due to her family's power. The narrative emphasizes the need for Alex to circumvent the official channels to prove her innocence, highlighting a deep-seated mistrust in the institutions designed to uphold justice.

title: Murphy's Law
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Jack Murphy, is framed for murder, highlighting the potential for corruption within the police force. He is arrested and jailed, and even his colleagues seem to believe in his guilt, indicating a failure of the system to protect the innocent. Murphy escapes custody, further demonstrating his distrust in the legal system's ability to deliver justice. The dialogue reveals that even after presenting evidence of his innocence, he is met with skepticism and betrayal, forcing him to operate outside the law to clear his name.

title: Manhunter
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film. The protagonist, Will Graham, is a former FBI agent who quit, implying dissatisfaction with the institution. He is brought back due to his unique skills, suggesting the FBI needs unconventional methods to solve cases. Dialogue such as "Atlanta PD swears they dusted everything, and their guy is pretty good. He is good. He's not as good as Price" indicates a hierarchy of competence within law enforcement, implying some are less effective. The reliance on Graham, who is portrayed as psychologically vulnerable, further suggests the limitations of standard institutional procedures. The film also shows the media, represented by Freddie Lounds, as intrusive and sensationalist, hindering the investigation and endangering lives, which reflects a distrust of media institutions.

title: Care Bears Movie II: A New Generation
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The primary conflict stems from Dark Heart's ability to exploit and corrupt individuals, leading to the capture of the Care Bears and Cousins. Christy's initial desire to be 'camp champ' leads her to make a deal with Dark Heart, highlighting how easily individuals can be manipulated. The Care Bears must actively fight against Dark Heart's influence, which has infiltrated the summer camp and turned children against each other. The narrative emphasizes the need for collective caring to overcome Dark Heart's evil, suggesting that traditional institutions are insufficient to combat such pervasive negativity. The story revolves around the Care Bears circumventing Dark Heart's plans and ultimately restoring goodness through their own actions.

title: Wise Guys
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts law enforcement and the justice system as deeply compromised, with Judge Overton and Chief Barkley receiving monthly bribes. This corruption is structural, enabling organized crime to flourish. Characters like Moe and Harry must navigate this corrupt system, often resorting to illegal activities to survive. The dialogue explicitly reveals the pervasive corruption, such as Santo mentioning increasing the judges' 'monthly allowance,' highlighting the systemic nature of the problem.

title: Something Wild
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not the dominant engine. The film opens with Charles, a newly promoted vice president, being confronted for not paying his lunch bill. He attempts to avoid involving the police ("No! No, don't tell...") suggesting a distrust of law enforcement or a desire to avoid bureaucratic involvement. Later, Ray, an ex-convict, expresses disdain for the legal system ("Take your laws and shove it down your goddamn throat!"). The film also portrays the police as ineffective, arriving only after significant violence has occurred, and failing to prevent Ray's actions.

title: Lucas
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. While there are instances of authority figures being unhelpful or out of touch, these do not form the central conflict of the narrative. For example, the school principal, Mr. Kaiser, is portrayed as somewhat insensitive and bureaucratic, initially dismissing Lucas's concerns and later attempting to prevent him from playing football due to perceived safety risks. However, he is ultimately ineffective in stopping Lucas. Similarly, the football coach is initially dismissive and even abusive, but this is more a reflection of individual character flaws than a systemic failure. The film does not depict widespread corruption or a system actively working against the protagonist, but rather isolated instances of institutional limitations and individual failings.

title: Haunted Honeymoon
justification: The subtitles present a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The police are portrayed as initially dismissive and slow to respond to reports of murder, requiring the threat of mayoral intervention to elicit action. This suggests a degree of distrust in their responsiveness and effectiveness. However, the police do eventually arrive and investigate, indicating that the system, while flawed, is not entirely broken. The narrative does not heavily rely on characters actively fighting or circumventing the system, so the cynicism is not structurally central.

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Lefty Enright, a former Texas Ranger, is actively fighting against the dismissive attitude of local law enforcement regarding a series of murders. Lieutenant Enright attempts to dissuade Lefty from investigating, stating, "This is just an accident. Just a couple of wild punks out raising hell." Lefty believes the "laws... shy away from piecing it together as murder," and hopes that publicizing the evidence will force them to "stop trying to shut me up and start helping me." This systemic failure forces Lefty to operate outside of official channels, relying on a radio DJ, Stretch, for assistance.

title: The Best of Times
justification: The film exhibits a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While there are no explicit instances of corruption, the narrative portrays institutions as somewhat ineffectual and disappointing. The town's repeated football losses to Bakersfield High are presented as a systemic failure, contributing to the town's overall sense of decline. Jack's frustration with the bank's bureaucracy is evident when he has to call in a purchase over $50 at the massage parlor, highlighting the absurdity of certain rules. The school shop teacher's belief that Taft is the safest place in America in case of nuclear war is presented as delusional, suggesting a disconnect between the institution and reality.

title: Quicksilver
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in the film. The protagonist, Jack, loses his and his parents' money due to a buyout, highlighting the volatile and potentially destructive nature of the financial system. Later, Hector's attempts to secure a loan for his hot dog cart are thwarted by bureaucratic obstacles and prejudice, as the loan officer implies Hector won't get a loan because of his ethnicity. Jack also expresses cynicism when he tells Hector that sometimes things don't work out the way you plan and can backfire on you. Terri's experiences as a messenger, where she is used to carry "dirty work" for others, further illustrates the exploitation within the system.

title: Maximum Overdrive
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a world where machines turn against humanity, indicating a systemic failure of technology and the systems that rely on it. Characters like Bubba Hendershot exploit parolees, highlighting corruption within the justice system. The radio broadcasts explicitly state that 'no machine is to be trusted,' underscoring a complete breakdown of faith in technology. The characters are forced to survive by circumventing or fighting against these now-hostile systems, indicating a world where institutions have failed to provide safety or order.

title: Runaway Train
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative revolves around Oscar Manheim's escape from Stonehaven prison, highlighting the corruption and brutality within the system. Warden Ranken is portrayed as a cruel and manipulative figure, willing to bend the rules to maintain control, as evidenced by his illegal confinement of Manheim and his desire to see him killed. The dialogue reveals a deep-seated mistrust of authority, with prisoners openly defying and insulting Ranken. The railroad system is also shown as flawed, with employees prioritizing company reputation over safety, leading to a near-disaster.

title: The Boy Who Could Fly
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The narrative includes instances where institutions are portrayed as flawed or untrustworthy. For example, the state institute is depicted as a place that could harm Eric, leading Milly and her family to actively resist their attempts to take him away. Mrs. Sherman, a teacher, also expresses concern about the institute. Additionally, the school system is shown as bureaucratic and somewhat uncaring, as evidenced by Louis's initial struggles and the notes sent home. While these instances don't dominate the entire story, they significantly influence character choices and actions, making institutional mistrust a recurring element.

title: The Name of the Rose
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative revolves around the distrust and manipulation of institutions, particularly the Church and the Inquisition. The abbot is shown to be more concerned with covering up events than seeking justice, demonstrated by his initial desire for William to 'cover up' the truth. The arrival of Bernardo Gui and the Inquisition highlights the corruption and abuse of power within the Church, as they prioritize maintaining authority over uncovering the truth. William actively fights against the Inquisition's unjust verdict, showcasing the system's failure to deliver justice and the need for rogue actions.

title: Blue City
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Chief of Police, Reynolds, is deeply corrupt, protecting Perry Kerch and ultimately admitting to killing the protagonist's father and others. Dialogue such as "I'm real sorry, Billy, but I'm not gonna be able to cover for you anymore" and his fabricated story about the motel incident highlight the systemic corruption. The protagonist, Billy, actively fights against this corrupt system, seeking justice outside of it. The dialogue between Billy and Ortiz also suggests a widespread understanding of the police force's corruption, further emphasizing the institutional failure.

title: She's Gotta Have It
justification: The provided subtitles contain very little to suggest institutional cynicism. The characters primarily focus on interpersonal relationships, particularly romantic and sexual ones. There is no dialogue that explicitly criticizes or questions the trustworthiness of institutions. The narrative revolves around personal choices and interactions, with no indication that characters are battling against or circumventing any systemic issues. The only hint of anything beyond personal relationships is the mention of Greer's career taking off, but this is not presented in a way that suggests any institutional support or hindrance.

title: Nine 1/2 Weeks
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. There are no clear instances of characters actively fighting against or circumventing institutions. The narrative primarily focuses on interpersonal relationships and personal struggles, with institutions playing a negligible role. The dialogue does not suggest any widespread corruption or incompetence within formal systems, nor does it portray institutions as obstacles to justice. Therefore, institutional cynicism is not structurally central to the story.

title: The Trip to Bountiful
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. The primary instance is the mother's pension check being consistently late, leading to suspicion and anxiety. This is explicitly stated: "I just don't understand the government. Always late." Additionally, the bus station employee's rigid adherence to the 'book' preventing the mother from purchasing a ticket to Bountiful, despite her insistence it exists, highlights bureaucratic inflexibility. The police are also portrayed as dismissive of the family's concerns, advising them to ignore the mother's attempts to leave, suggesting a lack of effective support from law enforcement. These instances, while present, do not fundamentally drive the plot, but rather serve as background elements contributing to the mother's desperation and the family's struggles.

title: Just Between Friends
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The news station is portrayed as somewhat superficial and driven by ratings, as seen in the producer's focus on entertainment value and the anchor's concerns about her appearance. Sandy's frustration with her career is evident when she says, "I keep having to make these wrenching decisions between my career, which I'm good at, and my life, which I'm not. It just really fucks me up." However, this is more about personal struggles within the system than a systemic critique. The seismology center is presented as a place of work, but there's no indication of corruption or incompetence.

title: Hoosiers
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Hoosiers." The townspeople initially distrust Coach Dale, questioning his qualifications and experience ("I ain't interested in talking defence and I don't have a hair of a notion why we hired someone who's been in the water for the last ten years."). This distrust escalates to a town meeting where a referendum is held to remove him as coach, highlighting a lack of faith in the school board's decision. The refereeing in several games is biased, demonstrating corruption or incompetence within the officiating system ("Long enough to recognise a hometown referee!"). While the team ultimately succeeds, they do so despite, rather than because of, the support of the community and the fairness of the game.

title: A Fine Mess
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The police are portrayed as largely ineffective and easily manipulated, as seen when Spence reports his car stolen but is not believed, and later when they are outsmarted by Tony Pazzo. The legal system is also shown as flawed, with the mob boss Tony Pazzo operating with impunity. The narrative relies on characters circumventing or being failed by institutions, such as the police and the racing commission, to drive the plot forward, highlighting a distrust in their ability to deliver justice or maintain order.

title: Beverly Hills Cop II
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative showcases law enforcement institutions as flawed and easily manipulated. Axel Foley frequently circumvents official channels, relying on his street smarts and connections rather than formal procedures. Captain Bogomil's suspension and subsequent shooting highlight the vulnerability of those who try to uphold integrity within the system. The ease with which criminals like Dent and Thomopolis operate, exploiting loopholes and corrupt officials, further underscores the systemic failures.

title: Fatal Attraction
justification: The subtitles present a moderate level of institutional cynicism. The legal system is shown as somewhat ineffective, as the police are unable to act without concrete evidence of harassment or threats, even when a character expresses fear for their family's safety. The lieutenant states, "We can't arrest people for what they might do," and later, "It's his bed. I'm afraid he's gonna have to lie in it." This suggests a limitation in the institution's ability to proactively protect individuals. However, this is not a central plot driver, and the characters do not actively fight or circumvent the system in a significant way.

title: 3 Men and a Baby
justification: The subtitles contain a limited amount of institutional cynicism. The primary focus is on interpersonal relationships and the unexpected responsibility of caring for a baby. There's a brief encounter with a police officer, Detective Melkowitz, who is investigating a drug smuggling operation, but the police are portrayed as doing their job, not as corrupt or incompetent. The characters do try to avoid the police, but this is due to their accidental involvement in a crime, not a general distrust of law enforcement. The narrative doesn't structurally rely on institutional failure or corruption.

title: The Untouchables
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts widespread corruption within the Chicago police force, requiring Eliot Ness to assemble a team of 'Untouchables' who are incorruptible. Dialogue such as, 'This town stinks like a whorehouse at low tide. First, who can you trust? Nobody. The cops, nobody,' highlights the pervasive distrust. Ness actively fights against the corrupt system, circumventing it to bring Capone to justice. The film also shows the legal system being manipulated, with jury bribery and the need for extraordinary measures (switching juries) to achieve a conviction.

title: The Secret of My Success
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The protagonist, Brantley, encounters systemic issues such as nepotism, corporate espionage, and general incompetence within Pemrose Corporation. He initially gets fired due to a hostile takeover, highlighting the instability of corporate structures. He later observes that 'Nobody knows what anybody else is doin',' and that 'Something happens to a man when he puts on a necktie. Cuts off all the oxygen to his brain,' indicating a critical view of corporate culture. Brantley actively circumvents the established hierarchy by assuming a false identity and leveraging inside information to expose corruption and ultimately take control of the company, demonstrating a clear distrust in the existing system.

title: Stakeout
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the FBI and local police as flawed and self-serving. Detectives Lecce and Reimers are assigned a low-priority stakeout by the FBI, who are more concerned with taking credit for capturing Montgomery than with actually solving the case. Lecce expresses his frustration: "What you're asking is, you'd like us to sit on our butts On some low-Priority shit detail...So you can make the arrest and get the keys to the city?" The captain's dismissive attitude towards the detectives' concerns further highlights the institutional indifference. The detectives also circumvent procedure by illegally entering Maria's house to gather evidence, indicating a willingness to bypass the system to achieve their goals.

title: Lethal Weapon
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative reveals that a clandestine group of ex-CIA mercenaries, "Shadow Company," is running a heroin smuggling operation, using a legitimate company as a front. This corruption extends to figures like General McAllister, who commands the operation. The protagonist, Murtaugh, actively fights against this corrupt system, and Riggs, initially suicidal, finds purpose in dismantling it. Dialogue such as Hunsaker's plea to "find them and kill them" and Riggs's line, "We bury the fuckers," highlights the extrajudicial approach necessitated by the institutional failure.

title: The Witches of Eastwick
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. Felicia's rant about the local newspaper focusing on trivial matters while ignoring important issues like toxic waste suggests a distrust of local media. She also criticizes the town for selling the Lenox mansion, a landmark building, implying a failure of the town's preservation efforts. However, these instances are relatively isolated and do not drive the main plot, which focuses more on the supernatural and interpersonal relationships.

title: Predator
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The initial mission is revealed to be a false pretense orchestrated by Dillon to further CIA interests, leading Dutch and his team into a dangerous situation without their knowledge or consent. Dillon admits to using them as "expendable assets" to achieve his goals, highlighting a deep mistrust of authority and the willingness of institutions to sacrifice individuals. The military command also demonstrates a lack of concern for the team's safety, denying extraction and prioritizing the extraction of the female guerrilla, further emphasizing the expendability of the soldiers. Dutch's disillusionment and his eventual fight against both the Predator and the system that betrayed him underscore the theme's importance.

title: Dragnet
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme. The film presents the police department as somewhat bureaucratic and constrained by regulations, as seen in Friday's strict adherence to rules and dress codes. Captain Gannon is portrayed as more concerned with appearances and political fallout than with justice, initially dismissing Friday's investigation and later siding with Commissioner Kirkpatrick over clear evidence. The commissioner herself is depicted as politically motivated, prioritizing public image over truth, and readily dismissing Friday despite his dedication. While the film ultimately upholds the law, the narrative highlights the challenges and compromises officers face within the system, suggesting a degree of institutional mistrust.

title: Dirty Dancing
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film portrays institutions like Kellerman's management and societal expectations as flawed and restrictive. Max's exploitative treatment of the entertainment staff, emphasizing their limited roles and prohibiting 'funny business,' highlights a cynical view of power dynamics. Robbie's abandonment of Penny and the back-alley abortion underscore the failure of societal safety nets. Baby's father's initial distrust of Johnny and the subsequent accusation of theft, despite lacking evidence, exemplify institutional bias and the protagonist's fight against these prejudices.

title: La Bamba
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. There are instances of law enforcement being viewed negatively, such as the song "Framed" where the singer is unjustly accused by police. Additionally, the character Bob expresses distrust and resentment towards the music industry, viewing it as exploitative. However, these instances are isolated and do not drive the main plot, which focuses more on personal relationships and Richie's rise to fame. The institutions themselves are not structurally central to the narrative's conflicts or resolutions.

title: RoboCop
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. OCP's control over the Detroit police force is a major plot point, with Dick Jones, a senior OCP executive, orchestrating criminal activities and manipulating the police for personal gain. The police force is portrayed as ineffective and easily manipulated by OCP, as evidenced by the police strike and the inability of officers to arrest Jones due to 'Directive 4.' RoboCop's creation and programming highlight the corporation's disregard for individual rights and its willingness to exploit law enforcement for profit. The dialogue emphasizes the corruption and the struggle against a system where corporate interests supersede justice.

title: Outrageous Fortune
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The CIA is portrayed as incompetent, as evidenced by Weldon's bumbling attempts to manage the situation and his initial disbelief in the actresses' abilities. The police are ineffective, requiring the actresses to apprehend criminals themselves, highlighted by their success in capturing the passport forgers. The film also depicts the KGB as infiltrating the New York theatre community, suggesting a deep-seated corruption within seemingly benign institutions. The protagonists must actively circumvent these flawed institutions to achieve their goals, relying on their own ingenuity and resourcefulness rather than trusting in official channels, as seen when they decide to track down Michael themselves.

title: The Living Daylights
justification: Institutional cynicism is a recurring theme in this film. The defection of Koskov is initially presented as a major intelligence coup, but Bond uncovers that it is a staged event to manipulate Western intelligence agencies. Koskov's manipulation of the British and the KGB, as well as Whitaker's arms dealing, highlight the untrustworthiness of individuals within these institutions. Bond's skepticism towards orders and his willingness to act on his own instincts, such as not killing the cellist, further emphasize a distrust of formal protocols. The film also portrays the KGB as ruthless and willing to use deception and violence to achieve their goals, contributing to the overall theme of institutional mistrust.

title: Full Metal Jacket
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film portrays the military, a core institution, as brutal and dehumanizing, prioritizing the creation of killers over ethical considerations. Sergeant Hartman's dialogue exemplifies this, stating, "You will be a weapon, you will be a minister of death praying for war." The dehumanization process is further highlighted by the recruits being called "pukes" and "the lowest form of life." Later, the Colonel states, "inside every gook there is an American trying to get out," which shows the dehumanization of the enemy. The film also shows the military's propaganda efforts to paint a positive picture of the war, even when the reality is grim.

title: A Nightmare On Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the mental health institution as ineffective and even harmful. Doctors dismiss the patients' shared nightmares as "group psychosis" and prescribe experimental drugs against the advice of a more insightful colleague. The institution's policies, such as locking doors and evening sedation, render the patients defenseless against Freddy. The police are also portrayed as unhelpful, with Nancy's father initially dismissing her concerns about Krueger's return, highlighting a systemic failure to protect the children.

title: Blind Date
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. The legal system is briefly touched upon, with the judge being portrayed as potentially corruptible, as evidenced by the father's offer to bribe him in exchange for an acquittal. However, this is a minor plot point and does not drive the overall narrative. The film primarily focuses on interpersonal relationships and comedic situations, rather than systemic issues or institutional failures. The police are shown arresting Walter, but this is a direct result of his actions, not a reflection of institutional bias or incompetence.

title: Roxanne
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme, though not dominant. The fire department, while staffed by well-meaning individuals, is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and reliant on luck. The fire chief expresses frustration that people might not trust the fire department to respond effectively to a fire, indicating a potential lack of confidence in the institution. The mayor seems more concerned with public image and promotions than with the actual effectiveness of the fire department, suggesting a degree of institutional self-interest over public service. The fire department's reliance on volunteer work and promotional gimmicks further underscores a sense of inadequacy and the need to circumvent traditional institutional structures to achieve success.

title: Planes, Trains & Automobiles
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Planes, Trains, and Automobiles." The airline is portrayed as incompetent and uncaring, delaying and bumping Neal from his first-class seat, leading to his initial encounter with Del. The car rental agency is equally inept, giving Neal keys to a car that doesn't exist, forcing him to walk miles. The train system is also flawed, with tickets not being honored and routes changing unexpectedly. These institutional failures directly drive the plot, forcing Neal and Del to rely on each other and other unreliable means of transportation to get home. While not the dominant engine, these failures significantly impact the characters' journey and choices.

title: Spaceballs
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in "Spaceballs." The primary conflict arises from Planet Spaceball's need for air, leading President Skroob and Dark Helmet to attempt to steal it from Planet Druidia. They aim to kidnap Princess Vespa and hold her hostage, demonstrating a willingness to bypass diplomatic solutions and resort to coercion. The Spaceballs' incompetence and corruption are highlighted through their bungled attempts to capture the princess, such as the radar malfunction and the self-destruct sequence. The film also satirizes bureaucracy, as seen in the Spaceballs' rigid adherence to orders, even when nonsensical, like 'combing the desert'.

title: Mannequin
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. Jonathan Switcher is repeatedly fired from various jobs for arbitrary reasons, highlighting the instability and lack of fairness in the employment system. B.J. Wert, the regional manager at Illustra, embodies corporate greed and a willingness to sabotage Prince and Company to facilitate its acquisition, suggesting a corrupt business environment. However, these instances are somewhat balanced by Mrs. Timkin's genuine care for her store and her eventual decision to resist the acquisition, indicating that institutions are not entirely devoid of positive elements. The dialogue reveals flaws and self-serving behaviors within institutions, but these do not become the central driving force of the narrative.

title: Eddie Murphy Raw
justification: The provided subtitles primarily consist of stand-up comedy routines, personal anecdotes, and observational humor. There is minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The comedian discusses personal experiences, relationships, and societal observations, but these do not inherently critique or undermine formal institutions. The jokes about marriage and relationships suggest a skepticism towards those institutions, but it's more about personal dynamics than systemic failures. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but not a driving force in the narrative.

title: Throw Momma From the Train
justification: The subtitles present a limited degree of institutional cynicism. The writing class, as an institution, is portrayed as somewhat farcical, with the teacher, Larry, struggling to provide meaningful feedback and the students producing questionable work. For example, Owen's murder mystery is criticized for lacking motivation, and Mr. Pinsky's work is deemed "whacking material." However, these instances primarily serve as comedic elements and do not structurally drive the plot or suggest a systemic failure of educational institutions. The police are shown as somewhat competent, but also easily misled, which contributes to a minor sense of distrust.

title: The Running Man
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays a dystopian society where the government and media (ICS) are deeply corrupt and manipulative. The Justice Department is complicit in a system where innocent people are falsely accused and exploited for entertainment, as seen with Richards being framed for the Bakersfield massacre. The Running Man game show exemplifies this, showcasing state-sanctioned violence and propaganda. Characters like Killian embody the amorality of the system, prioritizing ratings over truth and justice, as evidenced by his willingness to manipulate events and even kill to maintain control of the narrative.

title: No Way Out
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the Department of Defense, the CIA, and the US government as deeply flawed and easily manipulated. Secretary Brice is willing to abuse his power to cover up his affair and potential involvement in Susan Atwell's death, leading to a false flag operation to find 'Yuri.' The CIA is portrayed as self-serving, willing to inflate estimates to maintain its power. The dialogue highlights this, with characters like Brice expressing distrust in institutions and a willingness to circumvent them to achieve personal or political goals, such as terminating the phantom submarine program despite congressional resistance.

title: Summer School
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The narrative portrays the school administration (Gills and Kelban) as self-serving and primarily concerned with avoiding lawsuits and maintaining appearances, rather than genuinely caring about the students' education. Gills blackmails Shoop into teaching summer school to secure his tenure recommendation, highlighting the corrupt nature of the system. The students' files are presented as inaccurate and misleading, further demonstrating the institution's failure to understand or support them. Shoop is arrested due to the institution's policies, and the administration is more concerned with appearances than with Shoop's genuine efforts to help the students.

title: Like Father Like Son
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Dr. Larkin's repeated clashes with hospital policy regarding uninsured patients highlight the institution's prioritization of profit over patient care. He actively circumvents these policies, stating he doesn't give a "rat's ass about hospital policy." The board meeting scene further emphasizes this, with the board members prioritizing financial burdens over the well-being of patients, leading to Dr. Larkin's frustration and Dr. Hammond's eventual support. The film also shows the main character's father losing the Chief of Staff position due to the hospital's liability insurance policy.

title: Adventures in Babysitting
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative showcases multiple instances where characters encounter untrustworthy or ineffective systems. The police are absent or unhelpful, requiring the protagonists to navigate dangerous situations independently. The hospital is portrayed as chaotic and indifferent, failing to provide adequate assistance. The protagonists are forced to rely on their own resourcefulness and the help of morally ambiguous individuals like Pruitt to survive, highlighting a systemic failure of institutions to protect and aid them.

title: The Lost Boys
justification: The subtitles contain a few instances that suggest a mild cynicism towards institutions, but it is not a central theme. The most relevant example is the line, "ghouls and werewolves occupy high positions at City Hall," which implies corruption or untrustworthiness within the local government. However, this statement is made by characters who are presented as eccentric and possibly unreliable, diminishing its impact. The narrative does not focus on characters actively fighting or circumventing institutions; instead, the focus is on a more personal struggle against vampires. Therefore, institutional cynicism is present but not structurally significant.

title: Wall Street
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Bud Fox, is drawn into a world of insider trading and corporate raiding by Gordon Gekko, who explicitly states, "If you're not inside, you are outside." Gekko's actions, such as planning to dismantle Bluestar Airlines for profit, demonstrate a disregard for the well-being of employees and the community. Bud's father, Carl Fox, expresses distrust of management and corporations, saying, "That scum built the company up with one plane in 30 years...and made something out of nothing. If that's a scum, I'll take it over a rat any day." The narrative highlights how institutions can be manipulated for personal gain, leading to widespread consequences.

title: Can’t Buy Me Love
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. The high school is present as a social structure, but not as an institution that is actively failed or distrusted. There are no clear examples of characters fighting against or circumventing the school system itself. The focus is more on social dynamics and personal growth than on any systemic issues within institutions.

title: The Princess Bride
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Prince Humperdinck manipulates the legal system to start a war with Guilder by framing them for Buttercup's murder, showcasing the institution's susceptibility to corruption. The Thieves' Forest inhabitants are unjustly targeted and arrested on the wedding day, highlighting the abuse of power. Miracle Max, a former employee of the King, was fired by Humperdinck's son, indicating a flawed system where talent is disregarded. The Pit of Despair, a secret prison accessible only to the Prince and his associates, demonstrates the clandestine and oppressive nature of the ruling power. The Prince's manipulation of the wedding and planned murder of his bride to incite war further emphasizes the corrupt nature of the monarchy.

title: Harry and the Hendersons
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. George Henderson initially attempts to report the Bigfoot encounter to the police, but Sergeant Mancini dismisses his claims and threatens him with legal repercussions if he wastes police resources, stating, "So unless you wanna be responsible for wrongfully turning your neighborhood into a war zone I suggest you drop this whole thing right now." This forces the family to deal with the situation on their own. Later, Richard Smith from the U.S. Forestry Service investigates, but it's revealed he's actually Jacques LaFleur, a hunter, highlighting the untrustworthiness of official institutions and their potential for misuse. The narrative emphasizes the family's need to circumvent official channels to protect Harry, solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: Police Academy 4: Citizens on Patrol
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Captain Harris actively undermines Commandant Lassard's C.O.P. program, viewing it as a threat to the police force's authority and job security. He states, "Lassard's program is a mistake...and anyone who thinks otherwise is wrong. Pure and simple." Harris consistently sabotages the program, expressing disdain for citizen involvement in law enforcement. The C.O.P. program itself is portrayed as flawed, leading to a major undercover operation being compromised, highlighting the potential for citizen involvement to disrupt established procedures. The narrative also shows the justice system being circumvented when the judge allows Mahoney to enroll the skateboarders in the C.O.P. program instead of sending them to jail.

title: Tin Men
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant and recurring theme in this film, affecting major character choices. The Home Improvement Commission hearings reveal a system where individuals are penalized for deceptive sales practices, but the justification for these practices is questioned, suggesting a flawed system. Tilley's cynical view of the IRS and his attempts to evade taxes highlight a distrust of governmental institutions. The film also portrays the legal system as somewhat ineffective, as seen in the characters' attempts to settle disputes outside of formal channels, such as the pool game to decide Nora's future.

title: Black Widow
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in this film, though not dominant. The protagonist, Alex, works for the Justice Department but faces skepticism and resistance from her superiors (Bruce) and local law enforcement regarding her suspicions about a series of murders. Bruce initially dismisses her data analysis work as just a job with "green windows" and suggests she's unhappy because she needs a date, implying her professional concerns are secondary. Later, local law enforcement is reluctant to investigate the wealthy McCorey, stating, "If that's what the Justice Department calls evidence...then that is the scariest part of this whole conversation." This resistance and the need for Alex to circumvent official channels to pursue her investigation highlight a degree of mistrust in the system's ability to deliver justice.

title: Broadcast News
justification: The film portrays a news network driven by ratings and entertainment value rather than journalistic integrity. Characters express concerns about the 'star system' influencing news and the pressure to take a 'loyalty oath.' The film also shows the network's willingness to prioritize sensationalism over substantive reporting, as evidenced by the decision to run a feel-good homecoming story instead of covering a major policy change in SALT II. The characters often manipulate the news for their own gain, such as staging a news scene in Nicaragua. The film also shows the network's willingness to hire unqualified people based on looks and charisma, as well as the network's willingness to fire people based on budget cuts.

title: Nuts
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The legal system is portrayed as flawed and bureaucratic, with characters actively trying to manipulate it. The initial plea bargain negotiations between the lawyers ("WHAT ARE YOU GONNA GIVE ME ON HIM?") show a transactional approach to justice. Claudia's case highlights the system's potential for abuse, as she is nearly railroaded into a mental institution against her will, with her own lawyer initially complicit ("WE'RE TRYING TO DO WHAT WE FEEL IS BEST FOR YOU."). The judge's impatience and focus on efficiency over justice further underscore the system's shortcomings ("LET'S GET THIS ONE OUT OF HERE.").

title: *batteries not included
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a corrupt real estate developer, Lacey, who employs thugs to force tenants out of their homes. The police are portrayed as ineffective and unwilling to protect the tenants, stating they'll have 18 witnesses saying they were somewhere else. Mr. Riley and other tenants are left to fend for themselves against these forces, highlighting the failure of law enforcement to provide justice. The historical preservation society is also shown as bureaucratic and unsympathetic, prioritizing structural integrity over the human element, further emphasizing the inefficacy of formal institutions.

title: Baby Boom
justification: The film presents a mild form of institutional cynicism. J.C.'s initial corporate environment is portrayed as demanding and somewhat dehumanizing, where personal life is sacrificed for professional success. This is evident in dialogues like Fritz saying, "Normally I don't think of you as a woman. But in this case, I do have to look at you as a woman/partner." and "I mean, what if he expects a wife?" However, the primary focus isn't on systemic corruption or failure, but rather on J.C.'s personal journey and choices. The institutions themselves aren't actively malicious, but they are shown as potentially detrimental to personal well-being, leading J.C. to ultimately reject that lifestyle.

title: Ernest Goes to Camp
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The primary conflict arises from Krader Mining's attempt to seize Kamp Kikakee for petrocite mining, highlighting the corruption and disregard for legal and ethical boundaries. The legal system is portrayed as easily manipulated, as seen when Krader's attorney tricks the chief into signing away the land. The adults in charge of the 'Second Chance' program are dismissive and prejudiced towards the boys, further emphasizing the failure of institutions to provide genuine support. Ultimately, the protagonist and the boys must resort to vigilantism to protect their home, indicating a deep mistrust in the ability of formal institutions to deliver justice or fairness.

title: Raising Arizona
justification: Institutional cynicism is a relevant theme in "Raising Arizona." The film opens with Hi in prison, highlighting the structured and impersonal nature of the correctional system. Dialogue reveals a distrust of the system's ability to rehabilitate, as Hi admits to telling the counselor what he wants to hear to gain release. Ed's disillusionment with criminal justice leads her to resign from the police force, indicating a loss of faith in the institution. The FBI's investigation into the kidnapping is portrayed as somewhat inept, focusing on irrelevant details and failing to produce leads, further suggesting institutional ineffectiveness.

title: Revenge of the Nerds II: Nerds in Paradise
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Tri-Lambs face constant obstacles from the United Fraternity Conference and the Alpha Beta fraternity, who actively work to exclude and humiliate them. The hotel manager, Buzz Mussinger, exemplifies this, stating, "I don't want nerds staying in this hotel." Roger Lattimore, chairman of the UFC, orchestrates events to sabotage the Tri-Lambs, including a fake party and framing them for car theft. The police are used as tools to arrest the Tri-Lambs based on false accusations. The narrative structurally relies on the Tri-Lambs fighting against these biased and corrupt systems to achieve acceptance and justice.

title: Jaws 4: The Revenge
justification: The film presents a moderate level of institutional cynicism. While not a dominant theme, there are instances where institutions are portrayed as flawed or unhelpful. For example, the police department is shown dealing with trivial matters like "cow tipping" while a serious hazard (a dock piling) remains unaddressed. The Bahamian Fisheries Department is depicted as underfunded and bureaucratic, hindering Michael and Jake's research. However, these instances don't fundamentally drive the plot; the characters primarily rely on their own initiative and resources to confront the shark threat, rather than actively fighting or circumventing institutional failures.

title: Hello Again
justification: The film contains some elements of institutional cynicism, but it is not a central theme. The hospital, Knickerbocker, is presented as somewhat bureaucratic and concerned with appearances, as seen when Dr. Scanlon is pressured to take leave due to the media attention surrounding Lucy. However, the hospital also facilitates Lucy's medical tests and Dr. Scanlon genuinely tries to help her understand her condition. The Board of Education is mentioned as having Lucy's records wrong, stating she is dead, which presents a minor bureaucratic hurdle. Overall, institutions are more flawed than malicious, and the plot is not driven by characters actively fighting or circumventing them.

title: Critical Condition
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative depicts a hospital administration (Chambers) as self-serving and incompetent, prioritizing cost-cutting over patient care, and actively covering up negligence. The legal system is portrayed as flawed, with Lennihan facing a disproportionate sentence and the psychiatric evaluation process being easily manipulated. The police are shown as corrupt and easily manipulated, as evidenced by Stucky's presence and actions. The dialogue highlights this cynicism, with characters frequently expressing distrust and frustration with the system, such as when Rachel says, "You've been running this hospital into the ground." and when Lennihan says, "I'm part of the justice because I'm not just."

title: Innerspace
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. Vector-Scope, a government-funded research lab, is portrayed as deeply flawed and insecure, leading to the miniaturization experiment going awry. The dialogue reveals a lack of trust and competence within the organization, as characters like Pete Blanchard prioritize personal gain over the safety of Tuck Pendleton. The theft of the microchip and the subsequent attempts to cover up the incident highlight the corruption and lack of accountability within the institution. Characters actively circumvent the system, relying on rogue actions and vigilantism to resolve the crisis, indicating a significant distrust in formal channels.

title: Overboard
justification: The film presents a mild level of institutional cynicism. While there are no explicit instances of corruption, the narrative does feature a brief scene where the principal of the Elk Cove school, Adele Burbridge, is portrayed as somewhat dismissive and judgmental towards Dean Proffitt and his children, suggesting a lack of empathy or understanding from the educational system. However, this is a minor element and does not significantly drive the plot. The hospital staff is portrayed as somewhat indifferent to Joanna's amnesia, but this is more for comedic effect than a systemic critique. Overall, institutions are present but not structurally central to the plot's progression.

title: The Principal
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Rick, takes a job as principal at Brandel High, a school explicitly abandoned by the system. The head of security states, "The high school isn't exactly the highest priority for the police around here." He also notes that expulsion is ineffective because "most of the students here have already been expelled from someplace else, permanently." Rick is told, "There's nothing stopping you from bending the law. It's a tradition at Brandel." Rick's actions, such as deputizing teachers as security, demonstrate his need to circumvent established procedures to maintain order.

title: Suspect
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative reveals corruption within the justice system, specifically a fixed case from 1968 involving Judge Lowell and prosecutor Helms, who accepted bribes for political favors. This corruption is exposed by Elizabeth Quinn, a Justice Department clerk, leading to her murder to protect the guilty. The protagonist, Kathleen Riley, actively fights against this corrupt system, facing obstruction and threats, highlighting the systemic failure and the need to circumvent the established order to achieve justice. The film culminates in the exposure of a sitting judge as a murderer, underscoring the deep-seated institutional rot.

title: The Believers
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The film depicts the police force as deeply flawed, with evidence of corruption and incompetence. Lieutenant McTaggert's inability to effectively investigate the child murders, the disappearance of autopsy reports, and the pressure to close the case prematurely all point to systemic issues. Tom Lopez's descent into paranoia and his inability to get help from within the system further highlight the institution's failure. The protagonist, Cal, ultimately has to circumvent the official channels and take matters into his own hands to protect his son, indicating a profound distrust in the ability of institutions to provide justice or safety.

title: Some Kind of Wonderful
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of institutional cynicism. While there are authority figures present, such as teachers and parents, their actions do not drive the plot through corruption or incompetence. For example, Mrs. Albright gives Amanda detention for cutting class, but this is a standard disciplinary action, not an abuse of power. Mr. Sauner lets Amanda off the hook for detention, but this is more of a personal failing than a systemic issue. The school system is portrayed as somewhat ineffective, but not inherently malicious or corrupt.

title: Project X
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays the Air Force as prioritizing potentially inhumane experimentation on animals (chimpanzees) in the name of national security, overriding ethical concerns. The protagonist, Garrett, initially complicit, becomes disillusioned and actively works against the institution, ultimately stealing a plane to free the chimpanzees. Dialogue such as "They radiate the chimps to see how long they can fly before they die" and the Colonel's willingness to cover up the events to avoid a court martial highlight the institution's disregard for ethical boundaries and its self-preservation.

title: The Big Easy
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Remy, is a cop who operates within a corrupt system, accepting 'perks' and bending the law. The assistant district attorney, Anne, investigates police corruption, highlighting a deep mistrust in the police force. Dialogue such as Remy stating, 'If all the codes were enforced in this city, you wouldn't have a single restaurant that could stay open,' and Anne's question, 'Is everything for sale?' demonstrate the pervasive corruption. The climax involves Remy uncovering a heroin-dealing operation run by his superior, Jack, further solidifying the theme of institutional failure and the need to fight against the system.

title: Born in East L.A.
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Rudy, is wrongfully deported despite being a US citizen, highlighting the incompetence and potential for abuse within the immigration system. His attempts to navigate the system are met with bureaucratic indifference and hostility, as exemplified by the border patrol officer who dismisses his claims and mocks his identity. The film depicts law enforcement as actively working against the protagonist, forcing him to circumvent the system through illegal means (coyotes) to return home. The factory owner's repeated exploitation by immigration raids further underscores the systemic failure to protect vulnerable workers.

title: Masters of the Universe
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The Sorceress, the figurehead of order, is captured and imprisoned, rendering her powerless. Skeletor declares the war is over and that those who do not pledge themselves to him shall be destroyed, indicating a complete takeover and corruption of the existing power structure. Man-at-Arms, a high-ranking military figure, is unable to prevent the initial attack, highlighting institutional failure. The police force on Earth is portrayed as ineffective and easily manipulated, as seen when Evil-Lyn uses the Collar of Aldruber to control a police officer.

title: Angel Heart
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative portrays institutions, particularly law enforcement and psychiatric hospitals, as deeply flawed and easily corrupted. Dr. Fowler falsifies records for a bribe, and the police are portrayed as either incompetent or easily manipulated, as seen in their interactions with Angel and their assumptions about the murders. The legal system is also shown as easily bypassed, with characters like Cyphre operating outside its bounds. The protagonist, Harry Angel, must actively circumvent these systems to uncover the truth, highlighting their ineffectiveness and untrustworthiness.

title: Empire of the Sun
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The protagonist, Jamie, is separated from his parents during the Japanese invasion of Shanghai, highlighting the failure of British authorities to protect their citizens. He ends up in a Japanese internment camp, where the existing social order is upended and survival depends on bartering, scavenging, and exploiting the weaknesses of the system. The adults in the camp are shown as flawed and self-serving, further eroding any faith in established structures. Jamie's experiences demonstrate a world where institutions have collapsed, and individuals are left to fend for themselves in a brutal and chaotic environment.

title: Burglar
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme. The narrative features a corrupt cop, Ray, who extorts Bernie for money and a mink coat, leveraging his knowledge of Bernie's past crimes: "I want $20,000 and a mink coat for my wife, and I want you to get it." The police are portrayed as inept and easily manipulated, as seen when Bernie tricks them into raiding the wrong apartment. The legal system is also shown as flawed, with characters like Cynthia Sheldrake able to exploit loopholes and connections to attempt to evade justice. The narrative relies on the failure of law enforcement to maintain order and uphold justice, forcing the protagonist to navigate a world where institutions are unreliable and easily corrupted.

title: Over the Top
justification: Institutional cynicism is a central theme in this film. The protagonist, Hawk, faces legal and social institutions that actively work against him. Jason Cutler, the wealthy grandfather, uses his influence and resources to manipulate the legal system and attempt to bribe Hawk, demonstrating a belief that the system can be bent to his will. The custody battle and the attempts to intimidate Hawk highlight a distrust in the fairness and impartiality of the legal system. The dialogue explicitly shows Cutler's willingness to 'bend the law' to get his way, and the secretary's offer of money to leave the state underscores the corrupting influence of wealth.

title: Benji the Hunted
