justification: The dialogue suggests institutions are manipulative and untrustworthy, particularly through the character Spike, who represents a hellish television network. He says, "Here at Hellvision, We've turned the process of soul acquisition Into an entertainment extravaganza." Also, the police are portrayed as easily fooled and manipulated, as seen in the French Revolution scene.

title: Jurassic Park
justification: Several characters express distrust and contempt for the park's systems and John Hammond's hubris. Malcolm states, "You didn't earn the knowledge for yourselves so you don't take any responsibility for it." and later, "You've never had control! That's the illusion."

title: The Fugitive
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of legal processes. The marshal states, "I don't bargain," indicating a willingness to bend the rules to achieve his goals. Also, the lawyer is asked to "harbor and aid a convicted felon."

title: The Firm
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with legal and governmental institutions. Mitch says, "Wouldn't it be funny if I went to Harvard and you went to jail and we both ended up surrounded by crooks?" and later, "Being a tax lawyer's got nothing to do with the law. It's a game."

title: Sleepless in Seattle
justification: The radio show host is portrayed as somewhat exploitative, pushing Sam to talk about his deceased wife on air. One character expresses distrust in institutions by saying, "It's easier to be killed by a terrorist than it is to get married over 40.", indicating a belief that societal systems are failing.

title: Indecent Proposal
justification: The bank repossesses their property without warning, highlighting a lack of empathy. David expresses distrust, saying, "Don't deal with these people! They sold us out. They'll sell you out, too." This suggests a belief that institutions are self-serving and untrustworthy.

title: Cliffhanger
justification: The FBI suspects an inside job with the Treasury agents. Qualen, a former member of military intelligence, orchestrates a heist, highlighting distrust in government employees. The dialogue reveals a systemic failure where institutions are easily infiltrated and manipulated.

title: Free Willy
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and institutions. Jesse's probation officer, Dwight, is portrayed as jaded and overworked, while the Adventure Park owners are shown to be greedy and exploitative, willing to harm Willy for profit. The characters ultimately bypass the legal system to free Willy, indicating a lack of faith in its ability to protect him.

title: The Pelican Brief
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions. Characters express fear of surveillance ("Are you recording this? Can this call be traced?") and acknowledge corruption at high levels ("The President asked Voyles to back off?"). The FBI is suspected of covering up murders ("The FBI friend was killed yesterday.").

title: Groundhog Day
justification: The protagonist, Phil, expresses frustration and disbelief towards the weather authorities and their predictions. He sarcastically states, "Don't you listen to the weather? I make the weather," and later questions the reliability of long-distance lines and satellite communication, implying a distrust in the system's functionality.

title: Dave
justification: Characters scheme to manipulate the President and the First Lady. They orchestrate events and lie to the public. The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and manipulation of the political system for personal gain.

title: Rising Sun
justification: Characters express distrust and navigate around formal systems. Dialogue such as, "Absolutely, Chief. By the book. Absolutely. But everything was not absolutely by the book. Absolutely not," and "We're cops. Why the fuck are we running? We're not running. We're eluding," shows a need to bypass the rules.

title: Cool Runnings
justification: The coach, Irv Blitzer, is revealed to have cheated in the past, leading to his disgrace. The Olympic committee changes the qualifying rules specifically to exclude the Jamaican team, showing bias and distrust. Despite qualifying, they are initially disqualified due to a policy change, highlighting the arbitrary nature of the institution.

title: The Crying Game
justification: The dialogue suggests a distrust of authority and a sense that the characters are operating outside the bounds of the law. Fergus is tasked with killing Jody, and Jude seems to be manipulating Fergus. The line, "You're never out, Fergus," implies a lack of agency and a forced involvement in illegal activities.

title: Rookie of the Year
justification: The team owner is willing to sell a child to another team for money. The manager says, "I make the decisions!" and "He's my client!" showing a disregard for the child's well-being.

title: The Three Musketeers
justification: The Cardinal is portrayed as manipulative and power-hungry, willing to betray the King for his own ambition. The Musketeers are disbanded, suggesting a distrust in the formal military structure. Characters frequently bypass or defy authority, indicating a systemic failure of trust in institutions.

title: Dennis the Menace
justification: The police are only briefly present, and the main interaction with them is the thief's comment: "You can tell everybody at the big house you met our Dennis Mitchell." This implies a lack of respect for the law. The mother's work situation is also portrayed negatively, with her boss being unsympathetic to her childcare needs.

title: Demolition Man
justification: The dialogue reveals a society where freedoms are suppressed, and institutions like the police are seen as tools of control. Spartan's repeated fines for 'verbal-morality statute' violations and his disgust at the lack of toilet paper highlight the absurdity of the system. The revelation that Phoenix was secretly enhanced, not rehabilitated, underscores the corruption within Cocteau Industries.

title: Sommersby
justification: The Knights of the White Camellia represent a rogue, lawless element acting outside and against the formal justice system. The dialogue, "We are God's hand and He is our eyes...and we are His vengeance!" shows a distrust of the legal system. Also, the teacher says, "You are the liar! The real reason you are here is...to stop me from selling land to a colored man...who'd then be a landowner on a level with yourself."

title: The Nightmare Before Christmas
justification: The Mayor is portrayed as incompetent, stating, "I'm only an elected official here. I can't make decisions by myself." The police are also portrayed as ineffective, as they are confused by the strange toys and unable to stop Jack's actions.

title: Sister Act 2 Back in the Habit
justification: The movie portrays the Catholic school system as financially unstable and more concerned with property value than the students' well-being. Dialogue like "It's more valuable as a parking lot than a school" and "We're lucky to be open at all" shows a lack of institutional support and a focus on closure rather than solutions. The nuns must circumvent the administration to save the school, indicating a distrust in the formal system's ability to prioritize the students' needs.

title: Made In America
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. The mother's experience with the sperm bank highlights incompetence and potential corruption: "I distinctly asked for a black man." and "Why? Why do all complaints have to come in writing? It's obvious to me you people can't read."

title: The Good Son
justification: The therapist, Alice Davenport, is portrayed as ineffective, as Mark says, "She just thinks I'm some screwed-up little kid." Wallace and Susan also dismiss Mark's warnings about Henry, showing a failure to protect him and Connie.

title: Beethoven's 2nd
justification: Regina uses the court system to get the dog in the divorce settlement, not out of love for the dog, but to extort money from George. She says, "It's about alimony. And since I got the court order, the dog stays with me...until we negotiate our little divorce."

title: Addams Family Values
justification: Gomez is denied justice by the police when he reports his brother's situation: "I demand justice!"..."Denied!". The police are portrayed as dismissive and unhelpful, even threatening Gomez with arrest: "Don't make me call Ringling Brothers."

title: Wayne’s World 2
justification: The characters need to fill out 'the application for authorisation, approval from the guilds and unions' to get a permit for Waynestock. Wayne sarcastically says, 'We would love to put on a rock concert... not!' when asked about the permit.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. Walker manipulates the Daimio for profit, and the turtles frequently bypass or mock authority figures, like when Raphael says, "Fighting's for grown-ups and that's only if you got no other choice. You guys are kids."

title: Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the pound, with Chance stating, "The pound is where humans lock you up when they don't want you anymore." Later, despite the police finding them, Chance still fears the authorities, saying, "They took us to the pound! I told you!"

title: Falling Down
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police and government. The protagonist bypasses the police to take matters into his own hands, and the police are portrayed as incompetent and uncaring: "We don't appreciate you interfering with our investigation." and "Next time there's a proposition...to cut the number of patrol cars on the street, vote no, okay?"

title: Hocus Pocus
justification: The police officer dismisses Max's warning about the witches, saying "They thought I was a real cop." This shows a lack of belief in authority. The officer is more concerned with being mocked than protecting the community.

title: What's Love Got to Do With It
justification: The dialogue shows Ike bypassing medical advice to force Tina to perform, highlighting a disregard for professional expertise. Additionally, Ike's repeated offenses and lack of legal consequences suggest a failure of the justice system to protect Tina. Finally, the mother's advice to "keep him happy" normalizes abuse and discourages seeking help from external authorities.

title: Hot Shots! Part Deux
justification: Several lines indicate distrust or incompetence within the government and military. The President's advisors are concerned about him appearing incompetent, and the CIA is worried about another failure. The President himself seems detached and out of touch.

title: The Beverly Hillbillies
justification: The Beverly Hills police are easily manipulated by Drysdale to incarcerate Granny. Drysdale uses the police to protect his reputation, showing a distrust of the law as a fair system: "We want the wheels of justice to spin quickly...before our client finds out what happened."

title: Alive
justification: The mechanic states, "The batteries are in the tail, and the tails gone!" when asked about the radio. Later, when asked about emergency supplies, he replies, "No. Nothing like that." These lines suggest a lack of preparedness and a failure of the institution to provide necessary resources.

title: Sliver
justification: The doormen are described as only being around when they want tips, and the police are portrayed as slow to investigate and easily manipulated. Vida says, "Damn doormen. I really tip them well too. Everybody does. That's why they're never around when you need them."

title: Robin Hood: Men in Tights
justification: Prince John is portrayed as an illegitimate ruler who abuses his power through unjust taxes. Robin Hood actively resists the Sheriff of Rottingham and Prince John's authority, viewing them as obstacles to justice. The dialogue highlights a distrust of the legal system and a need for rogue action.

title: Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story
justification: Several characters express distrust and negative experiences with American institutions. The history teacher's anecdote about Chinese railroad workers and the gym owner's prejudice highlight systemic racism. Bruce's final speech about being seen as "just another gook" in America further emphasizes this cynicism.

title: Carlito’s Way
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Kleinfeld is a lawyer who is deeply corrupt and involved in criminal activity, and Lalin is working as an informant for the D.A. to avoid prison.

title: The Joy Luck Club
justification: The dialogue shows arranged marriages and a mother-in-law who is displeased with her daughter-in-law's inability to produce grandsons. The matchmaker admits mistakes happen in Heaven, suggesting a lack of accountability.

title: The Sandlot
justification: The police are mentioned in a negative light when the character Squints says, "My grandpa, Squidman Palledorous, was police chief back then. And he ordered Mr. Mertle to turn his backyard into a fortress and chain up The Beast and put him under the house, where he could never get out to eat children and stuff." This shows the police are viewed as an obstacle to the character's goals.

title: The Age of Innocence
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of societal norms and expectations, particularly regarding marriage and divorce. Characters express a desire to bypass or subvert these expectations, indicating a level of cynicism towards the established order: "Our legislation favors divorce, but our social customs don't."

title: Hard Target
justification: The police detective is initially dismissive of Natasha's missing person report, stating, "Well, generally, in order to be considered missing, you need somewhere to be missing from." Later, Detective Mitchell is helpful, but Dr. Morton assists in covering up the murders, showing corruption within the system.

title: Cop and ½
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust in the system. Devon has to cut a deal to get the police to do their job, and the police are willing to let a child ride along and put him in danger. The line, "Ever hear of 'quid pro quo'? One hand washes the other? Why don't you get me some soap?" shows the transactional nature of justice.

title: The Secret Garden
justification: The dialogue indicates a distrust of authority figures, particularly Mrs. Medlock, who is portrayed as controlling and dismissive. Mary states, "It's revolting how these people behave toward me," showing a negative perception of the adults in charge. Additionally, the uncle's neglect and the staff's fear of him suggest a dysfunctional power dynamic.

title: Point of No Return
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of authority and a willingness to bypass or subvert the system. Characters like Bob manipulate Maggie, and the government uses her as a tool. Maggie herself expresses cynicism, saying, "Everything's fucked!"

title: Grumpy Old Men
justification: Ariel says, "Taking mail is a federal offense." John replies, "I know." This shows a flippant attitude toward the law. Also, Elliot Snyder from the IRS is portrayed as a nuisance.

title: Poetic Justice
justification: The characters are engaging in illegal activities such as drug use and mail truck theft. There is a general disregard for the law, but no specific dialogue criticizing institutions. The characters are more focused on personal relationships and survival.

title: A Perfect World
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement willing to bend rules and prioritize outcomes over procedure. Red states, "In Texas, the bottom line is who you know and what they owe you," indicating a corrupt system. Additionally, Red admits to manipulating the juvenile justice system, highlighting a distrust in the fairness of legal institutions.

title: Son in Law
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for authority figures, particularly parents. Rebecca refers to her mother as "Connie" and dismisses her concerns. Zack is disrespectful to his father, and the parents are portrayed as out of touch and ineffective.

title: My Life
justification: The main character, Bob, expresses distrust and frustration with medical institutions, particularly after receiving a grim prognosis. He questions the doctor's authority and seeks alternative treatments outside of conventional medicine. This indicates a mild distrust in the established medical system.

title: The Man Without a Face
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for institutions. Catherine says she hates the idea of her son "becoming one of those brush-cut flyboys," implying a negative view of the military. Charles's essay title, "Why the system must be changed now!" also indicates a critical stance toward established systems.

title: The Adventures of Huck Finn
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the law and a willingness to bypass it. Characters are willing to steal, lie, and even consider violence to achieve their goals, indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to deliver justice or fairness. Jim's fear of being caught and sold back into slavery highlights the perceived injustice of the legal system.

title: Rudy
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the admissions process at Notre Dame, viewing it as biased towards certain types of students. Rudy encounters skepticism and discouragement from authority figures like Father Cavanaugh and Coach Parseghian, who initially dismiss his aspirations due to his background and academic record: "Notre Dame is for rich kids...smart kids...great athletes. It's not for us."

title: Guilty as Sin
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system. Characters express skepticism towards lawyers, viewing them as machines focused on winning rather than justice. The judge forces the lawyer to continue representing a client, despite the lawyer's objections and safety concerns.

title: Nowhere to Run
justification: The dialogue shows the land developer using corrupt tactics to force Clydie to sell her land, including threats and violence. The police are portrayed as being in the pocket of the developer, as evidenced by Lonnie's actions and Dunston's past. Sam, the protagonist, is an escaped convict who is distrustful of the legal system.

title: Super Mario Bros.
justification: The dialogue shows the police arresting people for being plumbers and the government is run by a corrupt dinosaur. Characters frequently bypass or undermine the established order. "Are you tellin' us that you can arrest a guy for bein' a plumber? Get outta here!"

title: Another Stakeout
justification: The detectives bypass standard procedure by leaving bugging equipment behind: "We could leave the bugging equipment and recorder...I suppose. Of course, we could write down what they say." This shows a willingness to bend the rules for convenience. The line "This assignment gets blown, it's not my butt, it's Archie's butt" also shows a lack of concern for the consequences of their actions.

title: Fire in the Sky
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in law enforcement's ability to find the truth, with characters questioning the investigation's fairness. Dallis expresses distrust in lie detectors, suggesting they can be manipulated or misinterpreted: "I think those devices are very dangerous, man."

title: Untamed Heart
justification: The dialogue includes a scene where a customer steals a quarter from a cigarette machine, and the waitress, Caroline, confronts him. She says, "It happens to be a very good investment once it's all paid off," indicating a belief in the system, but also the need to defend it against those who would exploit it. The overall tone is not overtly cynical, but there is a sense that one must be vigilant to protect their interests.

title: Born Yesterday
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of government and legal systems. Harry states, "I am the law," indicating a belief that he is above the rules. Billie's comment, "I don't wanna do anything that's against the law. That's for sure," followed by Harry's response, suggests that his actions are often legally questionable.

title: CB4
justification: The film portrays record company executives as exploitative and untrustworthy, exemplified by the line, "All these record company punks is a bunch of bitches." Additionally, the police are shown arresting the group for indecency during a performance, suggesting an overreach of authority and censorship.

title: A Bronx Tale
justification: The priest seems more concerned with the legal implications of a murder confession than with spiritual guidance. Sonny's philosophy is that "nobody cares" and that institutions like Mickey Mantle won't help you, so you shouldn't care about them.

title: Sidekicks
justification: Some characters display a lack of respect for authority figures, such as when Barry's dad jokes about what he would do to Mr. Horn. Also, the karate instructor, Mr. Stone, is portrayed as a fraud and a blowhard. Finally, the gym teacher, Mr. Horn, is portrayed as mean and insensitive.

title: Geronimo: An American Legend
justification: The dialogue expresses deep distrust of the "White-Eye" (government/settlers), accusing them of lies and land theft. Phrases like "Don't trust the White-Eye. With them there is no right way" and "Everything they said to me was a lie" highlight this cynicism.

title: Heart and Souls
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of institutions, but it's not a central theme. One character mentions bankruptcy hearings and creditors pushing for liquidation, suggesting a potentially adversarial relationship with financial institutions and the legal system. Another character expresses frustration with parking tickets and the police, indicating a minor level of cynicism towards law enforcement.

title: In the Name of the Father
justification: The dialogue is filled with accusations of police brutality, fabricated evidence, and a justice system that seems determined to convict innocent people. Gerry states, "They beat me...and then they threatened to kill my father. I'd have fucking signed anything after that," highlighting the extreme distrust and fear of the authorities.

title: Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as easily manipulated and somewhat incompetent ('I will straighten everything out. Randy, what am I gonna do?'). The bounty hunter, Duke, distrusts the police and operates outside the law, highlighting a systemic failure to deal with the threat effectively ('Those FBI idiots destroyed Jason's body so now he needs a new one.').

title: Indian Summer
justification: Lou admits to kicking a black counselor out of camp because he wouldn't "fit in." Jack got kicked out for protesting this action. This shows a distrust of Lou's authority and the camp's policies.

title: Body of Evidence
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the legal system. Characters manipulate evidence, lie under oath, and engage in blackmail. The lawyer, Frank, seems to be the only one trying to uphold the law, but even he is willing to bend the rules to win the case.

title: The Crush
justification: The police arrest Nick based on Adrian's false accusations, highlighting a distrust in the justice system's ability to discern truth. Michael, Nick's boss, prioritizes a sensational story over Nick's well-being, showing a disregard for ethical journalistic practices: "The editors haven't touched it. The article's fine as it stands."

title: Used People
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, particularly regarding mental health. One character says, "Do you really think I would let you rub your dirty little hands all over my son's brain?" Another character is seeing a psychiatrist behind their mother's back.

title: Man's Best Friend
justification: The dialogue shows the police being unhelpful and dismissive of the scientist's concerns about a dangerous animal. The scientist says, "This bullshit is not gonna do anything. What we gotta do is go out there and rescue my dog," indicating a lack of faith in the police's ability to help.

title: A Far Off Place
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with local figures of authority. Adams complains about Murray, the mechanic, and his work ethic: "Murray's not the sharpest tool in the shed...he does nothing but bitch and complain about his workload." This suggests a general dissatisfaction with the competence and reliability of local institutions.

title: Weekend at Bernie's II
justification: The characters repeatedly break the law (forgery, breaking and entering, stealing a body) and express distrust in the legal system. Dialogue like "We'll never break the law again" said sarcastically to an officer and "Someday they'll catch up to us" shows a disregard for the law.

title: Undercover Blues
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. For example, the police captain tells Sawyer to investigate Blue, but Sawyer goes behind his back to the FBI. Also, Blue mentions he blackmailed the guy at the FBI.

title: Forrest Gump
justification: Lieutenant Dan states he is "living off the government tit. Sucking it dry!" when asked what he does for a living in New York. He also says, "God is listening? What a crock of shit," showing his distrust in religious institutions.

title: The Lion King
justification: Scar manipulates Simba and the hyenas, leading to Mufasa's death and his own rise to power. Scar's reign is marked by mismanagement and disregard for the well-being of the Pride Lands, as evidenced by the lionesses' complaints: 'Scar, there is no food. The herds have moved on.'

title: True Lies
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, with characters bypassing or manipulating them for personal gain. Harry's double life as a spy and Helen's recruitment highlight the exploitation of individuals by government agencies. The casual disregard for legal boundaries, such as unauthorized wiretaps, further emphasizes the cynical view of authority.

title: The Santa Clause
justification: The main character is initially skeptical of the Santa Claus legend and the 'Santa Clause' contract. He expresses disbelief and resists accepting the responsibilities associated with becoming Santa, indicating a distrust of the imposed role. He says, "I'm just gonna call the police. I’ll carry this stuff up there. Let them deal with it, okay?”

title: The Flintstones
justification: Fred and Barney express distrust in the company's management, with Fred stating, "Cooped up inside some swank office all day, kissing the big shot's feet. Not Fred Flintstone." Later, Fred is framed for embezzlement by company executives, highlighting corruption within the institution.

title: Clear and Present Danger
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dialogue such as "They're stealing my money!" and "You lied under oath..." demonstrates a breakdown in trust and highlights corruption within the system.

title: Speed
justification: The bomber is a disgruntled ex-cop seeking revenge for being dismissed and feeling unappreciated. He states, "I got a medal, too, Jack, a medal and a pink slip and a 'sorry about your hand'." This shows a deep distrust and resentment towards the police institution.

title: Maverick
justification: The dialogue shows a lawman, Coop, who is willing to bend the rules and accept bribes: "THE COURTS ARE OVERWORKED. I'LL GIVE YOU A BREAK." Also, the characters often bypass the law and take matters into their own hands.

title: Interview with the Vampire
justification: The dialogue contains no explicit distrust of formal systems. However, the characters operate outside societal norms, suggesting a disregard for conventional institutions. For example, the vampire says, "God kills indiscriminately...and so shall we."

title: The Client
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement officials manipulating a child, withholding his rights, and invading his privacy. The lawyer states, "You attempted to interrogate a child...outside the presence of his mother and without her consent. He asked you if he needed a lawyer and you said no...stating as one of your reasons that lawyers are a pain in the ass."

title: Schindler’s List
justification: Characters express distrust and fear of the Nazi regime and its arbitrary power. Dialogue such as "Your government is in the wrong country!" and "The more you see of the Herr Kommandant, the more you see there is no set rules that you can live by" demonstrates a complete lack of faith in the system.

title: Philadelphia
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and accusations of corruption within the legal system and workplace. Characters express concerns about discrimination, concealed illnesses, and sabotaged files, indicating a systemic failure of trust and fairness. Joe says, "These people make me sick. But a law's been broken."

title: Ace Ventura: Pet Detective
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and authority figures. Ace bypasses police procedure, and the police are portrayed as incompetent, focusing on the wrong leads and dismissing Ace's insights. Einhorn manipulates the police force for personal revenge.

title: Star Trek: Generations
justification: While Starfleet is generally portrayed positively, there are hints of distrust. Riker questions contacting Starfleet Command, and Picard overrides protocol to investigate Soran immediately: "You want me to contact Starfleet? Is there a problem?"

title: Stargate
justification: O'Neil is reactivated against his will and is clearly a 'mess'. The military is portrayed as secretive and manipulative, using Jackson's research for their own purposes without full disclosure. O'Neil was ordered to blow up the Stargate if he found any possible danger.

title: Dumb & Dumber
justification: The police officer is portrayed as corrupt, drinking the alcohol he confiscated. The kidnapping plot also suggests a distrust of authorities, as the family initially avoids involving them.

title: Pulp Fiction
justification: Marsellus uses violence to enforce his own rules, bypassing any legal system. Butch defies Marsellus's orders and escapes, showing a lack of respect for authority. The dialogue suggests a world where personal power and violence are more effective than legal recourse.

title: The Specialist
justification: Several characters express distrust in the law and police. May says, "Go to court, use the law. The law's been bought. Use a bullet." Also, Joe León bribes the Chief of Police to get what he wants.

title: Four Weddings and a Funeral
justification: The vicar makes mistakes during the wedding ceremony, calling the Holy Spirit the 'Holy Goat'. This suggests incompetence. Also, the characters are frequently drunk at the wedding, suggesting a lack of respect for the institution of marriage.

title: The Little Rascals
justification: The kids are denied a loan because they are kids. The bank teller says, "You can't treat people this way, mister." The banker replies, "You're not people. You're kids."

title: Disclosure
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the company's HR and legal processes, with characters believing the system is rigged against them. Tom says, "She set me up," and later, "The legal system is supposed to protect people like me," indicating a belief that institutions are not fair or helpful.

title: The Crow
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and ineffectiveness: "Department of Housing! Code violations? Safety hazards? Place looks fine to me." and "You're a beat cop now, so be a beat cop." The characters frequently bypass or mock the law.

title: Angels in the Outfield
justification: The manager, George Knox, is portrayed as someone who bends the rules and relies on unconventional methods (angels) rather than trusting the system. He is eventually fired for his beliefs. The dialogue, "You're telling me, there's real angels in the ballpark?" and the subsequent firing suggest a distrust of authority and a reliance on outside forces.

title: When a Man Loves a Woman
justification: The counselor at the rehab center seems dismissive and bureaucratic, focusing on rules rather than Alice's immediate needs: "I just want to make a phone call." "Two more days, hon. You can do this." The police are not present, but the mention of an "armed robber" being around the children is a sign of societal breakdown.

title: D2: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The coach prioritizes sponsors over team colors, saying, "It's business stuff, Charlie. Don't worry about it." Later, the team faces unfair treatment in stores due to being unsupervised children, highlighting societal biases.

title: Timecop
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Lyle says McComb "already owns most of the guys we work with!" and Max states, "He killed my agency."

title: City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly’s Gold
justification: The characters are mostly focused on personal relationships and treasure hunting, with only a few instances of distrust towards external systems. One character lies to his wife about his activities, indicating a lack of faith in her understanding or acceptance: "What was I going to do, tell her the truth? That I'm jeopardizing my career to rent burros and go hunting for buried treasure? I'm sure she'd be real supportive."

title: Beverly Hills Cop III
justification: Axel consistently disregards jurisdictional boundaries and police procedure, indicating a lack of respect for the system. He openly mocks the Beverly Hills police and their adherence to rules, and he manipulates situations to his advantage, showing a belief that the system is ineffective or easily bypassed. The fact that DeWald, a respected figure, is corrupt further reinforces the idea of institutional failure.

title: On Deadly Ground
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Hugh Palmer states he's "rolled over for you bastards long enough," indicating prior corruption. Jennings orchestrates sabotage and covers up environmental damage, showing a disregard for regulations.

title: It Could Happen To You
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with authority. A cop is dismissive of a citizen's concerns ("What's with this cop? He's got nothing better to do than write tickets? With all the crime in this city?"), and another character states, "She'd work if she was dead!" about a Korean shop owner's wife, implying a distrust of his explanation and a general cynicism towards people's honesty.

title: The Paper
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the police and the justice system. Marty says her friend at the Justice Department "hates me now," and later, "I couldn't get anything out of Justice." Henry says, "All cops wanna talk. They just don't know they wanna talk."

title: Junior
justification: The university claims ownership of the baby, seeing it as "university property." Dr. Hesse is forcibly taken to an ambulance. The characters must go into hiding to escape the institution.

title: I Love Trouble
justification: The dialogue shows reporters bypassing official channels and using informal contacts to get information.  There's a general distrust of authority and a willingness to bend the rules to get the story.  The reporters are willing to lie and deceive to get the information they need.

title: Major League II
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and circumvention of the law. Rick mentions his cousin dating a judge who helped him avoid legal consequences after a high-speed chase. The owner Roger Dorn is portrayed as prioritizing profit over the team's well-being, indicating a cynical view of institutional priorities.

title: Blank Check
justification: The film portrays the police as incompetent, as seen when Biderman's henchmen run over a child's bicycle in a park while chasing Preston. Additionally, the realtor is portrayed as a crook, as evidenced by the line, "Are you Realtors just a bunch of crooks? Is that it?"

title: Blown Away
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and government. Jimmy says, "You do that and you'll end up behind bars!" and Max says, "Don't know what this city's comin' to. Bad as bloody Belfast."

title: A Low Down Dirty Shame
justification: The dialogue shows a blatant disregard for legal procedures and a reliance on personal favors. Shame asks Eddie for a file without proper paperwork, and Eddie agrees, highlighting a corrupt system where favors and personal connections outweigh official processes. Additionally, the lieutenant's dismissive attitude towards Shame's investigation and his willingness to let him go despite being a suspect further exemplifies the ineffectiveness and potential corruption within law enforcement.

title: My Father the Hero
justification: The beach security guard is portrayed as somewhat officious and condescending. Niki's father is portrayed as having been in prison. Niki lies to impress Ben, indicating a distrust of authority.

title: Wyatt Earp
justification: Several instances show distrust: the deputy who won't risk his life because "they don't pay me enough to commit suicide," and the town marshal who was fired for being "too much of a hard-ass." Also, Curly Bill's line, "There ain't an honest cowboy can get a fair shake in this town," shows distrust in the legal system.

title: Ri¢hie Ri¢h
justification: The police arrest Cadbury based on planted evidence, showcasing corruption within the legal system. Richie is essentially imprisoned in his own home by Van Dough, who exploits legal loopholes to control him. The dialogue highlights a distrust of authority and the manipulation of institutions for personal gain.

title: Blue Chips
justification: Characters frequently discuss bending or breaking rules to achieve their goals, particularly in the context of college athletics. For example, Mrs. Mcrae states, "A foul is not a foul unless the referee blows his whistle," indicating a belief that rules are only enforced when authorities choose to do so. Additionally, the dialogue reveals a system where "friends of the program" provide illicit benefits to athletes, highlighting corruption within the university.

title: Street Fighter
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Guile disobeys orders: "Our superiors say the war is canceled...Well, I'm not going home." There are also complaints about corruption: "Bison is getting paid off for his crimes, and our friends who have died here...will have died for nothing."

title: The Air Up There
justification: The film portrays the main character as willing to bend the rules and bribe officials to get what he wants. The tribal chief distrusts outsiders, and the community is threatened by a corrupt businessman who exploits legal loopholes and violence to seize their land. The army commander is also implied to be corrupt, as he is willing to oversee the bet between the tribe and the businessman.

title: Intersection
justification: The dialogue contains some complaints about bureaucracy and the need to bypass formal channels. For example, one character says, "Please sign off these specs for the tenly project. They're going crazy," indicating frustration with bureaucratic processes. Another character mentions, "I had dad call him. They went to school together," suggesting leveraging personal connections to expedite things.

title: Iron Will
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete rejection of institutions. Will Stoneman expresses distrust towards the race organizers, saying "I know what you're doing, Mr Harper, and I don't like it." However, this is more about personal fairness than a systemic critique.

title: Little Women
justification: Amy expresses a negative view of her school, saying she's "degradatated" and that if you don't bring limes, "you might as well be dead." Marmee also says the school is appalling and that Mr. Davis said it was as useful to educate a woman as to educate a female cat.

title: With Honors
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of government systems. Wilder expresses disdain for the government and the Constitution, viewing them as flawed and untrustworthy. He also mocks the Social Security system and expresses skepticism towards authority figures, highlighting a cynical perspective on formal institutions.

title: Only You
justification: The airport security guard enforces "strict rules" despite a woman's desperate plea, showing a lack of flexibility. Later, when Faith asks for help finding Damon, the hotel clerk says, "We don't usually follow our guests," indicating a lack of willingness to assist beyond basic service.

title: Color of Night
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police and legal system. The cop, Hector, is portrayed as aggressive and potentially corrupt, and the protagonist expresses frustration with the police's lack of progress in the murder investigation: "Just like a cop! You're never there when you need one!"

title: 8 Seconds
justification: The dialogue contains no distrust of formal systems. The characters are focused on rodeo and personal relationships, not institutions. One character states, "People hurt you a lot sooner" which could be interpreted as a distrust of people, but not necessarily institutions.

title: House Party 3
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority figures and institutions. Uncle Vester advises Kid to disregard others' opinions, saying, "If people don't like you if you're being yourself, fuck them!" and the music industry is portrayed as exploitative, with characters focused on "getting paid big-time."

title: Sugar Hill
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the legal system and police. Characters frequently discuss illegal activities and taking the law into their own hands. "Harry will take care of the precinct" suggests police corruption.

title: The Professional
justification: The DEA agents are portrayed as brutal and corrupt, willing to kill children and cover up their crimes. Stansfield's line, "Death is whimsical today," shows a callous disregard for human life. The police are also shown to be easily bribed and manipulated.

title: Milk Money
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of law enforcement and a sense that individuals must operate outside the system to survive. V is a prostitute evading dangerous criminals and the police. Cash states, "Waltzer steals from Jerry, I steal from Waltzer. They think that this is their turf, but they're wrong. This all belongs to me. I'm the man."

title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare
justification: The police are dismissive of Heather's concerns about her son, and the doctors are quick to suggest mental instability and foster care. Heather must take matters into her own hands to protect Dylan, indicating a distrust of the system's ability to help.

title: Miracle on 34th Street
justification: The prosecutor, Mr. Collins, seems to be using his position to further a personal agenda, as suggested by his conversation with the judge. The judge also seems to be swayed by external influence, hinting at corruption within the legal system: "Money makes the world go around, eddie."

title: Lightning Jack
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of law enforcement and government. Characters frequently bypass or undermine the law, such as the sheriff being easily fooled and the open bribery of officials. The line, "A posse will never cross the county line," shows the limits of the law.

title: Blink
justification: The dialogue shows detectives dismissing Emma's testimony due to her vision, and generally acting unprofessionally. One detective says, "Crazy people, that's what you're talking about. Lonely people, people who like attention." Another detective is sleeping with the witness.

title: Baby’s Day Out
justification: The FBI agent admits he can't possibly understand the mother's feelings, highlighting a disconnect. The police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent, struggling to find the baby and relying on tips from the public. The kidnappers easily evade law enforcement, showcasing a lack of institutional effectiveness.

title: My Girl 2
justification: The father figure expresses distrust of strangers in Los Angeles, warning Vada about corrupt people and potential dangers like pregnancy and drugs. He also mentions the possibility of being beaten to an unrecognizable pulp by a surfer, highlighting a cynical view of the city's inhabitants and potential for violence.

title: The War
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government assistance ("Food stamps? God bless America. They... They give you a handout before they give you a job.") and the legal system's ability to provide justice or opportunity ("Law says you can't work for the city or state...if you've spent time in a mental hospital or corrective institution."). Characters express frustration with systemic barriers and perceived unfairness.

title: Terminal Velocity
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. Ditch's disregard for FAA regulations and the deputy district attorney's ineffectiveness highlight a systemic failure. The dialogue, such as the discussion about the F.A.A. violations and the deputy's inability to handle the situation, supports this.

title: The Shawshank Redemption
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the government and law. Andy says, "I had to come to prison to be a crook," and Red states, "Hope is a dangerous thing. Hope can drive a man insane. It's got no use on the inside."

title: Monkey Trouble
justification: A shopkeeper accuses Eva of shoplifting and threatens to call her father, showing a distrust of teenagers. The shopkeeper also mentions knowing her father and his charge account, implying a potential abuse of power or social standing. The dialogue doesn't indicate systemic corruption, but rather individual distrust and potential misuse of authority.

title: Above the Rim
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures. Kyle says, "It's not like anybody else had a good game," showing a lack of team responsibility. He also says, "This is my gym, man, and they called a bullshit foul," indicating a belief that the system is unfair and biased.

title: The Getaway
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement. Characters are constantly bypassing or evading the police, and there's a general sense that the legal system is an obstacle rather than a source of justice, as evidenced by Doc's prison escape and subsequent criminal activities.

title: No Escape
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and formal systems. Characters are prisoners in a corrupt system run by a warden who manipulates them, and the 'father' figure admits the prison authorities keep the place classified so the public wouldn't allow it if they knew.

title: Speechless
justification: The dialogue reveals a cynical view of politics, with characters acknowledging lying and manipulation as common tactics. Julia says, "The people who do anything to win, do anything to keep on winning," and Kevin admits to using the "Teleprompter" for political gain, highlighting a distrust of the political process.

title: Bad Girls
justification: The Pinkerton detectives are portrayed as easily bribed and more interested in rewards than justice. The lawyer states the law doesn't include the women, implying systemic bias. The marshal deputizes a random person and then abandons them.

title: Threesome
justification: The dialogue focuses on interpersonal relationships and personal experiences, with no mention of institutions. The characters are concerned with their own lives and relationships, not with the failures or corruption of any formal systems.

title: Toy Story
justification: The toys distrust Sid, who represents a failure of parental authority. They see him as a torturer, and Woody says, "He tortures toys, just for fun!" The toys must band together to save themselves.

title: Pocahontas
justification: Ratcliffe is portrayed as greedy and uncaring, focused only on gold and power, shown by his song "Mine, Mine, Mine" and his willingness to attack the natives for personal gain. Smith expresses doubt about the mission, questioning the need to fight the natives, but Ratcliffe dismisses his concerns and insists on violence. The men also express some cynicism, questioning the lack of gold and food while Ratcliffe lives comfortably.

title: Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls
justification: The consulate general is portrayed as corrupt, exploiting native tribes for guano. Ace says, "You can't legally take possession of the caves as long as the Wachatis inhabit the area, and you want that dookie so bad, you can taste it."

title: Die Hard: With a Vengeance
justification: The dialogue shows police requisitioning civilian vehicles and disregarding traffic laws, indicating a disregard for rules. The constant radio jamming and communication failures within the police force further highlight institutional incompetence. McClane's rogue actions and distrust of the FBI also contribute to the theme.

title: Goldeneye
justification: Several characters express distrust and contempt for institutions. Bond mocks the motor vehicles department, and M criticizes political analysts. Trevelyan's motive is based on the British government's betrayal of his parents.

title: Crimson Tide
justification: The Executive Officer (X.O.) questions the captain's authority and decisions, leading to a mutiny due to distrust in the captain's judgment regarding nuclear launch protocols. The X.O. states, "You know as well as I do that any launch order received without authentication is no order at all," showing a distrust of the chain of command without verification. The crew is divided, showing a breakdown in the unified chain of command.

title: Waterworld
justification: Characters frequently distrust authority. Mariner is constantly breaking rules and laws, and the Deacon is a corrupt leader who uses religion to control his followers: "Citizens of the good ship. Please now, hear me speak. I’ve had a vision." and "I promised them results, and l’ll get ’em if I gotta cut ’em out of her goddamn back."

title: Dangerous Minds
justification: The principal is portrayed as out-of-touch and more concerned with policy than student needs. Emilio expresses distrust towards the Board of Education, saying, "Since when has the Board of Education done anything for us, huh? Yeah, man, we fuckin' barely get lunch." The school system is also shown to be failing the students, with a lack of basic supplies like Xerox paper.

title: While You Were Sleeping
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. Saul mentions that Ox "fudged it over" to become Peter's godfather by donating 50 folding chairs to Father Shea's bingo night, suggesting a minor bending of rules or influence within the church.

title: Congo
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government and corporations. Monroe states, "I run a few guns, you sons of bitches ruin the world." Karen Ross, when asked why she left the CIA, replies, "Because they're a loveless bunch of sons of bitches."

title: The Bridges of Madison County
justification: Francesca expresses some dissatisfaction with her life in Iowa, despite acknowledging the niceness of the people and the community support. She says, "It's not what I dreamed of... as a girl." This suggests a mild disillusionment with the conventional life she has built.

title: Nine Months
justification: The initial doctor is out with pneumonia, and his replacement is a nervous Russian doctor who used to experiment on rats. Rebecca says, "That lunatic is not delivering me." This shows a lack of trust in the medical system.

title: Get Shorty
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. Harry hires Chili to handle problems outside legal channels, and Ray Bones openly flaunts the law. 'I'm not going to pop her, okay? It was just a thought.'

title: Outbreak
justification: Multiple characters express distrust and frustration with the government and military. Daniels disobeys orders, saying, "Fuck the charter. It's not about a charter. People are dying. It's about being a doctor!" and later accuses his superior of prioritizing the weaponization of the virus over saving lives.

title: Legends of the Fall
justification: Several lines show distrust of government. For example, Colonel Ludlow says, "Congress is government, sir. I worked for the government once," and later, "I've seen nothing in its behavior since then that would persuade me...it has gained either in wisdom, common sense or humanity."

title: Bad Boys
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust. Characters bypass legal channels, with lines like "Screw you, that's illegal" and "All his files are blocked...unblock it."

title: The Living Sea
justification: The documentary focuses on the beauty and importance of the ocean, and the efforts of scientists and conservationists to protect it. There is no dialogue that expresses distrust or cynicism towards institutions. The U.S. Coast Guard is shown performing rescues.

title: Species
justification: The team tracking Sil must bypass official channels to hunt her down, such as stopping trains. Fitch prioritizes 'protocol' over saving his team, leading to their deaths. Lennox states he is a 'freelance solution to our government's problems,' implying distrust in formal systems.

title: Jumanji
justification: The police officer, Carl, is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Alan distracts him. Additionally, Alan's father uses his wealth to avoid legal consequences for Alan's actions, suggesting a distrust in the justice system: "Just because you're a Parrish doesn't mean you can hang around my girlfriend."

title: Babe
justification: The duck, Ferdinand, expresses distrust in the farm's rules, seeing them as obstacles to his survival: "It's against the rules... but this is bigger than rules. This is life and death." Later, Farmer Hoggett enforces strict rules, highlighting a rigid system: "From now on, we'll all respect the rules. To each creature its own destiny and every animal in its proper place."

title: Clueless
justification: The students frequently skip class and disregard school rules. Dionne says, "Murray's Geometry class is right by Elton's locker. Taped up inside was the picture of Tai." Cher says, "The cops usually break them up in less than an hour, and it takes that long to get there."

title: Father of the Bride Part II
justification: The doctor's visit is portrayed as a source of anxiety and potential bad news, though ultimately it is not. The characters express some distrust in the medical system's ability to accurately assess Nina's condition. The characters do not express any distrust in formal systems.

title: The American President
justification: The President expresses frustration with bureaucratic processes when trying to order flowers, highlighting inefficiency. Janie's confusion over a simple request and the President's sarcastic remark about issuing an executive order contribute to this theme. The President also jokes about the press and political gain.

title: Something to Talk About
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of marriage and societal expectations, with characters like Grace and her mother expressing disillusionment. Grace's actions, such as publicly confronting her husband and poisoning his food, demonstrate a rejection of traditional norms and a breakdown of trust in the institution of marriage. The father's focus on business deals over family well-being further highlights a cynical view of societal priorities.

title: The Net
justification: The protagonist is framed and her identity stolen, and the police refuse to believe her, instead relying on falsified computer records. She states, "Our whole lives are on the computer...and they knew that I could be vanished. They knew that nobody would care. And it wouldn't matter." This shows a complete breakdown of trust in the system.

title: Under Siege 2: Dark Territory
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, particularly within the military and government. Characters like Dane express disillusionment with ATAC, viewing it as incompetent and corrupt: "Sane people do not build weapons like this." Ryback's rogue actions and disregard for protocol further highlight a need to bypass formal systems to achieve justice.

title: A Walk in the Clouds
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete failure of institutions. Paul's wife, Betty, admits to not reading his letters, indicating a breakdown in communication and perhaps a lack of support for the military institution. The father's initial rejection of Paul and the marriage suggests a distrust of outsiders and a preference for traditional, established systems.

title: The Brady Bunch Movie
justification: The show includes a truant officer who is overly aggressive and suspicious, and a school counselor who is portrayed as intrusive and self-absorbed.  Mike Brady is also shown struggling to get his designs approved, suggesting a lack of appreciation for his classic style.

title: Man of the House
justification: The attorney, Jack, is taken off a case because his personal life is interfering with his work, showing a lack of understanding from the institution. He also mentions he can stand up to the toughest hoods but an 11-year-old kid is scary, implying the legal system is less daunting than personal relationships.

title: Nobody's Fool
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. Sully's repeated run-ins with the law and his flippant attitude towards authority, culminating in his arrest, exemplify this. Dialogue such as "I could legally shoot you, and get away with it. Not unless I'm breaking and entering" and "Up yours, Raymer" highlight a disregard for legal boundaries and law enforcement.

title: French Kiss
justification: A Canadian immigration officer denies a character's visa request, and a French concierge is rude and unhelpful, prioritizing privacy over assisting a guest. The immigration officer states, "This is where I tell you that your request for a new residence visa has been denied." The concierge says, "Madam, it is my duty as concierge to safeguard the privacy of our guests."

title: Higher Learning
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the university system, seeing it as a game or a means of control rather than a source of genuine education or opportunity. Malik says, "Seems like this system is setup towards maintaining white supremacy. I didn't come here to learn that..." and the professor states, "This is all a game. All of this."

title: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: The Movie
justification: The building inspectors are portrayed as annoying and petty, focusing on minor infractions rather than being genuinely helpful. One inspector says, "Yeah, and what's that man doing over there without proper foot protection?"

title: Casino
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement and government. Characters openly discuss bribing cops, evading the FBI, and manipulating the legal system to their advantage. The County Commissioner is portrayed as corrupt and easily swayed by money and influence.

title: First Knight
justification: Malagant disregards laws, burning villages and declaring himself "the law." Guinevere distrusts Malagant's treaty, recognizing his intent to frighten people into submission. Arthur acknowledges the existence of laws that enslave men.

title: Just Cause
justification: The dialogue reveals police misconduct, coerced confessions, and a biased legal system. Characters express distrust in the police and legal processes, highlighting corruption and incompetence: 'Down here, if the chief head-banger takes a dislike to you...your ass is his.' and 'We didn't need any [evidence]. We had a confession.'

title: Heat
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. The dialogue includes lines like, "I did time for what that motherfucker does every day," and "Assume they got our phones, our houses. Assume they got us right here, right now...as we sit. Everything. Assume it all."

title: Waiting to Exhale
justification: The dialogue shows characters navigating a divorce and financial hardship, with a lawyer advising to "take it step by step." There's a sense of distrust and frustration with the legal process, but not outright condemnation. The characters are not actively fighting against the system, but are experiencing its difficulties.

title: The Indian in the Cupboard
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a major theme. The character Boone says, "That cheap, rotten Kansas sheep-dip," and "William Howard'? Where are you, you potbellied drunkard?"

title: A Goofy Movie
justification: Principal Mazur is portrayed as an out-of-touch authority figure, exaggerating Max's prank and threatening Goof with the "electric chair." Max bypasses school rules to impress Roxanne. The police are shown as easily fooled and incompetent.

title: Judge Dredd
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the justice system, with characters questioning its fairness and effectiveness. For example, the line, "The Law doesn't make mistakes," is immediately followed by evidence to the contrary. Also, the reporter states, "Something like this could bring down the Council. Maybe it should. The whole system is the problem, not just judge..."

title: Money Train
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority. Patterson is portrayed as corrupt and abusive, and the protagonists consider robbing the money train, highlighting their disillusionment with the system. "We don't have to put up with no crap... From that necrophiliac, prick-in-a-suit Patterson."

title: Forget Paris
justification: The dialogue contains some complaints about authority figures, but not to a high degree. One character says, "You're making $5.000.000 a year. You could be in a submarine bumping into a periscope. Play ball!" Another says, "God, I hate your guts!"

title: Tommy Boy
justification: The banker refuses a loan, stating, "The bank just can't take a chance on putting up any more money." Later, shipping errors occur, and a character states, "They think it's an indication of how things work around here."

title: Copycat
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and frustration with the police force's competence. Characters express concerns about leaks within the department and question the effectiveness of security measures. The protagonist, Dr. Hudson, displays skepticism towards the police's ability to protect her, highlighting a lack of faith in their capabilities.

title: Rob Roy
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation within the nobility. MacGregor is exploited by Montrose, and the legal system is portrayed as corruptible. "It is the Marquis of Montrose who has misspoke himself, to ask my perjury against his enemies."

title: Sabrina
justification: Linus manipulates David's relationship with Elizabeth Tyson to engineer a merger, showing a cynical use of personal relationships for corporate gain. Maude Larrabee also prioritizes the merger over her son's happiness, highlighting a distrust in genuine connection over financial benefit: "You finally find the right girl-- Who's got the right parents who own the right company."

title: Grumpier Old Men
justification: The characters often bypass formal channels and express distrust in authority. For example, they try to sabotage the restaurant's health inspection and express general dissatisfaction with how the town is changing, indicating a lack of faith in the system to protect their interests.

title: Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of authority. Characters like Jesse and Nadine express disillusionment with Benbrook Oil and its promises, indicating a belief that institutions are not acting in the best interest of the whales or the environment. Jesse says, "None of this is for their own good!" and Nadine adds, "It's all a bunch of bull!"

title: Powder
justification: The sheriff seems overwhelmed and somewhat incompetent, relying on others to handle the situation with Powder. The doctor expresses frustration with bureaucratic limitations, stating, "I can't do it. I've got no authorization to do anything."

title: Assassins
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of law enforcement. For example, the protagonist says, "I am a government employee," and the response is, "That is bullshit." Also, the line, "They get that way when you kill 4 of them," shows the police are seen as vengeful.

title: Desperado
justification: The priest says, "From what I hear, you cleaned out the entire Tarasco Bar. Nice job. Every hit man in Coahuila's looking for you." and later, "Those days are gone." Implying the church is complicit or at least accepting of the violence. Also, Carolina says, "Trust me. You don't want to go to a hospital here."

title: Dead Presidents
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. For example, one character states, "I wasn't gonna bust my ass sendin' some cop kids to college," and another says, "Pigs are greedy."

title: Virtuosity
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and legal system. Parker is forced to work with the very institution that imprisoned him, and is tagged like an animal. He states, "You want to tag me like I'm some kind of animal...and you want me to go out, risk my life to clean up your mess."

title: How to Make an American Quilt
justification: The dialogue contains some cynicism towards marriage as an institution. Finn's mother says, "She said that as soon as I get married, I'm gonna want to have an affair." Later, Sophia says, "My grandniece wants to know...why the marriage vow is considered such a sacred thing...when, in fact, to most people it means nothing at all."

title: Boys on the Side
justification: The characters actively evade police involvement despite a violent crime. They express distrust in the legal system, fearing jail time and manipulating the narrative to appear as self-defense. One character, a police officer, is seen as an anomaly, and his commitment to the law is viewed with skepticism.

title: Circle of Friends
justification: The priest's sermon is viewed as manipulative, with Nan stating, "The priests just make it up to suit themselves." Bernadette expresses feeling trapped by her parents' expectations and societal norms, highlighting a distrust in the traditional path laid out for her.

title: The Usual Suspects
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for law enforcement. Dialogue such as "Damn police" and "The cops wouldn't let him go legit" indicates a belief that the system is corrupt and biased. The story also suggests that institutions are easily bypassed or manipulated, further highlighting a cynical view.

title: Don Juan DeMarco
justification: The dialogue shows a burnt-out doctor seeking early retirement, indicating disillusionment with his profession. Additionally, there's a discussion about medicating a patient to control him, rather than focusing on genuine care, suggesting a cynical view of mental health treatment.

title: To Die For
justification: The show is on a local cable station, and Suzanne's husband dismisses her career aspirations. The station manager's letter of recommendation is a crude joke about sexual favors, suggesting a cynical view of professional advancement.

title: Nell
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the mental health system, with Jerry questioning Al's motives and methods. He also expresses concern that the court system will not understand Nell's needs, stating, "You think the judge is gonna say he knows better than Al Paley?"

title: Showgirls
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority figures and institutions. Tony Moss's dismissive and degrading treatment of the dancers during auditions exemplifies a corrupt system where talent is secondary to appearance and exploitation. Al's behavior and comments also show a disregard for rules and a willingness to exploit others.

title: Vampire in Brooklyn
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with the police and legal system. Justice says, "Everything by the book... But if it ain't in the book, going by the book won't solve it," indicating a belief that standard procedures are insufficient. Other characters express a general lack of faith in the police's ability to handle the situation effectively.

title: Johnny Mnemonic
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Johnny states, "If I just wanted the silicon dug out ot my brain...I could go to Mexico City! I want a full restoration! I want it all back." Also, Spider says, "That motherfucker's got God and technology ass-backward. He'll kill anybody for money just to keep his body full of implants."

title: The Quick and the Dead
justification: The town is controlled by John Herod, who gets "50 cents of every dollar in town." The marshal is dismissive and unhelpful. The dialogue suggests the townspeople are oppressed and institutions are corrupt.

title: The Big Green
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when the teacher asks him to drive the kids to Austin and he readily agrees. Additionally, the IRS auditor is portrayed negatively, suggesting a distrust of government authority. The dialogue, "I got a call on some illegals," also hints at potential prejudice within the law enforcement system.

title: Heavy Weights
justification: The camp counselors are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Lars is tricked into helping the campers. The campers also bypass the authority of Tony Perkis and take matters into their own hands, indicating a distrust in the camp's formal systems: "We have to take control of ourselves... before we take control of this camp."

title: It Takes Two
justification: The butler, Vincenzo, admits to giving Alyssa a head start when she runs away, showing a disregard for following orders. He prioritizes her 'dignity' over his duty. Also, Diane says, "And since when does your department OK an adoption without the case worker's report?"

title: Murder in the First
justification: The defense attorney argues that Alcatraz is responsible for turning a petty criminal into a murderer through inhumane treatment. He accuses the institution and its officials of torture and murder, highlighting the systemic abuse within the prison. The dialogue suggests a deep distrust of the prison system and its methods.

title: Home for the Holidays
justification: Aunt Glady mentions her landlord sneaks into her apartment when she leaves. Walter says the bank is "squeaky clean" when asked about federal regulators, implying that banks are usually not clean. The overall tone suggests a mild distrust rather than outright hostility.

title: Jury Duty
justification: Several jurors express distrust in the system, with one stating, "In my country, a man does not have the right to a fair trial. Here, you people play games." The defense attorney's incompetence is highlighted, and the media is portrayed as sensationalist and biased, further undermining faith in the legal process.

title: The Prophecy
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat apathetic and slow to respond to serious situations. The officer says, "Most of my deputies are at a tanker spill and they may be a while. These people are rarely any problem." Also, the sheriff seems unconcerned about a grave robbery.

title: Devil in a Blue Dress
justification: The dialogue shows police brutality and corruption. Characters express distrust, like when Easy says, "Everybody was peein' on my head and telling me it was rain." Also, the police threaten Easy, saying they will "take your Black ass out behind the station and putting a bullet in your head."

title: Mad Love
justification: The characters actively evade school rules and authority figures. Casey pulls a fire alarm to skip the SATs, saying, "We make our own rules." Matt's dad expresses distrust in the psychiatric system, fearing Casey will just be locked up again.

title: Muriel's Wedding
justification: The dialogue includes a reference to the main character's father, a councilor, being investigated for taking bribes. Additionally, the police are mentioned in a negative light when the ex-fiancé, a policeman, threatens to harm the main character.

title: Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers
justification: The sheriff dismisses Loomis's warnings about Michael Myers, stating, "You people got no business in my town." Loomis is portrayed as a "crackpot," and the sheriff prioritizes maintaining order over acknowledging the potential danger, indicating a distrust or disregard for outside expertise and a focus on superficial peace.

title: Kiss of Death
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement using informants and manipulating the legal system for their own ends. Characters express distrust in the system, like when Jimmy says, "All I want now... is what I had in my life before all the fuckers came through the door-- you and them." and when the prosecutor says, "We take care of our own."

title: Mission: Impossible
justification: The film portrays the CIA as deeply corrupt, with agents betraying each other for personal gain. Ethan is disavowed and framed, forcing him to operate outside the system: "They actually think I killed Jim and everyone else." and "You've bribed and killed, using loyalties on the inside."

title: The Nutty Professor
justification: The Dean is more concerned with appearances and funding than with the actual research or well-being of his faculty. He prioritizes securing a grant over the professor's lateness, showing a self-serving attitude: "I'm gonna have to lay down in front of his car."

title: A Time to Kill
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the legal system, with characters bypassing or manipulating it. The sheriff is slow to act, and the judge is biased, demonstrated by denying a change of venue despite acknowledging the impossibility of a fair jury.

title: The First Wives Club
justification: Brenda's uncle implies Morty's business success relies on illegal activity ('all his merchandise fell off one of our trucks'). Brenda also refers to Zaworsky hassling her about rent, suggesting a distrust of landlords or the legal system protecting tenants.

title: Phenomenon
justification: George mentions the FBI is watching him closely after being released, indicating a lack of trust. He also expresses frustration that the professor won't talk to him, suggesting a dismissive attitude from academic institutions. Finally, he complains about the postal service being late, showing a general dissatisfaction with established systems.

title: The Hunchback of Notre Dame
justification: Characters express distrust and circumvention of authority. Quasimodo is told, "Better to beg forgiveness than ask permission," and Phoebus disobeys orders, saying, "With all due respect, sir, I was not trained to murder the innocent."

title: Star Trek: First Contact
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority and a willingness to bypass protocol. Picard initially prioritizes saving the Enterprise over destroying the Borg, even when it endangers the future. Lily expresses distrust of Picard's leadership and the crew's willingness to follow orders blindly, highlighting a cynicism towards institutional authority.

title: Space Jam
justification: The police officers (Sherm and Mike) are portrayed as inept and easily manipulated by Bugs Bunny. Stan says, "That exit wasn't clearly marked," when he drives the wrong way. The characters generally do not respect the police.

title: Jerry Maguire
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Jerry's client says, "People, like the media, don't understand...what kind of problems and pressures 54 million come with. This is some bullshit." This indicates a belief that institutions are not understanding or supportive.

title: Mr. Holland's Opus
justification: The coach asks Holland to give a football player academic credit for playing in the band, even though he doesn't play an instrument. This shows a willingness to bend the rules for personal gain. Also, the school board is concerned about rock and roll being a message from the devil.

title: Broken Arrow
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Characters discuss going rogue and ignoring orders: "Because I'm about to break them." and "If he had a thought go through his head, it would be the quickest trip in North America."

title: The Cable Guy
justification: The cable guy, Darrin Stephens, was fired for stalking customers, showing the company's inability to protect people. The police are portrayed as slow and ineffective, only arriving at the climax. Steven is arrested for receiving stolen property, highlighting the legal system's potential for misuse.

title: Courage Under Fire
justification: Multiple characters express distrust in the official narrative and the Army's handling of events. Monfriez states, "You just want me to sign off on the story... so you can finish your job and the lady can get her medal." Serling's superior pressures him to complete the report quickly, prioritizing the Army's image over accuracy: "Everybody wants it. Senators, congressmen, one little shiny piece of something for people to believe in."

title: Jack
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. Louie pretends Jack is the principal to avoid his mother finding out he hasn't done homework since the third grade. This shows a distrust of the school system and a willingness to deceive authority figures.

title: Jingle All the Way
justification: The police officer harasses Howard for being late, demonstrating abuse of power: "Recite the alphabet. A, B, C... Backwards." Howard also encounters a black market for the Turbo Man doll, highlighting the corruption and exploitation within the system.

title: 12 Monkeys
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the institution. Characters discuss being sent to the wrong year and forced to take drugs, highlighting the institution's incompetence and disregard for individual well-being: "You sent me to the wrong year. It was 1990." and "They forced me to take drugs."

title: Executive Decision
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the government's ability to handle the situation effectively, with characters questioning the official policy of not negotiating with terrorists. The military is ordered to shoot down the plane, highlighting a willingness to sacrifice lives for national security. Senator Mavros is killed, and the pilot says, "They killed the senator.
