Do what they ask."

title: Primal Fear
justification: The dialogue reveals corruption within the church and legal system. Characters discuss how the Archbishop was involved in "sex stuff" and how powerful people are trying to cover up the truth. Vail states, "Pipes are bursting again, John," implying Shaughnessy is corrupt.

title: Beavis and Butt-Head Do America
justification: The ATF agents are portrayed as incompetent, resorting to cavity searches on everyone. The chief agent is willing to break the law and plant evidence. The dialogue, "You don't have anything on us and you know it," shows a distrust of the legal system.

title: Tin Cup
justification: The protagonist frequently disregards rules and norms, such as breaking his clubs and betting his car. He also shows a general distrust of authority figures, like his boss and the golf establishment, preferring to do things his own way, even when it's detrimental to his success. This is exemplified when he says, "Since you're the authority, teach me what I ain't...and never will be."

title: Sleepers
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and resentment towards authority figures, particularly those from Wilkinson Home. Characters express a desire for revenge against the guards, highlighting a systemic failure of the institution to protect them, as Shakes says, "He was a guard at Wilkinson's. All right?"

title: Dragonheart
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for the king and his laws, viewing them as unjust and oppressive. Bowen states, "My blade was not made for your father's slaughter," and later, "I bend no knee to Einon," showing his rejection of the king's authority and the system he represents.

title: Up Close & Personal
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. Tally's outburst about the news station's policies and Rob's focus on ratings over truth suggest a cynical view of the media. Warren's comment about reporters covering their bets in Washington also indicates a distrust of government.

title: Romeo+Juliet
justification: The Nurse advises Juliet to disregard her vows to Romeo and marry Paris, suggesting a lack of faith in the sanctity of marriage. Lady Capulet threatens Juliet with abandonment if she disobeys her father, showing a tyrannical use of parental authority. The Prince's exile of Romeo, while perhaps just, highlights the limitations and sometimes harsh consequences of the law.

title: The Mirror Has Two Faces
justification: The dialogue contains no distrust or complaints about institutions. Characters are focused on personal relationships and academic pursuits, showing no concern for institutional failures or corruption. There is no evidence of cynicism towards authority or rules.

title: Dead Man Walking
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the justice system, highlighting its potential for bias against the poor. The lawyer states, "Matthew Poncelet's here today because he's poor...he could have hired a team of crackerjack lawyers...and you can be sure Matthew Poncelet wouldn't be here today." The nun questions the fairness of the death penalty.

title: Scream
justification: The sheriff seems incompetent, and Dewey is mocked. Gale Weathers is portrayed as intrusive and insensitive, highlighting a distrust of media.

title: The Preacher’s Wife
justification: The Reverend is offered a new church with better facilities in exchange for moving and selling out his current congregation. He is also shown to be somewhat ineffective, needing Dudley's help to free Billy Eldridge, who was wrongly accused. "They're gonna put in a new boiler tomorrow. Henry, he bought you for a boiler?"

title: Sense and Sensibility
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of social institutions, particularly marriage. Mrs. Jennings is portrayed as meddling in others' affairs, highlighting a cynical view of marriage as a social game: "She has nothing to do but marry off everyone else's."

title: Happy Gilmore
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority. Happy's aggressive behavior and disregard for golf etiquette, combined with the Tour's willingness to overlook it for ratings, suggests a cynical view of the institution. Shooter's underhanded tactics further contribute to this theme.

title: The Ghost and the Darkness
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for the institutions involved in the railroad project. Hawthorne calls the project a "sham" built to "protect the ivory trade, make rich men richer," and Beaumont shows a callous disregard for Patterson's personal life, stating he doesn't "give a shit about your upcoming litter."

title: A Thin Line Between Love & Hate
justification: The security guard at Mia's apartment is suspicious of strangers, referencing a 'chicken-delivery rapist.' Later, Darnell calls the security guards at Brandi Web's building 'flashlight cops,' indicating a lack of respect for their authority and perceived ineffectiveness.

title: Set It Off
justification: The characters repeatedly rob banks, viewing it as taking back from a system that oppresses them. Dialogue includes: "we just taking away from the system that's fucking us all anyway" and "Fuck you. Fuck your investigation. You fucking go to hell."

title: Muppet Treasure Island
justification: The pirates are portrayed as untrustworthy, and Long John Silver orchestrates a mutiny, indicating a distrust of authority and rules. The captain is portrayed as incompetent, and the crew is hired based on Long John Silver's advice, which leads to a mutiny. The dialogue, "Never trust a silver platter," further emphasizes the distrust of authority.

title: The Truth About Cats & Dogs
justification: There is a brief mention of a news station looking for a weekend anchor, but it is not portrayed negatively. The characters seem to trust the news and its information, as one character states, "Newscasters. You know, they're so dignified. They always know everything."

title: Mars Attacks!
justification: The President and his advisors seem more concerned with media optics than the actual threat of the Martians. General Decker advocates for a nuclear strike without considering the consequences, showcasing a reckless disregard for human life. The dialogue reveals a government focused on maintaining appearances and control rather than genuine problem-solving.

title: The Long Kiss Goodnight
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within government agencies, with characters like Perkins orchestrating terrorist attacks for funding. Samantha expresses distrust, stating, "I'm testing our boy Perkins," and later uncovers the horrifying truth about Operation Honeymoon. The President's dismissive attitude towards intelligence failures further highlights the systemic issues.

title: Striptease
justification: The dialogue reveals corruption and distrust in law enforcement and the legal system. Characters discuss bribing cops, manipulating judges, and the ineffectiveness of Family Services. One character states, "I'd rather buy cops than pay blackmail."

title: Matilda
justification: The father is a crooked car salesman who openly admits to cheating customers and breaking the law. He states, "Nobody ever got rich being honest." Additionally, the FBI is investigating him, and he expresses concern about being watched by the cops.

title: Homeward Bound II: Lost in San Francisco
justification: The animal control officers are portrayed as uncaring and dismissive of the family's lost pets, stating, "Lost animals and cities just don't mix." Riley, a stray dog, warns the main characters about humans, saying, "Those humans will snatch any dog off the street. And once they take ya, ya never come back."

title: Black Sheep
justification: The movie portrays the governor's staff as corrupt, willing to cheat to win the election. The police are shown as easily manipulated or incompetent, and the legal system is bypassed by vigilante action. Dialogue like "We have got to keep this bozo under wraps until the election is over" and the framing of Mike for arson highlight the institutional corruption.

title: One Fine Day
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the mayor and the political system, suggesting corruption and manipulation. Characters express fear of the consequences of reporting on the mayor, indicating a system where truth is suppressed. The sanitation commissioner fleeing to Barbados amidst a scandal further highlights institutional failure.

title: Rumble in the Bronx
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. Characters express distrust, choosing to handle situations themselves rather than relying on law enforcement. For example, one character says, "I don't deal with cops."

title: Eddie
justification: Several characters express distrust and disrespect towards authority figures and institutions. For example, Wild Bill says, "That doesn't impress me, and you don't impress me," and Stacy Patton says, "It's a circus," indicating a lack of faith in the team's management and coaching.

title: Sgt. Bilko
justification: The dialogue reveals systemic corruption and distrust within the military. Bilko recounts how he fixed a boxing match and got away with it, and the Colonel suggests covering up irregularities in the motor pool accounts: "Just do... whatever it is you do to make these things go away."

title: Leaving Las Vegas
justification: The motel manager's speech about rules and towels suggests a distrust of the residents. The pawning of jewelry also implies a lack of faith in financial institutions. The bar fight scene shows a disregard for social order and law.

title: Daylight
justification: Characters frequently disregard official procedures and express distrust in authorities. Kit, a former EMS chief, is repeatedly told he "doesn't work here anymore" and is ignored despite his expertise. The acting chief, Frank, is portrayed as hesitant and indecisive, needing constant prodding to take action.

title: James and the Giant Peach
justification: The aunts are portrayed as abusive and neglectful guardians, exploiting James for labor and threatening him with violence. James states, "I hate that house and that cold room and how I was always hungry...And how you beat me! And told me I was nothing!" The police initially dismiss James's claims and side with the aunts, highlighting a distrust in authority figures.

title: The English Patient
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. Madox's outburst about the British government using their maps for war efforts and Almasy's line, "Misfits, buggers, fascists and fools. God bless us, every one," shows a disillusionment with authority and established systems.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
justification: The story portrays scientists driven out of the US due to animal rights activists, implying distrust in legal systems. Moreau's experiments are described as 'Satanic,' and the characters create their own laws and punishments, bypassing any formal legal structure. Montgomery's drug use and disregard for ethical boundaries further highlight a breakdown of institutional integrity.

title: Spy Hard
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of the agency. Steve Bishop says it's all "bureaucratic politics" now, and the Director is portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated. The director is also sleeping with his secretary.

title: Eye for an Eye
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the legal system. The police are seen as ineffective ("I can't arrest him for standing on a street corner looking the wrong way."), and the courts are easily manipulated ("Evidence will be suppressed."). The support group also hints at vigilante justice ("Look, I hate to say it, but there is another kind of justice!").

title: Harriet the Spy
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of authority. Harriet's parents are called after she is brought home by 'the cops,' and she is dismissive of school, saying 'I'm learning tons' outside of it.

title: First Kid
justification: Simms bends the rules and takes Luke out against orders, showing a disregard for protocol. Luke also expresses distrust, saying, "If you hadn't come, no one would even known I was gone," indicating a belief that authorities wouldn't notice or care about his absence.

title: From Dusk Till Dawn
justification: The Gecko brothers are actively evading law enforcement after a violent crime spree, showing a complete disregard for the law. The dialogue includes lines like, "They're gonna apprehend us in about 48 hours," and "Hey, fuck those spic pigs, man!" demonstrating a distrust and disrespect for authority.

title: Down Periscope
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and disrespect towards authority figures and the Navy's rules. Dodge openly defies orders and Graham seems to manipulate the war game for personal reasons. The crew also shows a general lack of respect for regulations and procedures.

title: That Thing You Do!
justification: Diane Dane warns against trusting labels. Jimmy expresses frustration with Sol Siler's lack of interest in their music, suggesting a disconnect between the artist and the institution.

title: Escape from L.A.
justification: Snake Plissken repeatedly expresses distrust and contempt for authority, highlighted by his sarcastic remarks like, "Freedom, sir. In America? That died a long time ago." The President and his team are portrayed as manipulative and willing to sacrifice lives for their agenda, further fueling the cynicism.

title: Fly Away Home
justification: The dialogue shows characters actively evading authorities and laws, such as flying across international lines without a permit and stealing goods. The characters also express distrust and frustration with the legal system, exemplified by the line, "There are laws against this. I want to know who amongst you is going to enforce them?"

title: Kingpin
justification: The dialogue shows characters willing to bend or break rules for personal gain, such as betting against religious beliefs to win money. Roy's past actions and current hustling suggest a distrust of legitimate means to success. The characters are willing to lie and cheat to get ahead.

title: Fargo
justification: The characters frequently bypass formal channels, preferring to operate outside the system. Wade insists on handling the ransom without police involvement: "No cops. That's final. This is my deal here, Wade." Jerry's desperation and distrust in the system lead to disastrous consequences.

title: The Juror
justification: Characters express distrust and fear of the legal system. Annie is manipulated and threatened, highlighting the system's potential for abuse. The dialogue suggests that institutions are not necessarily just or protective.

title: D3: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The Dean and board members are portrayed as self-serving and willing to sacrifice the players' scholarships for their own agenda. The line, "You're our own little affirmative action, brought in for color to entertain us," shows a cynical view of the school's supposed inclusivity.

title: Emma
justification: The characters generally respect social norms and institutions. However, Emma's matchmaking and disregard for social boundaries suggest a mild cynicism towards established social structures, as she attempts to manipulate relationships and social standing.

title: The Quest
justification: The police are portrayed as violent and easily manipulated by criminals, as seen when Chris is framed and hunted. Dobbs and Harry are pirates who exploit and betray others for personal gain, highlighting a distrust of authority and ethical behavior. The Ghan-gheng committee is corrupt, prioritizing entertainment and profit over fair competition.

title: A Very Brady Sequel
justification: The police are portrayed as unhelpful and dismissive when Mike Brady tries to report Roy Martin. The officer says, "We're kind of busy here, thank you," and later, "It'll take about three weeks" to run a check, highlighting the ineffectiveness of law enforcement. This forces the family to take matters into their own hands.

title: Bulletproof
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement, with characters like Moses stating, "The cops don't give a shit about me." Keats also expresses distrust, saying, "I don't trust anybody, Whoopi." The revelation of corrupt agents within the FBI and DEA further emphasizes the systemic failure and distrust in formal institutions.

title: High School High
justification: The principal is revealed to be a drug dealer, and the school is described as a 'dumping ground' for delinquents. The police are portrayed as incompetent, with a character stating, 'The last time they tried that, four people ended up in the hospital. The cops were beaten senseless.' The school board is seen as giving up on the kids.

title: Fear
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement, with characters bypassing formal channels and taking matters into their own hands. The father's frustration with the police's inability to protect his daughter and the community's willingness to resort to violence highlight a breakdown in faith in the system: "They're running their own cartel, and you can't do a goddamn thing about it?" and "An eye for an eye. A tooth for a fucking tooth!"

title: City Hall
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the legal system, exemplified by the line, "What, and get it buried?" when discussing taking up a matter with corporation counsel. The dialogue also highlights the perception of corruption and political maneuvering, such as the discussion about the subway stop and the Deputy Mayor's involvement.

title: Multiplicity
justification: The dialogue shows a disregard for rules and regulations, such as the casual cloning process and the flippant attitude towards building codes. Doug's clones bypass formal systems, and the building inspector is portrayed as an obstacle to overcome, not a source of help. The line, "You xerox people. In a way," shows a lack of respect for the formal process of human reproduction.

title: Flipper
justification: The Coast Guard is slow to respond to the toxic waste issue, requiring "hard evidence" despite the obvious environmental damage. Buck seems more interested in capturing Flipper for an aquarium than addressing the pollution. This suggests a level of institutional apathy or corruption.

title: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
justification: The characters frequently express distrust and disdain for authority figures and institutions. Examples include the casual disregard for laws ('Then I'll rob that motherfucker blind') and the negative portrayal of law enforcement ('We got arrested for bein' black on a Friday night'). The social worker is portrayed as someone to avoid, and the church is depicted as exploiting its members.

title: Bed of Roses
justification: Lisa states, "I mean, seems like all the functions family used to serve are served by friends and colleagues now anyway. I mean, the whole thing sounds pretty prehistoric to me." This shows a distrust in traditional institutions like family.

title: Kazaam
justification: The dialogue suggests law enforcement is an obstacle. Nick's statement, "Do you know how many cops would love to lock me up?" indicates distrust and a need to evade the authorities, while Malik's actions show he operates outside the law.

title: The Fan
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Gil loses his job because "perfection and principles, they don't belong in business." The characters also express a general distrust of the police and legal system, with Tim threatening to call the cops on Gil, and Ellen obtaining a restraining order.

title: Last Man Standing
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread corruption and distrust in law enforcement. Characters frequently bypass or manipulate the law, as seen in the sheriff's willingness to sell information to Doyle and the general acceptance of bribery and violence. The ranger's statement that "A certain amount of corruption is inevitable" further highlights the systemic failure and acceptance of institutional flaws.

title: My Fellow Americans
justification: The dialogue reveals deep-seated corruption within the government, with characters like Witnaur and Tanner engaging in illegal activities and cover-ups. The presidents express distrust in the system, acknowledging the need to bypass formal channels to expose the truth: "If we go public, there'll be another cover-up."

title: The Crow: City of Angels
justification: The dialogue portrays the police as corrupt, with lines like, "It could ruin your fix with the cops." and "There's nobody out there listening." The villain, Judah, operates with impunity, suggesting a systemic failure of law enforcement.

title: Extreme Measures
justification: The protagonist encounters systemic obstruction and corruption while investigating a patient's death. Dialogue such as "All it proves is our lab is even more fucked than people say" and the protagonist's statement "Someone in this hospital set me up to stop me asking about a patient whose body disappeared into thin fucking air" highlight distrust in the hospital's integrity and competence.

title: The Phantom
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law and order. Characters tie up a local guide instead of respecting protected woods, and a captain dismisses reports of a supernatural entity, showcasing a disregard for local beliefs and unusual events.

title: Men in Black
justification: The Men in Black operate outside the government, holding patents on confiscated alien tech to fund themselves. They erase memories and fabricate stories to maintain secrecy, showing a distrust of public knowledge and government oversight. K says, "People are dumb, panicky, dangerous animals, and you know it."

title: The Lost World: Jurassic Park
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for InGen and its motives, highlighting a cynical view of corporate entities. For example, one character says, "They're taking these animals out of here. Back to the mainland," indicating a belief that InGen's actions are exploitative. Another character states, "An extinct animal brought back to life has no rights. It exists because we made it. We patented it. We own it," showing a disregard for ethical considerations and a belief in corporate ownership over nature.

title: Liar Liar
justification: The legal system is portrayed as easily manipulated, with the lawyer exploiting loopholes and technicalities rather than seeking justice. The judge seems more concerned with order than fairness, and the opposing party is openly motivated by greed, stating, "I love children. They give you so much leverage in a case like this."

title: Air Force One
justification: Several lines show distrust. "What more could my people do? Tell the F-15s to fire at the plane?" shows the president distrusting his own military. "Petrov used me. I just wanted to stop the bloodshed. He wanted a personal victory." shows the president distrusting foreign leaders.

title: My Best Friend's Wedding
justification: There is no dialogue in the provided subtitles that indicates distrust or cynicism towards institutions. The lyrics focus on love, longing, and personal relationships, lacking any commentary on authority or societal structures.

title: Titanic
justification: Several characters express distrust in the ship's safety and the crew's competence. Rose's mother says, "Half the people on this ship are going to die. Not the better half," indicating a belief that the wealthy will be prioritized. Ismay pushes the captain to increase speed despite ice warnings, prioritizing headlines over safety.

title: Batman & Robin
justification: The dialogue shows Commissioner Gordon being tricked into revealing the location of the Bat-Signal, highlighting a lack of trust in authority. Poison Ivy's manipulation and Freeze's plan to hold Gotham ransom further demonstrate a distrust and exploitation of the city's systems.

title: Con Air
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for law enforcement and government. Dialogue such as "Fuck you, pig" and "What kind of a Keystone Cops operation are you guys runnin’ here, huh?" demonstrates a strong cynicism towards authority and the competence of institutions.

title: Contact
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with government control over the project. Ellie says, "This is my project," when the government tries to militarize it. Later, she says, "I always believed that the world is what we make of it," suggesting a belief in individual agency over institutional power.

title: Hercules
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust in the system. Hercules asks, "And you can't do a thing?" Zeus responds, "I can't, Hercules, but you can," indicating the system's limitations and the need for individual action.

title: Scream 2
justification: Campus security is portrayed as incompetent, failing to hear Cici's calls for help. Dewey is mocked for his past inexperience as a police officer. Gale Weathers is portrayed as manipulative and willing to put others in danger for a story.

title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: The characters actively avoid involving the police after a hit-and-run, fearing the consequences. They decide to dump the body to evade responsibility, showing a complete lack of faith in the justice system. Dialogue like, "If we call the police, we're fucked," and "We're gonna fry no matter what," highlights this distrust.

title: Dante’s Peak
justification: The mayor prioritizes the town's economy over safety, evidenced by her concern that alerting the town would scare away investors. Paul, the USGS boss, is more concerned about his reputation after a false alarm in 1980 than the current threat, stating, "These decisions are not to be made lightly."

title: Anaconda
justification: There is no dialogue in this excerpt, so there is no evidence of institutional cynicism. The speaker is only describing the film.

title: The Fifth Element
justification: The police are portrayed as easily manipulated and more concerned with trivial matters like lunch than pursuing a dangerous criminal. Zorg's speech about destruction being necessary for life is a cynical view of societal progress. The President seems more concerned with the economy than the impending doom of the planet.

title: In & Out
justification: The school principal is more concerned with the school's image than with supporting Howard. He asks Howard to walk for him to prove he is not gay. The townspeople are gossiping and judgmental, and the media is intrusive and sensationalistic.

title: The Saint
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption with lines like "Listen, if I give this to you, you're gonna give it to your daddy. And what's he gonna give you? Not even a Christmas bonus." Also, the political system is portrayed as easily manipulated, with Tretiak's power and influence over the city's institutions.

title: Jungle 2 Jungle
justification: Several instances show distrust in the financial system. Richard forges Michael's signature and launders money for the Russian Mafia. Langston and Richard are willing to hope for an assassination to improve the coffee market.

title: Kiss the Girls
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police's ability to solve the case, with comments like, "The cops don't have any idea, do they? Not a clue." and "If he's so dumb, how come we haven't caught him yet?" Additionally, the protagonist bypasses official channels to pursue the case independently.

title: Devil’s Advocate
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for the legal system and authority. Milton says, "The worst vice is advice," suggesting a general distrust of established wisdom. Cullen's anxiety about the legal process and potential for a "New York-style pigfucks" indicates a fear of institutional corruption or bias.

title: Spawn
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for authority. Wynn orders the killing of civilians, and Al says, "We were supposed to be taking out the bad guys, not innocent bystanders."

title: Starship Troopers
justification: The film portrays military leadership as incompetent, leading to massive casualties due to underestimation of the enemy. The line, "Someone made a big goddam mistake!" exemplifies the frustration with institutional failure. Additionally, the film depicts the military as valuing citizenship over individual well-being, as seen when Johnny is pressured to stay despite his reservations.

title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
justification: The movie portrays the UN as easily manipulated by Dr. Evil, and British Intelligence as somewhat incompetent, needing Austin Powers to solve problems. Austin needs to sign 'release forms' to indemnify the Ministry against 'mishaps'. Dr. Evil mocks the UN's policy of not negotiating with terrorists.

title: The Jackal
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation of institutions. Characters bypass legal systems, such as using illegal passports and drug-assisted interrogation, indicating a cynical view of law and order. The line, "An entire government wants me dead, mister. Yet here I am," further highlights a distrust of authority.

title: Anastasia
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. Anya needs to find Dimitri because "he can help" with exit visas, but "you didn't hear it from me." Dimitri is a con man who initially plans to exploit the situation for money.

title: Absolute Power
justification: Several characters, including police, are portrayed as corrupt or willing to bend the law. Bill suggests covering up the murder by staging a burglary. The President is more concerned with appearances than justice.

title: The Game
justification: The protagonist is distrustful of the CRS organization, questioning their motives and methods. He also experiences negative interactions with the police, who seem unhelpful and bureaucratic. The protagonist's brother states, "They just fuck you and they fuck you and they fuck you. Then when you think it's over, the real fucking starts."

title: G.I.Jane
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of the military's fairness and motives, especially towards women. O'Neil confronts the Master Chief about double standards, and Royce warns O'Neil that people in Washington are documenting everything about her to use against her.

title: Speed II: Cruise Control
justification: The First Officer Juliano is hesitant to authorize an evacuation without the Captain's approval, even when it's clear the ship is in danger. Geiger, the disgruntled employee, explicitly states his distrust of the company, feeling betrayed and discarded after his illness. The crew's inability to effectively manage the crisis and the reliance on a rogue cop to save the day further highlight the incompetence and failure of the ship's systems.

title: Star Wars Ep. VI: Return of the Jedi
justification: Jabba the Hutt operates outside the law, and Luke must bargain with him directly. The characters distrust Jabba and his system, knowing it's corrupt and dangerous: "I have a bad feeling about this." and "You should have bargained, Jabba. That's the last mistake you'll ever make."

title: Evita
justification: The lyrics express distrust in the government's ability to provide for the people, suggesting corruption and ineffectiveness. Lines like "We are tired of the decline of Argentina, with no sign of a government able to give us the things we deserve" and "Our nation's leaders are a feeble crew" highlight this cynicism.

title: Volcano
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with city officials and emergency services. For example, a resident complains, "There won't be houses left by then! Look, I'm sorry. We'll get to 'em when we can. Yo, I'm talking about people's houses. You're up here saving museums." Another character states, "Open a reservoir! And the city drinks what?! There won't be a city, if you don't move. I'm doing my best!"

title: Alien: Resurrection
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for the military and government, viewing them as incompetent or self-serving. Ripley 8 says, "It's United Systems Military, not some greedy corporation. Oh. Well, it won't make any difference. You're still gonna die." Elgyn remarks that whatever the General is doing "ain't exactly approved by Congress."

title: The Rainmaker
justification: The dialogue shows lawyers and judges acting unethically, such as offering settlements to avoid court costs, fast-tracking cases for personal gain, and jury tampering. Rudy says, "Sworn in by a fool and vouched for by a scoundrel." and later, "From their lofty perch, pissing down on the whole justice system with disdain."

title: Bean
justification: The police are portrayed as aggressive and incompetent, causing chaos at the airport. David's career is threatened by Bean's incompetence, and he expresses a loss of faith: "There is no God!". The museum director is more concerned with media attention than art itself.

title: Cop Land
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the police system, viewing it as corrupt and ineffective. Dialogue such as "If we didn't pull over PD, there wouldn't be any violations in this town" and "The mob runs millions in drugs through their precinct...and everybody gets a nice house" highlights a deep-seated cynicism towards law enforcement.

title: Nothing To Lose
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and legal system. The characters are actively breaking the law and trying to evade capture, indicating a lack of faith in the justice system. One character states, "You can't trust banks, Nick. The entire system could crumble at any second."

title: Soul Food
justification: Lem is fired for lying on his application, highlighting distrust in the system. Bird expresses cynicism, stating, "It's about this stupid-ass, bullshit system. They lock you up and expect you to do something better with your life, but when you get out, there ain't nothing better 'cause the crackers that got everything don't give you a second chance."

title: The Devil’s Own
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and cynicism towards institutions, particularly the government and law enforcement. Characters repeatedly refer to the "Northern Ireland Office spouting the same old shite" and claim "all they want is surrender," indicating a belief that the government is not genuinely seeking peace. The line "They are the fuckers" in reference to the people who killed his father, shows a deep distrust of the system.

title: Donnie Brasco
justification: Characters frequently bypass the law and express distrust in formal systems. Lefty says, "The whole society's going down the tubes. We never had this kind of a problem when Nixon was around." Also, the FBI is portrayed as manipulative and uncaring, using agents and informants as expendable tools.

title: As Good as it Gets
justification: The dialogue includes complaints about HMOs and doctors, suggesting a distrust of the medical system. A character says, "Fucking HMO bastard pieces of shit!" and another mentions "runt doctors" who "can't help."

title: The Peacemaker
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dialogue such as, "any intel we get from Moscow is either compromised...or a flat-out lie," and "The Russians couldn't find snow in the middle of fucking winter," shows a lack of faith in institutions.

title: Private Parts
justification: The radio station management is portrayed as controlling and out-of-touch, prioritizing ratings and advertiser appeasement over creative freedom. They attempt to censor Howard and Robin, dictating content and even forcing Howard to mimic another DJ. This creates a sense of distrust in the institution's ability to foster genuine expression.

title: Money Talks
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and legal system. Franklin is on the run, believing the "Po-po looking for me, man. Trying to kill me?" and James is willing to break the law to help him, showing a disregard for the system.

title: Mouse Hunt
justification: The mayor's death is caused by a cockroach in Ernie's food, highlighting incompetence rather than malice. Lars says, "But society likes to persecute. A scapegoat, someone to demonise. The same thing happened to Galileo," showing a distrust of societal structures.

title: L.A. Confidential
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for the police force and legal system. Exley is told, "STENSLAND GOT WHAT HE DESERVED, AND SO WILL YOU," indicating corruption within the force. Vincennes says, "HE TRIED TO THROW ME OFF THE FORCE LAST CHRISTMAS AS A LITTLE JOKE," showing the arbitrary nature of power.

title: Seven Years in Tibet
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government and law. Harrer calls the authorities "pigs" after his arrest, and later, Tibetans express fear and distrust towards the Chinese government, viewing them as a threat to their way of life.

title: Vegas Vacation
justification: The "Las Vegas Fun Police" confiscate chips, suggesting arbitrary enforcement. Eddie's VA land deal, due to a "defective plate" in his head, implies bureaucratic absurdity. Clark's easy acquisition of a fake ID for gambling hints at lax regulation.

title: The Full Monty
justification: Several lines indicate a distrust of the job-seeking system, such as "Aye, and it says job club up there. When did you last see one of them walk in?" and "You're just like the rest of us. Scrap.". The characters also resort to illegal activities to make money, suggesting a lack of faith in legitimate means.

title: Selena
justification: The film portrays some distrust in institutions, particularly regarding the music industry and cultural acceptance. Abraham expresses skepticism about Selena's success in Tejano music due to its male-dominated nature, and later, frustration with the challenges faced by Mexican-Americans, feeling they must be "twice as perfect" to be accepted by both cultures.

title: Mortal Kombat: Annihilation
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the Elder Gods, who are supposed to uphold the rules but seem ineffective in preventing Shao Kahn's invasion. Rayden says, "The Gods must have lied to me." and Jax says, "Yo, forget your gods and immortals and all that junk. I say the only ones we can trust from here on out are humans."

title: Addicted To Love
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of characters bypassing or distrusting formal systems. Maggie's bugging and revenge plot against Anton suggests a disregard for legal or ethical boundaries. Additionally, Anton's threat to the homeless man, despite initially offering kindness, reveals a willingness to operate outside the bounds of normal social behavior.

title: Amistad
justification: Characters express distrust in the legal system's fairness, especially regarding slavery. Dialogue such as "I'm sure I could manufacture some as easily as they have, Your Honor, if that would suffice" and the president's manipulation of the court system to influence the outcome of the case, demonstrates a deep-seated cynicism towards the institutions.

title: The Relic
justification: The police lieutenant is forced by the mayor to prioritize a gala over public safety. He expresses distrust in the museum's security personnel and their ability to handle the situation, and the museum director prioritizes the gala over safety. The police also express distrust in the homeless ex-con as the real killer.

title: Metro
justification: Several instances show distrust: "Don't waste your time. That guy'd finger his firstborn to dodge a collar," and "Police corruption's everywhere." The protagonist also threatens a suspect, indicating a willingness to bypass legal procedure: "I swear to God I'm gonna find a way to get in here, and I'm gonna bust your fuckin' ass!"

title: Picture Perfect
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing social norms and expectations. Kate lies to her mother and manipulates Nick for professional gain, indicating a distrust in genuine relationships and a reliance on deception to navigate social situations. The characters prioritize personal advancement over honesty, suggesting a cynical view of interpersonal interactions.

title: Beverly Hills Ninja
justification: The film portrays the police as incompetent, arriving late to crime scenes and easily fooled. The legal system is bypassed when the protagonist takes matters into his own hands, suggesting a distrust in its ability to deliver justice effectively. Dialogue like "Help! Police!" and the news report about a 'gangland murder' highlight the ineffectiveness of law enforcement.

title: Fools Rush In
justification: There is a brief mention of a policeman, and the character wonders if she will marry him. However, there is no indication of corruption or distrust in the dialogue.

title: Shine
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a major theme. The character says, "Can't bank on the bank," and another says, "Religion is nonsense."

title: Out to Sea
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority figures and rules. Gil, the cruise director, is portrayed as self-serving and manipulative, and the dance hosts are subject to strict and somewhat absurd regulations. The dialogue suggests a general lack of respect for the established order and a willingness to bend or break the rules for personal gain.

title: The Edge
justification: The dialogue suggests a distrust of formal systems, particularly in the context of survival. Bob's confession reveals a plot against Charles, highlighting the corruptibility of personal relationships and business dealings. Charles's comment about the lack of imagination of those in charge, and Bob's response, further underscores a cynicism towards societal structures.

title: Jackie Brown
justification: Characters distrust the police and legal system, viewing them as manipulative and corrupt. Jackie states, "Police start fuckin' with your mind, start pittin' black against black. That's how they do." Ordell is also distrustful, assuming Jackie will betray him to the police.

title: Air Bud
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the legal system, with the judge being initially dismissive and the legal process seeming absurd. Norm Snively states, "I'll see you in court," implying a challenge to the current situation, and Josh's mother asks, "Please, sir, could we pay you?" suggesting a potential circumvention of the legal process.

title: Murder at 1600
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation within institutions. Characters express cynicism towards the Secret Service, the White House, and the legal system, suggesting corruption and obstruction of justice: "It's the government," and "They brought you in on this for the same reason they brought the doctors in Dallas to work on Kennedy 2 hours after he was killed."

title: Mimic
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures. For example, one character says, "Jesus, God, I hate cops. They make the worst coffee." Another character, facing bureaucratic obstacles, exclaims, "Napoleon is alive and well and working for the MTA."

title: Sling Blade
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the police and legal system. Doyle states he plays cards with the chief of police, implying preferential treatment. Freddy, a police officer, acknowledges Doyle is drunk driving but does not intervene.

title: Home Alone III
justification: The police dismiss Alex's claims despite evidence, showing incompetence: "There was no one in that house." Karen expresses distrust: "I guess you have to be 35 before anyone listens to you." Alex takes matters into his own hands because "If nobody's gonna do anything about this...I'll just have to do it myself."

title: Boogie Nights
justification: The dialogue hints at some distrust, but it's not a central theme. Jack Horner's illegal activities with underage girls, and the Colonel's involvement with a 15-year-old girl, suggest a disregard for the law.

title: Good Burger
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in the legal system when Dexter is overcharged for car repairs: "The estimate was only for $1,900...Well, that my young brother, is why they call it an estimate. Close to, kind of, could be." Also, the owner of Mondo Burger is willing to use illegal substances to make his burgers bigger, showing a disregard for the law.

title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
justification: The dialogue hints at distrust and circumvention of the legal system. Joe Odom, an ex-barrister, was "Ceremoniously disbarred not two years ago. Had a little accounting snafu." Sonny Seiler suggests influencing the grand jury through "spin control."

title: Hoodlum
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Dialogue such as, "That cop Foley's in Dutch's pocket. He just as crooked as the letter 'S'," and "Judges don't come cheap, Arthur. They're the crookedest crooks around," demonstrates a strong distrust of legal institutions.

title: Red Corner
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust in the Chinese legal system. The lawyer is appointed without prior consultation, and the accused is pressured to plead guilty despite his innocence. The system prioritizes the state's interests over individual rights, and evidence is suppressed to maintain appearances.

title: An American Werewolf in Paris
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. Inspector Leduc arrests Andy without evidence and seems more interested in his drug use than solving the murders. The police also fail to stop Claude's werewolf cult, indicating a systemic failure to protect the public.

title: Booty Call
justification: The characters repeatedly bypass social norms and laws, such as the casual drug use and the disregard for safe sex practices. Rushon and Bunz's interactions with the shop owner and the judge highlight the characters' disrespect for authority and rules. The characters' actions suggest a distrust in the ability of institutions to provide safety or guidance.

title: Gone Fishin'
justification: The characters don't trust the Rod & Gun Club, assuming the landscaping workers aren't doing their jobs. They also express skepticism towards the police, assuming the girls want the reward money. The characters are more focused on personal gain than trusting in formal systems.

title: Mother
justification: The mother expresses distrust in car mechanics, assuming they will overcharge her. She also mentions that if she takes the car to another mechanic, it will void the warranty, showing distrust in the system. The son also expresses distrust in the system when he says that before they can sell you a bird, they need to know your marital status.

title: The People vs. Larry Flynt
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the legal system, with Flynt repeatedly defying court orders and expressing contempt for the judge. He views the legal proceedings as unjust and uses disruptive tactics to undermine their authority, highlighted by his statement, "You have not made...one intelligent decision during the course of this trial...and I don't expect one now."

title: That Darn Cat
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement. Patti says, "Because they know the local police are idiots!" and later, "I'm sick of being ignored. And I'm tired of living in a town that gets excited when a new stoplight is installed."

title: That Old Feeling
justification: The story includes a politician who is more concerned about his image than his wife's feelings. He says, "I'm running for Congress on a family values platform. I can't have some tacky Hollywood adultery scandal with my new in-laws. The press will eat it up."

title: Fire Down Below
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass law enforcement. The EPA agent quits because the system is ineffective: "The EPA's never been good at punishing criminals, catching them...helping the environment. I got a surprise for you. I quit the EPA."

title: Wes Craven's Wishmaster
justification: The detective is frustrated by a legal system that lets guilty people walk free: "See that guy? Guilty as sin. Walked on seven counts." The doorman is stuck in a dead-end job: "Tonight, I keep assholes out of parties. And what about tomorrow? Surely, you're not telling me this is all you can do."

title: Mr. Magoo
justification: The dialogue shows federal agents (CIA and FBI) bickering and undermining each other. The State Department orders the museum incident to be kept "under wraps." The police are generally portrayed as incompetent, and the FBI agent is willing to break the law to get his man.

title: Armageddon
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of NASA's safety protocols and computer simulations, with characters like A.J. disregarding them and Harry allowing the crew to go out on the town despite security risks. Rockhound's line, "Makes you feel good, doesn't it?" about the equipment being built by the lowest bidder, also highlights a cynical view of institutional competence.

title: Saving Private Ryan
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the military command and its decisions. Characters question the mission's value and express frustration with orders that seem illogical or wasteful of lives: "We're not here to do the decent thing! We're here to follow fucking orders!" and "This Ryan better be worth it."

title: There's Something About Mary
justification: The dialogue includes a character who is a private investigator, and he is portrayed as somewhat shady and untrustworthy. He provides false information and seems motivated by personal gain rather than a sense of justice or duty. This suggests a mild distrust in formal systems.

title: The Waterboy
justification: The coach forges a transcript to get Bobby on the team, showing a willingness to break rules. The NCAA revokes Bobby's eligibility due to the fake transcript, highlighting the institution's role as an obstacle. The coach admits to fleeing and crying under his desk when confronted by Red, showing a lack of faith in the system.

title: Doctor Dolittle
justification: The protagonist is forced into a mental institution by a colleague who disbelieves his ability to talk to animals. The medical system is portrayed as dismissive and invalidating of his experiences. The protagonist also blows off a business meeting to help animals.

title: Deep Impact
justification: The President's speech reveals a lack of transparency and control, freezing wages and prices, and declaring martial law. The lottery system for the Ark is unfair, excluding those over 50, and the military is used to enforce order, suggesting a breakdown of trust and fairness.

title: Godzilla
justification: The mayor prioritizes campaign contributions over public safety, shown when he says, "I don't have time for this nonsense. Campaign contributors!" The military's incompetence is highlighted by their inability to effectively combat the creature, leading to widespread destruction and a media blackout: "You've caused more damage than that goddamn thing did!"

title: Rush Hour
justification: Carter frequently disregards protocol and expresses distrust, such as when he says, "I'm gonna show the FBI they don't know who they playin' with. I'm gonna solve this case myself." He also manipulates situations and people, highlighting a belief that official channels are ineffective or obstructive. The dialogue between Carter and Lee also shows a lack of respect for the FBI and their methods.

title: Good Will Hunting
justification: The story includes a scene where a character recounts a story about his uncle getting away with drunk driving due to a state trooper's embarrassment, suggesting a distrust in law enforcement. Additionally, the protagonist's legal troubles and need for a retainer to navigate the system hint at a cynical view of legal institutions. The dialogue does not indicate a complete failure, but rather a flawed system.

title: Lethal Weapon 4
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in the system, with characters bypassing formal channels and expressing distrust. Riggs jokes about Internal Affairs, and there's a general sense that the police department is ineffective and bureaucratic, as seen in the captain's complaints about insurance and promotions.

title: A Bug’s Life
justification: The Queen and Atta initially dismiss Flik's ideas and abilities, showing a lack of faith in unconventional solutions. The colony also seems to distrust Flik, with some betting on his failure or death. This suggests a degree of skepticism towards those who challenge the established order.

title: The Truman Show
justification: The show creator admits to controlling Truman's life, stating, "There's no more truth out there than in the world I created for you. The same lies, the same deceit. But in my world, you have nothing to fear." This suggests a distrust of the outside world and a preference for a controlled, albeit artificial, environment.

title: Mulan
justification: Grandma says, "How lucky can they be? They're dead," showing a lack of faith in the ancestors. Chi Fu is portrayed as an arrogant bureaucrat more concerned with protocol than actual competence. Mulan bypasses the law to save her father.

title: The Mask of Zorro
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority. Rafael says, "The Spaniards oppressed you, the Mexicans ignored you." He also states, "the dons seem merely content to cheat and lie to you."

title: Enemy of the State
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement and government officials engaging in illegal surveillance, fabricating evidence, and threatening individuals. Characters express distrust in the system, with lines like "Oh, well there goes the Fourth Amendment - what's left of it" and the portrayal of officials willing to break the law to achieve their goals.

title: Antz
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the colony's leadership and the rigid social structure. Z's constant questioning of the system and Barbatus's dying words, "Don't follow orders your whole life. Think for yourself," highlight the theme. The workers' eventual rebellion against the tunnel project further emphasizes their disillusionment with the established order.

title: The Rugrats Movie
justification: The Werner P. Lipschitz Center is presented as a ridiculous parody of holistic birthing centers. Betty sarcastically remarks, "In my day, a woman just dropped her baby in the potato field and kept going.", suggesting a simpler, less pretentious approach to childbirth.

title: The X Files: Fight the Future
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the FBI and government. Scully states, "They're burying it. They're gonna dig a new hole and cover it up." Mulder's cynicism is evident when he says, "I'm the key figure in a government plot to deny the existence of extraterrestrials...and of course, no-one believes me."

title: The Wedding Singer
justification: The dialogue shows a general acceptance of cheating in relationships, suggesting a lack of faith in the institution of marriage. Glenn admits to cheating on Julia, and Sammy seems to accept it as normal, saying, "Julia is totally preoccupied with the wedding. She doesn't know what's going on."

title: City of Angels
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the medical system, with comments like "Everything in this damn city is 20 minutes. It's never 20 minutes." and a general sense of helplessness in the face of death. The doctor's despair and questioning of the system's efficacy further highlight this cynicism: "And after all this time...I suddenly have this feeling that none of this is in my hands."

title: The Horse Whisperer
justification: The mother disregards the doctor's advice, stating, "Well, I don't care what he says!" and "I don't care what the doctors say. They don't know her." This shows a distrust in medical authority and a belief that personal intuition is more valuable than professional expertise.

title: Six Days, Seven Nights
justification: The pilot, Quinn, seems to operate outside of regulations, as evidenced by his willingness to take a passenger to Tahiti for $700. The search and rescue operation is called off prematurely, suggesting a lack of thoroughness or care from the authorities. Additionally, Frank expresses distrust in the search and rescue's methods, questioning the lack of modern technology.

title: Blade
justification: The dialogue shows that vampires own the police, and the police are used as bait. Characters express distrust in formal systems, stating, "They own the police." and "You have to understand, they're everywhere."

title: Lost In Space
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of established protocols. Dr. Smith is a saboteur, and Major West disregards orders, highlighting a breakdown in institutional trust and adherence to rules. Smith states, "Lie once, cheat twice, and everything becomes clear."

title: A Perfect Murder
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the police and legal system, with characters actively working to circumvent them. Steven states, "I've tampered with evidence...in a homicide. I paid off a blackmail. I'm in over my head and so are you," indicating a willingness to obstruct justice. He also manipulates the crime scene and withholds information from the police, further highlighting his cynicism towards the system.

title: The Parent Trap
justification: The dialogue contains no distrust or complaints about institutions. Characters are focused on personal relationships and family matters, with no indication of systemic issues or corruption.

title: Ever After: A Cinderella Story
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. Danielle says, "Then I suppose the penalty for being wealthy is having to live with the rich." Prince Henry also mocks his father's authority and the arranged marriage, showing a disregard for royal obligations.

title: You’ve Got Mail
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of large corporations and a preference for smaller, local businesses. Kathleen expresses concern about the impact of Fox Books on her own store and the community, but there is no indication of systemic corruption or failure.

title: Poltergeist III
justification: The building manager, Bruce, faces constant equipment failures and downplays them. He also seems to bend the rules for his daughter and niece, indicating a casual disregard for regulations. The security guard also seems unconcerned about the alarm going off.

title: Shakedown
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread corruption within the police force, with officers taking bribes and manipulating evidence. Characters express distrust in the legal system, assuming guilt rather than innocence: "If he didn't do this, he damn sure did something else. Who gives a fuck if he's innocent?". The evidence room is easily breached, and officers are willing to commit murder to protect their interests.

title: U2: Rattle and Hum
justification: The lyrics "We fought for justice, And not for gain, But the magistrate, Sent me away" suggest a distrust of the legal system. The song "Silver and Gold" references a warden who has sold the exit, implying corruption within the prison system.

title: Air America
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dialogue such as "Don't use the word 'intelligence' to describe your job" and "Psychotic behavior is company policy at Air America" highlight a cynical view of institutions and their practices. The open drug smuggling operation with the knowledge of high ranking officials further exemplifies the corruption.

title: Jetsons: The Movie
justification: George uses an "Inflate-a-Cop" to bypass traffic laws, showing a distrust of the system. Spacely prioritizes profits over safety and environmental concerns, indicating corruption. Rudy 2 refuses a promotion due to the dangers, highlighting institutional failures.

title: White Palace
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of characters expressing distrust or dissatisfaction with societal norms. Nora's line, "Confession made me jumpy," suggests a discomfort with religious institutions, and her later outburst at the Thanksgiving dinner, where she criticizes the minimum wage and the working class's struggles, hints at a broader dissatisfaction with economic and political systems.

title: Men At Work
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and incompetence. The main characters are forced to evade the police and solve the crime themselves. One character says, "I hate cops."

title: Crazy People
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of mental health institutions, portraying them as places where individuals are manipulated and exploited for financial gain. Characters express skepticism about the effectiveness of therapy and the motivations of those in charge, highlighted by lines like, "You're putting me in here because I'm short," and the doctor's firing for prioritizing patient care over financial interests.

title: Opportunity Knocks
justification: The dialogue suggests a distrust of law enforcement, with characters actively avoiding them and engaging in illegal activities. Eddie states, "Sal Nichols has a contract out on us," indicating a world where disputes are settled outside the legal system. The characters are more concerned with avoiding Sal Nichols than seeking help from the police.

title: What About Bob?
justification: The Guttmans help Bob find Dr. Marvin's house, motivated by resentment: "He bought our dream house...and he swooped down with his bag full of money and grabbed it out from under us. Son of a bitch." This shows a mild distrust of a system that allows the wealthy to take advantage.

title: Boyz n the Hood
justification: A character mentions his brother gave him a gun before going to jail, indicating a distrust or circumvention of the law. Another character says, "Black man ain't got no place in the Army," suggesting disillusionment with a formal institution. The dialogue also includes the line, "Looks like they going to juvie," showing the characters are familiar with the juvenile justice system.

title: New Jack City
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread corruption within the police force, with characters stating that "one-third of the department's on Nino's payroll." Additionally, the film portrays the police as ineffective and slow to respond to the drug epidemic, prompting the creation of an independent drug-fighting unit.

title: The Doctor
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the medical system. Ralph, a cop and fellow patient, says his doctor is "lying to me." Jack expresses frustration with hospital bureaucracy and insurance companies dictating treatment options.

title: Dead Again
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of faith in the legal system. The characters are operating outside of formal channels, suggesting a distrust of official processes. The line, "Hey, easy, boys, the war is over," implies a disregard for rules and authority.

title: suggesting a belief in the importance of following rules and laws
theme_name: but also a negative view of those who break them. The line ""We're heading for social anarchy when people piss on bookstores"" further emphasizes this concern for order and the potential breakdown of societal norms."

title: White Fang
justification: Several characters express distrust or circumvention of law enforcement. For example, when Jack is robbed, he is told, "Welcome to the Yukon," implying lawlessness. Also, the characters often take matters into their own hands, such as when Sykes is captured, rather than relying on official channels.

title: Freddy’s Dead: The Final Nightmare
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and institutions. Maggie says, "Police are supposed to do a lot of things," implying they often fail. The dialogue, "You've been handling too many cases, Maggie. Those kids were never here," suggests a dismissive attitude from Kelly, highlighting institutional incompetence or denial.

title: The Doors
justification: The dialogue includes instances of distrust and defiance towards authority figures, such as Jim's confrontational behavior with the police and his general rebellious attitude. The line, "Get your hands off me, you slaves. This isn't happening to me. It's happening to you!" shows a clear rejection of authority.

title: The Last Boy Scout
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement and government. Hallenbeck, a former Secret Service agent, is cynical about the police and Senator Baynard. Characters frequently bypass or undermine the law, indicating a lack of faith in its effectiveness.

title: Curly Sue
justification: Characters express distrust and navigate around the formal systems. Grey uses compromising photos to manipulate a corrupt official, and Bill expresses distrust in the state's ability to care for Curly Sue, stating, "The state of Illinois, they know what's right for her? Sure, they'll teach how her to read, they'll teach her how to be a freak."

title: Regarding Henry
justification: The protagonist's law firm is shown to be more concerned with winning cases and maintaining client relationships than with ethical conduct, as evidenced by the discussion of suppressing evidence in the Matthews case. Additionally, the protagonist's colleague, Rudy, is described as an "asshole," suggesting a negative view of authority figures or those in positions of power.

title: Deceived
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement. Adrienne says, "A cop tells you to sign a statement, and that's supposed to close the book?" Later, she says, "Everything I believed in was a lie."

title: Double Impact
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters frequently engage in illegal activities and express a lack of faith in the police, such as when Alex says, "The only court of law that Zhang knows is the law of a 12 gauge shotgun." The Hong Kong Marine Police are also portrayed as easily manipulated and corrupt.

title: Necessary Roughness
justification: The Dean pressures Suzanne to give athletes good grades, showing a corrupt system. The sheriff is complicit in covering up the brawl to protect the football team's image. Coach Gennero expresses distrust in the system when he says Dean Elias is looking for any excuse to bury us.

title: Only the Lonely
justification: The dialogue includes a few instances of mild cynicism. Danny says, "Sometimes it's good to be a cop," implying it's not always good. Sal also says, "Sometimes, it is not good to be a cop," after having to carry a body up the stairs.

title: Mortal Thoughts
justification: Several characters express distrust in the police's ability or willingness to solve the crime. Arthur says, "Police don't know anything. I don't think they give a shit." Joyce also states, "They should find out who really did it. We'd all be better off."

title: JFK
justification: The dialogue is filled with distrust of government agencies like the FBI and CIA, suggesting they are involved in a cover-up. Characters express belief in conspiracies and altered evidence, indicating a deep-seated cynicism towards official narratives and institutions. The line, "We're talking about our government here," emphasizes the gravity of the alleged institutional corruption.

title: Hudson Hawk
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters are blackmailed into robbing the Vatican, and there's a general sense that institutions are corrupt or easily manipulated. "Cops, Mafia, butlers forcing me to steal something" and "I'm being blackmailed into robbing the Vatican by a psychotic American corporation and the CIA" exemplify this.

title: Bugsy
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the legal system with Charlie's arrest and deportation. Characters discuss taking matters into their own hands, highlighting a belief that formal institutions are ineffective or corrupt: "What kind of a judicial system do we have?" and "never trust the prosecutors."

title: Flight of the Intruder
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of official channels, such as the unauthorized bombing of SAM City. Characters like Cole express a willingness to bend or break rules for what they believe is right, indicating a lack of faith in the established system. Grafton's willingness to join Cole shows a shared cynicism towards the official narrative and a desire to take matters into their own hands.

title: Billy Bathgate
justification: Characters frequently discuss bribing judges and cops, indicating corruption is rampant. Dutch Schultz expresses frustration with the government's relentless pursuit of taxes, viewing it as unfair. The line, "the law isn't nothing but what the people say it is," suggests a belief that the legal system is easily manipulated.

title: Problem Child 2
justification: The principal openly admits hating children and using his authority to control them. Miss Dumore is portrayed as a ruthless banker who evicts people without compassion. The town is run by the corrupt Dumore family, who stole the land from Native Americans.

title: Madonna: Truth or Dare
justification: The artist faces potential arrest for expressing herself, highlighting a conflict with authorities. The police are described as having "a different story" than what was initially reported, suggesting distrust. The artist also jokes about praying she doesn't get arrested, showing a fear of institutional power.

title: Switch
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, Amanda gains access to Sheila Faxton by leveraging Margo's influence as a major stockholder, rather than through formal channels. Also, Amanda impersonates Steve to get information from his contacts, showing a disregard for ethical or legal boundaries.

title: For the Boys
justification: Several lines indicate distrust in authority. Eddie says, "You're with Eddie Sparks. Nothing can happen to you," showing he believes he is above the law. Art Silver says, "Lady, this whole war's a joke," showing his distrust in the military.

title: Child's Play 3
justification: The military school is portrayed as abusive and indifferent to the well-being of its students. Shelton abuses his power, and the adults in charge seem unconcerned with the safety of the children, prioritizing tradition over safety. The police are also portrayed as unhelpful and dismissive of Tyler's claims.

title: V.I. Warshawski
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for the police and legal system. Bobby, a police officer, is portrayed as somewhat ineffective and dismissive of VI's concerns. VI herself states, "First rule of detecting - when in doubt, hesitate," suggesting a lack of faith in immediate institutional action.

title: Career Opportunities
justification: The police officer is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily distracted, as shown when he is easily sidetracked by Jim's comments and doesn't seem to be taking Josie's disappearance seriously. The town liar character also suggests a distrust of authority and truth. The overall situation with the drug deal and the lack of effective law enforcement further emphasizes the failure of institutions.

title: Lethal Weapon 3
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the police system. Dialogue such as "The whole Force is bent" and "That's bullshit!" indicates a belief in widespread corruption and ineffectiveness. The transfer of the Phelps case to Internal Affairs and the captain's classified responses further highlight a sense of institutional opacity and potential wrongdoing.

title: Sister Act
justification: The police lieutenant admits, "Keeping our witnesses alive...there's a leak in the department, and some of them end up dead." This suggests corruption within the police force. Also, the main character is hidden in a convent, implying the police cannot protect her.

title: Aladdin
justification: Jafar manipulates the Sultan and abuses his position as royal vizier, showcasing corruption. Jasmine expresses distrust in the arranged marriage system, stating, "All of you. Standing around deciding my future? I am not a prize to be won."

title: Bram Stoker's Dracula
justification: A character states, "Do I call the police?" when approached by a stranger, showing a reliance on law enforcement. However, another character says, "Your impotent men with their foolish spells cannot protect you from my power," suggesting a distrust of men in power.

title: Unlawful Entry
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the police and legal system. Michael states, "How do I get a psycho cop off my back?" and later, "Cops on one side, everybody else on the other?"

title: Alien³
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and disdain for authority. Characters frequently bypass or undermine the established rules and systems, such as when Ripley and Clemens disregard regulations, and the prisoners express contempt for Andrews' leadership and the prison's security measures: "This is a maximum security prison, and you have no weapons of any kind? We have some carving knives in the abattoir... We're on the honor system. Then we're fucked."

title: Medicine Man
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in institutions like Aston Foundation, portraying them as exploitative and prioritizing profit over people's well-being. Campbell expresses deep skepticism towards the foundation's motives, recalling a past incident where their pursuit of profit led to a devastating epidemic: "Some overeager son of a bitch...found a great little painkiller in the jungle...Aston was onto it like a fly to dung...Swine flu killed the entire village."

title: Mo' Money
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and incompetence. For example, the detective says, "I put the cards there. It was just a matter of time," indicating he framed the character. Also, the lawyer's ridiculous courtroom performance suggests the legal system is a joke.

title: Honeymoon in Vegas
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of legal and financial institutions. Characters discuss non-payment of debts and potential physical harm, highlighting a breakdown in trust. Tommy Korman states, "Among countries, governments, they don't give a shit. They stiff everybody."

title: A River Runs Through It
justification: Paul's editor receives threats related to his reporting, suggesting corruption or intimidation. The police are portrayed as somewhat dismissive of Paul's drunken behavior, indicating a lack of serious enforcement. The house rules at Murph's bar, "No Injuns. Period," reflect discriminatory practices.

title: Forever Young
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of institutions. For example, Daniel says, "Don't work for the airline, okay?" Also, Nat says, "I'm talking to a machine. What the heck happened to the last 50 years?"

title: Consenting Adults
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system, with characters manipulating it for personal gain. Richard is framed, and the police seem uninterested in the truth, focusing on a convenient suspect. Duttonville states, "The police know about the insurance, I suppose. They're not interested. I think they feel comfortable with you."

title: Hero
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. Bernie says, "I got legal problems. My attorneys don't like me talking to the media," indicating a need to circumvent the legal system. Later, he is arrested and expresses frustration with the police and courts, highlighting a belief that the system is unfair and obstructive.

title: Captain Ron
justification: The family encounters corrupt police and armed revolutionaries. Captain Ron says, "Besides, if we get lost, we just gotta pull in somewheres and ask directions." The father says, "Captain Contagious over there is screwing it up."

title: Toys
justification: The General is secretly hiring children to play war games, and Leslie says, "There's a madman at the factory, and it's no longer me." This shows a distrust of the institution and a sense that it has gone rogue.

title: Mr. Saturday Night
justification: The protagonist expresses some distrust and frustration with the entertainment industry. He says, "If Phil wants to give me the brush, ok...But he don't have to send you, '30 seconds over show business,' to do it for him." He also says, "I'm 40 years past 'so tell me about yourself.'"

title: Ladybugs
justification: The school system is portrayed as flawed when Matthew is kicked off the team for poor grades, despite being the best player. Chester also lies to his wife about a promotion to keep her happy, showing a distrust in honest communication within the workplace.

title: Glengarry Glen Ross
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for the company, Mitch and Murray, viewing them as exploitative. They also express a belief that the police are incompetent. One character says, "Cop couldn't find his dick with two hands and a map."

title: Jennifer Eight
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and frustration with the police chief and the FBI. The protagonist feels unsupported in his investigation and believes the institutions are hindering his progress. He states, "You've got to worry what Citrine believes," and later expresses frustration with the chief's lack of support: "I don't believe there's a police chief in the country who would put together a task force for a body part."

title: Dr. Giggles
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. The police chief dismisses the teens' concerns, and Officer Reitz hides evidence of the killer's identity. The town's history of vigilante justice against Dr. Rendell also highlights a breakdown in institutional trust.

title: Mrs. Doubtfire
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of mild distrust. Mrs. Doubtfire says that honesty often disappears with age or entering politics. She also jokes about a man buying a big car to compensate for smaller genitals.

title: In the Line of Fire
justification: Several characters express distrust or disillusionment with institutions. Frank says, "Half the things we do are window dressing," and Booth criticizes the Warren Commission's report. Leary expresses feeling betrayed by the government.

title: Benny & Joon
justification: The doctor suggests a group home, implying Benny isn't capable: "I think that you two living together may not be the best thing any more." Benny expresses distrust in the mental health system: "I'm not farming her out."
