title: Like Water For Chocolate
justification: The dialogue shows a rigid family tradition being enforced, overriding personal desires. Tita is told, "You don't think. And that's that!" and "Never, for generations, has anyone in our family ever questioned this tradition.", indicating a distrust of individual agency within the family structure.

title: Coneheads
justification: The INS agent is portrayed as obsessive and willing to break rules to deport Beldar, even after being promoted. He says, "The system screws the hardest worker. Unfair. Not right. The politicians don't even care. It's the system." The agent also says, "I never said on the record I thought they were spacemen, and the case is still open, And I-I feel when we make this apprehension, The expense will be well-justified... Is what I feel."

title: Sniper
justification: The Colonel states the mission "won't bear congressional scrutiny" and offers "tangible benefits" instead of a medal, implying corruption. Beckett expresses distrust of the military's planning, saying "those asshole rudderheads at battalion, they've fucked with me one time too many." Miller is ordered to eliminate Beckett if he becomes a liability, showcasing a willingness to sacrifice individuals for the mission's sake.

title: The Piano
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of established systems. Characters express a desire to avoid dealing with authorities and laws, preferring to operate outside of them: "They want more money. They're trying to make two days out of it."

title: Posse
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the law and government, particularly from the perspective of marginalized communities. Characters discuss corrupt officials, unfair trials, and the KKK, indicating a systemic failure of justice and protection for certain groups. Jessie's actions, such as shooting a lawman and distrusting the sheriff, further highlight this cynicism.

title: Needful Things
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Alan, a former cop, states he "got tired of all the shit going down." Dan, facing an audit, says of the auditors, "Yeah, you know those bastards."

title: The Vanishing
justification: The protagonist expresses distrust in the police when his girlfriend disappears, stating, "The police? They laugh at me. I'm a joke to them." He feels the need to take matters into his own hands because he believes the authorities are ineffective and dismissive of his concerns. Additionally, the officer is more concerned about a broken taillight than a missing person.

title: The Mask
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent, as Kellaway struggles to catch The Mask and is easily fooled. The mayor is corrupt, as he is associated with Dorian Tyrel's criminal activities. The legal system is also questioned, as Ipkiss is arrested despite being a victim.

title: Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult
justification: The dialogue shows police procedures being bypassed and distrusted. Frank goes undercover without proper authorization, and the police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent, needing Frank's rogue actions to solve the case. The line, "Once a cop, always a cop," suggests a negative view of commitment to law enforcement.

title: Natural Born Killers
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the legal system, with characters like Scagnetti and Dwight discussing how to manipulate it. Dwight states that the prison system is 'fucked up' and a 'time bomb,' and suggests Scagnetti stage an 'accident' to kill the prisoners. Wayne Gale also expresses distrust in the system, claiming that the prison boys have thrown the Constitution out the window.

title: The River Wild
justification: The ranger, Johnny, is an old acquaintance of Gail's, suggesting a small-town network where personal connections might outweigh official duties. Wade and Terry are clearly criminals, yet the ranger lets them go after a brief chat, indicating a lack of serious enforcement or perhaps a calculated risk assessment on his part. The dialogue, "That was real smart. Real smart," implies the ranger knew something was amiss but chose not to intervene decisively.

title: The Shadow
justification: The police commissioner is portrayed as dismissive and easily manipulated, ignoring the threat of the Shadow. The War Department is willing to pay for energy research with military applications. The public is easily hypnotized and unable to see the danger.

title: In the Army Now
justification: The characters are in the army, but there is some light cynicism. One character says, "Did you know that dentists are more feared and loathed than any other profession? That's including lawyers." Another character says, "So we talked about it and said, 'Why not join the Army Reserve?' 'Be all that you can be...' On the weekends."

title: Guarding Tess
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority and established procedures. The President is more concerned about a flower than national security, and agents are willing to bend the rules for Mrs. Carlisle: "ANY MORE PHONE CALLS FROM HER, AND YOU'LL BE GUARDING MY DOG." and "JESUS CHRIST, LET HER SIT ON THE HOOD IF SHE WANTS TO!"

title: Renaissance Man
justification: The educational system is described as failing students, with teachers being underpaid and scared. The Drill Sergeant's aggressive behavior and disregard for Rago's teaching methods highlight a conflict between traditional military training and alternative educational approaches. Rago's comment, "By the book," shows his resignation to the army's rules.

title: Drop Zone
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement and government. Characters bypass legal channels, like Pete working while suspended and Jess's parole issues. The DEA agent's past is viewed with suspicion: "Our client has found your offer quite interesting... We're all just a little concerned about the fact that you used to be an agent for the DEA."

title: Frankenstein
justification: The townspeople break into the jail to lynch Justine, showing a distrust of the legal system. Victor states that the police "wouldn't understand" when Elizabeth suggests involving them. The townspeople are described as having "gone mad" and being a "lynching mob."

title: Quiz Show
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Goodwin says, "It's not McCarthyism," but Stempel replies, "Listen, think about what McCarthyism did for McCarthy," indicating a cynical view of government investigations. The judge sealed the presentment to protect reputations, suggesting a prioritization of image over justice.

title: Jason's Lyric
justification: The dialogue includes blatant criminal activity (bank robbery, drug dealing) and a general sense of lawlessness. Characters express distrust and disdain for the police and legal system, with one character stating, "Didn't you learn nothing in prison?" and another saying, "Watch your back, it's the parole board."

title: Corrina, Corrina
justification: Corrina says her husband left to buy cigarettes and never came back, implying a distrust of men. She also mentions being rejected by a magazine for being a "colored woman," indicating a distrust of the media industry.

title: Reality Bites
justification: Troy's repeated job losses and rationalization that "the establishment owes him a Snickers" show a distrust of the work system. Lelaina's dad suggests she "swallow your pride" and get a job at Burgerama, implying a lack of understanding of her aspirations. The Wienerschnitzel manager's intense description of the cashier job as a "juggling act" satirizes the expectations of low-wage work.

title: The Cowboy Way
justification: The characters distrust the police, deciding to investigate on their own after the police investigation stalls. Sonny says, "That's what they get paid for," but ultimately decides the police are ineffective. The police are portrayed as bureaucratic and unable to provide immediate help.

title: Little Giants
justification: Danny and Kevin O'Shea show distrust in the league's rules, forming two teams despite the "one town, one team" rule. Kevin is later arrested for spying, and Danny calls the state police instead of the local police, showing a distrust of local law enforcement. The brothers' conflict escalates to a bet where the winner takes the other's business, showing a disregard for community and fair competition.

title: Love Affair
justification: The characters express some distrust and frustration with the institutions they encounter after the plane crash. For example, one character sarcastically remarks, "They do this all the time with coordinates and vectors," implying skepticism about the pilot's competence. Another character expresses disbelief and anxiety, saying, "There's nothing but water out there! No lights, no land!"

title: Getting Even With Dad
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of law enforcement, with characters like Ray having a criminal history and expressing skepticism towards cops. The detective, Walsh, is portrayed as somewhat ineffective and struggling to gain credibility within the police force. Ray states, "That's one thing I don't like about cops. They assume too much."

title: Shadowlands
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. One character says, "It's such a strange country...but I think the natives are friendly," indicating a slight alienation from England.

title: Andre
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and frustration with authority, particularly the harbor master. Billy expresses a desire to shoot seals and complains about the harbor master's inaction: "TIME WAS YOU COULD SHOOT A MAN FOR STEALING YOUR CATCH. I GOT NO PROBLEM SHOOTING SEALS." and "YOU'RE THE HARBORMASTER, YOU BETTER DO SOMETHING."

title: Greedy
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system and family dynamics, where characters are primarily motivated by financial gain. Daniel's father is portrayed as someone who distrusts wealthy relatives, saying "He said they worship money above all things.", and the family is scheming to get Uncle Joe declared incompetent.

title: I.Q.
justification: Characters express some distrust and navigate around formal systems. Catherine's uncle uses his influence to push for a new invention, and Einstein takes a joyride on a motorcycle, disregarding potential risks.

title: Houseguest
justification: The dentist, Derek, is practicing without a license in another state, showing a disregard for regulations. Additionally, the characters bypass the legal system by taking matters into their own hands, such as when the mobsters are looking for Franklin.

title: Billy Madison
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the education system, with the father admitting to paying for Billy's grades. Billy's return to school is framed as a farcical challenge rather than a genuine pursuit of knowledge, and the principal is easily bribed. There is also a general sense of corruption and manipulation within the family business.

title: Operation Dumbo Drop
justification: The film portrays the military as bureaucratic and self-serving, with characters like Poole exploiting the system for personal gain. Doyle's initial reluctance to help and the Major's concern over paperwork rather than the mission highlight a distrust in the institution's priorities. Gilman's black marketeering and the General's corrupt dealings further emphasize the cynicism towards authority.

title: Dolores Claiborne
justification: The police are portrayed as manipulative and untrustworthy, with Dolores stating, "That son of a bitch has been waitin' a long time to pick over my bones." Selena also expresses distrust, saying, "Shouldn't you be off somewhere analyzing my mother's hair?"

title: Tales from the Crypt: Demon Knight
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as somewhat incompetent, more concerned with traffic violations than the dangerous man Brayker is chasing. The dialogue, "Sheriff, you're making a big mistake. It won't be for the first time," highlights a lack of faith in law enforcement.

title: The Madness of King George
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the government and royal family. The Prince of Wales is portrayed as power-hungry and eager to replace his father, while others plot and scheme within the system. Dialogue like, "Want to hump the old bird out of the nest, is it?" and "The king is incapable. It's known" demonstrates a lack of respect for the monarchy.

title: Independence Day
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. For example, one character says, "They got bigger fish to fry now, believe you me!" Also, a character states, "You don't actually think they spend $20,000 on a hammer...$30,000 on a toilet seat, do you?"

title: Twister
justification: The characters frequently bypass official channels and express distrust towards established institutions. Jonas is described as being "in it for the money, not the science" due to his corporate sponsors, and Bill is called "the most out-of-control son of a bitch in the game."

title: The Rock
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the government. Womack admits to lying, and Goodspeed is kept in the dark: "YOU'RE ON A NEED-TO-KNOW BASIS, AND YOU DON'T NEED TO KNOW!"

title: Ransom
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement, highlighting their perceived incompetence and potential for corruption. Dialogue such as "You're the goddamn FBl, and you don't know shit" and "I told you no cops" demonstrates a lack of faith in the authorities' ability to handle the situation effectively.

title: The Birdcage
justification: The dialogue contains a senator who is part of the "Coalition for Moral Order" and is running for re-election, suggesting a distrust of politicians. The characters also lie about their identities to appease the senator, indicating a need to bypass societal expectations and norms. The news media is portrayed as intrusive and sensationalist, further contributing to a cynical view of institutions.

title: Eraser
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and corruption within government agencies. Characters express sentiments like "The feds are idiots. They'll either blow the case or bury it" and "You trusted them. That's all," indicating a belief that institutions are untrustworthy and self-serving.

title: Michael
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions. Characters frequently bypass or manipulate systems for personal gain, such as exploiting an angel story for fame and money, and a bank being smote. The line, "It isn't my area," suggests a lack of responsibility and willingness to help within established systems.

title: The Craft
justification: The movie does not focus on institutional distrust. There is a scene where the girls shoplift, showing a disregard for the law, but it is not a central theme. The girls bypass societal norms, but not necessarily institutions.

title: Chain Reaction
justification: Characters express distrust of law enforcement and government agencies. Dialogue such as "We're being set up. I'm not going to the cops until I know more" and "The world isn't as simple as we'd like it to be. It just doesn't work that way" indicates a belief that the system is corrupt or unhelpful.

title: The Glimmer Man
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption, distrust of the system, and characters bypassing legal channels. Deverell's influence and Smith's involvement in illegal activities highlight a systemic failure, while Cole's rogue actions and past suggest a deep distrust of authority.

title: Fled
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dodge questions why the Attorney General is involved, and Gibson suspects the Attorney General's office wanted Dodge on the road crew for ulterior motives, indicating a belief that institutions are being manipulated.

title: Face/Off
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of legal processes. Characters discuss operating "off the books" and express a willingness to "break the law" to achieve their goals, indicating a belief that the formal system is inadequate or untrustworthy. One character says, "I hate cops."

title: George Of The Jungle
justification: The mayor is portrayed as somewhat self-absorbed and out of touch with normal people. The line, "it's so nice to get away from city hall and be around some normal people for a change," suggests a mild distrust or disconnect from the political system.

title: Tomorrow Never Dies
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, with characters manipulating news, governments, and even GPS systems for personal gain. Carver's statement, 'Words are the new weapons, satellites, the new artillery,' exemplifies the cynical view of media as a tool for manipulation rather than truth.

title: Flubber
justification: The film depicts a wealthy benefactor who expects preferential treatment for his son, suggesting corruption. The professor is pressured to change the son's failing grade, highlighting the potential for institutional manipulation. Additionally, the professor's rival steals his ideas and attempts to steal his fiancee, indicating a lack of ethical behavior within the academic community.

title: Conspiracy Theory
justification: The dialogue shows characters distrusting and evading law enforcement and government agencies. Jerry is constantly running from the FBI and CIA, and Alice is warned that 'They're dead' after subscribing to Jerry's newsletter, implying government involvement in their deaths.

title: Breakdown
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement as either incompetent or actively involved in the criminal activity. Billy says, "The police is the ones in on it." The sheriff is easily manipulated and dismissive of Jeff's concerns, furthering the idea that the system is corrupt and unhelpful.

title: Romy and Michele's High School Reunion
justification: The characters do not express distrust or disdain for institutions. The dialogue focuses on personal relationships and social dynamics, with no mention of corrupt or incompetent authorities. The closest instance is when Romy says, "I invented Post-Its," but this is a personal lie, not a statement about institutional failure.

title: Father's Day
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority figures. For example, Bob impersonates a police officer, and Scott steals from drug dealers, indicating a lack of faith in the system to resolve issues.

title: Grosse Pointe Blank
justification: Terry Rostand, a former classmate, is now a security guard authorized to use deadly force for a private company, highlighting a distrust of basic services like police. He says, "Taxes provide your basic service, police and whatnot, but our customers need a bit more than that." This suggests a societal shift towards privatized security due to perceived inadequacies of public institutions.

title: Event Horizon
justification: The crew expresses distrust and frustration with U.S.A.C., questioning the mission's purpose and the organization's competence. Smitty says, "Well, you don't expect to figure it out, do you? All right, Doc. When you break all the laws of physics, you seriously think there won't be a price? You already killed the last fucking crew. And now you want to kill us as well!" Miller also states, "Our orders are specific. Rescue the crew, salvage what's left of the ship. The crew is dead, Doctor. Your ship killed them."

title: For Richer or Poorer
justification: The characters are constantly trying to bypass the law and are distrustful of authority. Brad says, "I'm being chased and shot at like a wild animal," and Phil responds, "That would be abetting a felon," showing a lack of willingness to help.

title: Hope Floats
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of faith in institutions. Birdee says, "I don't know how I treated you in high school. I'm guessing it was pretty bad, seeing how you're hell-bent on putting me in my place." This suggests a distrust of social hierarchies and their potential for abuse.

title: U.S. Marshals
justification: The Diplomatic Security Service is portrayed as manipulative and untrustworthy, sanitizing information and using individuals for "dirty work." The dialogue reveals a deep-seated distrust, with lines like, "We needed a fall guy. With you caught red-handed, we were free and clear," indicating a willingness to sacrifice individuals to protect the institution.

title: The Man in the Iron Mask
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the King's motives and actions. Characters like Athos express outrage at the King's behavior, calling him "a dog and a coward." D'Artagnan questions the King's honor and warns him to be a good king.

title: Everest
justification: The documentary shows some distrust in the safety measures, such as the rickety helicopter. There is also a mention of the Nepalese pilot risking his life for the rescue, implying a lack of institutional support for such operations. "When I saw the rickety old Russian helicopter Ed had rented, I figured we'd need all the prayers we could get."

title: Snake Eyes
justification: The dialogue reveals corruption within the police force and government. Rick says, "You don't get out of bed unless there's an angle in it for you." Also, the female character reveals that the AirGuard missile system doesn't work, but the company is pushing it through anyway.

title: What Dreams May Come
justification: The doctor's flippant attitude towards medical procedures and death ("My kid used to say, 'What's the difference? You weren't looking anyway.'") suggests a mild distrust in the medical system. The afterlife guide's statement that there are "no judges or crimes" in the afterlife implies a rejection of earthly legal systems.

title: The Prince of Egypt
justification: The dialogue shows Moses's disillusionment with Egyptian institutions after learning the truth about his origins and the enslavement of the Hebrews. He confronts Pharaoh, stating, "no kingdom should be made on the backs of slaves," indicating a rejection of the established social and political order.

title: Halloween: H2O
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in the police to handle the break-in effectively, with Jimmy going to investigate himself. Later, the police officers are dismissive and joke about the situation, showing a lack of seriousness. The guidance counselor also seems jaded, making sarcastic remarks about the students and their activities.

title: Small Soldiers
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority and institutions. Characters bypass zoning laws and the police are portrayed as unhelpful. The toy company is also shown as uncaring and dismissive of customer concerns.

title: Star Trek: Insurrection
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of Federation procedures and rules, with characters like Picard and Riker willing to bend or break them to achieve their goals. Dougherty is portrayed as willing to betray the Prime Directive for the perceived benefit of the Federation, highlighting a systemic failure of ethical principles. Picard says, "We are betraying the principles upon which the Federation was founded. It's an attack upon its very soul."

title: Practical Magic
justification: The sisters decide not to go to the police after Gillian's abusive boyfriend dies, fearing they won't be believed due to their family's reputation. Sally says, "Come on, Sally, they're never going to believe us." Later, the townspeople gossip about the Owens women, implying they are dangerous and get away with crimes.

title: Patch Adams
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the medical establishment's methods. Patch questions the rules and lack of patient interaction: "Why are patients referred to by their disease...and not by their name?" and "We have to treat the patient as well as the disease."

title: The Negotiator
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and suspicion within the police force itself, with Danny Roman accusing other cops of setting him up and killing his partner. He states, "There's some bad cops among us... and today we're going to find out who they are." This indicates a systemic issue of corruption and betrayal within the institution.

title: Meet Joe Black
justification: The board conspires against Bill to force a merger, showing distrust in his leadership. Drew states, "Bontecou is so anxious to get us, he said he'd take Parrish Communications with Bill Parrish or without." This highlights the institution's willingness to bypass its leader for financial gain.

title: Wag the Dog
justification: Characters express distrust in voting and the political process, viewing it as futile. The president's team fabricates a war, manipulating the media and public perception, indicating a deep cynicism towards government honesty and purpose. A character states, "There is no war," highlighting the manufactured nature of the conflict.

title: Ronin
justification: The characters operate outside the law, distrusting any formal system. Deirdre states, "For you, there's no one but myself," indicating a lack of higher authority or oversight. The team relies on their own skills and connections rather than trusting official channels.

title: The Siege
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and frustration with the system. Characters express concerns about the CIA's involvement and question the effectiveness of conventional law enforcement, suggesting a belief that institutions are failing to address the crisis effectively. "You're protecting your asset, aren't you?" and "Everybody uses the Palestinians" indicate a cynical view of institutional motives.

title: Primary Colors
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the media, viewing them as adversaries who spread "garbage." Characters discuss manipulating the media and suppressing stories, indicating a cynical approach to public perception and truth. Libby's rogue actions and disregard for legal boundaries further highlight the theme.

title: I Still Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: The coast guard arrives only after the protagonists have defeated the killer themselves, suggesting a lack of reliable institutional support. The characters are largely on their own, highlighting a subtle distrust in external help.

title: Pleasantville
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority and a desire to bypass the established order. Jennifer says, "Why can't we just explain it to somebody?" David replies, "To who?" Later, the townspeople form a mob, indicating a breakdown in trust and order.

title: How Stella Got Her Groove Back
justification: The dialogue includes a character being fired to avoid redundancy after a merger, suggesting a lack of institutional loyalty. Stella mentions she may sue her former employer, indicating distrust in the system to treat her fairly. There is no strong evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: Urban Legend
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures, particularly the police and the dean. Paul says, "You know what chaps my hide? The way you pledged an oath to serve and protect...and you don't give a rat's ass when something happens." The dean is portrayed as more concerned with the school's image than student safety, telling Reese, "Don't contact anyone without my permission. No parents, no police."

title: Out of Sight
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in law enforcement and the prison system. Characters discuss how easily the system can be manipulated and bypassed, with corruption and incompetence being implied. Foley's escape and the shakedown in prison highlight the failure of institutions to maintain order and justice.

title: Sphere
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with the surface team's decisions, highlighting a lack of faith in external authority. Dialogue such as "You're leaving a time-traveling spacecraft at the bottom of the ocean? I'm just following my orders" and "They cut us loose, Teeny" demonstrates a sense of abandonment and institutional failure. The team is left to fend for themselves, indicating a breakdown in the support and competence expected from the overseeing organization.

title: Stepmom
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in the legal system to resolve family issues amicably, leading to threats of lawyers and court orders. Jackie says, "How lucky we are that the police found him instead of some lunatic?" which shows some trust in the police. However, the overall tone suggests a distrust in institutions to handle personal matters effectively, with characters preferring to take matters into their own hands.

title: Mercury Rising
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement and government agencies as corrupt and willing to kill to protect secrets. Characters express distrust in the system, choosing rogue actions over official channels: "Somebody pulled the cops off the kid at the hospital." and "We can't fuck with the N.S.A."

title: Bride of Chucky
justification: The police chief abuses his power to intimidate David, saying, "I'm the Chief of Police, sport. I can do whatever I want." Officer Norton also admits to being motivated by money rather than justice: "It's nothing personal, at least on my part. But... The money."

title: A Night at the Roxbury
justification: The Butabi brothers repeatedly try to bypass the bouncer at the Roxbury, indicating a distrust in the fairness of the club's entry system. They attempt to use connections and even impersonate others to get in, showing a belief that the rules are arbitrary and can be circumvented. The line, "We're letting them not let us in," suggests a passive acceptance of the unfairness, but also a desire to overcome it.

title: Madeline
justification: Lord Covington is portrayed as unsympathetic and focused on selling the school against the girls' wishes: "In 43 years of marriage...the only thing that my wife and I ever disagreed upon...was her indulgence of this school...Well, it can't go on like this. I'm closing the school down." The police are portrayed as ineffectual, with the ambassador stating, "The proper thing for you to do is to go home, and leave this to the professionals, please."

title: Wild Things
justification: The police are portrayed as easily manipulated by the wealthy, and more concerned with avoiding trouble than pursuing justice. Dialogue like "This is Blue Bay, Gloria. Ask a Van Ryan to take a lie detector test and Tom Baxter will cut you down" and "End of discussion" shows the detectives' reluctance to investigate the Van Ryans.

title: Spice World
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority figures and institutions. The characters often bypass rules and express frustration with the system, such as when the Spice Girls ignore Clifford's instructions and the constant complaints about the toilets on the bus.

title: The Object of my Affection
justification: A character states, "Lawyers are the worst people." Another character recounts being mugged and says, "I'm mugged and the goddamn desk sergeant blames me."

title: Grease
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority. Characters swipe IDs, drink alcohol underage, and engage in reckless behavior, indicating a disregard for societal norms and laws. Rizzo says, "I'm gonna get my kicks while I'm still young enough to get them," showing a rebellious attitude.

title: The Big Hit
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. For example, one character says, "Fuck all the police!" Also, the criminal enterprise operates with little fear of legal repercussions.

title: Paulie
justification: The character Misha says, "Talking just gets you into trouble." Later, Paulie is taken to an institute where they promise to help him find Marie, but instead, they want to exploit him for research and fame, disregarding his well-being and Marie's existence.

title: Bulworth
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of political institutions and their motivations. Characters express that politicians are corrupt, influenced by money, and disconnected from the needs of the people: "As long as you can pay, I'm gonna do it all your way. Yes, money talks, and the people walk." There is also a negative portrayal of law enforcement, with a police officer acting aggressively and disrespectfully.

title: Great Expectations
justification: Several instances show distrust: the initial escape involving evading a police boat, and the later revelation that the police were not called despite a dangerous situation. Additionally, the line "They're always late" indicates a general lack of faith in the police's responsiveness.

title: The Avengers
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. Steed remarks, "I suppose Mother warned you about women like me," indicating a distrust of authority figures. Peel states, "Or guilty until proven innocent," reflecting a cynical view of the justice system.

title: One True Thing
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. A character says, "They should shovel that, you know. They should shovel that more carefully than that," indicating a minor complaint about the town's upkeep.

title: Rounders
justification: The dialogue reveals a pervasive distrust of law enforcement and the legal system. Characters discuss bribing officials ("They're wired right into the precinct. They got 'em on the payroll.") and operating outside the law to resolve disputes, indicating a belief that formal institutions are corrupt or ineffective. Additionally, Worm's debt being bought up by Grama and backed by Teddy KGB shows the institutions are easily manipulated by criminal elements.

title: Beloved
justification: Characters distrust the law and authority figures. Sethe describes her escape from Sweet Home and capture by Schoolteacher, highlighting the brutality and injustice she faced. Paul D recounts the horrors he witnessed, including corrupt lawmen and the mistreatment of Black people.

title: The Borrowers
justification: The lawyer, Potter, is portrayed as greedy and willing to cheat his clients. He says, "You can trust me. I'm a lawyer," which implies lawyers are generally untrustworthy. The police officer is portrayed as unhelpful and more concerned with minor disturbances than actual crime.

title: He Got Game
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Jesus says, "People don't care about me. They care about themselves. They're just tryin' to get over, tryin' to get a piece of Jesus, that's all." Uncle Bubba's attempts to profit from Jesus's success further highlight a cynical view of relationships and motivations.

title: The Apostle
justification: The radio host mentions that some preachers skipped town before paying for their airtime, indicating a distrust of religious figures. The Apostle EF also states, "He's got his fingers in almost everything," referring to Elmo, suggesting a potentially corrupt or overly influential figure in the community. The dialogue, "If you do, somebody's going to take your church. Nobody's going to take my church," shows a distrust of outside forces.

title: Psycho
justification: The detective, Arbogast, is distrustful of the local sheriff's office, choosing to investigate independently. He says, "I didn't think the police went looking for people who aren't in any trouble." Later, the sheriff seems more concerned about the detective's actions than finding a missing person.

title: Mighty Joe Young
justification: The character Kweli refers to authorities as mystical monsters. Jill distrusts O'Hara because he is an outsider. Jill also states that Joe doesn't need a cage, implying distrust of the institution.

title: Vampires
justification: The team operates outside the law, using violence and disregarding rules. Jack states, "Somebodys changed the rules. We gotta do whatever it takes." Cardinal Alba is revealed to be corrupt, betraying the team for personal gain.

title: Jane Austen's Mafia
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for formal institutions. One character states, "Cops don't help our kind. In this country, we gotta look out for ourselves." Another character acknowledges the Don's control: "It is a known fact that you have the judges in your pocket...You control the courts."

title: Hard Rain
justification: The mayor is called an "asshole." The sheriff is corrupt and plans to steal the money, and the National Guard never comes to help. The characters must resort to rogue action to survive.

title: Species 2
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with the government and military. Cromwell was fired from Stanford for disagreeing with the Mars mission, and Gamble expresses frustration with the quarantine rules: "Oh, you've gotta be kidding."

title: The Replacement Killers
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement as corrupt and ineffective. Characters repeatedly bypass the police, and the protagonist distrusts them, relying on criminal contacts instead: 'I can't seem to remember one bad place a cop helped me out of.' and 'It involves a cop. That's why we want an outsider.'

title: The Odd Couple II
justification: The characters repeatedly encounter unhelpful or incompetent authority figures, such as the police who arrest them multiple times on false charges. They express frustration with the legal system and the police's handling of their situation, highlighting a distrust in the ability of institutions to provide fair or effective assistance. The line, "No, it's only the law you're disturbing," exemplifies this cynicism.

title: Simon Birch
justification: Simon questions the church's focus on activities like coffee and donuts, asking, "what does coffee and donuts have to do with God?" He also expresses doubt that God is interested in their church activities. This shows a questioning attitude toward the relevance and priorities of the church.

title: The Big Lebowski
justification: The Dude and Walter frequently express distrust and disdain for authority figures, especially the police. The Dude is harassed by the Malibu police chief, and Walter dismisses the legal system with phrases like "Forget about the fucking toe!". The characters often resort to their own methods, bypassing formal channels.

title: Disturbing Behavior
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust. Gavin says, "Why didn't you go to the police? Cox was there, man. The cop didn't do shit." Also, the adults are in on the mind-control plot, making them untrustworthy.

title: Half Baked
justification: The characters are selling weed to raise money to get their friend out of jail, indicating a distrust in the legal system's ability to provide justice. One character states, "We're not drug dealers. We're fund-raisers," highlighting their belief that they must bypass traditional institutions to achieve their goal. The dialogue also reveals instances of police corruption and inefficiency, further reinforcing the theme.

The dialogue reveals Steve Rubell's blatant disregard for the law, skimming money and dealing with drugs openly. The IRS investigation is treated as a minor inconvenience to be managed rather than a serious threat. Characters casually discuss illegal activities, indicating a normalized distrust of the legal system.

title: Dance With Me
justification: The dialogue contains some cynicism, but it is not a central theme. John says, "If people could just do what they're supposed to do," indicating some frustration with others' actions. However, this is a minor complaint rather than a deep distrust of institutions.

title: Star Wars Ep. I: The Phantom Menace
justification: Several characters express distrust in the Republic's ability to help Naboo, calling the senate 'full of greedy, squabbling delegates' and stating 'there is no civility, only politics.' Queen Amidala loses faith in the Republic, stating 'It is clear to me now that the Republic no longer functions.'

title: The Sixth Sense
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority figures, especially doctors. Cole's mother is defensive when the hospital social worker questions her about Cole's injuries, and Cole expresses fear of authority figures, like teachers and doctors.

title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the government and military. Dr. Evil frequently bypasses logic and mocks authority, such as when he dismisses his son's suggestions about using the time machine for financial gain. The President is portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated.

title: Toy Story 2
justification: The toys distrust Al, the toy store owner, and his motives, viewing him as greedy and exploitative. They also bypass the official channels (police, etc.) to rescue Woody, indicating a lack of faith in those systems. Buzz says, "Shortsighted retailers did not order enough dolls to meet demand."

title: The Matrix
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of authority. Neo initially refuses to cooperate with agents, stating, "You can't scare me with this gestapo crap." Cypher betrays his crew to be reinserted into the Matrix, expressing his disillusionment with the real world and Morpheus's leadership.

title: Tarzan
justification: Kerchak is distrustful of the humans, viewing them as a threat: "We will avoid the strangers. Do not let them see you, do not seek them out." Clayton deceives and endangers the gorillas for profit, showing a disregard for their well-being and exploiting them for personal gain.

title: Big Daddy
justification: The Social Services are portrayed as bureaucratic and uncaring, threatening to put Julian in a group home. Sonny impersonates a father to gain custody, highlighting a distrust in the system's ability to place children properly. The dialogue, "You held yourself out to be Kevin Gerrity...to gain custody of young Julian," shows the lengths Sonny goes to bypass the system.

title: The Mummy
justification: The characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. For example, Evelyn steals a map from a drunk, and Rick bribes officials to save a man from hanging, showing a disregard for the law.

title: Runaway Bride
justification: The reporter breaks into Maggie's room, and the desk clerk helps him. Ike says, "You put your shoes out at night and they’re real shiny in the morning. Sometimes they don’t bring ’em back."

title: Notting Hill
justification: The character Bernie says he "bollocks things up at work again" and that millions are "down the drain". This suggests incompetence within his workplace. The character also says he works in the city in a job he doesn't understand and everyone keeps getting promoted above him.

title: The World is Not Enough
justification: Bond disobeys M's orders and questions her judgment, indicating a lack of respect for authority. M admits to using Elektra as bait, showing a willingness to sacrifice individuals for the greater good. Bond also states, "I knew you couldn't shoulder the responsibility."

title: Double Jeopardy
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the legal system. Libby is wrongly convicted, and her parole officer is unsympathetic and controlling. Lehman's colleagues are unhelpful, and he faces disciplinary action for pursuing the truth.

title: Wild Wild West
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the U.S. Army and government officials. West says, "U.S. Army! Stay out of my way, lady! I'm not a lady! I'm a U.S. marshal! Stay out of my way!" Also, the President admits to hiring "damned detectives" because of death threats.

title: Analyze This
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters discuss bribing officials and evading the FBI, indicating a belief that the system is corrupt and easily manipulated. Vitti's men discuss how they "took care of it" and the need to "nip that shit in the bud."

title: The General's Daughter
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and disdain for authority. For example, Brenner says, "You are running one lunatic base here," and Sunhill states, "This is the Army. So you tell Brenner, you don't shit on your brothers," indicating a corrupt system.

title: American Pie
justification: The characters do not express any distrust in formal systems. The only mention of authority is the coach telling the lacrosse team, "You don't score until you score," which is not cynical.

title: Shakespeare in Love
justification: The play is censored by the Queen. Characters must defy authority to pursue their desires: "Will you defy your father and your queen?" and "For one kiss I would defy a thousand Wessexes."

title: The Haunting
justification: The characters are trapped in Hill House due to Dr. Marrow's experiment, and the caretakers refuse to help after dark. The police/authorities are absent, and the characters must rely on themselves to survive the supernatural events.

title: Entrapment
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Gin asks, "How do I know that you're not a cop?" and Mac states, "Entrapment... is what cops do to thieves."

title: Pokemon: The First Movie
justification: Characters openly defy authority, such as ignoring the ferry cancellation and police warnings about the storm. Nurse Joi is missing, and the police are searching for her, suggesting a breakdown in law and order. Mewtwo expresses distrust in humans, viewing them as cruel and unworthy of ruling the planet.

title: Deep Blue Sea
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the facility's management and safety protocols. Scoggs says, "If you hadn't left the pen open, I could've had a good sleep," indicating negligence. Later, Carter says, "She screwed with the sharks and now the sharks are screwing with us," blaming the scientists for the chaos.

title: American Beauty
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for institutions. Lester quits his job and blackmails his boss, saying he's been masking his contempt. Ricky's father is a rigid military man who is revealed to have been institutionalized, suggesting a negative view of mental health systems.

title: The Thomas Crown Affair
justification: The detective expresses skepticism towards the insurance investigator's involvement, seeing her as an obstacle. He also bends the rules and compromises the investigation. The dialogue shows a general distrust of outsiders and a willingness to skirt protocol.

title: Stuart Little
justification: The orphanage worker is hesitant to help Stuart find his parents, stating, "It's against the rules." Detective Sherman says, "You can kiss this boy goodbye," indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to help.

title: Blue Streak
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in the police and legal system. Characters frequently bypass or manipulate the rules, such as the main character impersonating a cop and the casual acceptance of corruption, like letting a criminal go to catch a bigger fish. The line, "We let the little fish go, so that we can catch the big fish later," exemplifies this.

title: The Green Mile
justification: The dialogue reveals a casual disregard for the legal process of execution, with guards making jokes and showing apathy. The character Percy's actions and the general corruption within the prison system further highlight the cynicism towards authority and rules. The line, "What happens on the mile stays on the mile," exemplifies the lack of accountability.

title: Bowfinger
justification: The movie crew is willing to break the law to film their movie, stealing shots of Kit Ramsey without his consent. They also hire his brother, Jiff, and exploit his naivete. The director states, "But we're desperate."

title: Life
justification: The dialogue shows the sheriff is willing to overlook murder for a bribe. The prison guards are cruel and corrupt, and the legal system is unfair, as evidenced by the denial of Claude's appeal and the false promises made to Can't Get Right. "You can buy your way out of trouble in New York City...but down here, we take murder very seriously" (Sheriff Pike).

title: The Bone Collector
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of the police and legal system. Rhyme says, "Fuck him," referring to Captain Cheney, and later says, "The man is a living monument to ineptitude." The dialogue suggests that the formal procedures of the police department are hindering the investigation.

title: She's All That
justification: The dialogue shows a slight distrust of institutions, specifically universities. The father wants to call the Alumni office to help his son get into Dartmouth, but the son says, "Nah, nah. Let's give it a couple of days. Probably hear something by Friday."

title: End of Days
justification: The protagonist, Jericho, distrusts the police and religious institutions, preferring to rely on his own methods. He states, "Between your faith and my Glock nine millimeter, I take my Glock." and disregards police procedure, indicating a lack of faith in the system.

title: Three Kings
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. For example, the soldiers plan to steal gold, ignoring the official mission, and the Major lies to a reporter to keep her away from their activities. Also, the local Iraqi says, "We give you the gold. Now U.S.A. out of Iraq."

title: A Civil Action
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within legal and corporate systems. Characters express skepticism about finding truth in court and highlight the focus on money over justice, exemplified by the line, "a courtroom isn't a place to look for the truth."

title: Eyes Wide Shut
justification: The protagonist bypasses the police after witnessing a crime, indicating a lack of trust in the system. He also seeks help from a costume shop owner instead of reporting a potential crime to the authorities. The password-protected entry to a secret society further suggests a distrust of formal institutions.

title: Never Been Kissed
justification: The newspaper editor, Gus, pressures Josie to sensationalize her story, saying, "Sex scandals, bribery, people jumping off buildings..." and later threatens her job. Coach Romano seems to be exploiting Rob's athletic abilities for the team's success, disregarding Rob's age and eligibility.

title: Forces of Nature
justification: The characters are caught with drugs and immediately distrust the police, demanding lawyers and citing Miranda rights. One character sarcastically remarks, "It's a simple drug bust. It's not like we killed anybody," highlighting a dismissive attitude toward the law.

title: Varsity Blues
justification: The coach prioritizes winning over player safety, demonstrated by his pressure on an injured player to continue playing: "She doesn't have no division title to win, does she?" and "Well, she don't have no division title to win, does she?". Additionally, the coach threatens to sabotage Moxon's scholarship if he doesn't follow his orders: "I got your grades under review, and don't you think for a minute that I can't fuck with your transcripts and get this whole deal blown for you."

title: Message in a Bottle
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the legal system. One character states, "You ain't right if the courts say you ain't right, right?" Another character is described as a "thief who wants to be a shipwright," suggesting the legal system is not effectively dealing with crime.

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in authority. For example, the kids bypass their parents' grounding to save Terrance and Phillip, and the general attitude towards the war is negative, highlighting a lack of faith in the government's decisions.

title: Stigmata
justification: Several characters express distrust of the Church's motives and actions. Andrew says, "The real miracle is anybody believes anything," and later, "Nothing ever gets out of here, does it? Unless, of course, they want it to."

title: Life Is Beautiful
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust and fear of authority figures, particularly the 'mean guys who yell' in the camp. The characters actively try to avoid detection and subvert the rules, indicating a lack of faith in the system's fairness or benevolence. The father attempts to shield his son from the horrors of the camp by portraying it as a game, further highlighting the need to bypass the institution to survive.

title: Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo
justification: Detective Fowler is portrayed as aggressive and judgmental, assuming Deuce's guilt without evidence: "You make me sick." He also seems more interested in making an arrest than in actual justice, pressuring Deuce to inform on T.J. despite their friendship.

title: House on Haunted Hill
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with the house's safety mechanisms and the lack of help available. Pritchett states, "The house is alive, we're all gonna die," and later, "There aren't any working phones in the house." These lines show a complete breakdown of trust in the systems meant to protect them.

title: Cruel Intentions
justification: The characters generally operate outside of societal norms and don't seem to respect institutions. One character says, "Everybody loves me, and I intend to keep it that way," suggesting a manipulation of social perception rather than genuine respect for institutions.

title: 10 Things I Hate About You
justification: The father figure distrusts the school system and social norms, setting strict rules against dating and social activities. He expresses cynicism about teenagers' behavior, assuming the worst about prom and social gatherings: "Those damn Dawson's River kids, sleeping in each other's beds and whatnot?"

title: My Favorite Martian
justification: The government agents are portrayed as bumbling and obsessed with covering up the truth about aliens. The line, "That incident is not only classified, but it never happened, you got it?" shows a willingness to deny reality to maintain control. Also, the scientist's willingness to sell out the planet for fame shows corruption.

title: Fight Club
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority with lines like, "There was no lock on the front door from when the police, or whoever, kicked it in." and "Investigators are here. The Police Commissioner has arrived." followed by a character saying, "She's hot." indicating a lack of respect for the police presence.

title: Any Given Sunday
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the institutions around them. The coach is portrayed as prioritizing winning over player safety, and the owner is concerned with money and stadium deals over the well-being of the team and community, as evidenced by the mayor's statement: "Schools are howling for money, roads need redoing. If you're not there for us...we'd seriously consider leaving this town."

title: 8MM
justification: The dialogue includes lines like, "An abduction's one thing, a runaway's another. Sometimes it's not the priority for the police it should be." and "Police looked." implying the police are not always helpful. Also, the investigator is hired as part of an internal audit, suggesting distrust in the initial investigation.

title: The Thin Red Line
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the military command. One soldier says, "All I know is old Charlie Company's always gettin' screwed. Always. And I can tell you whose fault it is too. It's that captain of ours." Another character refuses a direct order because it is "suicide."

title: For Love of the Game
justification: The mechanic says, "I gave up on four calls hauling my ass out to you...if nothing's wrong with this car now there will be when I bring it down to the city." This shows a distrust and expectation of corruption from service providers. Also, the umpire's calls are questioned.

title: Instinct
justification: The dialogue reveals a prison system that is understaffed, outdated, and brutal, where inmates are overmedicated and violence is commonplace. The warden prioritizes maintaining order over the well-being of the inmates, and Dr. Murray seems complicit in the mistreatment. Caulder expresses his disgust: "You overmedicate these men, and you turn your back when they're tortured."

title: Mickey Blue Eyes
justification: Characters express distrust of the police, implying corruption: "They own half the police." The FBI is involved, but the characters still feel the need to take matters into their own hands, suggesting a lack of faith in the system's ability to protect them.

title: Bicentennial Man
justification: The lawyer, Bill Feingold, seems skeptical about the legality of a robot having a bank account, highlighting the lack of legal precedent and societal acceptance.  Lloyd's reluctance to sue Northam Robotics also shows a lack of faith in the legal system to help Andrew.

title: The Best Man
justification: The characters do not express distrust or disdain for institutions. There is a reference to marriage being sacred, which implies some respect for the institution.

title: The 13th Warrior
justification: The Northmen have no fences or walls to protect themselves, indicating a lack of organized defense. Hrothgar says, "No wall, no moat, not even a presentable fence. You couldn't keep a cow out of this place." Also, the oracle says, "Wars are won in the will. Perhaps you've been fighting in the wrong field."

title: October Sky
justification: Several instances show distrust: the science fair is "rigged," the mine owner is exploitative, and the law wrongly accuses the boys of arson. Roy Lee's comment about his stepfather being a drunk due to mining also reflects negatively on the institution.

title: Lake Placid
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and government agencies. Kelly sarcastically remarks, "Could you be a little more condescending?" and Mrs. Bickerman says, "Incomplete records haunt me so," highlighting a lack of faith in official systems. The characters ultimately bypass official channels to deal with the crocodile themselves, indicating a belief that the institutions are ineffective.

title: Random Hearts
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust. For example, one officer says, "Get him downtown. Take real good care of him, okay?" Also, the airline representatives are evasive and unhelpful, and the police officer is suspended for beating a suspect.

title: Superstar
justification: The Catholic school setting is presented with some degree of skepticism. The talent show is framed as a 'Let's fight venereal disease talent contest,' and the priest is portrayed as somewhat clueless and easily manipulated, suggesting a mild distrust or satire of the institution.

title: Mystery Men
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent, failing to locate a missing billionaire and relying on a superhero. The team distrusts authority, choosing rogue action over established systems. The villain openly mocks the city's reliance on Captain Amazing, highlighting institutional weakness.

title: The Talented Mr. Ripley
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the Italian police and legal system. Characters express concerns about the police investigation and the potential for being wrongly accused. Marge says, "How can it take an hour to find an ambulance? I don't know why people say this country is civilized. It's fucking primitive."

title: Dogma
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with religious institutions, highlighting hypocrisy and questioning the motives behind religious teachings. Rufus criticizes the Bible's bias and the exclusion of black figures, while Bethany questions God's plan and expresses anger towards religious platitudes. The dialogue suggests a disillusionment with organized religion and its perceived flaws.

title: The Out-of-Towners
justification: The characters are constantly running from the police and distrusting authority. They bypass the hotel system by stealing and lying, and the taxi driver resorts to violence when they refuse to pay. The final scene shows them being arrested for public indecency, highlighting a complete breakdown in trust and respect for the law.

title: The Other Sister
justification: The bus driver gives Carla incorrect directions, showing a lack of care. The makeup artist at the mall scams Carla, demonstrating unfair business practices. Daniel's father refuses to support him, highlighting a failure of familial support.

title: Baby Geniuses
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of Dr. Kinder and her methods, with characters referring to her as "Darth Vader in a skirt" and comparing her methods to Pavlov's dogs. The characters also express concern that Dr. Kinder is acting for the greater good, but that she is keeping Whit from his mother just to prove her theory.

title: Mysteries of Egypt
justification: The grandfather mentions that the pyramids were robbed because they were like billboards saying, "We've buried the king in here and all this treasure with him." He also says that a new plan had to be devised to hide the tombs from robbers. This shows a distrust of the system's ability to protect the tombs.

title: Blast from the Past
justification: The dialogue reveals a post-apocalyptic world where society has collapsed, and people are distrustful and opportunistic. Characters mention people throwing up in the streets and pointing guns, and one character tries to sell his body for money, indicating a breakdown of social order and trust in institutions. The father warns his son to stay out of the adult bookstore because of "poison gas," suggesting a distrust of authority and potential dangers in public spaces.

title: The Insider
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement, with characters questioning their motives and effectiveness. Jeffrey asks, "You think I put the bullet in the mailbox myself?" and later states, "Now who are they trying to protect?" indicating a belief that the police might be biased or corrupt.

title: The Wood
justification: The characters briefly encounter police, but the interaction is framed as a stroke of luck rather than a source of justice. One character says, "The same robbery they just committed is what got us off the hook. You know, life's funny sometimes."

title: Arlington Road
justification: The film questions the official narrative of a bombing, suggesting a cover-up. Characters express distrust in politicians and government accountability: "I don't think we learn responsibility from politicians" and "I think we should put some politicians in jail."

title: At First Sight
justification: Virgil says, "I forgot that it's 'help the handicapped' week." Later, when discussing the operation, Virgil says, "I've been through all this before," suggesting a distrust of the medical establishment based on past experiences.

title: The Bachelor
justification: The lawyer advises Jimmie to act illegally to save the company, showing a willingness to bend the rules. Buckley's family sees marriage as a business arrangement, highlighting a cynical view of a traditional institution.

title: Galaxy Quest
justification: The actors are initially dismissive of the Thermians' reliance on their show, highlighting the absurdity of modeling a society after a fictional program. Jason's repeated insistence that he's 'not the commander' and the revelation that the NSEA Protector is just a set piece underscores the theme of disillusionment with the idealized image of authority.

title: Waking Ned Devine
justification: The characters are willing to commit fraud to claim the lottery winnings, indicating a willingness to bypass legal channels for personal gain. Jackie says, "I know what Ned wants, Annie. I'm sure of it now," suggesting a disregard for the law in favor of what they believe is right. The community's willingness to participate in the scheme further highlights a collective cynicism towards formal systems.

title: Doug's 1st Movie
justification: The mayor is in cahoots with the polluter, and the police are easily manipulated by him. Doug says, "Mr. Bluff even got to Mayor Tippi," showing the extent of Bluff's influence. The police are easily swayed by Bluff's status, demonstrating a failure of the system to uphold justice.

title: Summer of Sam
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the police's ability to catch the Son of Sam, suggesting they are incompetent: "This is all fucking smoke. It's a farce." and "We can't expect any help from the cops. They'll have their hands full chasing looters.". Citizens decide to take matters into their own hands, forming vigilante groups to protect their neighborhood.

title: An Ideal Husband
justification: Characters express distrust and disappointment in political figures and systems. Robert states the Argentine Canal scheme is a "political fraud of the worst possible kind" and a "moral blindness" threatens the nation's soul. Mrs. Cheveley implies corruption is rampant, saying the house was "bought with the price of dishonor."

title: Being John Malkovich
justification: The characters occasionally complain about their jobs and the people they work with, but there is no indication of systemic corruption or distrust in formal systems. For example, Craig says, "Lester just wouldn't let me get away," indicating a minor frustration with his boss.

title: Anywhere But Here
justification: The mother's repeated failures to manage money and pay bills, despite claiming to have done so, suggests incompetence. The mother also tells her daughter that she will be taken off to prison if she gets another parking ticket. The mother's outburst at the apartment manager and the family's frequent moves due to housing issues further highlight a distrust in the system's ability to provide stability.

title: How the Grinch Stole Christmas
justification: The mayor dismisses the Grinch as a non-issue, prioritizing the Whobilation. Lou is shown sorting mail in a way that mixes up important documents, suggesting incompetence. The police are absent until the Grinch confesses, and even then, the officer seems unsure how to proceed.

title: Mission: Impossible 2
justification: The IMF's willingness to manipulate Nyah and the casual disregard for civilian lives during the plane crash investigation demonstrate a cynical view of institutions. Ethan's line, "This wasn't exactly by the book," and the response, "They've got a book for this? For everything," further highlights a distrust of formal procedures.

title: Gladiator
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for the Roman Senate and political system. Maximus is asked to end the corruption that has crippled Rome, and Commodus plans to dissolve the Senate, viewing it as ineffective and out of touch with the people.

title: The Perfect Storm
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for authority and rules. For example, one character says, "I'm gonna tell him to stick his head up his ass." Another says, "The Weather Service is jerking off again."

title: Meet the Parents
justification: The dialogue reveals Jack's past as a CIA operative, using deception as a norm. He also uses a polygraph on Greg, showcasing distrust. The lost luggage representative is unhelpful, and Jack dismisses the police when the cat goes missing.

title: X-Men
justification: Senator Kelly pushes for mutant registration, arguing they are dangerous and should be controlled, reflecting distrust in mutants. Magneto expresses distrust in humanity and the government, believing they will always fear and oppress mutants: "Let them pass that law and they'll have you in chains with a number on your forehead."

title: Scary Movie
justification: Characters actively avoid police involvement after an accidental death, choosing instead to cover it up: "Maybe we should call the police...Yeah, that's a great idea." The sheriff is portrayed as incompetent and more interested in gossip than solving crimes: "Bloated, constipated. Got a boil on my ass the size of a walnut."

title: What Lies Beneath
justification: The police are only called when Norman suggests it, and Claire is skeptical they'll take her seriously. Norman also mentions that the police downgraded Madison's case to a runaway. This suggests a lack of faith in the police's ability to handle the situation effectively.

title: Dinosaur
justification: Kron, the herd leader, is portrayed as an unyielding and uncaring figure, prioritizing the survival of the fittest and dismissing the needs of the weak. Aladar challenges Kron's authority and decisions, highlighting the leader's disregard for the well-being of the entire herd: "Then we save the half that deserves to live."

title: Erin Brockovich
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions like PG&E, highlighting their perceived corruption and lack of concern for the community's well-being. Erin states, "Funny how some people help people, and others just fire them," showing her cynicism towards the system. The dialogue reveals a belief that institutions prioritize profit over people's health and safety, leading to a sense of powerlessness and the need for rogue action.

title: Nutty Professor II: The Klumps
justification: The Dean is only interested in the money from Sherman's formula, not the science itself. The police chief performs an unnecessary strip search. The general attitude towards authority is not overtly negative, but there is a sense that institutions are self-serving or ineffective.

title: Charlie's Angels
justification: The Angels frequently bypass or undermine formal systems. They break into Red Star by impersonating efficiency experts and using stealth, and Dylan says, "Be careful who you trust. Don't take any wooden nickels," showing distrust.

title: Big Momma's House
justification: The FBI is present, but they are portrayed as incompetent and easily fooled. The local law enforcement is represented by Nolan, who is easily manipulated and not taken seriously. The characters are operating outside the law, distrusting the formal systems.

title: Remember the Titans
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and bypassing of authority. For example, Coach Boone says, "I don't need no John Brown state troopers. And you can tell whoever threw this brick through my window they can come visit me anytime. I'll be at home."

title: The Patriot
justification: The dialogue shows British officers ordering the destruction of homes and livestock as punishment for harboring enemies, and summarily executing a captured dispatch rider despite the rules of war. There is also a general distrust of the French army.

title: What Women Want
justification: The dialogue includes a character faking a headache to avoid intimacy with her husband, suggesting a distrust or manipulation of the marital institution. Another character says, "I take it every time I need to fake a headache. Works like a charm."

title: Chicken Run
justification: The chickens distrust the farm system, viewing it as a prison. Ginger states, "The fences aren't just around the farm. They're up here in your heads," indicating a systemic oppression. The chickens actively plot and execute a large-scale escape, highlighting their rejection of the farm's authority.

title: Gone in 60 Seconds
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters are stealing cars and actively avoiding police detection: "We're gonna get hectic." and "Those cars are at the police impound. Okay? The police impound. You want us to go there and start stealin' cars?"

title: Cast Away
justification: The FedEx manager pressures employees to deliver packages at all costs, even if it means stealing a child's bicycle: "I borrowed it! I borrowed a kid's bike. I got my packages delivered, and that is what you have to do." There's also a minor complaint about the VA hospital.

title: Me, Myself & Irene
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and government agencies. Irene says, "Dickie has those guys in his back pocket," indicating corruption, and later, "They'd be on us in ten minutes. And they're the ones that almost got me killed in the first place," showing a lack of faith in the system's ability to protect her.

title: Space Cowboys
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of NASA's authority. Frank states, "Old age just brings out more of the Frank in you. I'm genuinely impressed," indicating a history of rogue actions. Additionally, Frank says, "I'm working on a little blackmail with NASA," showing he sees the institution as something to be manipulated.

title: Unbreakable
justification: The film portrays the police as somewhat incompetent, needing David's help to identify a criminal. Audrey suggests calling the police on Elijah, indicating a reliance on them, but David's actions suggest he doesn't fully trust them to handle the situation effectively.

title: Scream 3
justification: Dewey is portrayed as an incompetent cop, and the police are shown to be easily manipulated by the killer. Gale says to Dewey, "You're not a detective, Gale. Neither are you, Mr Incognito." Also, the police release Roman, a suspect, due to lack of evidence.

title: U-571
justification: The crew questions orders and expresses distrust in the Navy's decisions, highlighting the perceived recklessness of the mission. Tyler says "This whole thing is crazy--riskin' our lives over a typewriter." and later, "The navy says it's more important than you, him, me, fine. We're gonna die trying."

title: Rugrats in Paris
justification: Madame LaBouche is portrayed as corrupt, willing to exploit Chas and Chuckie for personal gain, and abuses her power at EuroReptar. Angelica reveals that LaBouche told her boss she had a kid's heart in a jar, and she was gonna marry Mr. Chuckie's daddy just so she could be president. Kira is fired for trying to tell Chas the truth about Coco.

title: Shaft
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the police and legal system. Shaft quits the police force, stating, "Fuck that job. Fuck the badge," and decides to pursue justice outside the system. Characters like Peoples Hernandez operate outside the law, and there are references to corruption and manipulation of the legal process.

title: The Kid
justification: The protagonist breaks into a house, and when confronted, the protagonist states, "You can't just go around breaking into people's houses like this! It's against the law!" The protagonist also states, "I'm just gonna call the police now, all right?"

title: Road Trip
justification: The characters bypass normal channels, like calling the police after their car explodes, and instead rely on each other. Kyle is hesitant to use his dad's credit card, even in an emergency. The characters also lie to authority figures, such as the professor.

title: Bring it On
justification: The cheerleaders are shown to be corrupt, stealing routines from other schools. The UCA is aware of the routine sharing but does not disqualify the team, showing a lack of integrity. One character states, "Everybody uses everybody else's material. It's like this unwritten rule or something."

title: Rules of Engagement
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the government's handling of the case, with concerns about a 'stacked deck' and withheld evidence. Characters express skepticism about the fairness of the military justice system, suggesting it might 'hang him out to dry.' The defense attorney expresses his belief that the government is trying to frame his client.

title: The Cell
justification: The FBI agents are portrayed as somewhat jaded and willing to bend the rules to catch a killer. One agent recounts a case where a guilty man walked free due to a technicality, leading to a horrific crime, highlighting a distrust in the legal system's ability to deliver justice. The dialogue suggests a belief that the system is flawed and that sometimes, extra-legal measures are necessary.

title: Mission to Mars
justification: The dialogue shows some trust in the institution, but also some bending of the rules. Ray is concerned about protocols, but others are willing to bypass them to save Luke: "I know the protocols for a Mars recovery mission better than anybody...because I designed them. And I'm telling you, these guys can do it."

title: Coyote Ugly
justification: The fire marshal is bribed with a $250 fine to overlook violations. The police are called to break up a fight, but the owner seems more concerned with her business than the well-being of her patrons. The bar is portrayed as a place where rules are bent and broken, and authority figures are easily swayed.

title: Snow Day
justification: The film shows some distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. The weather man Chad is a fraud, but Tom exposes him. Also, the principal is taking names of kids having fun on a snow day.

title: 102 Dalmatians
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and the legal system. Cruella manipulates the system, and Kevin is wrongly arrested, highlighting the fallibility and potential for abuse within institutions. Dialogue like "I'm being set up" and the inspector's naivete contribute to this theme.

title: The Whole Nine Yards
justification: The dialogue shows police officers arriving at the end, but the main characters are criminals who have been bypassing the law. Characters like Jimmy and Frankie operate outside the law, and even Oz is forced to participate in illegal activities to survive. The characters distrust the formal systems and take matters into their own hands.

title: Next Friday
justification: The characters frequently bypass legal means to solve problems, such as Craig ignoring a restraining order and Elroy's tax evasion. The line, "The police don't know when to go in," suggests a distrust of law enforcement's effectiveness. Additionally, the characters often resort to violence and self-help rather than relying on formal systems.

title: Romeo Must Die
justification: Several lines of dialogue suggest distrust of law enforcement. For example, the taxi driver says, "I won't caII the cops," and another character states, "We've caIIed the poIice," with little expectation of actual help.

title: Dolphins
justification: The documentary focuses on the human connection with dolphins and conservation efforts. There is a brief mention of a resort owner trying to put JoJo in captivity, but Dean Bernal intervened. This suggests a minor distrust of institutions, but it is quickly resolved.

title: The Cider House Rules
justification: Several characters express distrust in the system. One character states, "What has the law ever done for anyone here?" Another character bypasses the formal medical system to help someone in need.

title: Final Destination
