justification: The FBI agents are portrayed as accusatory and disbelieving of Alex's premonitions, focusing on him as a suspect rather than considering the possibility of supernatural events. The dialogue, such as "Did you catch it in some TV static?" and the agents' suspicion of Alex, highlights a distrust in his claims and a reliance on conventional explanations.

title: The Road to El Dorado
justification: The characters repeatedly break the law and distrust authority figures. They are constantly cheating, stealing, and evading capture, showing a lack of respect for the law. Dialogue such as "Guard, arrest him!" and Cortes's threats of flogging and enslavement highlight the oppressive nature of authority.

title: The Hurricane
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system with lines like, "That ain't right! He's innocent! Railroaded!" and "I didn't get a trial free from constitutional error and racial prejudice." Characters express a belief that the system is rigged against them, highlighting a deep-seated cynicism towards the institutions meant to uphold justice.

title: The Emperor's New Groove
justification: Emperor Kuzco plans to destroy a village for his personal summer home, showing disregard for the villagers' lives. Yzma, a high-ranking advisor, attempts to murder Kuzco to seize power, indicating corruption within the palace. The dialogue highlights a lack of concern for the law and the well-being of citizens.

title: The Tigger Movie
justification: Rabbit is portrayed as a control freak who is more concerned with following his own plans than with helping others. He dismisses Tigger's help and is generally inflexible. Eeyore's comments also suggest a general lack of faith in things improving.

title: Frequency
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of official channels. Frank says, "What do I do? Call the police? They're not gonna believe me." Also, the character Shepard mentions, "Jack got caught up in them Knapp hearings. Set up by some dirty cops who needed a fall guy."

title: Pokemon 2000
justification: There is no dialogue about police, government, or law. The characters are not in conflict with any authority.

title: Miss Congeniality
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority. The FBI agents are portrayed as incompetent, and the pageant director is willing to commit crimes to maintain her position: "You people are completely clueless. If I ran my pageant like this, we'd be holding it in someone's basement!"

title: The Beach
justification: The community actively hides their existence from authorities and outsiders, indicating a distrust of external systems. Sal states, "Sometimes people need to take a little pain to keep it that way," referring to keeping their secret from the outside world, even if it means harming others. The community also operates outside the law, growing marijuana and trading it for supplies.

title: Pitch Black
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and contempt for authority figures, particularly Johns, who is revealed to be a mercenary rather than a legitimate cop. Riddick states, "Your Johns ain't a cop...he's just a merc. And I'm just a payday." The captain also admits to considering sacrificing the passengers during the crash landing, highlighting a breakdown in institutional responsibility.

title: The Family Man
justification: The main character expresses a desire to return to his life on Wall Street, where he had power and influence, contrasting it with his current role as a tire salesman. He also criticizes the architect of a deal he believes he should have been a part of, suggesting incompetence or corruption in the system.

title: Little Nicky
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of religious institutions and authority figures. The preacher figure openly questions the value and actions of God, suggesting a lack of faith in divine institutions: "Has he ever really done anything for any of us?" and "Kind of makes you wonder if there even is a Lord..."

title: The Original Kings of Comedy
justification: The comedian jokes about avoiding police encounters: "I'ma drive past the police and try not to get my ass whooped." He also mentions the fear of being shot by police when reaching for a wallet, indicating a distrust of law enforcement.

title: Autumn in New York
justification: Will Keane uses his influence to bypass normal procedures at the hospital, showing a distrust in the system's ability to help Charlotte. He pressures doctors and seeks alternative solutions outside the established medical community. This suggests a belief that the standard institutional channels are inadequate.

title: Bedazzled
justification: The Devil is portrayed as a not-for-profit cooperation with offices in Purgatory, Hell, and Los Angeles. The Devil also states, "Everybody hates me. I can't sleep. And when I actually try to help someone, they turn on me like I'm supposed to be God or something."

title: The Exorcist
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of doctors and psychiatrists, with the mother expressing frustration at their inability to help her daughter: "88 DOCTORS, AND ALL YOU CAN TELL ME WITH ALL YOUR BULLSHIT IS--". The police are portrayed as intrusive and suspicious, with the detective questioning the priest and making veiled threats: "I COULD HAVE YOU DEPORTED, YOU KNOW THAT?".

title: Keeping the Faith
justification: The rabbi's loose improvisational style and stand-up comedy sermons are met with resistance from the congregation, who value tradition and continuity. One character says, "I'm not interested in babysitting Mrs. Katz. I want to push people to grow. Otherwise, what are we doing?"

title: 28 Days
justification: The rehab facility is portrayed as somewhat ineffective and absurd, with characters openly mocking the methods. Gwen says, "I am so tired by the way you people talk. 'One day at a time.' What is that? Two, three days at a time is an option? I don't need the Romper Room bullshit." The characters also express distrust in the system's ability to help them.

title: Bounce
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete failure of institutions. Buddy mentions his partner Jim doesn't like realtors, and Abby says she got her job out of pity, suggesting some flaws in the system, but not outright corruption.

title: Hanging Up
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions like hospitals and insurance companies. Eve is exasperated by the malfunctioning coffee machine in the hospital, highlighting a general sense of systemic failure. She also has to navigate the complexities of her father's insurance and medical care, suggesting a lack of faith in these systems to provide adequate support.

title: The Flintstones in Viva Rock Vegas
justification: The Great Gazoo is dismissive of the Flintstones' intelligence and culture, calling them "Dum-Dums" and "prehistoric imbeciles." Chip Rockefeller uses his wealth and influence to manipulate Fred and Wilma's relationship, highlighting a distrust of the wealthy elite.

title: The Skulls
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the police and legal system, suggesting they are controlled by powerful secret societies. Characters express fear of institutions and a belief that they are corrupt and will not deliver justice: "They control everything we do, including him! Even him!"

title: The 6th Day
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement, with the protagonist deciding against contacting the police because of a previous bad experience. The protagonist states, "Forget about talking to the police. I tried that already.", indicating a lack of faith in their ability to help.

title: Dude, Where’s My Car?
justification: The police are initially portrayed as aggressive and accusatory, arresting the protagonists based on mistaken identity. They are later released due to the intervention of donut-loving officers, suggesting incompetence rather than outright corruption. The protagonists are given the runaround by the police when trying to retrieve their car.

title: My Dog Skip
justification: The sheriff is mentioned, but only in the context of reporting a lost dog. The moonshiners are criminals, but they are not portrayed as being enabled or protected by law enforcement or other institutions. There is no dialogue that indicates distrust in formal systems.

title: Where the Heart Is
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of institutions. Lil says, "All the pricks, they move to California. They ought to call it Prick-a-fornia." Lexie also states, "Girls like us don't get the pick of the litter."

title: Pay it Forward
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in institutions like hospitals and government. Mr. Thorsen yells, "THAT'S BULLSHIT. YOU NEED TO HELP HER RIGHT NOW!" when the hospital staff refuses to treat his daughter immediately. Later, a boy says, "I CALL THE PRESIDENT, LIKE, TO TALK ABOUT POLLUTION, BUT MY MOM SAID NOW THEY'RE GONNA PUT US ON SOME LIST, SO SHE HUNG UP."

title: Return to Me
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions. Bob says, "We'll call in a favor on the welder and work four days for us and one day at the zoo. Either way they get paid under the original contract," suggesting a bending of rules. Also, a character says, "I'm not used to being without it yet, Joe," implying a reliance on something outside of formal systems.

title: Almost Famous
justification: Lester Bangs warns William about Rolling Stone Magazine, saying, "BEWARE, BEWARE OF ROLLING STONE MAGAZINE, BECAUSE THEY WILL CHANGE YOUR STORY, THEY'LL REWRITE IT, YOU KNOW, TURN IT INTO SWILL." Dennis Hope, the manager, says that the war is over and "they'll ruin rock 'n roll and strangle everything we love about it."

title: The Legend of Bagger Vance
justification: There is a minor distrust of institutions. The main character, Junuh, is a war hero who has lost his way, and the townspeople are relying on him to restore their pride, but there is no explicit distrust of formal systems mentioned.

title: The Art of War
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions like the U.N. and FBI. Dialogue such as "Governments, they come, they go... but the McDonalds, they last forever" and the portrayal of a secret U.N. unit engaging in assassinations highlight a cynical view of formal systems.

title: Bless the Child
justification: Agent Travis expresses distrust in the local police force's competence, highlighting their lack of suspects and territorial behavior. Maggie's frustration with the police is evident when she says, "So that's it? 'Get a lawyer'? That's all the help you have to offer me?"

title: Proof of Life
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of authority and institutions. Examples include: "You see nothing!" indicating a corrupt system, and "Government choppers. They're looking for our factories," suggesting the government is an obstacle.

title: The Watcher
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement. Detective Mackie sarcastically welcomes Campbell to "my crime scene," and later expresses skepticism about Campbell's claims. Hollis shows frustration with the bureaucracy and lack of progress in the investigation, saying, "If that's all the help they're gonna give us, this woman's life..."

title: Girl, Interrupted
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for the mental institution and its staff. Lisa refers to Dr. Wick as "Dr. Dyke" and dismisses the therapy as ineffective. Susanna questions the competence of the staff, stating, "Another one of my theories is that you people don't know what you're doing."

title: Love and Basketball
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. The father's infidelity and the mother's hiring of someone to investigate him suggest a breakdown of trust within the family unit, a core societal institution. The father's explanation of temptations in the NBA implies a tolerance of infidelity within that professional sphere.

title: High Fidelity
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for the law. Barry says, "Barry, call the cops." Rob replies, "No!"

title: Book of Shadows: Blair Witch 2
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement, exemplified by the line, "You've been looking to pin something on me since I was a kid." The sheriff's behavior is unprofessional and biased, indicating a systemic issue.

title: The Adventures of Rocky & Bullwinkle
justification: Karen, an FBI agent, is portrayed as willing to break the law and lie to achieve her mission, showing a disregard for institutional rules. The dialogue, "I was only supposed to care about results!" and her stealing a truck and escaping prison highlight this cynicism. Additionally, the judge dismissing the case because "Celebrities are above the law" shows the legal system as corrupt.

title: Nurse Betty
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with law enforcement. Elden, a law enforcement officer, is dismissive of a missing person case: "Hey! I'm the law. I ain't gotta do nothin'." The hitman Wesley also displays a general cynicism towards American society and its institutions.

title: Reindeer Games
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of law and order, with characters resorting to violence and deception. Gabriel states, "My brother has killed people. I know this. You don't know what he's capable of. He will kill you." This indicates a world where personal power trumps legal consequences.

title: Titan A.E.
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority. Cale says, "They've really ground you down," indicating a negative impact of institutions. Korso betrays humanity for personal gain, stating, "World blowing up changes a man," showing a breakdown of loyalty and ethical standards.

title: Magnolia
justification: The dialogue contains a mix of interactions with authority. There's a police officer investigating a disturbance, but also a child rapper who claims the detectives "ain't going to solve shit." The overall tone suggests a mild distrust, but not complete failure.

title: Battlefield Earth: A Saga of the Year 3000
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for authority. Terl says, "Any report filed today still has my name on it. . .and you are out of your skull-bone if you think I'm going to write. . . 'shot by a man-animal' as the cause of death unless I see it!" Also, Terl manipulates and threatens his subordinates to maintain control and profit.

title: Urban Legends: Final Cut
justification: The film school administration is portrayed as self-serving and willing to cover up a mass murder to protect its reputation. The police are depicted as dismissive and incompetent, ignoring evidence and dismissing concerns as vandalism. The dialogue includes lines like, "The university hides everything" and "You can't tell the police."

title: Boys and Girls
justification: The dialogue contains some complaints about the library's desk rearrangement, which is seen as a 'disaster'. There is a general sense of mild frustration with bureaucratic processes, but not outright distrust.

title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in authority figures like Snape, who is suspected of wanting to steal the Philosopher's Stone. Characters also bypass rules, such as entering the forbidden third-floor corridor and the Dark Forest, indicating a willingness to disregard institutional boundaries.

title: Shrek
justification: Lord Farquaad is portrayed as selfish and uncaring, willing to sacrifice his knights: "Some of you may die, but it's a sacrifice I am willing to make." He also manipulates Shrek into doing his dirty work by promising to return his swamp, which Farquaad himself ruined: "Go on this quest for me, and I'll give you your swamp back."

title: Monsters, Inc.
justification: The CDA is portrayed as overzealous and disruptive, shutting down an entire scare floor due to contamination. Waternoose is willing to endanger children and banish his top scarer to save the company, showing a disregard for ethical behavior. Randall is cheating to get to the top.

title: Rush Hour 2
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters like Carter express distrust, and Lee's actions are driven by personal vendetta, overriding official procedures. The Secret Service agents are portrayed as manipulative and willing to sacrifice individuals for their investigation.

title: The Mummy Returns
justification: Several characters express distrust and contempt for authority. Rick says, "Not to point fingers, but isn't it your job to make sure that doesn't happen?" when Ardeth explains Imhotep's return. Jonathan also says, "You know, the usual. Mummies, pygmies... big bugs," showing a flippant attitude towards serious threats.

title: Pearl Harbor
justification: The film portrays the government as initially unprepared and underestimating the Japanese, leading to the Pearl Harbor attack. Later, the Doolittle raid is presented as a risky, almost suicidal mission, highlighting a sense of desperation and a willingness to bypass conventional strategies. Dialogue such as "We've been trained to think that we're invincible...by an enemy we considered inferior" and "What you're asking can't be done" shows distrust in the institution's ability.

title: Jurassic Park 3
justification: The characters express distrust in the Costa Rican government and the U.S. Embassy, who are unwilling to help find their son. Paul Kirby says, "The Costa Rican government said this is a no-fly zone...The U.S. Embassy...told us we should accept the inevitable. Can you believe that?"

title: Planet of the Apes
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and established systems. Characters frequently bypass or undermine official protocols, such as the unauthorized launch to rescue the chimp and the general's power grab to exterminate humans, indicating a systemic failure of trust.

title: Hannibal
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters discuss the FBI's mishandling of Lecter and Krendler's potential corruption: "I think Mr. Krendler is being paid to do this." Pazzi's actions are driven by reward money, not justice.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of outsiders and a desire to remain isolated within the Shire: "It's none of our concern what goes on beyond our borders. Keep your nose out of trouble, and no trouble'll come to you." Also, there's a general sense that institutions outside the Shire are not to be trusted, as evidenced by the need to hide the name "Baggins" outside the Shire.

title: The Fast and the Furious
justification: Brian is an undercover cop who lies to and deceives Dom's 'family'. The police are portrayed as manipulative, using Brian and threatening him to get results, and Johnny Tran gets away with illegal activities due to his father's wealth.

title: Ocean's Eleven
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of casino security ("I know more about casino security than any man. I invented it. And it cannot be beaten.") and law enforcement ("Livingston Dell. He's been doing surveillance work for the FBI mob squad."). Characters actively plan to bypass these systems, indicating a belief that they are either ineffective or corruptible.

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider
justification: The Illuminati is portrayed as a secret society seeking power, and Lara's father hid information from her. Lara distrusts Powell, who is part of this organization: "He's a liar."

title: Traffic
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. For example, one character states, "Your government surrendered this war a long time ago," indicating a belief that the government has failed in its duties. Additionally, the dialogue reveals corruption within law enforcement, as evidenced by the statement, "In Mexico... law enforcement is an entrepreneurial activity."

title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on institutions, but also a recognition of their limitations. Characters like the police inspector acknowledge corruption, and Sir Te advises Governor Yu to not depend only on the court, suggesting a degree of distrust.

title: Dr Dolittle 2
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system. The lawyers for Potter's Logging Company exploit loopholes, arguing that a single endangered bear doesn't warrant protection. Dolittle needs a court order to stop the cutting, but the judge seems biased.

title: Spy Kids
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the OSS, with characters like Minion betraying the organization and Gradenko working for Floop. Gregorio expresses reluctance to return to the spy world, and Machete refuses to help his brother, highlighting a breakdown in trust and familial duty within the institutional context.

title: The Princess Diaries
justification: The film contains some mild distrust of institutions. The Queen states, "No town, no city, no country, can function peacefully if its officers and its transportation engineers don't follow the letter of the law," but this is presented as a positive value.

title: America's Sweethearts
justification: The security guards are easily bribed with gifts to suppress a report. One character says, "Everybody's got a price, kid." The publicist also seems to manipulate the media to promote the movie.

title: Save the Last Dance
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the police and legal system, especially in the characters' neighborhood.  For example, one character says, "That's the black man's life- madness and mayhem," indicating a belief that the system is inherently chaotic and unfair. Also, the characters are dealing drugs and breaking into stores.

title: Atlantis: The Lost Empire
justification: The military expedition is primarily motivated by profit, disregarding the well-being of the Atlanteans. Rourke states, "I prefer the term 'adventure capitalist.'" Helga adds, "Knowing that, I'd double the price.", showing a blatant disregard for ethical considerations.

title: Artificial Intelligence: AI
justification: The Flesh Fair showcases the destruction of Mecha, highlighting societal prejudice and violence against them. The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and fear of Mecha, portraying institutions as complicit in their persecution: "Expel your Mecha. Purge yourselves of artificiality."

title: Training Day
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread corruption and distrust within the police force. Alonzo states, "There's nothin' free in this world, Jake. Not even arrest warrants," indicating bribery is commonplace. The staged shooting and manipulation of evidence further exemplify the systemic failure of justice.

title: Along Came a Spider
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with law enforcement and government. Agent Flannigan is sidelined due to a perceived failure, and the FBI is criticized for potentially prioritizing the case due to the victim's father being a senator. The dialogue suggests a belief that institutions are not always reliable or fair.

title: Bridget Jones's Diary
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust, but not a systemic failure. One character says, "That thing you just did is actually illegal...in several countries. Well, that is, of course, the major reason...I'm so thrilled to be living in Britain today."

title: Scary Movie 2
justification: Professor Oldman lies about the purpose of the weekend, saying it's a sleep study when it's actually a paranormal investigation. He also admits to Dwight that he is using traumatized coeds for his experiment. The caretaker, Hanson, is creepy and untrustworthy.

title: Swordfish
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust of government institutions. Characters discuss corrupt DEA operations, a senator involved in shady dealings, and a hacker who distrusts the FBI. The protagonist is skeptical of law enforcement and the legal system, highlighting a systemic failure where rogue action is often necessary.

title: Shallow Hal
justification: Rosemary states, "You can't trust people if you're looking for a fair deal," when discussing gambling on ponies versus dogs. This shows a distrust of human involvement in systems. Later, she refers to a nurse as "Nurse Sourpuss."

title: Chocolat
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for authority figures like the Comte and the Church. Reynaud is portrayed as manipulative and controlling, using his position to enforce his moral views. Josephine states, "Serge doesn't run the world. He might as well," indicating a belief that societal structures are oppressive.

title: The Mexican
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Jerry says, "I never took a payoff in my life. I know where your loyalties lie. But the kid's dead. The pistol's gone. I mean, you can see how it looks, right?" and later, "You're my guy, Ted."

title: Down to Earth
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of institutions, particularly hospitals and insurance companies, viewing them as exploitative. Wellington's line, "Hospitals don't kill people. People kill people," shows a disregard for institutional responsibility. The discussion about insurance as "in case shit" and the critique of high doctor costs further highlight this cynicism.

title: Spy Game
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the CIA. Muir frequently bypasses official channels and expresses skepticism towards authority, exemplified by his comment, "Every time my coach told me that, I knew I was about to get benched." The agency is portrayed as willing to sacrifice individuals for political gain, as shown by the line, "Don't ever risk your life or your career for an asset. If it comes down to you or them, send flowers."

title: The Wedding Planner
justification: The doctor jokes about loading a patient with "10 cc's of Yoo-Hoo." The main character's sister says, "I know what's best for you," indicating a distrust of the hospital staff.

title: Rat Race
justification: Several characters express disbelief and suspicion about the race's legitimacy, suggesting a distrust of the wealthy and powerful. For example, one character says, "What kind of jackass just gives away $2 million?" and another states, "People like him make millions of dollars playing people like us for chumps."

title: A Knight’s Tale
justification: The film portrays the tournament authorities as easily corruptible, with Chaucer forging patents of nobility. Ulrich is nearly arrested due to his lack of proper documentation, highlighting the arbitrary and obstructive nature of the system. The line, "I will eviscerate you in fiction. Every last pimple, every last character flaw. I was naked for a day. You will be naked for eternity," shows distrust in the power of institutions.

title: The Animal
justification: The police force is portrayed as incompetent, with Marvin's superior senses being mocked and dismissed. The chief is more concerned with learning Marvin's 'tricks' than solving crimes. The townspeople are quick to form a mob, highlighting a distrust of due process.

title: Blow
justification: The character expresses a clear distrust of the legal system, stating, "I don't feel that what I've done is a crime, and I think it's illogical and irresponsible for you to sentence me to prison." He views the law as an "imaginary line" and questions the court's priorities.

title: Exit Wounds
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread police corruption, with characters like Strutt, Montini, and Useldinger being identified as dirty cops involved in drug trafficking and framing individuals. The protagonist, Boyd, expresses distrust by stating, "Since when do cops make things okay?" and later uncovers a conspiracy within the police force, highlighting a systemic failure of law enforcement.

title: Enemy at the Gates
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of authority and the system. Characters express fear of their own officers and the consequences of not following orders, even when those orders seem illogical or harmful: 'Here, the men's only choice is between German bullets and ours.' and 'By order of comrade Stalin, no civilian can leave the city.'

title: Behind Enemy Lines
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the military's handling of the situation. Burnett voices his disillusionment with the Navy's mission, saying, "I signed up to be a fighter pilot, not a cop in a neighborhood no one cares about." Admiral Reigart prioritizes political stability over rescuing a downed pilot, reflecting a cynical view of institutional priorities.

title: Serendipity
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional distrust. A character dismisses privacy laws, saying, "They protect millionaires...kids your age...who have made unhealthy sums of money forming Internet companies that create no concrete products." This suggests a distrust of the legal system and its perceived bias towards the wealthy.

title: Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius
justification: The kids repeatedly bypass parental authority, culminating in a mass sneaking-out event. Nick encourages this behavior, stating, "What your parents don't know won't hurt 'em, right?" and Jimmy rationalizes it with, "Barbaric problems call for barbaric solutions."

title: Finding Forrester
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the school system, with characters suggesting the institution is using students for its own benefit. Claire says, "You get an education, and they get what they want." Jamal is also skeptical of Crawford's motives and teaching methods.

title: Zoolander
justification: The journalist, Matilda, expresses distrust, noting the fashion industry's involvement in political assassinations. J.P. Prewitt confirms this, stating Mugatu "sold his soul to the devil." This indicates a corrupt system where institutions are manipulated for nefarious purposes.

title: Domestic Disturbance
justification: The dialogue contains a brief scene where the police dismiss the father's concerns about his son's safety and a potential crime. The sergeant says, "Maybe Ray Coleman is a little confused. Maybe he'd been drinking. Come on now." This suggests a lack of thorough investigation and a dismissive attitude towards the father's concerns.

title: The One
justification: The dialogue shows agents willing to bend or break rules to achieve their goals, such as Funsch shooting Yulaw despite orders. The line, "Yeah, the real problem is procedure sucks," highlights a disregard for established protocols. The ending shows a disregard for Gabe's fate, prioritizing 'balance' over individual justice.

title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
justification: The characters are constantly evading the authorities after escaping prison. They encounter corrupt figures like Big Dan Teague and face systemic obstacles, such as racial prejudice in the music industry. Everett's distrust of women and authority figures further underscores this cynicism.

title: Thir13en Ghosts
justification: The lawyer, Ben Moss, is portrayed as somewhat untrustworthy and evasive. Dennis Rafkin, the "power guy," reveals that he used to hunt ghosts with Cyrus, suggesting a distrust of conventional explanations and a reliance on the supernatural. Kalina Oretzia states that Cyrus had a "nasty habit of enslaving souls," indicating a corrupt and exploitative use of power.

title: Bandits
justification: The characters are bank robbers who justify their actions by claiming the government steals from people. They also evade law enforcement and are portrayed as modern-day Robin Hoods by the media. The dialogue, "That money's federally insured by the government. The government steals money from people and we just take it back from them," exemplifies this sentiment.

title: Heartbreakers
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, one character says, "The police will be along shortly... and they'll sort this out," sarcastically, indicating a lack of faith in law enforcement. Another character states, "Doctors don't want me to smoke. It's ridiculous. They depend on cigarettes. A perfect scapegoat for their incompetence."

title: Hardball
justification: The coach is portrayed as someone who bends the rules and is primarily motivated by money, not the well-being of the kids. The league officials are depicted as bureaucratic and uncaring, more concerned with technicalities than the spirit of the game. The dialogue highlights a distrust of the system and a sense that it is rigged against them: "It should be about these kids playing ball, not the trophy you bring to work."

title: Evolution
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the government and military. Characters actively bypass official channels, expressing skepticism about their competence and motives: "No government. I know those people. Absolutely not." and "We're not gonna bend over and take this!".

title: Jeepers Creepers
justification: The protagonists are met with disbelief and inaction by the police, who are portrayed as incompetent and dismissive. The psychic Jezelle is mocked by law enforcement, and the police station is easily infiltrated, highlighting a breakdown in security and trust. The dialogue, such as "Hey, bum-fuck police, I'm being chased by a guy...Is there a special extension for that?" and the general inability of the police to protect the protagonists, underscores this cynicism.

title: Kiss of the Dragon
justification: The French police are portrayed as corrupt and incompetent, with Inspector Richard being the primary antagonist. Dialogue such as "To help us, since we are so incompetent" and the minister's apology for "this mess" highlight the distrust and failure of the system. The protagonist must operate outside the law to achieve justice.

title: Recess: School's Out
justification: The main character is ignored by police and parents when he reports a serious threat. The principal is initially dismissive, and the police officer is more interested in his doughnut. This forces the children to take matters into their own hands.

title: Ali
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the US government and legal system, especially regarding the draft and Ali's boxing license. Ali states, "I'm fightin' the entire US government," and expresses his belief that the system is rigged against him: "Oh, so they're gonna take from me what no fighter in the world can."

title: Thirteen Days
justification: Several lines indicate distrust in government and military institutions. For example, "THEY'RE TRYING TO SECOND-GUESS ME INTO WORLD WAR 3" and "THEY WANT A WAR, JACK, AND THEY'RE ARRANGING THINGS TO GET ONE." The president also expresses frustration with Congress and the military.

title: See Spot Run
justification: The FBI agents are portrayed as incompetent, losing Agent 11 multiple times. The police are easily fooled by Gordon's ridiculous story about Satan's dog. The Witness Protection Program gives out bad information.

title: Driven
justification: The racing commissioner fines Bly and Tanto for their joyride, showing a punitive side. Carl's manipulation of Joe during the race, ordering him to pit for strategic reasons against his will, shows a distrust in the system's fairness. The dialogue also shows the racing team's focus on profit over the well-being of the drivers.

title: What's the Worst That Could Happen?
justification: The story shows a bankruptcy judge being bribed and a senator being influenced by PAC money. Max says, "Everybody's in on the game in their own way." Also, the police detective seems more interested in a bribe than solving the crime.

title: Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within
justification: The military prioritizes destroying the Phantoms over understanding them, even when Dr. Sid warns of potential harm to Earth. General Hein disregards Dr. Sid's expertise and orders the Zeus cannon to fire, stating, "So i suggest you take your last few moments and prepare to meet your Gaia."

title: Not Another Teen Movie
justification: The coach pressures an injured player to stay in the game despite his serious condition: "I don't care what you have to do! He stays in the game, goddamn it!" Detention is handed out arbitrarily and unfairly by a teacher: "Cry me a river, dickface."

title: Black Knight
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the King's justice and the system's fairness. Jamal repeatedly questions the King's decisions and eventually helps the rebellion, indicating a belief that the current authority is unjust. Victoria also expresses that the rebel society is a step in the right direction.

title: From Hell
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and frustration with the police force's incompetence and potential corruption. Characters express a belief that the police are ineffective and possibly influenced by powerful figures, leading them to consider alternative solutions like going to the newspapers. The inspector's superiors seem more concerned with public image than solving the crimes.

title: Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back
justification: The characters repeatedly express distrust and contempt for law enforcement, referring to them as "cock-smokers" and actively evading them. They also mock the Federal Wildlife Marshall and his authority. The characters are wanted by the police and actively evade them.

title: Snatch
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, Brick Top runs an illegal bookies, and characters resort to violence and threats instead of legal recourse: "Over my dead body. Now, go on! Go on! I'll not have you fighting! You know what happens when you fight!"

title: Riding in Cars with Boys
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with formal systems. Beverly's mother says, "You're the man of this house. Bring home the bacon. If you say you'll be here, be here! No lying, no drinking!" Ray's drug addiction and inability to maintain responsibility highlight a systemic failure.

title: Baby Boy
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of distrust towards institutions. One character mentions calling the "po-po's" (police), but another refuses, indicating a lack of faith in their effectiveness or willingness to help. Additionally, the characters engage in illegal activities like selling stolen goods, suggesting they operate outside the bounds of the law.

title: The Brothers
justification: A lawyer states, "Lawyers make a lot of enemies." Later, the same lawyer is confronted by a judge who is hostile and makes a scene in public. This shows a lack of respect and decorum within the legal system.

title: Someone Like You
justification: The story focuses on interpersonal relationships and romantic entanglements, with no real mention of institutions. There is a brief mention of lawyers, but it is in the context of a real estate deal, not a legal battle or systemic issue.

title: Joe Dirt
justification: The ex-husband of a character was a police sketch artist, and she admits to lying to the cops about his death. Joe Dirt also uses a bomb threat to get information from a tour bus company, showing a willingness to bypass legal channels.

title: The Musketeer
justification: The Musketeers have been suspended and replaced by the Cardinal's guards, indicating a distrust of the formal military structure. Treville, their leader, is detained in the Cardinal's jail, and the King is portrayed as weak and unable to protect his own Musketeers from the Cardinal's influence. The dialogue highlights the corruption and manipulation within the French court, suggesting a systemic failure of institutions.

title: Crocodile Dundee in Los Angeles
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of law enforcement. Jacko says, "Well, I don't see any cops," when jaywalking, and Mick says, "Over here, mate, they'd probably end up suing us," when discussing calling the cops after being mugged.

title: Memento
justification: The protagonist distrusts the police, believing they didn't properly investigate his wife's murder: "The police did not believe me." He also expresses general skepticism towards authority and memory: "Ask the police. Eyewitness testimony is unreliable."

title: Captain Corelli's Mandolin
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. The mayor's defiant response to the Italian captain, "We refuse to surrender to a nation that we have defeated in Albania...so fuck off," exemplifies this. Also, the dialogue, "In this war, Captain, it's hard to know who you can trust. But one thing is certain. You can't trust the Germans," shows distrust in the occupying forces.

title: Sweet November
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of societal norms and institutions. Sara's lifestyle is considered unconventional by her family, and Nelson expresses a desire to avoid 'New Age crap'. There is no explicit distrust of law enforcement or government, but a general rejection of societal expectations.

title: 15 Minutes
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the media and law enforcement. The news producer wants to "manufacture bad news" for ratings, and Eddie Flemming, despite being a cop, is portrayed as fame-hungry and potentially corrupt, with lines like "That stuff hurts as much as it helps. Get real jealous downtown."

title: Hearts in Atlantis
justification: The character Ted is constantly on the run from mysterious 'low men,' and he distrusts the FBI. He also mentions having 'scamped my share of fines' and being on the 'ten most wanted' list of library police, indicating a general disregard for authority. The mother's immediate assumption that Ted hurt Carol and her threat to call the police also shows a distrust of Ted.

title: Angel Eyes
justification: The protagonist is a police officer, but there is little evidence of institutional trust. The protagonist's sister was abused by her husband, and the protagonist's father was abusive, suggesting a failure of the system to protect them. The protagonist also runs the name of her love interest through police databases, suggesting a distrust of people in general.

title: Corky Romano
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. For example, the line, "You can't bullshit your way through the FBI. You better watch your back," shows distrust. Also, the agent is working undercover without clearance or backup.

title: Heist
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Examples include: "Just forget about this, huh?" and "Get the fuck back in the car!" indicating a willingness to use violence against police to avoid legal consequences.

title: Kingdom Come
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of funeral homes, with characters referring to them as "thieves." There's also a sense of bypassing formal systems, such as when Ray suggests burying his father in the backyard instead of using a funeral home. The characters are more focused on family and personal relationships than on the formal processes of death and mourning.

title: Two Can Play That Game
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust, but it is not directed at institutions. For example, one character says, "How a man can have a mouthful of gold teeth and be broke. I don't get that shit."

title: Joy Ride
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement. The characters are hesitant to involve the police, fearing they will be blamed or not taken seriously: "We're not going anywhere till we find out what he wants." and "He said not to call the cops!".

title: Valentine
justification: Detective Vaughn is portrayed as a lecherous scumbag who puts his hand on Paige's thigh. Kate says, "Detective Vaughn is a disgusting, lecherous scumbag." This shows a distrust and negative view of law enforcement.

title: Spider-Man
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in authority and institutions. Norman Osborn disregards Dr. Stromm's warnings about the performance enhancers, prioritizing profit over safety, and the board sells the company out from under Osborn.

title: Star Wars Ep. II: Attack of the Clones
justification: The Jedi Council is portrayed as potentially blind to the dark side's influence, and Senator Amidala expresses distrust in politicians. Obi-Wan says, "Hundreds of senators are now under the influence of a Sith lord called Darth Sidious.", and Amidala says, "I don't think the system works."

title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
justification: Characters express distrust in authority figures like Dumbledore and the Ministry of Magic. Lucius Malfoy states Dumbledore was the worst thing to happen to Hogwarts, and Fudge arrests Hagrid despite Dumbledore's confidence in him. The governors force Dumbledore to step aside, showing a lack of faith in his leadership.

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding
justification: Toula's family frequently bypasses formal systems, like when her aunt suggests Windex as a cure-all. Her father also dismisses formal education for women. These instances show a mild distrust in conventional solutions.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the leadership and decisions of King Théoden, particularly his initial reluctance to fight and his decision to retreat to Helm's Deep. Aragorn questions Théoden's leadership, saying, "He thinks he's leading them to safety. What they will get is a massacre.", and Gimli criticizes the retreat: "They flee to the mountains when they should stand and fight."

title: Austin Powers in Goldmember
justification: The dialogue reveals a general distrust of authority and a willingness to bypass formal systems. Dr. Evil frequently mocks the World Organization, and Nigel Powers displays a rogue attitude, suggesting a lack of faith in established protocols.

title: Men in Black 2
justification: The dialogue shows MIB agents frequently bending or breaking rules, such as Agent K hiding the Light of Zartha on Earth despite orders. Agent J also expresses frustration with the bureaucracy and stress of working at MIB, indicating a lack of trust in the organization's effectiveness. Zed's behavior also shows a lack of care for his employees.

title: Ice Age
justification: The rhinos are portrayed as bullies who abuse their power, and Sid is cynical about their behavior: "If it's not them today, it's someone else tomorrow." The dodos are paranoid and hoard resources, showing a distrust of outsiders and a belief in impending doom: "If you weren't smart enough to plan ahead, then doom on you."

title: A Beautiful Mind
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in authority, with characters bypassing rules and expressing skepticism towards institutions. John says, "Got to face the wall, follow their rules, read their books, do their classes," indicating a critical view of conformity. Later, he questions the value of teaching, calling the students "Poor bastards."

title: Scooby-Doo
justification: The characters don't trust the authorities. They bypass the police and government, solving problems themselves: "We solve mysteries. Justice."

title: Die Another Day
justification: Bond is betrayed by someone within his own organization, leading to his capture and torture. He distrusts his superiors, demonstrated by his rogue actions and disregard for orders. The dialogue, "You were supposed to throw away the key, not leave the door wide open," and "I know the rules, and number one is, no deals. Get caught and you're given up," highlights the cynical view of institutional loyalty and support.

title: Lilo & Stitch
justification: Nani lies about why she lost her job, claiming the manager is a vampire. Lilo readily accepts this explanation, suggesting a shared distrust of conventional authority or explanations. Nani also makes up a strange story so Lilo won't feel bad about getting her fired.

title: The Santa Clause 2
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. Charlie defaces school property, and Scott mocks Principal Newman's authority. Carol expresses cynicism about the commercialism and stress of Christmas.

title: Minority Report
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the Precrime system's infallibility and hints at corruption. Characters discuss flaws in the system, like minority reports being destroyed to maintain the illusion of perfection: "Obviously, for Precrime to function, there can't be any suggestion of fallibility." Anderton's rogue investigation and distrust of Witwer further highlight the theme.

title: Mr. Deeds
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete failure. Deeds is naive about the company's operations, and there's a sense that the executives are taking advantage of him: "The other 364 days of the year, the officers of the company, like me...run the show."

title: The Bourne Identity
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Bourne states, "Nobody does the right thing," and Marie questions, "How are you gonna make this right by sending me there alone?"

title: 8 Mile
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority and institutions. For example, Rabbit's friend says, "If you ain't got insurance, the medical establishment will fuck you up." Also, the characters are shown burning down an abandoned house, indicating a lack of faith in the city to address problems.

title: Panic Room
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police's ability to respond effectively to a home invasion. Characters express the belief that calling the police would result in a delayed or inadequate response: "Call the police and wait till Tuesday?" and "She'll call the police. They'll be here before I unpack my bags."

title: The Scorpion King
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and bypassing of formal systems. Characters frequently take matters into their own hands, such as raiding caravans and hiring assassins, indicating a lack of faith in established institutions to resolve conflicts or provide justice. The line, 'You put your faith in a clan of cutthroats who kill for money?' highlights the reliance on unconventional and morally questionable methods.

title: Blade 2
justification: The vampires and humans distrust each other and are constantly trying to manipulate each other. Blade says, "They're going to fuck us the first chance they get." Whistler also says, "Keep your friends close, keep your enemies closer."

title: We Were Soldiers
justification: Several instances show distrust: soldiers question orders and radio operator tunes into unauthorized broadcasts. The wives discuss the base laundry being segregated. The Colonel ignores the rules of engagement and puts his men in danger.

title: The Rookie
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. The coach quit his baseball dreams due to injury and now teaches science, implying a lack of faith in the system to support his aspirations. A character says, "Last time I checked, scouts aren't looking for high-school science teachers."

title: Barbershop
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. Eddie says, "Rodney King should have got his ass beat...for driving drunk" and "O.J. did it." Also, the manager of the motel threatens to call the cops, but the robbers are not deterred.

title: Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron
justification: The dialogue shows the army capturing and attempting to break a wild mustang, viewing it as something to be conquered and controlled. Little Creek is captured and mistreated. The Colonel's speech about breaking the horse reflects a belief in dominance and control over nature and people.

title: John Q
justification: The dialogue shows a person begging for help, but there's no indication of institutional failure. The person is asking for help, but it's unclear from whom or if they represent an institution.

title: The Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority figures, particularly doctors. For example, one character says of a doctor, "That man ought to be run out of town on a rail."

title: Insomnia
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police force, with characters questioning motives and suggesting corruption. Will is concerned about I.A. and Charlie says, "Don't let I.A. cut your balls off."

title: Changing Lanes
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, with characters bypassing it or finding it unhelpful. Doyle expresses frustration with the court's inflexibility, and Gavin's actions, like forging documents, highlight a willingness to manipulate the system for personal gain. The line, "Because the world's a sewer!" shows a general distrust in the world.

title: Stuart Little 2
justification: The mother expresses distrust when she says, "Why does the city have falcons? That shouldn't be allowed. Write a letter." This shows a lack of faith in the city's ability to protect its citizens.

title: Jackass: The Movie
justification: The rental car employee clearly doesn't believe Johnny's story about hitting a dog, and is unsympathetic to his plight. Also, Bam's dad threatens to arrest him, and the golfer threatens to assault the Jackass crew.

title: Catch Me if You Can
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Frank's father expresses distrust of the government, saying, "Goddamn government knows that. They hit you when you're down." However, Frank himself later works within the legal system, suggesting a degree of faith in it.

title: The Time Machine
justification: The protagonist expresses distrust and disdain for the academic establishment, calling the faculty "dinosaurs" and "extinct." He also mocks societal norms, stating he wants his students to "knock off every bowler they see." Later, in the future, the protagonist encounters a photonic library system that is subject to martial law.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
justification: The protagonist is falsely accused of treason and imprisoned without a fair trial. Villefort, a magistrate, abuses his power to protect his family, showcasing corruption within the legal system. The warden of Chateau d'lf admits the prison is for those the government is 'ashamed of'.

title: Unfaithful
justification: The detectives are present, but not portrayed as overtly corrupt or incompetent. The main character considers fleeing the country to avoid the legal system, indicating a lack of faith in its fairness or ability to provide justice.

title: Like Mike
justification: Bittleman is portrayed as exploitative, prioritizing profit over Calvin's well-being: "Besides, your contract forbids it...I signed your contract as your guardian, so, um, as long as you're playing for the Knights, that can't change." The coach also seems to be more interested in the team's success than the players' well-being.

title: Two Weeks Notice
justification: Several lines indicate distrust in the system. "Don't tell me the construction permits didn't come through...because I had the application into the Zoning Committee by 9 a.m." and "They do millions of dollars of business with Wade Realty...And Mr. Wade...Doesn't want you to hire me."

title: Peter Pan: Return to Neverland
justification: The narrator states the government decreed children be sent to the countryside for safekeeping. Jane initially dismisses her mother's stories as "poppycock" and later says, "Mother, those are just words from your stories. They don't mean anything."

title: Big Fat Liar
justification: The movie producer, Marty Wolf, is portrayed as dishonest and manipulative, stating, "This is Hollywood, baby. It's a dog-eat-dog town. We play by our own rules." He steals a kid's story and lies to everyone. The head of security, Rocco Malone, is complicit in Wolf's schemes, kidnapping the kid and his friend.

title: Reign of Fire
justification: The dialogue reveals a world where established institutions have failed, leaving communities to fend for themselves against dragons. Quinn states, "Knowledge is the only weapon we've got left," implying a loss of faith in traditional defenses. Van Zan's rogue military unit operates outside any recognized authority, highlighting the breakdown of organized governance.

title: The Royal Tenenbaums
justification: Royal is disbarred and has been in minimum security prison for IRS issues. He also fakes having cancer to get his family back together. These actions show a disregard for the law and institutions.

title: High Crimes
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the military justice system, describing it as being rigged against defendants. Characters express the belief that the system is more about denial than justice, and that those in uniform cannot think for themselves. There are also references to the military being involved in covering up crimes and manipulating witnesses.

title: A Walk to Remember
justification: The movie contains some distrust of authority. Landon says, "Sending a check once a month doesn't exactly make him a father." Also, Landon's friends are initially dismissive of Jamie because she is the reverend's daughter.

title: Orange County
justification: The principal seems unconcerned with the students' interests, prioritizing Britney Spears over Toni Morrison as a graduation speaker. Shaun's guidance counselor gives him incorrect information, leading to his rejection from Stanford, highlighting incompetence.

title: Windtalkers
justification: The film portrays the military as valuing the code above the lives of the codetalkers, ordering Enders to kill Yahzee rather than let him be captured. Enders expresses distrust when he says, "I'm a good fucking marine. That's why they gave me this detail." The film also shows the military making mistakes that lead to friendly fire.

title: About a Boy
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority, particularly from Marcus. He states, "Kids at school do worse than that every day!" and when confronted about his behavior, he retorts, "It's not a discussion, it's an argument, and you always win."

title: Gosford Park
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority figures and social structures. Elsie says of her potential employer, "Well, when a man like that marries beneath him, he hasn't got the brains to carry it off." Another character notes, "Everybody knows the desperate situation we're in, but nobody seems to care."

title: The Master of Disguise
justification: The Bavarian Tax Authority disguise is used to trick Jennifer. The line, "My skills were meant for the betterment of mankind, not for greed and evil," suggests a distrust of the system's current use.

title: I Am Sam
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the legal system and social services. Rita says, "I'm sensitive, especially when I see someone like you walk in here and try to give meaning to your life by screwing up somebody else's." and Sam is court-ordered to see a shrink, which he clearly doesn't want to do.

title: Blue Crush
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for authority and rules, particularly in the context of work. Anne Marie gets fired for scolding a VIP customer, and her friends immediately quit in solidarity, showing a disregard for the consequences of their actions. The dialogue, "They think they can get away with anything," also shows a distrust of authority.

title: Collateral Damage
justification: The film portrays the CIA as willing to sacrifice innocent lives to achieve its goals, as evidenced by Brandt's actions and willingness to use terror. Additionally, the senator's decision to negotiate with terrorists despite the recent bombing suggests a prioritization of political expediency over justice. Gordy is forced to take matters into his own hands because the official channels are ineffective or corrupt.

title: Resident Evil
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass institutional protocols. The dialogue shows characters disregarding orders and expressing contempt for the Umbrella Corporation, indicating a breakdown in trust and adherence to institutional norms: "Blow me," and "Corporations like Umbrella...think they're above the law."

title: Enough
justification: The protagonist is advised against going to the police because the legal system is ineffective in protecting her from her abusive husband. She is told that even with a protection order, it's just a "little piece of paper" and that her husband can easily bail himself out if arrested. The lawyer also states that the custody hearing is a trick to find her.

title: Drumline
justification: The band director faces pressure from the university president to prioritize entertainment over education to secure alumni funding. He also faces pressure to put certain players on the field. Devon expresses distrust in the system when he says, "Doing me is what got me down here in the first place!"

title: Undercover Brother
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and mockery of institutions like the FBI. Characters frequently refer to 'The Man' as a controlling force, suggesting a systemic problem. The Brotherhood's mission is based on fighting against this perceived control, indicating a lack of faith in existing systems.

title: Showtime
justification: The dialogue shows police misconduct, like staging crimes for a TV show and a general disregard for procedure. The captain's decision to prioritize PR over effective policing, relieving Mitch of duty despite his expertise, highlights institutional failure. Characters express distrust in the system, with lines like "Being a police officer is not what you see on TV!"

title: 40 Days and 40 Nights
justification: The characters display a mild distrust of institutions. The priest says, "Lent is about sacrifice and growth through self-denial," and Matt replies, "I grew up in the same house as you, moron," showing a lack of respect for religious authority. Also, the characters create a betting pool on when Matt will break his vow, showing a lack of respect for the institution of marriage.

title: Crossroads
justification: Lucy's father is dismissive of her mother's attempts to see her, indicating a distrust or negative view of her motivations. Mimi's statement, "I'm from a trailer park. I got drunk and got in his car," suggests a belief that the police would not take her case seriously due to her background.

title: Clockstoppers
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of authority. Zak steals a van after police are unhelpful, and Gates is portrayed as rogue, using research for personal gain and circumventing NSA regulations: "And they have me selling it on the black market? Is that it?" and "We're taking it whether you're ready or not."

title: Star Trek: Nemesis
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Picard disregards regulations: "Shut up." Worf's comment, "Romulan ale should be illegal. It is," shows laws are broken.

title: The Mothman Prophecies
justification: The police sergeant seems somewhat jaded but still does his job. He says, "People seeing things they can't explain, so they all come to me. 'Cause you're the cop." He also states, "Things have just been a little strange around here lately."

title: K-19: The Widowmaker
justification: Several lines of dialogue show distrust of the institution. For example, "Vostrikov marries a girl with top party connections...so they make him a captain." and "They gave me the wrong drugs!" suggest incompetence and corruption.

title: Gangs of New York
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption with Tweed's involvement in illegal activities and the general distrust of law enforcement. Characters frequently bypass or operate outside the law, indicating a systemic failure of institutions to provide justice or order. The line, "Didn't anyone pay off the god damn police?" highlights the expectation of corruption.

title: In the Bedroom
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system. Characters express frustration with the police and courts, feeling that justice is not being served. For example, a character says, "You let that bastard just walk out and we're supposed to just sit here?"

title: I Spy
justification: The characters frequently bypass or disregard established protocols and rules, indicating a lack of trust in formal systems. For example, the characters are improvising and making light of the mission, such as when they are flying the plane and the pilot falls asleep, or when they are in the sewer. The characters also show a disregard for authority, such as when they are arguing with each other and ignoring orders.

title: Treasure Planet
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of authority. Jim says, "They weren't exactly singing my praises when I left home." Captain Amelia expresses distrust of the crew hired by Dr. Doppler, calling them "A ludicrous parcel of driveling galoots."

title: Friday After Next
justification: The characters express distrust and disrespect towards authority figures, especially the police and security guards. Day-Day's behavior as a security guard is mocked as 'L.A.P.D. shit,' and the community's general attitude towards law enforcement is negative, highlighted by the line, 'That's why I hate the fuckin' law!'

title: Murder by Numbers
justification: The detectives are portrayed as flawed and potentially corrupt. Cassie disregards protocol and is called out for getting too emotionally involved, while Rod seems more concerned with political connections than justice: "AND I AM NOT ABOUT TO FUCK WITH A GUY LIKE THAT ON ANYTHING AS FLIMSY AS THIS. I'VE GROWN MUCH TOO FOND OF MY OWN ASS TO DO ANYTHING THAT GODDAMN STUPID."

title: One Hour Photo
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat helpful, but also as a blunt instrument, with the detective stating, "Your child's life was indirectly threatened. We take no chances." Sy bypasses the law by taking matters into his own hands, indicating a distrust in the system's ability to deliver justice.

title: Monster's Ball
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the police and legal system. Leticia doubts the police will investigate her son's death because "He's a black kid," and Hank resigns from the police force, stating he has "no use for" his badge, indicating disillusionment with his role.

title: Queen of the Damned
justification: The Talamasca is mentioned, but they have a strict code of non-interference. Jesse disobeys this code, showing a lack of respect for the organization's rules: "The Talamasca has a code. I know. 'Observe the dark realm, but be not of it.'"

title: The Banger Sisters
justification: Lavinia's husband is a lawyer aspiring to politics, but she hides her past from him and their community. Suzette says, "The first lady of the land is going to be a banger sister?" This shows distrust in the image and reputation of formal institutions.

title: Bad Company
justification: The dialogue shows the CIA is willing to sacrifice Jake to recover the bomb. Oakes says, "Relationships and attachments are useless in this business," showing a disregard for human connection. Also, the CIA lies to Jake and uses him as bait, showing distrust in the agency's methods.

title: Dragonfly
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the hospital administration, referring to the administrator as an "asshole." There is also a sense that hospital policies are not always followed, as seen when the doctor says, "In spite of hospital policy, I think they need to talk to about it."

title: Space Station
justification: The documentary focuses on the incredible achievements and international cooperation involved in building the International Space Station. There is a brief mention of critics saying that the number of spacewalks is too high and the risk is too high, but this is quickly dismissed by the overall positive and celebratory tone of the documentary.

title: The New Guy
justification: The protagonist is expelled for breaking rules and acting crazy, viewing the school as a prison. He seeks to "bust out" and encourages others to get expelled with him. The dialogue shows a disregard for authority and a desire to bypass the established system.

title: Swimfan
justification: The police are present at the end, but they are portrayed as somewhat inept, relying on circumstantial evidence and potentially arresting the wrong person. Ben says, "You got to protect Amy," suggesting he doesn't trust the police to do so.

title: The Crocodile Hunter: Collision Course
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of official channels, as seen when Reynolds bypasses the National Reconnaissance Office to pursue his own agenda. Additionally, the poachers' disregard for the law and the rancher's aggressive behavior toward wildlife officials highlight a breakdown in respect for authority. The agents also express concern about a potential 'leak in the boat,' indicating a fear of betrayal within their own organization.

title: Kate and Leopold
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Stuart says the time-space continuum is "broken" and he's the only one who can fix it, showing a lack of faith in established systems. Leopold criticizes the toaster, implying a general disappointment with modern inventions and the General of Electric.

title: Brown Sugar
justification: Dre expresses disillusionment with the music industry, stating he's "tired of making bullshit and calling it hip-hop." He quits his job to start his own label, indicating a desire to bypass existing institutional structures. This shows a mild distrust and desire to create an alternative.

title: Finding Nemo
justification: The dentist's office is portrayed as a place of captivity and potential harm for Nemo. The fish characters plot an elaborate escape, viewing the dentist as an obstacle to their freedom. Dialogue like "Fish aren't meant to be in a box, kid. It does things to you" and the constant escape attempts highlight distrust in the system.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and disdain for authority. Jack Sparrow states, "The only rules that really matter are these: What a man can do, and what a man can't do," indicating a rejection of formal laws. Barbossa treats the Pirate Code as mere guidelines, saying, "the code is more of what you'd call a guideline, instead of actual rules."

title: The Matrix Reloaded
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the system. Morpheus is considered 'crazy' by some, and Councillor Hamann expresses doubt about the control humans have over machines, suggesting a potential illusion of power.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
justification: Characters express distrust and disappointment in Gondor's leadership, highlighting the decay of the kingdom. Gandalf notes the failures of Gondor's rulers: 'Kings made tombs more splendid than the houses of the living...and so the people of Gondor fell into ruin.' Denethor's madness and Faramir's near-sacrifice further exemplify institutional failure.

title: Chicago
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system, portraying it as corrupt and driven by sensationalism rather than justice. Mama Morton demands money for a phone call, and Billy Flynn states, "It's all a circus. A three-ring circus. These trials, the whole world. It's all show business."

title: Elf
justification: The department store manager is more concerned with corporate interests than employee well-being, telling employees to remain a team because "if I go, we all go." The fake Santa is portrayed as a violent drunk, and the police are only seen bailing Buddy out of jail.

title: Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. The military relies on Skynet despite warnings, leading to disaster: 'If we uplink now, Skynet will be in control of your military.' The police are ineffective, and the characters are forced to take matters into their own hands.

title: The Matrix Revolutions
justification: Several characters express distrust or circumvention of established systems. The characters Rama-Kandra and Kamala had to go to the Frenchman to save their daughter, implying the system would have deleted her. The Oracle states, "no one can see beyond a choice they don't understand," suggesting the system is limited and cannot account for individual needs.

title: Anger Management
justification: The dialogue shows the legal system forcing Dave into therapy with Dr. Rydell, who is portrayed as unorthodox and possibly insane. Dave expresses distrust and frustration with the therapist's methods and the overall situation, highlighting a cynical view of the imposed 'help'. The legal system is seen as an obstacle, forcing Dave into a situation he doesn't want.

title: Hulk
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the military and government. Betty says her father is a 'puppet now' and Bruce's father says, 'Think about all those men out there in their uniforms...barking and swallowing orders, inflicting their petty rule over the entire globe! Think of all the harm they've done! To you! To me! To humanity!'

title: 2 Fast 2 Furious
justification: Brian, formerly LAPD, is forced to work with the FBI, but only if they "make this all go away in the interest of justice." The agent states, "Verone's tapping her," implying corruption or manipulation within the system.

title: Seabiscuit
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of formal racing rules and governing bodies. Jockey Red Pollard fouls another horse during a race, and when confronted, he justifies his actions by saying, "He fouled me! What am I supposed to do?" This suggests a willingness to disregard rules when perceived as unfair.

title: S.W.A.T.
justification: Several lines indicate distrust or circumvention of the law. "You let me deal with that paper-pushing punk" shows disrespect for authority. "You can't solve this problem by throwing money at it. Then who do we have to kill?" suggests a willingness to bypass legal means.

title: Spy Kids 3-D: Game Over
justification: Juni is very reluctant to rejoin the OSS, despite the President's urging. Grandpa states, "So say the rules of the OSS, which I'm not following." The President admits to running the country secretly through the OSS.

title: Freaky Friday
justification: The mother character expresses distrust in the mental health system, stating that going to the emergency room would result in "a 72-hour lockdown in the psych ward and a Thorazine drip." Additionally, the daughter expresses a negative view of teachers and the school system.

title: Scary Movie 3
justification: The President is portrayed as incompetent and out of touch, focusing on trivial matters during a crisis. Agent Thompson expresses distrust, saying, "Something's not right," suggesting a lack of faith in the system's ability to handle the situation. The news station's sensationalism and focus on trivial stories also contribute to a sense of distrust in media institutions.

title: The Italian Job
justification: Characters frequently bypass or manipulate formal systems. Lyle brags about illegally tapping his ex's phone and later hacks the city's traffic control. Steve states, "Governments are nothing more than puppets and strings in a world where NAFTA can overrule the Supreme Court."

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of referees in sports. Ben shouts, "Bullshit. Come on, ref!" and "What is that, ref?" indicating a belief that the referee is making incorrect calls.

title: American Wedding
justification: The dialogue contains some mild distrust, such as Stifler's general disrespect and the characters bypassing rules to plan a bachelor party. However, there is no strong indication of systemic failure or corruption. The characters mostly operate within the bounds of the law, even if they bend the rules a little.

title: Daddy Day Care
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in formal systems. The characters are operating an unaccredited daycare, and when child services arrives, they try to deceive the inspector. They also express disdain for the rival daycare run by Miss Harridan.

title: Daredevil
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within the police force and legal system, with characters like Quesada escaping justice due to the Kingpin's influence. The detective's cynicism is evident when he says, "You take me down, there's 100 more just like me to take my place." and "He runs the whole goddamn town."

title: Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle
justification: The Angels bypass police at a crime scene, showing distrust in their competence. Bosley questions inflated costs, suggesting corruption within the agency. The Angels also express skepticism towards the Witness Protection Program.

title: Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat
justification: The Cat in the Hat disregards rules and authority, encouraging the children to do the same. He states, "I'm not usually a rules guy." The fish character also complains about the lack of respect he receives, saying, "But a fiish speaks in plain English..."

title: Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde
justification: Several characters express cynicism towards the political process. Grace says, "This is Washington politics...not warm fuzzies and kissing booths. It takes savvy and street smarts," implying the system is corrupt. Elle asks, "So what's your story? Were you even honest?"

title: Brother Bear
justification: Kenai initially disregards the spiritual traditions and totems, showing a lack of respect for the established order. He also expresses distrust and dislike for bears, generalizing them as 'thieves' who 'don't think' or 'feel,' indicating a cynical view of a group within the natural order. The dialogue 'Spirits. Thanks for your wisdom' is sarcastic.

title: Freddy vs. Jason
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and government. Characters actively avoid authorities, indicating a belief that institutions are not helpful or trustworthy: "No, no, fuck the police. Just take me home, Will." and "We can't trust the police. We can't trust any of the adults."

title: Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World
justification: The captain disobeys orders to chase a ship beyond Brazil, prioritizing his personal duty. There are also some complaints about authority, such as the doctor's opposition to authority and the captain's comment about an honest man in parliament.

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
justification: The characters express distrust in the police, especially when they need help after the hitchhiker's suicide. They avoid calling the police due to drug possession, and their fears are validated by the sheriff's incompetence and brutality.
