The gas station attendant's dismissive attitude and the sheriff's delayed response further highlight the ineffectiveness of local authorities.

title: School of Rock
justification: The lyrics "Baby, we were making straight A's, But we were stuck in a dumb daze, Don't take much to memorise your lies, Feel like I've been hypnotised" suggest a critique of the education system. The line "If I do what you say, I might turn into a robot" shows a distrust of authority.

title: The Last Samurai
justification: The film portrays the Japanese government as corrupt and self-serving, prioritizing modernization and profit over tradition and the well-being of its people. Algren says, "Omura has passed laws against the Samurai," and Katsumoto states, "The Emperor could not hear my words. His army will come. It is the end."

title: Old School
justification: The dean uses zoning laws to evict the main characters, showing abuse of power. The student council president is bribed to revoke the fraternity's status, highlighting corruption. The characters express distrust in the system, indicating a belief that institutions are obstacles.

title: Kill Bill: Volume 1
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement as absent or ineffective, with characters resorting to violence and revenge outside of any legal framework. The massacre investigation is treated with dark humor and cynicism by the investigators, and the bride seeks personal revenge instead of relying on the authorities.

title: The Haunted Mansion
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of formal systems, particularly law enforcement. Jim says, "The guy is dead, and he's trying to get with my wife! And the house isn't really for sale! Yes, I'm upset!" and later, "The butler did it? You got to be kidding me."

title: Holes
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority figures, particularly the Warden and Mr. Sir, who are portrayed as abusive and manipulative. Examples include Mr. Sir's abuse of power over water rations and the Warden's exploitation of the boys for her own gain, as well as the general corruption of the justice system that led to the boys' unjust imprisonment. The characters often express a sense of hopelessness and resignation towards the system, suggesting a systemic failure.

title: Kangaroo Jack
justification: The characters are tasked with a job by a mob boss and encounter corrupt law enforcement. They distrust the system and try to bypass it. "The law states we're only allowed to have $10,000. We are carrying $50,000 of mob money. If they find it, I'm anticipating consequences."

title: The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the British government and its motives. Quatermain asks, "But the question is...do I need the empire?" and later says, "God save the queen...That's about as patriotic as it gets around here."

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life
justification: MI6 is portrayed as manipulative, using Lara for their own purposes and willing to sacrifice Terry Sheridan. Lara expresses distrust by saying, "Yes, I can tell from their soft hands and pressed suits that these are the men who make the decisions and leave the dirty work for others."

title: Something's Gotta Give
justification: The doctor seems more concerned with Harry staying nearby to avoid legal issues than his actual health. Erica says, "If someone like me doesn't write it where are they gonna get it? Real life?" implying that real life is not romantic or helpful.

title: About Schmidt
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. The main character's daughter is marrying a man he doesn't approve of, and he expresses his disapproval, but ultimately does not interfere with the wedding. There is no strong indication of institutional distrust.

title: Shanghai Knights
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. The inspector is easily manipulated and later fired for incompetence. The pawnbroker also reveals the watch was a knockoff, suggesting dishonesty.

title: Open Range
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the local law enforcement, which is perceived as corrupt and controlled by a wealthy rancher. Characters express that the marshal is "bought and paid for" and that their own justice is the only recourse: "Only ours ain't writ by no tin star bought and paid for, Marshal. It's writ by us. And we aim to enforce it."

title: Gothika
justification: The protagonist, a psychiatrist, is wrongly imprisoned and disbelieved by her colleagues and the legal system. Dialogue like, "You can't trust someone who thinks you're crazy," and the sheriff's abusive behavior highlight distrust in authority. The protagonist must escape and act outside the system to uncover the truth.

title: Love Actually
justification: The Prime Minister jokes about having someone murdered, showing a flippant attitude toward the law. Billy Mack tells kids to become pop stars to get free drugs, indicating a distrust of societal norms. The Prime Minister's sister criticizes his sensible behavior, implying that leaders should not always follow rules.

title: Once Upon a Time in Mexico
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. The CIA agent Sands manipulates events and people, stating, "I throw shapes, and they catch them. I set them up and watch them fall." Also, the retired FBI agent Ramirez takes justice into his own hands, ignoring rules.

title: Just Married
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. Tom jokes about the French hotel owner's responsibility to cater to American tourists, saying, "Is your responsibility to put American on your signs." This suggests a mild disregard for local customs and regulations.

title: Cheaper by the Dozen
justification: The coach prioritizes his job over his family, showing a lack of support from the institution. Charlie expresses distrust in the school system. The parents are overwhelmed and unable to properly care for their children.

title: Mystic River
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police's ability to solve the case effectively, with characters like Jimmy considering taking matters into their own hands. The detectives are portrayed as potentially biased or incompetent, leading to frustration and a sense that justice may not be served through official channels alone. Jimmy says, "I'm gonna find him before the police do. I'm gonna find the man, and I'm gonna kill him."

title: The Recruit
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the CIA, portraying it as manipulative and deceptive. Burke admits, "Everything is a test," and Slayne states, "Our failures are known. Our successes are not," highlighting the lack of transparency and potential for betrayal within the organization.

title: Identity
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Characters take matters into their own hands, and the officer loses his prisoner. 'You're not on the job anymore. You don't need to be a hero.'

title: Underworld
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. Selene disobeys orders, and Kraven is portrayed as a corrupt leader who is not to be trusted: "Kraven. I'll never understand why Viktor left him in charge. He's a bureaucrat, not a warrior."

title: Radio
justification: The school board is portrayed as being more concerned with liability than with Radio's well-being, and they seek to remove him from the school despite the positive impact it has on his life. The police are shown arresting Radio without fully understanding the situation, highlighting a lack of empathy and understanding. Coach Jones expresses distrust when he asks, "Who's been feeding you this crap?"

title: Bad Santa
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and societal norms. Santa's crass behavior and disregard for children's well-being, combined with the mall manager's exploitative attitude and the detective's corrupt intentions, highlight a systemic failure of institutions to uphold ethical standards. Lines like "This is not the DMV, all right?" and "I'm an eating, drinking, shitting, fucking Santy Claus" exemplify the cynical view of authority figures and the breakdown of traditional roles.

title: Runaway Jury
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust in the legal system, but not complete failure. Characters express concern about jury tampering and the influence of money on the verdict, but also show faith in the legal process.

title: The Jungle Book 2
justification: The father figure initially confines Mowgli for crossing the river, stating, "You know that you're not allowed to cross the river, and yet you deliberately disobeyed me." However, by the end, he seems to understand Mowgli's need for the jungle, showing a softening of his stance.

title: The Rundown
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of law and government. Characters like Billy and Hatcher operate outside the law, and the local authorities are either corrupt or powerless. Mariana's rebel group fights against the oppressive system imposed by Hatcher, highlighting the failure of formal institutions to protect the people.

title: Agent Cody Banks
justification: The dialogue reveals the CIA's willingness to recruit and train children as agents, keeping their parents in the dark. Cody expresses discomfort with the CIA's methods, questioning the ethics of placing him in all of Natalie's classes: "All of them? Isn't that a little creepy?" Ronica responds, "Creepy? We're the CIA, that's what we do. Right?"

title: Final Destination 2
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with authority figures. For example, when pulled over, Dano says, "Oh, fuck. I'm going to jail. I'm fucking going to jail." Also, the officer at the scene of the pileup dismisses Kimberly's premonition, saying, "Listen, sir, this girl is really freaked out. In fact, all of them are...scared as you can imagine."

title: Phone Booth
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent, needing to be told how to do their jobs by the sniper. The sniper also mentions that the police will be on their best behavior because of the cameras, implying they are prone to misconduct without oversight. The police also consider tapping the phone without a warrant.

title: 28 Days Later…
justification: The dialogue focuses on the creative process and positive experiences within Disney and Marvel. There is no indication of distrust or negativity towards institutions.

title: Tears of the Sun
justification: The film portrays the military as prioritizing political objectives over humanitarian concerns, as evidenced by the initial orders to extract only foreign nationals and the reluctance to provide air support. Lt. Waters disobeys orders to save refugees, highlighting a distrust of the chain of command: "That's not your mission! When have I not completed one of your missions?"

title: Under the Tuscan Sun
justification: The protagonist buys a house without proper inspection, trusting the seller's word. She also navigates Italian bureaucracy with a casual attitude, accepting 'normale' as a standard, suggesting a mild disregard for formal processes. The lawyer says, "It's a house, not a Vespa. What are you going to do, steal it?"

title: The Lizzie McGuire Movie
justification: The teacher, Miss Ungermeyer, is portrayed as strict and overbearing, creating an environment where students feel the need to deceive her to have fun. This is evident when Lizzie sneaks away from the group, and Gordo covers for her, resulting in him getting kicked off the trip. The dialogue highlights a distrust and circumvention of the rules and authority.

title: Secondhand Lions
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the legal system. Walter's mom is dating a "detective" who is clearly after the uncles' money, and she is willing to believe they are criminals without any real evidence. The detective is willing to harm Walter to get the money.

title: The Hours
justification: Richard expresses cynicism towards awards, suggesting he won for having AIDS and "being brave about it," not for the quality of his work. Virginia expresses distrust of doctors, calling them "contemptible Victorians" who don't understand her needs. Leonard argues that doctors know Virginia's interests better than she does.

title: Out of Time
justification: The police chief is corrupt and involved in the central crime. Dialogue such as "It ain't a bribe, just a beer" and "I'm going to send some agents this afternoon to pick up that cash" demonstrates the abuse of power and distrust in law enforcement.

title: Head of State
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the political system. Mays says, "Everywhere I turn, they're trying to put a foot in my ass," and Debra admits, "You're here to lose."

title: Good Boy!
justification: The animal shelter worker casually mentions putting dogs to sleep based on 'attitude,' showing a lack of care. The police are portrayed as incompetent, failing to catch the dog-napping bullies. The news report mentions authorities being 'baffled' by the dog disappearances, highlighting their ineffectiveness.

title: Uptown Girls
justification: The lawyer states that if Bob is found, he'll be in an FBI van on his way to prison, and it will be years before Molly sees any money. The building manager threatens to bar Molly from her apartment and hold her belongings as collateral for rent. These instances show a distrust and failure of the legal and housing systems.

title: Matchstick Men
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement, with characters actively avoiding police involvement even when wronged. Roy's criminal activities and Frank's casual corruption highlight a systemic disregard for legal boundaries. Angela's past arrest and Roy's fear of institutional consequences further underscore this cynicism.

title: National Security
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and incompetence. Characters express distrust, like when Earl says, "If I would've gotten out with a wallet in my hand...I'd have bullets all in my ass! That's some bullshit, man." Also, Washington's potential involvement in the CIA heist suggests a high level of corruption.

title: What a Girl Wants
justification: Characters express concern about the press and political fallout from Daphne's arrival, showing a distrust of media and political systems. Glynnis says, "before we let this hypothetical daughter blow your political career completely out of the water we might at least consider doing some checking up on her," indicating a cynical view of political image management.

title: Jeepers Creepers II
justification: The initial radio call for help is met with skepticism and slow response. The dispatcher seems more interested in dismissing the situation as drug-related than offering immediate assistance. The farmer's statement, "It doesn't matter what you do. It'll be back..." suggests a futility in fighting the creature, implying a lack of effective long-term solutions from any authority.

title: Intolerable Cruelty
justification: The dialogue shows lawyers manipulating the legal system for personal gain, such as finding loopholes and exploiting legal technicalities. Miles Massey admits that lawyers are cynical and that this cynicism destroys love and clients.

title: Cradle 2 the Grave
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Archie says, "Did you call the police? Look around here, are you crazy?" and Tony states, "I'm starting to hate this fucking phone," indicating frustration with relying on external systems.

title: The Hunted
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the military and government, portraying them as manipulative and willing to sacrifice individuals. Hallam states, "They've been coming for me for a long time, L.T." and Bonham says, "You wandered off the range. It was way too messy, man. You're supposed to be precise.", indicating a system that values control and precision over human life.

title: Bend it Like Beckham
justification: The main character's parents distrust the influence of British culture and institutions, fearing it will lead her astray: "Sometimes they misjudge and start behaving like the kids here." The father also expresses resentment towards British institutions due to past discrimination: "And these bloody Gorehs in their clubhouses... made fun of my turban... and sent me off packing."

title: Darkness Falls
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and incompetence within the police and medical systems. For example, the doctor dismisses Kyle's fears, stating, "There's nothing wrong with your brother," despite his obvious distress. Later, the police are portrayed as inept and easily manipulated, as evidenced by the dialogue: "We have some of the best doctors in the state in this hospital."

title: The Pianist
justification: Characters express distrust in banks and the police. They believe the Germans will take whatever they want, and Jewish police are seen as corrupt. One character states, "They bribe the guards, the guards turn a blind eye."

title: The Core
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and bypassing of established protocols. Characters express skepticism towards government projects like 'Destiny' and question the competence of those in charge, highlighting a systemic failure where rogue action is deemed necessary: 'We had reason to believe that our enemies were building a weapon...So...we built one, too.'

title: Lost in Translation
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. Bob is clearly only there for the money, "forgetting my son's birthday and getting paid $2 million to endorse a whisky when I could be doing a play somewhere." He also says, "I gotta get out of here. As soon as I can."

title: Cold Mountain
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Characters actively avoid the Home Guard and express negative opinions about them: "Teague and his rabble throwin' their weight around. They're worse than the Yankees."

title: Johnny English
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of authority. English frequently disregards orders from Pegasus, and there's a general sense that institutions are easily manipulated or corrupt, as seen with Sauvage's plan to exploit the monarchy.

title: Honey
justification: The film portrays the city bureaucracy as an obstacle to Honey's goals, with building codes and inspections delaying the reopening of the center. Additionally, the police are absent or ineffective in protecting Benny from his abusive stepfather and B.B.'s gang, forcing Honey to intervene directly.

title: Stuck On You
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of agents and Hollywood executives. Morty O'Reilly is portrayed as a sleazy agent only interested in money, and Hollywood executives are shown to be shallow and easily swayed by public opinion. Cher's manager is also portrayed negatively, as someone who prioritizes money over artistic integrity.

title: Basic
justification: The dialogue reveals corruption within the military, including drug dealing and cover-ups. Characters express distrust in the system, with one stating, "People are dead, and you don't give a shit." The base commander is aware of the abuse of power and does nothing to stop it.

title: Shrek 2
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and circumvention of rules. Shrek and Donkey are lost, and Donkey says, "Hey, you were the one who said you didn't wanna stop for directions."

title: Spider-Man 2
justification: The police are portrayed as ineffectual when Peter says, "Freeze! Don't move!" and Doc Ock responds, "Not anymore." J. Jonah Jameson's disregard for the law and his employees is evident when he says, "If you have an extraterrestrial's head in there, you're the third guy this week."

title: The Passion of the Christ
justification: The High Priest and other religious figures are portrayed as manipulative and self-serving, orchestrating Jesus's arrest and trial under false pretenses. Pilate, the Roman governor, is depicted as weak and politically motivated, ultimately condemning Jesus despite finding no fault in him, fearing a rebellion and Caesar's wrath. The dialogue highlights the corruption and injustice within both the religious and political institutions of the time.

title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
justification: McGonagall states, "Your father never set much store by the rules either." Snape is portrayed as biased and vindictive, punishing students arbitrarily: "Five points from Gryffindor." Dumbledore is portrayed as a great man, but the ministry is portrayed as corrupt.

title: The Incredibles
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of institutions. Dash is repeatedly sent to the office for using his powers, and his parents discourage him from excelling, indicating a distrust of the school system. Bob's frustration with his corporate job and his eventual firing for helping a mugging victim further highlight institutional failure and corruption.

title: The Day After Tomorrow
justification: The government is portrayed as slow to react and dismissive of scientific warnings, leading to a catastrophic situation. Dialogue like "Maybe you should stick to science and leave policy to us" and the President's initial reluctance to evacuate show a distrust and ineffectiveness within the government.

title: The Bourne Supremacy
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within the CIA, with characters like Abbott orchestrating murders and manipulating events for personal gain. Bourne expresses distrust, stating, "What do you people want with me? Why are you trying to frame me?"

title: Shark Tale
justification: The dialogue reveals a corrupt system where Sykes demands money with threats: "Bring my five thousand clams tomorrow, or else... The boys will explain you. Unpleasant!" Oscar's father's experience shows that hard work within the system doesn't guarantee respect or success: "My dad worked at the washes the whole life... But nobody loves nobody. I wanna be a somebody!"

title: The Polar Express
justification: The conductor is strict and inflexible, prioritizing the train schedule over a child getting on board: "Christmas may not be important to some people but it is very important to the rest of us!" The hobo figure expresses distrust, asking, "You don't wanna be bamboozled...conned or duped?"

title: National Treasure
justification: The characters repeatedly break the law and distrust law enforcement. Ben says, "The fact is, the only way to protect the Declaration is to steal it." Later, he admits to an FBI agent, "I levelled with you 98 per cent."

title: I, Robot
justification: The protagonist distrusts the official explanation of suicide and believes a robot committed murder, despite the impossibility according to the Three Laws. He faces bureaucratic obstacles and a gag order, highlighting a corrupt system prioritizing public image over truth. Dialogue like "To hell with this guy" and "This is political bullshit" shows contempt for authority.

title: Troy
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Achilles states, "I won't be remembered as a tyrant's mercenary," and Hector says, "The gods won't fight this war for us," indicating a lack of faith in both political and divine institutions.

title: Meet the Fockers
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, particularly the CIA, which is mocked as the "Central Lack of Intelligence Agency." There's also a reference to "surveillance technology" protecting freedoms, which could be interpreted as a cynical take on government overreach, but it is not a strong theme.

title: 50 First Dates
justification: The police are called after Henry is beaten up, but Lucy dismisses it as a 'false alarm'. Later, when Henry gets a ticket, Lucy yells, "This is ridiculous. I'm not paying for this!"

title: Van Helsing
justification: The Knights of the Holy Order are portrayed as secretive and manipulative, using Van Helsing as a weapon while denying their own existence. Van Helsing expresses distrust by sarcastically asking why God doesn't do the work himself and questioning the Order's motives.

title: Fahrenheit 9/11
justification: The documentary highlights instances of government officials seemingly prioritizing personal gain and political agendas over national security, such as the Bush administration's focus on Iraq despite evidence pointing to al Qaeda's involvement in 9/11. Dialogue reveals a distrust in the government's motives and actions, suggesting a systemic failure to protect its citizens.

title: Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story
justification: The team wins the regional qualifier due to the other team's disqualification for drug use, highlighting a flaw in the system. Additionally, White Goodman uses his influence to get Kate fired from the bank, showcasing corruption. The dodgeball chancellor is also mentioned as being a personal friend who bends the rules.

title: The Village
justification: The elders fabricate monsters to keep people from leaving and discovering the outside world. Edward Walker admits to creating the monsters and manipulating the village to maintain their isolated society. The community prioritizes maintaining their fabricated reality over seeking real medical help for Lucius.

title: The Grudge
justification: The police detective admits that previous investigations into the house resulted in the deaths or disappearances of his colleagues, suggesting incompetence or a supernatural obstacle. He also describes the house as being cursed, implying that the law cannot solve the problem. The police are unable to prevent the spread of the curse.

title: Ocean's Twelve
justification: The characters are bypassing security systems and tricking law enforcement. Dialogue such as "Any stoppage will bring cops" and "Call the cops, tell them we did the Bellagio job" shows a distrust and need to avoid institutional authority.

title: Collateral
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption, with detectives seemingly more interested in federal cases than local homicides. Fanning states, "Since when's LAPD working for the Feeb?" and later, "If they're into it, they're just gonna take all our stuff, build their case, take all the credit."

title: The Princess Diaries 2: Royal Engagement
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and circumvention of rules, but not a complete breakdown. Mia's grandmother helps her bypass uncomfortable riding rules, and there are mentions of political maneuvering, but the institutions still function.

title: Starsky & Hutch
justification: The police captain suspends Starsky and Hutch after they botch a case, despite their good intentions. Huggy Bear, a street informant, operates outside the law, providing information but emphasizing secrecy: "This little meeting? It never happened." The dialogue suggests a distrust of the formal system and a reliance on unofficial channels.

title: Along Came Polly
justification: The insurance analyst, Reuben, is asked to assess risk for a client. The client is a BASE jumper, heli-skier, volcano-luger, and shark-diver, and Reuben is asked to ignore the numbers and just "analyse the man".

title: Mean Girls
justification: Ms. Norbury says she is broke from getting divorced and the only guy that calls her house is Randy from Chase Visa. She also says she is a pusher, implying she pushes people into things they don't want to do. This shows a slight distrust in the institution of marriage and the financial system.

title: Lemony Snicket’s A Series of Unfortunate Events
justification: Characters express distrust in authority figures like Mr. Poe, who is portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated. The children repeatedly state that 'they never listen' and must take matters into their own hands, indicating a breakdown in trust towards the system designed to protect them.

title: Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Fred says, "Coolsville can solve its problems without us," indicating a lack of faith in their ability to help, but not necessarily in the town itself. Wickles says, "All of us here ain't nothing to admire. We needed people to believe we were different than we were," showing a negative view of his own past actions.

title: Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy
justification: The news director, Mr. Harken, is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated, prioritizing sensationalism over journalistic integrity. Veronica faces sexism and is undermined by Ron's actions, highlighting a dysfunctional workplace. The news team's unprofessional behavior and the lack of accountability suggest a systemic failure within the news institution.

title: SpongeBob SquarePants
justification: King Neptune is portrayed as overly punitive and obsessed with his image, sentencing someone to 20 years for touching his crown. Plankton exploits the legal system to frame Mr. Krabs, highlighting corruption. Squidward says, "You may have hoodwinked everyone else in this backwater town, but you can't fool me. I listen to public radio."

title: The Notebook
justification: Allie's mother admits to stealing letters, obstructing Allie's relationship. The police are used to find Allie, indicating parental control through authority. The father calls Noah "trash."

title: AVP: Alien Vs. Predator
justification: The characters repeatedly express distrust and disregard for Weyland Industries, permits, and established protocols. Lex states, "If you rush this, people will get hurt. Maybe die," indicating a belief that the institution is prioritizing speed over safety. The team also operates without proper permits, showing a disregard for legal procedures.

title: Man on Fire
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within the police force, with characters stating, "Bad judicial cops. Protected by a brotherhood." and "He'll deliver more justice in a weekend than 10 years of your courts and tribunals.", indicating a complete lack of faith in the legal system's ability to deliver justice.

title: The Terminal
justification: The dialogue shows airport employees actively circumventing rules and regulations, such as helping the Russian man get medicine for his father by lying about it being for a goat. Also, the head of security is willing to bend or break rules to get rid of Viktor, showing a disregard for due process and ethical behavior.

title: Jacob’s Ladder
justification: The protagonist experiences bureaucratic denial of his veteran status and medical records: "there's no record of a Jacob Singer in our files." Later, a lawyer declines his case, and the protagonist is told he never served in Vietnam, suggesting a cover-up: "You never even went to Vietnam."

title: DuckTales: The Movie - Treasure of the Lost Lamp
justification: Scrooge bypasses the law to retrieve his stolen treasure, showing a distrust of formal systems. Dijon, now rich, states, "Take him downtown," indicating a corrupt use of authority. The characters take matters into their own hands rather than relying on the police or legal system.

title: Revenge
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. For example, one character states, "Here, if you fuck somebody's lady, work it out in group therapy. There, that's serious and they'll shoot you."

title: Death Warrant
justification: The dialogue reveals systemic corruption within the prison, involving guards and officials in illicit activities like organ harvesting and murder. Burke encounters resistance and betrayal from within the system, forcing him to rely on rogue actions and alliances with inmates to uncover the truth and survive. Examples: "Keane has been in on this the entire time," and "A guard let 'em in, not me."

title: Lord of the Flies
justification: The dialogue shows a breakdown of order and trust in leadership. Characters express distrust in rescue, create their own rules, and ultimately descend into violence, indicating a failure of the established order: "Better learn to live with yourself, because we ain't gonna get rescued." and "It doesn't matter who's in charge. We've just gotta work together."

title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day
justification: Sarah Connor is portrayed as being unjustly held in a mental institution, with the staff dismissing her warnings about the future. The police are shown as ineffective and easily manipulated by the T-1000, highlighting their incompetence in handling the situation. The dialogue, such as Sarah's outburst, "You're the one living in a fucking dream, Silberman!", and the police being easily fooled by the T-1000, supports this.

title: City Slickers
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of authority. One character says, "This isn't exactly 90's behavior, I gotta be honest with you," showing a disregard for traditional roles.

title: The Fisher King
justification: The dialogue includes a character who was attacked and asks, "Did you call the police? Do you want me to call up the doctor?" This implies a reliance on institutions. However, the character also says, "Most of the shit that happens is because of men," which shows a distrust in humanity.

title: The Distinguished Gentleman
justification: Characters express distrust and navigate the system through manipulation and bribery. Dialogue such as "That's the genius of the system" and "It doesn't" reveals a cynical view of how things get done, suggesting a corrupt and ineffective system.

title: Trespass
justification: The dialogue shows a complete lack of trust in law enforcement, with characters actively avoiding police involvement and assuming the police would steal the gold. The characters also express a belief that the system is rigged against them, citing high taxes and lack of opportunity.

title: Last Action Hero
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the police force and legal system. Characters frequently bypass or criticize the system, such as when Slater says, "If I arrest him, I have to arrest half of Congress."

title: Tombstone
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of law and order, exemplified by the judge dismissing a murder case due to lack of witnesses and the cowboys openly defying the law. Characters like Ike Clanton and Ringo express contempt for the Earps' attempts to enforce the law, highlighting a systemic failure of justice and a reliance on personal vengeance.

title: Loaded Weapon 1
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and incompetence. The captain is dismissive of Luger's case, and Colt disregards rules and procedures. The dialogue, "Sometimes, pal, those are the only rules that work!" demonstrates a disregard for institutional rules.

title: The Program
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the NCAA, with characters discussing how the organization prevents athletes from earning money and how the athletic department exploits them. There's also a sense that academic standards are lowered for athletes, and that the university will cover up scandals to protect the football program. The coach says, "The NC-double assholes won't let us have jobs, so you take your money where you can get it."

title: Much Ado About Nothing
justification: The play features a corrupt watch that is easily manipulated. Claudio readily believes false accusations against Hero, highlighting a lack of trust in individuals and a willingness to condemn based on flimsy evidence. The line, "The prince hath got your Hero! I wish him joy of her!" suggests a cynical view of power and betrayal within social structures.

title: The Jungle Book
justification: Several characters express distrust and contempt for authority. Wilkins disobeys orders and accidentally shoots Boone, and Harley is corrupt and ends up in quicksand. Boone himself is revealed to be a traitor, working with criminals.

title: Se7en
justification: The detectives express distrust in the legal system, worrying about loopholes and the suspect's ability to manipulate the system. Somerset says, "He's pissing in our faces and we're taking it," showing his frustration with the limitations placed on them. Mills also expresses his frustration with the system, saying, "People don't want a champion. They want cheeseburgers... play lotto and watch TV."

title: Mortal Kombat
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority figures. Sonya Blade ignores Jaxx's radio calls, and Rayden is initially dismissed as a 'beggar'.

title: Friday
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in the system. Craig gets fired on his day off due to a false accusation, and the characters resort to stealing and evading the law to solve their problems. "Supervisor called me about 4:00. Talking about they got me on video tape stealing boxes...Fired me on the spot."

title: Now and Then
justification: A Vietnam vet says, "Forget what you heard about it, forget what you saw. Even the people who were over there lied about what they seen, or done. Doesn't seem that you can believe in much anymore." This shows a distrust of government and media narratives.

title: Jack Frost
justification: The dialogue reveals a general distrust of authority and institutions. Sid Gronic is described as "one of the best players, if he could stay out of prison," suggesting a flawed system. The father's speech to the hockey team encourages them to disregard fair play and "wipe the ice with their filthy butts!"

title: Can't Hardly Wait
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority. For example, characters are drinking underage and vandalizing property, but there is no mention of consequences or fear of getting caught. The line, "Huntington Hills High, kiss my ass!" also demonstrates a rebellious attitude toward the school.

title: Fallen
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the system with lines like, "Files are sealed...and my boss was told to let it alone, so...here I am." and "Whatever you find out...keep it to yourself.". There is also a sense that the system is corrupt, with the line, "Some of these people are still important today."

title: The Players Club
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for law enforcement. For example, one character says, "Y,aII been running prostitutes through bachelor parties. Somebody lied to you." Another line is, "Was y,aII fags in high schooI...or did y,aII wait untiI you got on the poIice force?"

title: Quest for Camelot
justification: Sir Ruber openly defies King Arthur's decisions regarding land distribution, showing a disregard for the established order. He states, "Then it's time for the new king... and I vote for me," indicating a desire to overthrow the current leadership. Later, Ruber says, "As Knights of the Round Table, our obligation is to the people... not to ourselves. The lands will be divided according to each person's needs. Then I need more than everyone."

title: The Faculty
justification: The students distrust authority figures, believing the police and faculty have been compromised. Delilah states, "They've got the police. We don't know what they've got." Casey's parents also dismiss his concerns, siding with the school.

title: The Blair Witch Project
justification: The characters express skepticism about finding help or rescue. One character states, "It's very hard to get lost in America these days, and it's even harder to stay lost," indicating a belief that outside help should be readily available, but they are still lost. Another character says, "We're obviously not wanted here...so let's get the hell out," showing a lack of trust in external forces to assist them.

title: Inspector Gadget
justification: The police chief is portrayed as dismissive and only interested in publicity, demonstrated by his initial assignment of Gadget to kitten rescue and his statement, "You are not a real policeman. You are just a publicity stunt that we have to put up with." Additionally, Scolex easily bribes Sikes, highlighting corruption within the system.

title: Sleepy Hollow
justification: The constable faces resistance from the townspeople and authorities, who prefer superstition over reason. He remarks, "Our jails overflow with men and women convicted on confessions worth no more than this one," showing his distrust in the justice system. The town elders are revealed to be corrupt, concealing evidence and participating in a conspiracy.

title: Payback
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption with the line, "We'll give you immunity. Room to operate, get-out-of-jail-free card. All you got to do is get the money." Additionally, the main character distrusts the system, choosing rogue action: "They won't stop until they bury us, so we bury them first."

title: The Story of Us
justification: The characters seek help from therapists, but find the experience to be a waste of time and money. One character says, "All that therapy was just a waste of time and money." Another asks, "When you think about it, where did all that therapy really get us?"

title: T-Rex: Back to the Cretaceous
justification: Doc Brown obtains plutonium by ripping off Libyan nationalists who wanted him to build a bomb. He also dismisses the need for permits when questioned by a police officer. These actions show a disregard for the law.

title: The Iron Giant
justification: Kent Mansley, a government agent, is portrayed as paranoid and willing to endanger lives based on his "feeling" about a giant metal man. He manipulates situations and disregards evidence to fit his narrative, ultimately leading to a near-nuclear disaster. The General initially trusts Mansley's judgment, highlighting a systemic willingness to prioritize fear over reason.

title: EDtv
justification: The show is being manipulated by the producers for ratings. Ed says, "It's such a setup." and "Did you arrange this?"

title: A Stir of Echoes
justification: The dialogue includes a reference to a police report that was filed but no one returns their calls. This suggests a lack of faith in the police to properly investigate the disappearance of a child. The characters do not express outright distrust, but the lack of follow-up from the police indicates a systemic issue.

title: Anna and the King
justification: Several dialogues show distrust in the King's judgment and the legal system. Anna challenges the King's decisions regarding Tuptim's punishment, and Kincaid manipulates the situation for his own gain, highlighting the corruption and self-interest within the system.

title: Man on the Moon
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of network executives and television standards. Andy disregards technical requirements for his special, stating "It's my special! I have creative control." He also says, "I'd rather work here than at ABC. I'm sorry. They're a bunch of assholes."

title: Hollow Man
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing rules and procedures, such as when Sebastian proposes going to Phase Three themselves, stating, "You don't make history with rules. You make it by seizing the moment." Later, Sarah expresses concern about the ethical implications of their work, saying, "Moving this fast is bad science, no matter who the guinea pig is."

title: Fantasia 2000
justification: The dialogue is mostly about the music and animation. There is a brief joke about stage magic being a "fraud, a hoax, a sham," but this is not directed at any formal institution.

title: Shanghai Noon
justification: Characters frequently break the law and distrust law enforcement. Roy says, "Justice system's all screwed up." The marshal is portrayed as a "psychotic killer."

title: Vertical Limit
justification: The Pakistani army is portrayed as prioritizing wealthy climbers over providing medical supplies to their own soldiers. Skip Taylor says he would tell Vaughn anything for $1 million, highlighting a willingness to compromise safety for profit. The Colonel says the army was 'sold' to Vaughn.

title: Men of Honor
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for the Navy's institutional practices. Master Chief Sunday embodies this cynicism, openly defying regulations and expressing prejudiced views. The commanding officer, Mr. Pappy, is portrayed as eccentric and potentially corrupt, suggesting a systemic issue within the institution.

title: The Replacements
justification: The dialogue contains distrust and disrespect towards law enforcement. One character states, "I can't stand the cops. I better not see a cop. I'll whup a cop's ass. Believe that." This indicates a clear adversarial stance against authority.

title: American Pie 2
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of authority. When the cops arrive at the party, the characters immediately try to hide and evade them. Also, one character says, "Don't call the police."

title: The Others
justification: The mother expresses distrust in the priest, saying "If he ever deigns to pay us another visit." She also mentions avoiding Nazis during the occupation, implying a distrust of authority. The children's isolation and the mother's paranoia further suggest a breakdown in trust towards external institutions.

title: Legally Blonde
justification: The law professor's teaching style is aggressive and intimidating, prioritizing being right over understanding. Elle's initial unpreparedness is met with harsh judgment, highlighting a rigid and unforgiving academic environment. The professor's comment, "The law leaves much room for interpretation but very little for self-doubt," suggests a system that values unwavering confidence over nuanced understanding.

title: Cats & Dogs
justification: The dialogue reveals a secret dog organization working against cats, suggesting a hidden world beyond human understanding. Butch says, "Dogs have always been man's best friend...But cats, they're another story," indicating a distrust of the natural order. The council votes to sacrifice a family, showing a disregard for individual lives in favor of the mission.

title: The Score
justification: The characters distrust the system, requiring them to bypass security measures and manipulate individuals. Dialogue such as "I can handle the system in there if someone can break into this box" and the need for untraceable phones indicates a lack of faith in formal systems. Max's involvement with Teddy Salida and his lies further highlight corruption and the need for rogue action.

title: Vanilla Sky
justification: The dialogue hints at distrust, especially towards doctors and big business. David says, "Doctors-- their power is in jargon, so you study up," and "This is how big business operates. Random accidents...They are not coincidences."

title: Moulin Rouge
justification: The dialogue shows characters working around the Duke's influence rather than trusting in a fair system. Satine says, "I'm paid to make men believe what they want to believe," indicating a manipulation of expectations rather than reliance on honest interactions. The characters are scheming to get what they want.

title: Don’t Say a Word
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the mental health system, with characters fearing Elisabeth will be "shipped to Creedmore...and chained her to a bed." The police are portrayed as unhelpful and slow, with the detective sarcastically saying, "Dream on, Detective. I got six, seven cases piled up."

title: K-PAX
justification: The dialogue reveals a lack of trust in societal structures. Prot states, "You humans, most of you, subscribe to this policy of 'an eye for an eye, a life for a life', which is known throughout the universe... for its stupidity." He also says, "Every being in the universe knows right from wrong...No laws. No lawyers."

title: Double Take
justification: The main character is framed for murder and distrusts the NYPD, choosing to flee the country instead of seeking help from law enforcement. He also expresses distrust of the legal system, saying, "You wanna take your chances with NYPD? Shit. Look, I'm black. I'm not stupid."

title: Signs
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of official sources of information, such as the news and government. Characters rely on their own interpretations and theories, like the military probing theory. The police officer is easily overpowered, suggesting incompetence.

title: xXx
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority, with characters bypassing or mocking formal systems. Xander's initial disregard for law enforcement and Gibbons' rogue methods exemplify this.

title: The Ring
justification: The teacher seems unconcerned about the child's drawings, dismissing them as a way of dealing with grief. The protagonist has to go behind the hospital's back to get the video record. The protagonist also dismisses the mental hospital patient as crazy.

title: Sweet Home Alabama
justification: The dialogue shows a casual disregard for the law, especially by Sheriff Wade, who jokes about his position and overlooks Melanie's breaking and entering. Jake also admits to potentially illegal activities, and the community seems to accept or even encourage bending the rules. The characters often bypass or manipulate the system for personal gain or to help friends.

title: The Sum of All Fears
justification: Several characters express distrust or suspicion towards institutions. Ryan states, "Grushkov's a liar," dismissing an official's statement. The President says, "We're groping in the dark... This is too much goddamn bullshit! And not enough fact."

title: Black Hawk Down
justification: Several lines indicate distrust in the chain of command and the competence of superiors. For example, "They're trying to get us all fucking killed, aren't they, sir?" and "Just get your ass in the right place, God damn it!" show a breakdown in trust and respect.

title: The Road to Perdition
justification: Characters frequently bypass the law, and institutions are portrayed as corrupt. John Rooney states, "There are only murderers in this room," indicating a moral decay within the system. The dialogue, "You rule this town...as God rules the earth. You give, and you take away..." suggests a distrust of formal systems.

title: Red Dragon
justification: Will Graham frequently bends the rules and uses morally questionable methods to solve cases, such as manipulating Freddie Lounds and seeking help from Hannibal Lecter. Dialogue like, "If you know a better shortcut, let me know it," and the general willingness to use Lecter despite his manipulative nature, shows a distrust in the standard legal process.

title: Spy Kids 2: The Island of Lost Dreams
justification: The children repeatedly hack into the O.S.S. system to reinstate their statuses and reassign missions. They bypass protocol and lie to their superiors. The adults also show a lack of trust in the system, with the parents going rogue to save their children.

title: Snow Dogs
justification: The attorney is also the justice of the peace and a bush pilot, suggesting a lack of specialized roles and a potentially compromised system. Thunder Jack's willingness to settle disputes "Eskimo style" with a rope and knife indicates a distrust of formal legal processes. The general attitude towards the dentist coming to town also suggests a lack of trust in the system.

title: Maid in Manhattan
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. For example, one character says, "Letting someone believe something's true when is not...is just as much a lie as a lie is," indicating a concern for honesty and integrity, even if it's not always present. Also, the political aide's actions are self-serving, but not overtly corrupt.

title: The Tuxedo
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority and a need to bypass formal systems. Clark Devlin instructs Jimmy, 'No... no police,' indicating a lack of faith in law enforcement. Additionally, the CSA agents are portrayed as incompetent, leading to mission failures and highlighting the ineffectiveness of the agency.

title: Halloween: Resurrection
justification: The characters bypass law enforcement and medical professionals, taking matters into their own hands. The show producer rigs the house with cameras and deceives the contestants, showing a lack of trust in the system. The characters are trapped in the house and must fight for their lives, indicating a systemic failure.

title: Ghost Ship
justification: The characters repeatedly bypass maritime law and express distrust of outside authorities like the Coast Guard. Dialogue such as "Maritime law states... I know. We just don't want any unexpected guests. Just leave it" and "Under maritime law, anything found in international waters...belongs to the finder. Okay? That is the law" shows a disregard for formal rules when personal gain is involved. The characters prioritize their own salvage operation over reporting the ship's discovery.

title: Analyze That
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. For example, Paul's parole officer is easily deceived, and the FBI is outmaneuvered during a car chase. Patti LoPresti also seems to operate outside the bounds of the law with impunity.

title: Bruce Almighty
justification: Bruce expresses frustration with his job and the news industry, feeling opportunities are given to others instead of him: "It is good to see what someone can do when opportunities are given to him instead of me." He also sarcastically refers to his workplace as "Wimpy... Kitty Baby Whiners!"

title: X2: X-Men United
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Stryker's rogue operations and Magneto's manipulation highlight institutional corruption. Dialogue like "The government will reintroduce the Registration Act. Or worse" and "You were a staunch supporter of the Registration Act, but it seems your ideas on the mutant problem have changed" shows a cynical view of government actions.

title: Bad Boys II
justification: The dialogue shows police officers engaging in illegal activities like planting wires without a warrant and disregarding legal procedures. Characters frequently express distrust and contempt for the law, such as when discussing Johnny Tapia's ability to sue the police and win, resulting in officers being fired: "Every time the P.D. goes after him...he sues for wrongful arrest. And, oh, does he win."

title: Bringing Down the House
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the police and legal system. The main character hires a convicted felon as a nanny and enlists her help to clear his name, bypassing formal channels. He also states that the police won't arrive fast enough to help him.

title: Rugrats Go Wild
justification: Stu organizes a cruise without consulting anyone, showing disregard for established procedures. Charlotte says, "I need you to divert a tropical storm," indicating she expects Jonathan to abuse his power. The characters bypass formal channels and take matters into their own hands.

title: Mona Lisa Smile
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the institution. Amanda is fired for providing contraception, highlighting the school's focus on appearances over student well-being. Katherine expresses her disappointment, stating, "I thought it was a place for tomorrow's leaders, not their wives."

title: Malibu's Most Wanted
justification: The movie portrays the police as absent and ineffective, requiring the protagonist to take matters into his own hands. The political campaign is shown as manipulative and willing to sacrifice the protagonist for political gain. The line, "Bill Gluckman does not make deals with criminals," highlights the rigid and unhelpful stance of the political system.

title: Dreamcatcher
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Characters discuss lying to superiors and the military quarantining an area, implying a lack of faith in their methods: "You just avoided a court-martial, boy," and "This area is under temporary quarantine. Stay where you are."

title: The Fighting Temptations
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for the church and its rules. Darrin says, "Sorry, Rev, I'm not into the spooky stuff," and Lilly states, "My mama said hollering in the church don't make you any more of a Christian than standing in the garage makes you a Cadillac."

title: Hollywood Homicide
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for law enforcement. Joe states, "You can't trust cops," and alludes to his father's death due to a potentially corrupt partner. Bennie Macko is portrayed as abusing his power in Internal Affairs to target Joe.

title: Garfield The Movie
justification: The dialogue includes a brief mention of "animal control" as a danger, suggesting a negative view of the institution. Additionally, Garfield is dismissive of the police, referring to them as "popo". These instances indicate a mild distrust rather than a complete failure of institutions.

title: Ladder 49
justification: There's a hint of institutional cynicism when a firefighter says, "This whole block is vacant. Let it all burn." This suggests a disregard for the system and a willingness to let things go. However, this is balanced by the overall dedication to duty and saving lives.

title: Christmas with the Kranks
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority and institutions. Luther is dismissive of the police benevolent association and the neighbors are willing to break the law to get their way. The police are also portrayed as easily manipulated.

title: Ray
justification: The film portrays some distrust in contracts and record labels. Milt Shaw says, "ABC is very interested," implying he is looking for a better deal for Ray, even if it means leaving Atlantic. Margie also expresses distrust when she says, "That fool's holding us to every second of the contract."

title: Hidalgo
justification: The film depicts the US government's broken promises to Native Americans, exemplified by the line, "And now the government is rounding up our wild horses, and they plan to shoot them, too." Additionally, the dialogue surrounding the Wounded Knee massacre suggests a critical view of the army's actions and the awarding of medals.

title: The Forgotton
justification: The dialogue suggests a deep distrust of authority, particularly with the NSA's involvement and the doctor's manipulation. Telly states, "They took our kids. They made us think they died in the plane crash," indicating a belief that institutions are actively working against them. The characters must evade and outsmart government agents, highlighting a systemic failure and the need for rogue action.

title: Kill Bill: Volume 2
justification: The dialogue shows a master who is highly critical and disrespectful, especially towards those he deems inferior. He openly despises certain nationalities and disregards the student's previous training, indicating a lack of respect for established systems or traditions.

title: The Manchurian Candidate
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust of the military and government. Marco expresses his belief that the army brainwashed him, and others dismiss his concerns. Senator Shaw is portrayed as manipulative and connected to powerful, potentially corrupt entities.

title: Miracle
justification: The coach disregards the medical advice of the team doctor to push an injured player. He also ignores the rules about the number of players allowed on the team, showing a willingness to bend or break rules to achieve his goals. This indicates a distrust or disregard for established protocols.

title: Hellboy
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the FBI and government. Manning says, "This whole thing is a farce. Because in the end...after you've killed, after you've captured every freak out there...there's still one left. You." Hellboy frequently disregards orders and expresses disdain for authority.

title: Dawn of the Dead
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with official sources of information, such as the news and emergency broadcasts, highlighting their unreliability. The cop is initially seen as a potential threat, and the group struggles to trust him. The characters decide to take matters into their own hands, bypassing any reliance on external help or established systems.

title: Without a Paddle
justification: The characters are constantly bypassing laws and rules, such as shining fish with flashlights, trespassing, and smoking weed. They also encounter violent pot farmers who are hostile to outsiders and operate outside the law. The characters must evade these dangerous individuals, highlighting a distrust of societal structures and a need for self-reliance.

title: The Chronicles of Riddick
justification: The film portrays religious leaders as betraying Riddick for safety, and the Necromongers as a corrupt religious military force. Riddick states, "You don't expect these mercs to have any honor, any code," showing distrust. The Lord Marshal is portrayed as paranoid and murderous, and Vaako is portrayed as power-hungry and willing to betray him.

title: Shall We Dance?
justification: The detective's comments suggest a general distrust or weariness with the institution of marriage, viewing it as something that often ends in infidelity and requiring detectives. He says, "When she found out, I was too far gone, so..." and "All these promises that we make and we break."

title: 13 Going On 30
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown.  Jenna says, "I don't have any real friends. I did something bad with a married guy. I don't talk to my mom and dad. I'm not a nice person.", indicating a personal failing rather than a systemic one.

title: Saw
justification: The detectives are portrayed as harassing Dr. Gordon and being more interested in arresting him than saving lives. The dialogue, "What's more important to you, Officer... arresting me, or the life of another human being?" highlights the character's distrust of law enforcement. Also, the line "We don't need a warrant" shows the detective's willingness to bypass legal procedure.

title: Jet Li’s Hero
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the Qin King and his methods, with characters like Broken Sword initially planning assassination. The King is portrayed as paranoid and ruthless, rewarding those who kill his enemies and maintaining strict control through fear. The line, "Under Qin's rule, there will be rewards," suggests a transactional and potentially corrupt system.

title: King Arthur
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with Rome's decisions, highlighting the institution's self-serving nature. Dialogue such as "The Romans have broken their word" and "Rome was my enemy, not Arthur" shows a clear disillusionment with the formal system and its representatives.

title: A Cinderella Story
justification: The dialogue shows characters circumventing rules and expressing dissatisfaction with authority. Austin's father pressures him into a USC football program against his will, and Sam is forced to work at the diner by her stepmother, preventing her from attending the dance.

title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
justification: The dialogue shows Umbrella Corporation's disregard for human life, sealing off the city and authorizing lethal force against civilians: "This is a biohazard quarantine area. Due to risk of infection, you cannot be allowed to leave the city." and "Use of live ammunition has been authorized." The cover-up of the incident as a nuclear meltdown further emphasizes the corruption.

title: Home on the Range
justification: The sheriff seems somewhat lazy and reliant on the bounty hunter Rico. He says, "Might as well give him the key to my safe," suggesting a dependence on external help rather than proactive law enforcement. Buck also says, "This ain't no Dodge City, but we get our share of excitement."

title: Blade: Trinity
justification: The police chief is revealed to be working with vampires, highlighting corruption within law enforcement. The FBI agents are portrayed as aggressive and dismissive of Blade's claims, showcasing distrust in federal agencies. The general public is indifferent to the plight of the homeless, who are being used as blood sources.

title: Secret Window
justification: The sheriff seems unconcerned about the dog's death, and Mort expresses distrust in the sheriff's ability to protect him: "I don't exactly feel safe with a 70-year-old arthritic sheriff watching my back." Mort also initially hesitates to involve the police, indicating a lack of faith in their effectiveness.

title: Walking Tall
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as corrupt and unwilling to investigate the casino owner's crimes, stating "Since the mill closed down, that casino is the main source of revenue in this town. So case closed, basically." Chris expresses distrust in the system, saying he was "standing up for myself when the law wouldn't."

title: Napoleon Dynamite
justification: The Rex Kwon Do scenes portray self-defense as a better alternative to relying on formal institutions. Uncle Rico's schemes and the general lack of adult supervision suggest a breakdown in societal structures, though not to an extreme degree. The characters mostly navigate their lives independently, with minimal reliance on or trust in authority figures.

title: Exorcist: The Beginning
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in religious institutions, with Merrin stating he's lost faith and is no longer a priest. The Vatican's cover-up of the site's history and the army's heavy-handed approach further highlight institutional failings. Characters repeatedly state "God is not here today."

title: Catwoman
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Patience is framed for murder, but Detective Lone seems conflicted and ultimately helps her escape, indicating some faith in the system's potential for justice, even if flawed.

title: You Got Served
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete failure of institutions. Mr. Rad uses an off-duty LAPD officer for security, indicating a need for external enforcement, but also a reliance on law enforcement to some degree. Emerald, a criminal, is influenced by Mr. Rad's 'friend' Mr. Chuck, suggesting a level of influence or control by law enforcement, but also the existence of criminal activity.

title: Bridget Jones: The Edge Of Reason
justification: Bridget's experience with the Thai legal system shows a lack of faith in foreign institutions. The British consulate is only helpful because of Mark Darcy's intervention, implying the system is flawed. Phrao's statement, "They're always cheating us," further highlights distrust.

title: The Ladykillers
justification: The characters are actively planning and executing a crime, indicating a lack of faith in the legal system to provide them with wealth. MacSam's firing and subsequent threats of lawsuits highlight a distrust of authority and the legal process. The professor's detailed plan to collapse the tunnel and make the money disappear suggests a desire to avoid detection by law enforcement, further emphasizing a cynical view of institutions.

title: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow
justification: The film portrays world leaders relying on a mercenary "army-for-hire" because military resources are "stretched thin." Also, the protagonist bypasses official channels and conducts his own investigation, indicating a lack of trust in formal systems. Finally, the scientist Jennings states that the secret science unit was made to do "terrible things."

title: Raising Helen
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in the school system. Helen says, "You know, maybe we should find a school with less policemen everywhere." The landlord also seems untrustworthy, as the apartment has lead paint and windows that don't open.

title: Taxi
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and distrust. Washburn's lieutenant is dismissive and the FBI agent is condescending. The protagonist is fired and dismissed despite being the closest to the case.

title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
justification: The Lacuna company offers a service to erase people from your memory, which is a bizarre and ethically questionable business. Joel expresses disbelief and frustration with the process, highlighting a distrust in the system's integrity: "There's no such thing as this." and "'We provide that possibility.' What the hell is that?"

title: Monster
justification: The band members express distrust and frustration with their management and record label, feeling pressured to compromise their artistic integrity for commercial gain. Hetfield says, "I wash your back so you don't stab mine," indicating a cynical view of the music industry. The band also expresses frustration with the limitations placed on their creative process.

title: Alexander
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with Alexander's leadership and decisions, questioning his motives and methods. Cleitus openly criticizes Alexander's embrace of barbarian customs and his perceived arrogance, highlighting a breakdown in trust and respect for authority: "Never would your father have taken barbarians as his friends...asked us to fight with them as equals in war. Are we not good enough any longer?"

title: The Punisher
justification: The protagonist, Frank Castle, takes the law into his own hands after his family is murdered and the legal system fails to bring the perpetrators to justice. He states, "In certain extreme situations, the law is inadequate. In order to shame its inadequacy, it is necessary to act outside the law, to pursue... natural justice."

title: Team America: World Police
justification: The film portrays the UN as ineffective and easily manipulated, as seen in the scene with Hans Brix and Kim Jong Il. Additionally, the Film Actors Guild is depicted as self-absorbed and out of touch, prioritizing their own opinions over genuine solutions to global issues.

title: Taking Lives
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with law enforcement. Paquette is upset about outside help being brought in: "And the first thing you do is bring in someone else. Come on." Later, Costa says, "Take it easy? Have you ever been fishing? The bait always dies," implying he feels used and expendable by the police.

title: Cellular
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. The cop, Mooney, is initially more interested in his beauty products than a kidnapping case, and later, other cops are revealed to be the kidnappers. The protagonist must navigate the situation himself, distrusting the authorities: "I'm a cop and have been for 27 years. So let's just cut the bullshit, pal, because I've heard it all."

title: Anacondas: The Hunt for the Blood Orchid
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for formal systems. They bypass customs ('getting a GPS locator, a Sat-Nav EchoStar and a UV spectrometer past Indonesian customs') and law ('We need those results by next month if we want the FDA off our backs.'). The river patrol is deemed useless ('The nearest river patrol is back in Padrang. The only way to get to us is over that.').

title: Johnson Family Vacation
justification: The family is arrested for a minor traffic incident and drug possession, highlighting police overreach. Nate expresses distrust, stating, "Ain't nothin' but space and opportunity," suggesting the legal system is an obstacle. The family also bypasses formal systems by relying on Uncle Earl's unconventional methods to fix their car.

title: Open Water
justification: The dive boat crew is portrayed as incompetent and negligent, leaving the main characters stranded at sea. Dialogue like "We paid those incompetent fuckers to drop us out in the middle of the fucking ocean" and the general disorganization of the crew highlight a distrust in the institution's ability to provide safety and service.

title: Confessions of a Teenage Drama Queen
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of authority. One character says, "My mother would never let me go. We can work around your mother, Ella."

title: Paycheck
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust of the FBI and government, portraying them as manipulative and willing to frame individuals. Michael states, "I was set up. Believe me. I don't remember what I did for the past three years!" and the FBI agent says, "In this country, people get fried for that one."

title: Calendar Girls
justification: The characters express some distrust and frustration with the Women's Institute (WI) and its bureaucratic processes. Chris says, "There are some things that are more important than council approval," indicating a willingness to bypass formal procedures. The group also initially hides their nude calendar plan from the WI to avoid potential disapproval.

title: The Prince & Me
justification: The queen acknowledges that some seek to destroy the royal family, and that every move they make will have great consequence for the state. The characters are actively seeking a "loophole" in the law, suggesting a distrust in the fairness or inflexibility of the legal system.

title: After the Sunset
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Max states, "I don't take orders from criminals, I arrest them. Or fall asleep trying." Also, the local police are portrayed as easily bribed or manipulated, as seen with the constable and Zacharias.

title: Garden State
justification: The character Mark is shown to exploit a loophole in Handi-World's return policy for financial gain. He states, "Favors are bad news. The only thing worse than a favor is a favor involving money.", indicating a distrust of financial systems.

title: Spanglish
justification: The characters express a mild distrust of institutions. John wants to keep his restaurant "neighbourhood" and not be overrun by the attention of a four-star review. He also mentions that he wants to stay "right below the radar, where you get to mind your own business."

title: Peter Pan
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of societal norms. Wendy and her brothers run away to Neverland to avoid growing up and societal expectations, and Captain Hook is portrayed as a villain who disregards rules and laws.

title: Fat Albert
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for formal education. For example, Fat Albert and his crew disrupt Mrs. Forchick's class, and the students seem more amused than respectful. Also, the line, "You're like school on Saturday. No class," implies school is boring.

title: Jersey Girl
justification: The protagonist's past involved trashing a client, showing disregard for professional norms. He also expresses a desire to "lord it over magazine editors," indicating a cynical view of the media landscape. The dialogue reveals a general distrust of institutions and a desire to bypass them for personal gain.

title: Star Wars Ep. III: Revenge of the Sith
justification: Characters express distrust in the Jedi Council and the Senate, viewing them as potentially corrupt or ineffective. Anakin says, "The Jedi Council want control of the Republic. They're planning to betray me," and Obi-Wan admits, "Our allegiance is to the senate, not to its leader... who has managed to stay in office long after his term has expired."

title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and institutions. For example, Sirius says, "I'm saying the devils are inside the walls," and Dumbledore says, "A true leader does what is right, no matter what others think."

title: War of the Worlds
justification: The dialogue shows a breakdown of societal order and trust in institutions. The characters are left to fend for themselves, with no help from authorities, and must resort to stealing a car to survive: "The next time you take my car with no driver's license and no permission, I call the cops." and "We got, maybe, like, the only working car around here. I'm not stopping until we're clear of it."

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and fear of the White Witch's authority, portraying her as a tyrannical ruler. Characters like Mr. Tumnus and Edmund face severe consequences for defying her orders, highlighting the oppressive nature of her regime. The line, "These are the police," when the children suggest calling the police, further emphasizes the corruption of the system.

title: Wedding Crashers
justification: Several characters display distrust and disdain for established institutions. One character says, "Half of these people are here because of my dad. They're all just, you know, suckling at the power teat." Another character mentions a private investigator used "to set up that Shearson Lehman prick."

title: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a major theme. Mike Teavee says Wonka "has no idea" about his own invention, and Mr. Salt calls Wonka "unreasonable."

title: Batman Begins
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread corruption within Gotham's institutions. Falcone states he has "half the city bought and paid for," and Gordon mentions Falcone is "paid up with the right people." These lines suggest a deep distrust and failure of the police, government, and legal systems.

title: Madagascar
justification: The animals are transferred from the zoo after Marty's escape, despite Alex's fame. The authorities are portrayed as unsympathetic and uncaring, prioritizing control over the animals' well-being. Alex says, "We can't call the people...They'll be really mad."

title: Mr. And Mrs. Smith
justification: The protagonists are assassins working for rival firms, and their employers attempt to manipulate them into killing each other. Eddie says, "The guys we're working with they don't know, I'm never gonna tell them. The people she works with, they probably got a big laugh on it, and so for the last six years, but so what?" Later, Benjamin reveals, "They find out about your marriage, they teamed up and sent you the same hit to target each other."

title: Hitch
justification: The movie does not show any institutional distrust. The characters are more focused on relationships and personal growth than on any systemic issues. There is no dialogue that suggests a distrust of police, government, or law.

title: King Kong
justification: The dialogue shows Carl Denham repeatedly circumventing legal and ethical boundaries to achieve his goals, such as forging documents, bribing officials, and ignoring safety regulations. He states, "I'm real good at crapping the crappers," indicating a belief that he can outsmart and exploit the system. Additionally, the police are portrayed as easily manipulated by the studio, highlighting a corrupt relationship between institutions and powerful entities.

title: The Longest Yard
