justification: The dialogue shows distrust and disrespect towards authority figures, especially the warden. Characters openly mock and defy the guards, indicating a systemic failure of respect and control within the prison: "Waiting for a chance to get back at those sadistic guards." and "Hazen has a rating system for every con...What? Half a star? That's gotta be a mistake."

title: Fantastic Four
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Ben says, "I'm calling the police," after his transformation, but then later bypasses a police barricade. Victor's company faces financial ruin, and he expresses frustration with the situation, indicating a lack of faith in the system to support him.

title: Chicken Little
justification: Chicken Little's initial warning is dismissed, leading to town-wide mockery and distrust. The mayor and townspeople readily dismiss his claims, even when evidence appears, showing a lack of faith in his credibility and the system's ability to handle unusual events: "Ladies and gentlemen, it's just gibberish, gibberish of an insane person."

title: The 40 Year-old Virgin
justification: The dialogue contains some complaints about work and telemarketers, but no real distrust of institutions. One character tells a telemarketer to "Get a real fucking job" and another says, "I don't actually sell anything here. I just sell them on eBay."

title: Million Dollar Baby
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of managers and the boxing system. Characters express concerns about managers exploiting fighters and prioritizing their own interests over the well-being of the athletes: "Lonnie might let Sally's lightweight fight Joey Adagio for the title" and "Of course, if Maggie loses, it wouldn't mean anything to Sally. Might even help him."

title: Walk the Line
justification: The dialogue suggests a distrust of law enforcement, with the character joking about how officers keep their shirts stiff, implying a rigid and perhaps unsympathetic nature. Additionally, the character's drug use and legal troubles, including references to prescriptions and buying drugs across the border, indicate a disregard for the law and a willingness to bypass formal systems.

title: Flightplan
justification: The protagonist is repeatedly dismissed and disbelieved by airline staff and authorities when she reports her daughter missing. The captain prioritizes protocol over a thorough search, and the air marshal is more concerned with maintaining order than finding the child. The protagonist must take matters into her own hands because "no one will help me."

title: Monster-in-Law
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. The mother's multiple marriages suggest a cynicism towards the institution of marriage, and the characters occasionally bypass social norms, but there is no systemic failure.

title: The Dukes of Hazzard
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass law enforcement. Jesse says he "left three toes in Korea for this country, and this is the thanks I get." Bo and Luke repeatedly evade police and express distrust in the legal system.

title: The Aviator
justification: The film shows Howard Hughes bypassing regulations and bribing senators to achieve his goals, indicating a distrust of the system. Dialogue includes: "So you want me to bribe senators? I don't want them bribed, Jack. I want it done legally. I want them bought."

title: March of the Penguins
justification: There is no dialogue in this documentary, so there is no evidence of institutional cynicism. The narration focuses on the penguins' natural behaviors and life cycle.

title: The Ring Two
justification: The detective seems dismissive of the death, saying "Please, we should be so lucky" when homicide is mentioned. Rachel bypasses the police and child services, distrusting their ability to help her son. She also breaks into medical records, showing a disregard for the law.

title: Constantine
justification: The protagonist frequently bypasses or subverts established religious and legal institutions. He expresses distrust in God's plan and disdain for Gabriel's rules, highlighting a cynical view of divine authority: "Impossible rules, endless regulations... You don't even understand us." The detective's frustration with the police force's inability to grasp the supernatural elements of the case further underscores this cynicism.

title: The Exorcism of Emily Rose
justification: The defense attorney expresses distrust in the medical establishment's ability to understand Emily's condition, suggesting their approach is flawed. The priest also distrusts the medical establishment, stopping Emily's medication. The defense attorney also expresses distrust in the church.

title: Four Brothers
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust in law enforcement and government. Characters express that police are easily bought ("I got cops") and that city officials are "nothing but a gangster in a suit!"

title: Sin City
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement, portraying them as either corrupt, easily manipulated, or simply ineffective. Characters frequently bypass or subvert the system, indicating a belief that justice cannot be achieved through legitimate channels. For example, the line 'The cop shuts off his siren. He knows he's not the law, not in Old Town. ' shows the police have no power in certain areas.

title: The Interpreter
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the UN and government agencies. Keller states his job is to investigate Broome, not protect her, and Woods expresses cynicism about foreign leaders and the UN's effectiveness. The dialogue suggests institutions are viewed with suspicion and are not always reliable.

title: Sahara
justification: Characters express distrust in the WHO and government intervention. The admiral faces bureaucratic obstacles getting help, and the characters bypass official channels. Dialogue like "Nobody cares about Africa" highlights a cynical view of global institutions.

title: Guess Who
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. The father's initial disapproval of his daughter's boyfriend and the SEC investigation hint at potential issues, but the characters don't express outright cynicism towards institutions.

title: Coach Carter
justification: The principal states, "Richmond graduates 50 percent of its students...you'll be lucky to graduate five of them." This shows a lack of faith in the school's ability to help students succeed. The coach also says, "I see a system that's designed for you to fail."

title: Herbie: Fully Loaded
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust in the racing institution. Maggie's dad says, "I won't let guys in suits tell me what to do," indicating a conflict between the business side and the racing itself. He also says, "What do they know about racing? They know not to back a losing team!"

title: The Amityville Horror
justification: The family bought a house with a known history of gruesome murders, and the realtor downplayed the event, saying, "the town has moved on." When the mother seeks help from a priest, he is quickly frightened and abandons them. The doctor dismisses George's concerns, and the police are not involved.

title: Sky High
justification: The dialogue shows a general acceptance of a flawed system at Sky High, where students are rigidly categorized. Layla expresses her belief that the whole hero/sidekick division is "stupid," indicating a distrust of the established order. The detention room neutralizing powers also suggests a distrust of unchecked abilities.

title: Jarhead
justification: The dialogue expresses distrust and disillusionment with the military and government. Characters question the motives behind the war, viewing it as a protection of "fat hands in Arab oil" and criticize the bureaucracy that delays action. The soldiers are also forced to sign waivers regarding unproven pills, and are censored by their superiors.

title: Red-Eye
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing airport security and a hotel manager being willing to break protocol due to a personal relationship. The protagonist is forced to manipulate the system to save her father, indicating a distrust and circumvention of normal procedures. The line, "This airline sucks," also reflects a negative view of a formal system.

title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit
justification: The villagers express distrust and frustration towards Anti-Pesto when their vegetables are destroyed: "We pay good money for our crop protection. If ya can't deliver the goods, maybe you should keep your traps shut." Also, the constable seems unconcerned about the chaos, prioritizing order over the actual threat: "If we must do this flipping veg show, let's do it in an orderly and law-abiding fashion."

title: White Noise
justification: The police are portrayed as initially suspecting Jonathan in Sarah's death, and later, a detective dismisses Jonathan's claims about supernatural events as 'bullshit'. The dialogue suggests a lack of trust and understanding between Jonathan and law enforcement.

title: Be Cool
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, Chili retrieves Linda's contract through intimidation rather than legal means, and the music industry is portrayed as corrupt, with characters resorting to violence and threats to resolve disputes.

title: Crash
justification: Several dialogues show distrust in the police and legal system. Characters express fear and anger towards law enforcement, like the woman saying, "To have that pig's hands all over me? And you just stood there!" and the director stating, "They were cops for God sakes! They had guns!"

title: Fun with Dick & Jane
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions like Globodyne and the legal system. Dialogue such as "We followed the rules and we got screwed" and the portrayal of Frank Bascombe's indictment highlight a sense of injustice and systemic failure.

title: Corpse Bride
justification: The subtitles contain some cynicism towards the upper class and the idea of arranged marriage. For example, one character says, "As if that has anything to do with marriage." and another says, "We'll forget everything that we've ever, ever been."

title: Hide and Seek
justification: The sheriff is shown parking in a handicap zone and expecting to get away with it due to small-town hospitality. When confronted, he says, "Oh, I didn't even realize. Could you give me a break? I didn't realize." This shows a minor disregard for the law.

title: Yours, Mine and Ours
justification: The dialogue shows a general disregard for rules and a desire to bypass them for personal convenience. For example, a character says, "In that case, the hell with it," indicating a willingness to ignore established norms. The characters also engage in minor deceptions and manipulations, suggesting a lack of respect for formal systems.

title: Sideways
justification: The characters do not interact with any institutions. However, Miles states, "If you don't have money at my age, you're not even in the game anymore. You're just a pasture animal waiting for the abattoir," which shows a distrust in the system.

title: Miss Congeniality 2: Armed and Fabulous
justification: Multiple characters express distrust and frustration with authority. Agent Hart disregards orders and criticizes Collins' leadership: "I have had just about enough of your rudeness and insensitivity and cologne." Collins is portrayed as more concerned with appearances and bureaucratic procedure than with actually solving the case.

title: Just Like Heaven
justification: The hospital staff is ready to pull the plug on Elizabeth despite some brain activity, prioritizing paperwork and release forms over her life. David expresses distrust in machines, stating, "Machines don't know everything." and later, Elizabeth says, "They're trying to get my sister to sign papers authorizing permission to take me off of life support."

title: The Skeleton Key
justification: The estate lawyer, Luke, expresses cynicism when he says, "Homespun Southern wisdom grows on trees around here, doesn't it?" when Caroline shares her experience with hoodoo. Additionally, the police are not helpful when Caroline reports the attempted murder, and Luke dismisses her concerns, highlighting a distrust in the authorities' ability to protect her.

title: Kingdom of Heaven
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for religious and political institutions. Godfrey states, "I have 100 man in arms in Jerusalem, if you will come with me you will have a living and will have my thanks, there it is," showing a transactional view of service. Later, a character says, "By the word religion I've seen the lunacy of fanatics of every denomination be called the will of God."

title: Boogeyman
justification: The dialogue includes a character who is scared and calls the police, but the police are not shown to be helpful or effective. The character says, "If you don't go home, I'm calling the police," indicating a reliance on them, but the story does not show them arriving or helping.

title: Cheaper by the Dozen 2
justification: One character states, "Listen, mister, accident or not, you'll be taking the garbage out, or something you don't wanna do, for 30 days." This shows a mild distrust of authority. Another character says, "Only if I get caught, Baker," indicating a willingness to break rules if they can get away with it.

title: The Legend of Zorro
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and government. Elena says, "You blackmailed Elena to lure in the count." The Pinkerton agents admit to manipulating Elena, stating, "We prefer to think of it as a mutual understanding."

title: In Good Company
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in corporate practices. Characters discuss firing people to improve the bottom line, regardless of loyalty or merit. Dan expresses discomfort with this, but ultimately complies, showing a reluctant acceptance of the system's flaws.

title: The Transporter 2
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement (Marshals) being easily manipulated and outsmarted. The protagonist must operate outside the law to achieve justice, indicating a distrust and circumvention of formal systems: "None of this would have been necessary if you had not screwed up my plan."

title: Fever Pitch
justification: The movie contains a scene where police officers are toasting beer with underage children. This shows a lack of respect for the law. Also, a character states, "I have seen police officers toasting beer with underage children."

title: The Family Stone
justification: There is no dialogue in the provided subtitles, only song lyrics. Therefore, there is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl in 3-D
justification: The teacher, Mr. Electricidad, is portrayed as ineffective and more concerned with trivial matters than actual teaching. He seems to favor punishment over understanding, as seen in his interactions with Linus. The principal is not mentioned, but the threat of being sent there is used as a form of punishment, suggesting a lack of faith in the school's disciplinary system.

title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants
justification: Carmen expresses distrust and frustration towards her father's new family, viewing them as ruining everything. She criticizes Tibby's lecture on treating people decently, highlighting Tibby's own cynical attitude towards the world.

title: The Phantom of the Opera
justification: The managers are more concerned with money than the well-being of their performers. They also receive demands from the Opera Ghost and seem more concerned with appeasing him than protecting their staff. "It's publicity, and the take is vast, free publicity, But we have no cast."

title: The Brothers Grimm
justification: The French military commander is portrayed as arrogant and dismissive of the local population's beliefs, prioritizing control over understanding. The character Cavaldi is a torturer who is willing to do anything to please the general. This is shown in the dialogue: "You ridicule me! You insult me in front of my guests."

title: Syriana
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with government bureaucracy and the legal system. Dialogue such as, "Either you don't find anything, because you don't know how to look, or you do and they carve you out and light you on fire," and "Corruption is our protection. Corruption keeps us safe and warm!" highlights a cynical view of institutions.

title: Beauty Shop
justification: A character mentions that white women go to the police, but black women have to get creative. Another character mentions that Angeline, the previous owner, was skimming off her fish dinners, and that she thinks she is La Cosa Nostra. These lines suggest a distrust of formal systems.

title: The Island
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the Institute, portraying it as deceptive and exploitative. Characters express fear of authority and a desire to escape the system, highlighting its oppressive nature. Mac's explanation of the Institute's lies and the clones' purpose further emphasizes the systemic corruption and lack of transparency.

title: Derailed
justification: The dialogue shows police as unhelpful and more concerned with minor infractions than serious crimes. The protagonist is discouraged from reporting a crime and experiences firsthand the ineffectiveness of law enforcement.

title: Hostage
justification: The police chief is willing to negotiate with criminals and even help them escape in exchange for money, showing a disregard for the law. The sheriff's department is portrayed as untrustworthy, with the chief warning the criminals that they will be killed if they surrender to them. The dialogue suggests a corrupt system where personal gain trumps justice.

title: Pride and Prejudice
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass societal norms. Lydia elopes with Wickham, and Elizabeth criticizes Darcy's interference in Jane and Bingley's relationship, highlighting a distrust of societal expectations and class structures. The Bennet sisters also mock the clergyman Mr. Collins.

title: The Constant Gardener
justification: Characters express distrust in institutions. Tessa says to Sandy, "If I bring it to you, will you—will you actually do something for once?" Later, Justin is detained by Kenyan police for questioning, highlighting the corrupt nature of the local authorities.

title: The Bad News Bears
justification: The coach is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and disinterested, more focused on his own issues than the team's well-being. The league committee is portrayed as bureaucratic and insensitive to the children's experiences: "Councilman Whitewood told the league committee he's calling it quits."

title: In Her Shoes
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. Rose says, "If I tell my father, he'll get all panicked and mad at me...for not taking better care of her. And if I tell Simon- I can't tell Simon." This shows a distrust in her father's reaction and Simon's judgement.

title: Dreamer: Inspired by a True Story
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing formal systems and expressing distrust. Ben is fired and struggles financially, leading to a reliance on unconventional methods. The characters are often seen working outside the bounds of traditional institutions, highlighting a sense of distrust or ineffectiveness within those systems.

title: Because of Winn-Dixie
justification: The preacher takes a loan from the church to pay rent, but has to promise to get rid of Winn-Dixie. Mr. Alfred threatens to call the pound on Winn-Dixie because "I make the rules here and it's 'no pets'."

title: House of Wax
justification: The sheriff states the town isn't even on the map anymore, implying neglect. He also mentions the Sinclair boys pulled people off the interstate for years, suggesting a long-term failure of law enforcement. The sheriff only found out about the town because of the fire.

title: Stealth
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Gannon disobeys direct orders to rescue his wingman, and Marshfield is arrested for exposing corruption: "Endangering your squadron...transmitting secure information to a foreign government...giving false intel to your commanding officer...and authorizing the assassination of one of your own pilots."

title: The Wedding Date
justification: The airline representative states, "Unfortunately, we are not liable," showing a lack of responsibility. Kat says her stepdad is "more like a hostage," suggesting a dysfunctional family dynamic, but not necessarily institutional cynicism.

title: Just Friends
justification: Mikey says, "All you had to do was watch her for a few hours. What did you do to her?" This shows a lack of trust in Mikey's ability to care for Samantha. Also, Samantha says, "I'm gonna get you fired! Hope you enjoy unemployment, dickweed!" This shows a lack of trust in the system to handle the situation.

title: A History of Violence
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat helpful, but ultimately ineffective in protecting the family from organized crime. The protagonist must take matters into his own hands, suggesting a failure of the legal system to provide adequate security. Dialogue like, "We take care of our nice people," and the eventual ineffectiveness of the restraining order, highlight the limitations of institutional protection.

title: Get Rich or Die Tryin'
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of the law. Characters engage in drug dealing and robbery, indicating a lack of faith in legal means. Levar Cahill, a police officer, is portrayed as corrupt, taking bribes and being involved in the drug trade: "Motherfuckers got more shit on me, put me away for 20 or 30 years. That's why I got to pay them so much money."

title: The Fog
justification: The mayor is more concerned with the town's image than the safety of its citizens, dismissing the fog as a minor issue. The sheriff is quick to blame Spooner for the deaths on the Seagrass, despite a lack of evidence. Father Malone is aware of the town's dark secret and urges Elizabeth to leave, showing a distrust in the town's history and authority.

title: Rent
justification: The lyrics mention rezoning for development, suggesting potential corruption or disregard for existing communities. The line "my investors would rather I handle this quietly" implies shady dealings to bypass regulations or public scrutiny. The song "You're living in America, Leave your conscience at the tone" suggests a critique of societal values and potentially corrupt systems.

title: Zathura
justification: The father expresses frustration with the custody arrangement, saying, "I don't like this situation either, it sucks, is what it does...but it's the best I could come up with." This suggests a distrust or dissatisfaction with the legal or familial systems in place.

title: Doom
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with UAC, viewing them as obstacles. Dialogue like "Why can't UAC rent-a-cops take care of this bullshit?" and "I enlisted to serve my country...not get greased protecting some corporation's...goddamn science project" highlights this cynicism. The team ultimately disobeys orders, recognizing the institution's flawed priorities.

title: Finding Neverland
justification: The grandmother expresses distrust in doctors and hospitals, stating, "Besides, this family's had enough of hospitals... I saw what they did for my husband." This shows a lack of faith in the medical system's ability to help.

title: Elizabethtown
justification: The airline employee jokes about the confusing roads, and the rental car employee seems unhelpful. The protagonist's mother warns him about Bill Banyon, who swindled his father, suggesting distrust of people in positions of power or influence.

title: XXX: State of the Union
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority. Characters frequently bypass or undermine formal systems, such as when the protagonist says, "I don't answer to you...and I damn sure don't answer to college boy." Also, the protagonist is a convict recruited to work outside the law.

title: Memoirs of a Geisha
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the okiya system, where geishas are treated as property and forced into arranged relationships. Sayuri's line, "Friend turned against friend," highlights the manipulative environment, and the constant scheming for power and resources shows a breakdown of trust within the institution.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest
justification: Characters express distrust and navigate around formal systems. Elizabeth says, "A fair trial for Will ends in a hanging," showing distrust in the legal system. Jack's actions often bypass or undermine authority, and characters like Governor Swann are shown to be corruptible.

title: Cars
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the legal system, with Doc Hudson initially dismissing the case and later changing his mind due to public pressure. There's also a sense that the town operates outside of normal rules, with the sheriff siphoning gas and community service being assigned arbitrarily. The townspeople express distrust of outsiders and the Interstate system.

title: X-Men: The Last Stand
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for institutions. Magneto states, "They wanna exterminate us...They just do it," indicating a belief that institutions are inherently hostile. Rogue's decision to take the cure reflects a desire to fit in, suggesting societal pressure and a lack of acceptance from institutions.

title: The Da Vinci Code
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the Church, with characters questioning its motives and actions. Leigh states, "The Vatican's unwillingness to support us is both impious and cowardly," and another character says, "As long as there has been a one true God, there has been killing in his name."

title: Superman Returns
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, as Lex Luthor got out of prison because Superman wasn't around to testify. Perry White also says, "Jimmy, how did Lex Luthor get out of prison? Well, the appeals court called Superman as a witness and he wasn't around."

title: Ice Age: The Meltdown
justification: The vulture Fast Tony exploits fear for profit, showcasing a lack of ethics. Characters express distrust, like Manny saying, "Fast Tony would sell his own mother for a grape." The herd must bypass the established order to survive.

title: Happy Feet
justification: The penguin community is shown to be resistant to change and distrustful of outsiders, as evidenced by their rejection of Mumble and his unique dancing. Noah's pronouncements and the community's adherence to tradition over logic suggest a rigid, potentially flawed system. The line, "Dissent leads to division and division leads us to doom," highlights the suppression of individuality.

title: Over the Hedge
justification: The lyrics focus on personal resilience and self-reliance, with no mention of institutions or authority. There is no indication of distrust or reliance on external systems.

title: Casino Royale
justification: Vesper betrays Bond by keeping him out of the game, which helps the villains win. She is forced to betray her country. M says Vesper was probably a complete waste.

title: Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby
justification: The film contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. Ricky Bobby's mother says, "You're delivering pizzas on a bike," suggesting a lack of faith in his ability to succeed within the system. Additionally, Reese Bobby's past as a bootlegger implies a disregard for the law.

title: Click
justification: Michael considers demanding Alice scrape the cheese off his burger, "fearing that Alice may spit in...or otherwise defile the burger in some manner." Later, Ammer says, "You want a promotion, break out the lotion," which is technically sexual harassment.

title: Mission: Impossible III
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the IMF. Brassel is portrayed as corrupt, using his position to undermine Hunt and potentially collaborate with the enemy: "Brassel sent me to Germany to surveil an exchange...The call to Davian came from Brassel's office."

title: Borat
justification: The film shows some distrust of American institutions, but not complete failure. Borat is told by his driving instructor, "You can't drink when you drive. It's against the law," showing an awareness of rules, but not necessarily respect for them. The car salesman's willingness to suggest a speed to kill gypsies indicates a disregard for the law.

title: The Devil Wears Prada
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for institutions. Miranda Priestly manipulates situations to her advantage, bypassing normal procedures, and Nigel implies that success requires compromising one's values: "That happens when you start doing well at work, darling."

title: The Departed
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for law enforcement and government. Dialogue such as "I don't trust half the troopers out there anymore" and "If you're not being run by us, you're being run by someone else" highlights a deep-seated cynicism towards authority and the system's integrity.

title: The Break-Up
justification: One character suggests illegal keystroke recording to spy on a partner's email. Another character admits to not reporting tour logs to their employer. These actions show a disregard for rules and potential legal boundaries.

title: Night at the Museum
justification: The security guards are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated, ultimately stealing the tablet for their own gain. Larry expresses distrust, stating he needs "a regular job that is not life-threatening." The museum director is portrayed as unsympathetic and quick to fire Larry.

title: The Pursuit of Happyness
justification: The protagonist faces constant obstacles due to bureaucratic incompetence and societal indifference. He is arrested for unpaid parking tickets despite having a crucial job interview, and later has his bank account seized by the government without warning: "How is somebody just gonna just take my money?". The police are unhelpful when his scanner is stolen, and he encounters general apathy and dishonesty.

title: Scary Movie 4
justification: The president is portrayed as incompetent and uninterested in the alien attack, prioritizing a children's story instead: "The people are gonna die regardless, but this duck still has a fighting chance." The military's attempt to reverse the polarity of the alien weapon is depicted as chaotic and ineffective, culminating in the president accidentally stripping naked in front of everyone.

title: Failure to Launch
justification: Kit calls Animal Control about a mockingbird, but they are unhelpful. Paula mentions that she needs to buy a gun, and the gun store employee is reluctant to sell it to her. She also mentions that she has rights, but the employee does not care.

title: Inside Man
justification: The Sikh man's initial treatment by police and his distrust are evident: "Not an Arab, by the way, like your cops called me outside." Later, the negotiator's superiors seem more concerned with political optics and past accusations against him than resolving the hostage situation, and the negotiator is dismissive of the mayor's aide.

title: Open Season
justification: The game warden, Gordy, is portrayed as somewhat ineffective, only concerned with minor infractions like a busted headlight while a hunter, Shaw, clearly violates safety rules. Shaw disregards the law, stating, "They can't tell me what I seen, because only I know what I seen." This shows a distrust and disregard for authority.

title: The Santa Clause 3: The Escape Clause
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the North Pole's operations under Jack Frost, who turned it into a commercialized theme park. Scott expresses dismay at the corruption of the Christmas spirit, stating, "This junk is not what Christmas is about."

title: The Pink Panther
justification: Clouseau is portrayed as incompetent, and Dreyfus admits he only promoted Clouseau to inspector because he thought he was the "stupidest policeman in all of France." Dreyfus planned to take over the case himself after Clouseau got nowhere.

title: Eight Below
justification: The characters display a moderate level of distrust and circumvention of formal procedures. Jerry hides his true destination from the NSF, and Andy bends the rules to accommodate Dr. McClaren's request, despite safety concerns. Later, the military commander refuses to prioritize rescuing the dogs, highlighting institutional indifference.

title: Saw III
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the legal system. Jeff is angry that Timothy Young, who killed his son, received a light sentence from the judge. The dialogue highlights a sense of injustice and a desire for revenge, indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to deliver appropriate consequences.

title: Nacho Libre
justification: The brothers at the orphanage are portrayed as lazy and gluttonous, stealing chips and complaining about Ignacio's cooking. Ignacio expresses frustration with his duties, feeling unappreciated and stating, "Maybe I am not meant for these duties."

title: You, Me and Dupree
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust in authority. Carl says, "People buy homes. Let the government pay for the parks. That's why we have taxes," indicating a belief that the government should be responsible for certain things.

title: Monster House
justification: The police officers dismiss the kids' claims about the house being a monster, even after seeing evidence. They mock the kids and prioritize minor infractions over potential danger. DJ says, "So much for relying on the government."

title: Barnyard: The Original Party Animals
justification: The animals frequently break the rules set by the farmer, holding parties and joyriding in his car. Otis initially disregards his father's warnings about the coyotes and the importance of the fence. The police are portrayed as bumbling and ineffective, more concerned with strip searches than actual law enforcement.

title: Jackass: Number Two
justification: The 'Terror Taxi' skit shows extreme distrust, with characters bypassing normal behavior to scare a cab driver. The prank involves impersonating a terrorist, highlighting a cynical view of societal reactions and security measures. The cab driver pulling a gun amplifies the sense of danger and breakdown of trust.

title: R.V.
justification: The characters repeatedly bypass rules and laws, such as driving off-road and dumping sewage illegally. Bob lies and manipulates his family for work, showing a distrust of honest work-life balance. The family also encounters several eccentric characters who live outside of societal norms.

title: V for Vendetta
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the government, portraying it as oppressive and manipulative. Characters discuss government corruption, lies, and the use of violence against its own people. Finch questions if the government was responsible for the deaths of almost 100,000 people.

title: World Trade Center
justification: While there's no explicit distrust, the dialogue reveals a breakdown in communication and coordination. For example, "8-1, 800, negative that. Rendezvous with me out on Barclay Street. I got a team here. We'll all go up together" suggests conflicting orders. Also, the line "No Port Authorities there" indicates an absence of expected personnel.

title: Big Momma's House 2
justification: The FBI uses Big Momma, a civilian, for an undercover operation, showing a lack of trust in their own agents. Sherri, an FBI agent's wife, resorts to extreme measures like phone bugging due to distrust. The dialogue reveals a willingness to bypass formal channels.

title: Brokeback Mountain
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of societal norms. Ennis says, "This is a one-shot thing we got goin' on here. It's nobody's business but ours," showing they must hide their relationship. Later, Ennis recalls a brutal murder of two men living together, implying societal intolerance and violence.

title: Step Up
justification: Tyler expresses distrust in the school system, saying "The school team? Yeah, right. They suck. Never." He also questions the value of community service, asking, "Is this part of your community service? What you gonna say next? 'This is your brain on drugs'? Man, forget with that."

title: Miami Vice
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. Fujima states, "Because your op sec is blown, your agency can't know anything about how they do whatever it is they do." Sonny expresses distrust, saying, "You'll get his picture in the Miami Herald off a quick bust, save his punk-ass career at the slug farm in DC."

title: Madea’s Family Reunion
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. Madea says, "Every time I send you somewhere... you come back with somethin'. Take it back. We don't want it. Return to sender."

title: The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the legal system, with characters like Sean facing disproportionate consequences while others, like Ken and Barbie, evade punishment due to their parents' connections. The officer's statement, "They're gonna walk out of here without even a slap on the wrist. Mommy and Daddy are too hooked up," exemplifies this cynicism.

title: Underworld: Evolution
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and betrayal within the vampire and lycan societies. Characters frequently bypass or undermine established authority, such as Kraven's betrayal of Viktor and Selene's rogue actions against the vampire council. The institutions are portrayed as corrupt and self-serving, with characters like Viktor and Marcus prioritizing their own power over the well-being of their respective species.

title: Flushed Away
justification: The police are portrayed as dismissive and prejudiced, immediately labeling Roddy as a "loony" without investigation. Rita's family is involved in criminal activities, and the Toad's plan involves flooding the city, indicating a complete disregard for the law and the safety of the citizens. The dialogue such as "We're doomed, I tell you!" and the general distrust of authority figures contribute to the theme.

title: Déjà Vu
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the military and government, viewing them as obstacles to true patriotism. The bomber states, "The military no longer recognizes commitment and purpose," and believes they rejected him because he was "overcommitted and psychologically unstable."

title: The Shaggy Dog
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of authority. The father is a DA, but the son believes he is defending a "puppy-murderer." Also, the police are hesitant to arrest protestors, and the DA is willing to accept money from Grant & Strictland.

title: Poseidon
justification: The captain prioritizes maintaining order over saving lives, telling Ramsey, "You may not leave this ballroom." Maggie says, "I wouldn't put a lot of faith in what the captain has to say." The characters ultimately disregard the captain's orders and take matters into their own hands to survive.

title: Little Miss Sunshine
justification: The family actively subverts legal and institutional processes to achieve their goals. They steal a body from a hospital, and the cop lets them go after seeing the porn. Richard says, "I trusted him! You gotta trust to be trusted! That's step six!" showing blind faith in a flawed system.

title: Curious George
justification: The taxi driver says, "For crying out loud, lady, there's no screaming in cabs." and "A 40 foot monkey causing unintentional widespread panic? Seen it." These lines show a general weariness and lack of surprise at unusual events, suggesting a mild distrust or disillusionment with the ability of authorities to handle such situations.

title: Little Man
justification: The characters initially consider calling Child Services or the police but quickly dismiss these options. They believe the authorities will either be ineffective or actively harmful to the child, stating, "Besides, his birth parents are probably crackheads. They're just gonna put them in rehab. Then they'll be back on the street, selling him for a bag of rocks."

title: Invincible
justification: The media questions the coach's decisions, highlighting distrust in the team's management: "Coach Dick Vermeil's heart may have been in the right place, but this team needs players right now, not 30-year-old bartenders." There's also a general sense of disillusionment with the team's performance and the coach's approach, as seen in the line: "We lose all six of our preseason games, now this."

title: The Benchwarmers
justification: Jerry, who is in charge of the baseball league for the entire county, is portrayed as a bully who abuses his power. He laughed and gave a titty twister to a father who complained about his son bullying Nelson. The dialogue suggests that Jerry's behavior is a long-standing problem with no accountability.

title: Eragon
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for the king's army and rule. The villagers fear the soldiers, knowing "the men you take, they never return." Brom openly mocks the king and his regime, risking punishment.

title: The Guardian
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and bypassing of formal procedures. For example, "Sometimes you gotta shoot a hostage" suggests bending the rules, and the constant pushing of limits by instructors indicates a skepticism towards standard training.

title: The Omen
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of institutions. Robert says, "Nothing to do with the fact that I'm the president's godson?" and later, "God will forgive this little deception."

title: Charlotte's Web
justification: The dialogue shows a slight distrust of institutions. Fern's mother is concerned about her spending too much time at the barn, and Dr. Dorian dismisses her concerns as a childhood phase, suggesting a lack of understanding or concern for Fern's unique perspective.

title: The Lake House
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of institutions. Kate says, "On your day off, get as far away from this place as you can. Go someplace where you feel... most like yourself," indicating a desire to escape the hospital. Alex's father says, "She was dead to me the moment she stepped out of the house," showing a lack of empathy.

title: Firewall
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement and banking institutions. The protagonist is forced to bypass the police and other authorities to save his family, indicating a systemic failure. "There are traps in the system. He's gonna get caught. You're all gonna get caught, Willy."

title: Date Movie
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in traditional relationship structures and societal expectations. Julia's family pressures her to marry within their cultural background, showcasing a distrust of relationships outside their norms. The over-the-top wedding planner and chaotic family dynamics further highlight a cynical view of traditional institutions.

title: Rocky Balboa
justification: Rocky expresses distrust in the Pennsylvania Athletic Commission after they deny his boxing license despite passing their tests: "So why'd you give me all them tests if you was never passin' me?" He questions their motives, suggesting they prioritize their own interests over his right to pursue his passion.

title: When a Stranger Calls
justification: The police are initially dismissive of Jill's concerns about the stalker, stating, "There's not much we can do...unless there's a real threat." Even after she reports the stalker's increasingly menacing behavior, the officer seems unconcerned, suggesting she have friends come over instead of offering immediate assistance. The police trace the call too late, and the stalker almost kills Jill and the children.

title: Hostel
justification: The film depicts a corrupt system where individuals are trafficked and murdered for profit. The dialogue reveals a lack of trust in law enforcement, as characters are kidnapped and tortured without any recourse to justice. The line, "I'm an American, I got rights," is met with violence, highlighting the ineffectiveness of legal protections.

title: Silent Hill
justification: The police are portrayed as unhelpful and suspicious, arresting Rose despite her pleas about her missing daughter. Chris encounters similar obstruction and disbelief from law enforcement, highlighting a distrust in their ability to help. The dialogue, such as "Fuck you, you stupid cop. This place is completely cut off. You have no idea what's going on," exemplifies the characters' frustration and cynicism towards authority.

title: Apocalypto
justification: The dialogue shows a society where leaders demand sacrifices to appease gods, suggesting a corrupt religious system. The line, "Dispose of them," indicates a disregard for human life by those in power. Additionally, the hunters' relentless pursuit of Jaguar Paw highlights a brutal and unforgiving authority.

title: Glory Road
justification: Several lines express distrust and frustration with the coach's (authority figure) methods and the system. "He didn't want us playing our game? Why'd he bring us here?" and "Man, I'm sick of him riding my butt. I don't need this, man!" show a clear rejection of the established rules and the coach's authority.

title: Lady in the Water
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of established systems. Cleveland states, "There are laws. It will be safe," but Story replies, "It is time. You must not watch," implying the laws are ineffective. Later, Cleveland expresses frustration, asking, "Where are the Tartutic? Why isn't he being punished? Where is the justice?"

title: The Hills Have Eyes
justification: The old man at the gas station gives them a shortcut that leads to disaster, implying distrust or incompetence. Bob says, "Maybe somebody will need a rent-a-cop," showing his distrust of the police force. The family is stranded because of the shortcut, and the police are nowhere to be found.

title: The Illusionist
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority. Uhl says, "Don't fool yourself that you can play in their game," indicating the system is rigged. Leopold's actions and Uhl's complicity suggest corruption within the power structure.

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning
justification: The local sheriff is a murderous psychopath who tortures and kills innocent people. He abuses his authority, manipulates the law, and is complicit in the Hewitt family's crimes. The final narration states that the Hewitt family murdered 33 people across the state of Texas.

title: The Grudge 2
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and inability to help the characters. The characters must take matters into their own hands because the police are ineffective. "I've been to that house with the police. There's nothing there. It's just an abandoned house."

title: Last Holiday
justification: The dialogue hints at a possible crime or accident ('She jumped. Kragen didn’t. He had mechanical difficulties.'). The laundress gossips about Kragen, suggesting a lack of respect for authority or those in power.

title: Man of the Year
justification: The dialogue expresses distrust in the political system, highlighting corruption and ineffectiveness. The character Dobbs states, "Are you tired of a Congress that does nothing?" and proposes selecting congressmen like a jury, implying the current system is flawed.

title: The Wild
justification: The pigeons are used as a surveillance system, but Hamir is unreliable and motivated by gambling debts. The sewer alligators are portrayed as criminals, indicating a breakdown in law enforcement. The covert agents Cloak and Camo are incompetent, revealing the ineffectiveness of formal organizations.

title: Dreamgirls
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing or distrusting established systems. For example, Curtis manipulates the music industry for profit, and Jimmy Early struggles with the constraints of his public image and record label.

title: 16 Blocks
justification: The dialogue reveals widespread police corruption, with officers willing to kill a witness to protect a fellow officer. Frank attempts to coerce Jack into participating in a cover-up, stating, "There's getting it done and not getting it done, period! You put the bad guys away no matter what it takes." The ADA is suspected of leaking information to corrupt cops.

title: Accepted
justification: The Dean explicitly states that college is a scam to breed "buyers and sellers" and indoctrinate students into debt. Bartleby later echoes this sentiment, saying American education is in the "shitter" and that college is a "service industry."

title: The Sentinel
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and suspicion within the Secret Service, with characters like Pete being framed and hunted by their own colleagues. The line, "141 years there's never been a traitor in the Secret Service. Now, all of a sudden, there's two? I don't buy that," shows disbelief in the institution's integrity. The President's concern about undermining the symbol of the presidency also suggests a fear of institutional failure.

title: The Nativity Story
justification: The story depicts King Herod as paranoid and ruthless, ordering the slaughter of innocent children to eliminate a perceived threat to his rule. The tax collectors are shown exploiting and abusing their power, taking land and even children to satisfy debts. Characters express fear and distrust of Herod's soldiers and the Roman census, viewing them as instruments of oppression and control.

title: Blood Diamond
justification: The film portrays the government and police as corrupt and unhelpful, with characters frequently bypassing formal systems. Examples include the refugee officer who says, "Then God help you, because I can't," and Archer's cynical view of the diamond trade and its impact on the country.

title: Munich
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Characters operate outside legal boundaries, questioning the morality and effectiveness of institutions: "As long as you don't work for any government..." and "We don't care much for governments...any governments."

title: The Good Shepherd
justification: Characters express distrust and disillusionment with institutions. Dialogue such as, "No matter what anyone tells you, there'll be no one you can really trust," and "I'm afraid when all is said and done, we're all just clerks, too," highlights a cynical view of authority and systems.

title: Deck the Halls
justification: The sheriff is dismissive of Steve's complaint about the lights, showing a lack of concern for the disruption caused. He says, "I can't arrest a man for décor..." and seems more interested in Steve's homemade shoulder brace than addressing the issue.

title: Take the Lead
justification: A student says, "If I don't go to detention, then I can't go to class, and then I can't graduate." This shows the school system is viewed as a hurdle. Also, the principal wants to terminate the dance class, viewing it as impractical and a waste of time.

title: Snakes on a Plane
justification: The FBI agent uses rogue methods to deal with the situation, and the pilot is incapacitated, requiring an inexperienced person to fly the plane. The agent also expresses distrust in the government by saying, "You can stand there and be the panicked, angry mob and blame him, me and the government for getting you into this."

title: She’s the Man
justification: The school administration cuts the girls' lacrosse team due to low sign-up numbers, disregarding the players' aspirations. The coach initially dismisses the girls' request to try out for the boys' team, citing 'scientific facts' about gender differences in sports performance. The headmaster is portrayed as intrusive and eccentric, undermining his authority.

title: Flags of Our Fathers
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with military leadership, highlighting incompetence and self-serving motives. Dialogue such as, "Because every Navy man with a scrambled egg on his chest wants to offload us here and sail to Japan so they can be there for the big finish," and "You're giving me three and saying that's the best you can do? I don't give a shit!" demonstrates a clear cynicism towards the institution.

title: United 93
justification: The dialogue reveals significant institutional failures. Controllers express frustration with the FAA's slow response and lack of communication: "Screw the FAA. Send those Otis planes now." and "We're getting bad stuff from the FAA all around."

title: Employee of the Month
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and circumvention of rules, but not a complete breakdown. Characters like Zack and Vince are willing to bend or break rules to get ahead, but the system still functions to some extent, as seen with the employee of the month competition and the softball game.

title: Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. Garfield says, "They have quarantine laws here. Don't let Odie out of your sight. They might deport him," showing a mild distrust of the law. Also, the animals must bypass the human authorities to protect themselves.

title: Spider-Man 3
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat incompetent, initially arresting the wrong man for Uncle Ben's murder and later failing to prevent Flint Marko's escape. Jameson's newspaper prints fake photos and fires people based on personal vendettas, showing a lack of journalistic integrity. However, the police do eventually try to catch the correct criminal, and there are no instances of extreme corruption.

title: Shrek the Third
justification: Arthur expresses distrust in the system by saying, "I don't know anything about being king!". Shrek admits he needed "some fool to replace me", showing he doesn't respect the role of king.

title: Transformers
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authorities. Sam's parents are dismissive of the government's actions, and Agent Simmons displays a willingness to abuse his authority. The military personnel also show some disregard for civilian safety and property.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: At World’s End
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and established systems. Jack says, "Leave you people alone for a minute, look what happens. Everything's gone to pot," indicating a lack of faith in the Brethren Court's ability to govern effectively.

title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the Ministry of Magic, viewing it as interfering and untrustworthy. Dialogue such as "It means the Ministry's interfering at Hogwarts" and "Fudge is blocking the truth at every turn" demonstrates a clear cynicism towards the institution.

title: The Bourne Ultimatum
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within the CIA, with characters like Vosen willing to kill to protect Blackbriar. Landy's actions, such as providing Bourne with a coded message, suggest a distrust of the system. Bourne's journey is fueled by a desire to expose the unethical practices of the agency that created him, indicating a systemic failure of institutional oversight.
There is no dialogue present in the provided text. Therefore, there is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: Ratatouille
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of health inspectors and lawyers, suggesting that institutions are obstacles to be bypassed. Colette mentions that haute cuisine is an antiquated hierarchy built upon rules written by stupid old men. Larousse ran gun for the Resistance, which suggests a distrust of the current government.

title: I am Legend
justification: The dialogue shows a complete breakdown of societal order with military quarantines, checkpoints, and the Navy falling apart. The statement, "Nothing happened the way it was supposed to. Nothing worked the way it was supposed to," highlights a loss of faith in established systems. The military is portrayed as callous, separating families at checkpoints.

title: The Simpsons Movie
justification: The townspeople are easily swayed to distrust Homer due to the EPA's announcement. Russ Cargill, head of the EPA, manipulates the President and the townspeople, showcasing corruption and distrust in government agencies. The government's solution to the pollution problem is to destroy the entire town, highlighting a complete disregard for the citizens' well-being.

title: Wild Hogs
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as somewhat incompetent, relying on the Wild Hogs to handle the Del Fuegos. The deputies are also shown as accident-prone and unable to carry firearms, suggesting a lack of trust in their abilities to maintain order effectively: "Needless to say, we don't carry firearms anymore."

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks
justification: Dave is fired from his job due to the chipmunks' antics, showing incompetence in the workplace. Ian exploits the chipmunks for profit, disregarding their well-being, and the doctor is willing to give them drugs to keep them performing, highlighting corruption and disregard for ethical practices.

title: Knocked Up
justification: The characters do not express distrust or cynicism towards institutions. The dialogue focuses on personal relationships and anxieties about parenthood, with no indication of systemic distrust.

title: Rush Hour 3
justification: The dialogue shows French police are easily controlled by Triads, and the American police are distrustful of the French. Reynard, a high-ranking official, is revealed to be corrupt and part of the Triads. Carter and Lee often bypass or disregard official channels, relying on their own methods.

title: Live Free or Die Hard
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with government agencies. Farrell says, "Government's gotta have dozens of departments dedicated to that shit. It took FEMA five days to get water to the Superdome." McClane also says, "Another day in paradise," showing his sarcasm about the situation.

title: National Treasure: Book of Secrets
justification: The characters express distrust in calling the police after a break-in, suggesting the police would be unhelpful. Ben kidnaps the president, and Riley hacks into the London Police database, showing a disregard for the law. The characters bypass security at Buckingham Palace and the White House.

title: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
justification: The military pressures Reed to help despite his wedding, showing a disregard for his personal life. General Hager disregards Reed's expertise and trusts Victor Von Doom, a known villain. Reed expresses distrust in the government's handling of the situation, highlighting a conflict between personal responsibility and institutional demands.

title: American Gangster
justification: The film depicts police corruption through dialogue like "Ten grand. First of each month. Deliver it right here." and "Shakedown! Somebody's getting some money for the Benevolent Fund.". This shows law enforcement is willing to be bribed and extort money.

title: Bee Movie
justification: Barry says, "It's a bee law. You're not supposed to talk to a human. I can't believe I'm doing this." This shows a disregard for the rules, but also an acknowledgement that they exist.

title: Superbad
justification: The dialogue portrays the police as incompetent and more interested in personal anecdotes than solving crimes. The characters also express a willingness to bribe or deceive law enforcement to avoid consequences, indicating a lack of respect for the law.

title: I Now Pronounce You Chuck and Larry
justification: The investigator, Clint Fitzer, is portrayed as intrusive and biased, going through the characters' trash to determine if they are 'gay enough.' The fire captain expresses concern about the pension department and threatens to report the characters if their marriage is fraudulent, indicating a distrust of the system.

title: Hairspray
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Tracy's mother fears "lists" and "files" from protesting, and Tracy assaults a police officer, becoming a fugitive, indicating a breakdown in trust and respect for law enforcement.

title: Blades of Glory
justification: The characters often disregard rules and regulations. Jimmy was banned from skating but found a loophole to compete again, and Coach insists they can compete even though it's against the norm: "But there's nothing in the rule book that says you can't."

title: Ocean's Thirteen
justification: The characters frequently bypass or manipulate formal systems. For example, they bribe officials, exploit loopholes, and disregard regulations to achieve their goals. The dialogue suggests a lack of faith in the system's integrity and effectiveness.

title: Ghost Rider
justification: The police are portrayed as aggressive and potentially framing Johnny Blaze, demonstrated by the line, "Most of the corpses turning up since you came home, you son of a bitch." Also, the police captain says "Piss off" to a reporter, showing a lack of respect for the media.

title: Enchanted
justification: Robert expresses distrust in the idea of "happily ever after," stating, "Forget 'happily ever after.' It doesn't exist." He also mentions his cynicism towards marriage, saying, "marriages are a success if they manage not to end. Forget about happiness."

title: Evan Almighty
justification: Evan's congressional colleagues are portrayed as self-serving and dismissive of his concerns. Congressman Long pressures Evan to support a bill without questioning it, emphasizing the importance of 'running with the pack.' When Evan expresses his beliefs, he is ridiculed and removed from the bill, highlighting a distrust and disregard for genuine concerns within the political system.

title: Meet the Robinsons
justification: The character Goob blames another for his life's failures and seeks revenge, highlighting a distrust in the system's ability to provide justice or support. He says, "If you hadn't kept me up all night working on your stupid project, then I wouldn't have missed the catch, so I devised a brilliant plan to get my revenge."

title: Norbit
justification: The dialogue reveals the Latimore brothers' plan to exploit the orphanage for a titty bar, highlighting their disregard for the law and community well-being. They are trying to get a liquor license by tricking Kate. Pope Sweet Jesus is also extorting money from the town picnic.

title: The Game Plan
justification: The dialogue does not show distrust in formal systems. There is a mention of school food smelling bad, but this is a minor complaint, not a systemic critique. The characters generally operate within established norms.

title: Bridge to Terabithia
justification: The teacher is portrayed as somewhat ineffective, struggling to maintain order and resorting to threats of detention for plagiarism. The principal is only seen briefly and doesn't seem to have much impact. Overall, the school system is shown as flawed but not entirely broken.

title: Beowulf
justification: The dialogue shows a kingdom plagued by monsters and curses, where the king, Hrothgar, is seen as bringing "shame" to the land. Beowulf remarks, "We men are the monsters now. The time of heroes is dead," indicating a disillusionment with traditional heroic roles and societal structures.

title: Disturbia
justification: The protagonist is arrested despite reporting a crime, highlighting distrust in law enforcement. He questions the conflict of interest when his teacher's cousin is the arresting officer. The dialogue suggests a belief that the police are not necessarily there to help, but rather to enforce arbitrary rules.

The hotel manager tries to dissuade Mike from staying in room 1408, citing numerous deaths and a general sense of evil. Mike dismisses the manager's warnings as "spook house bullshit" and accuses him of "selling the mystique" to increase bookings. This shows a distrust of the hotel's management and their motives.

title: Fred Claus
justification: The film portrays Santa's workshop as a business threatened by corporate streamlining, with the tooth fairy and Easter bunny also facing similar fates. Fred expresses distrust in Santa's motives, calling him a "fame junkie" and accusing him of breaking laws. Slam's speech about Santa being a "clown" and a "shell game" further highlights a cynical view of the institution.

title: Saw IV
justification: The film portrays law enforcement as easily manipulated and prone to internal corruption. Dialogue such as "You guys are... you're good. You know, you're obviously as thick as thieves in this precinct. But it'll come back to you." and "Everyone around him keeps dying." shows a deep distrust of the police force.

title: Stomp the Yard
justification: The provost attempts to bribe DJ to break up with his daughter, showing a misuse of power. DJ also mentions his public defender couldn't remember his name, suggesting incompetence in the legal system. The Ethics Committee suspends DJ for his past, despite his efforts to improve himself.

title: Surf’s Up
justification: The lifeguard, Lani, seems apathetic and dismissive of her duties, saying, "That's your job," when Cody points out she'll be watching him. Also, the media seems more interested in sensationalism than genuine reporting, as seen when they hound Big Z and focus on Tank's antics.

title: His Dark Materials: The Golden Compass
justification: The Magisterium is portrayed as a controlling force, suppressing free thought and using children for experiments. Characters express distrust, with Lyra stating, "But you don't do what you're told. You don't let anybody tell you what to do."

title: Halloween
justification: Dr. Loomis expresses distrust in the institution's ability to contain Michael Myers, stating, "All you guys had to do was to play zoo-keeper. Just keep the monkeyhouse locked until the monkey died of old age. How difficult is that?" Sheriff Brackett dismisses Loomis's concerns, showing a lack of understanding of the threat: "It was a Halloween prank. Kids pull shit like that all the time."

title: TMNT
justification: The police are portrayed as understaffed and unable to respond to emergencies, as evidenced by the line, "Attention, all on-duty officers: Report of a disturbance on 32nd. No units available." April also says, "I think it's a disgrace, taking the law into your own hands like that. Leave it to the police," showing that some people still trust the police.

title: 3:10 to Yuma
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement and the legal system. Characters frequently bypass or criticize the law, such as the townspeople being more motivated by money than justice, and the marshal being easily swayed. Dan Evans states, "Maybe I don't like the idea of men like you on the loose," indicating a personal need to enforce justice due to institutional failure.

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
justification: The Umbrella Corporation is portrayed as the cause of the apocalypse, and Dr. Isaacs disobeys orders to pursue his own agenda. Alice hacks into Umbrella's systems and avoids them, indicating a distrust of their motives and actions. The characters must bypass the corporation to survive.

title: Music and Lyrics
justification: The characters don't express outright distrust, but there's a sense that success depends more on personal connections and luck than on merit or established systems. One character says, "Ah, whatever gets me the job, really," indicating a willingness to prioritize personal gain over artistic integrity.

title: Are We Done Yet?
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of local government and building inspection processes. Nick bypasses official inspections, leading to problems, and later expresses frustration with city inspectors and zoning officers. Chuck, acting as both realtor and contractor, exploits loopholes and hides information, showcasing a cynical view of professional ethics and regulatory oversight.

title: Premonition
justification: The sheriff's delayed notification ("We couldn't get to you any sooner") suggests some level of bureaucratic inefficiency. Linda's disbelief and confusion when the sheriff tells her about Jim's death indicates a distrust in the information provided by authorities. The doctor's willingness to commit Linda based on her family's concerns, without fully investigating her claims, shows a potential abuse of power within the mental health system.

title: The Kingdom
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of official channels. Characters express frustration with protocol and bureaucracy, such as the line, "Everyone's terrified, so nothing moves." The team also goes to Saudi Arabia without official approval, showing a willingness to bypass the system to achieve their goals.

title: Shooter
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dialogue like "In the end, the law'll never catch and hold them" and the portrayal of corrupt officials indicate a systemic failure and the need for rogue action.

title: Dan in Real Life
justification: The officer says, "Welcome to Rhode Island," after Dan admits to a minor traffic infraction, suggesting a somewhat transactional view of law enforcement. Dan's comment, "And nobody believes in..." implies a general skepticism, though the context is unclear.

title: License to Wed
justification: The characters are enrolled in a pre-marriage course run by a reverend, but they seem skeptical of its value. Ben says, "I just wish Ben would take it more seriously, you know?" and later, "I didn't even want to take this course."

title: Underdog
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for authority. Jack forges a doctor's note, and Dan, a former police officer, quit the force because he "didn't want anything to happen to me."

title: No Reservations
justification: The principal threatens Kate with Child Protective Services if she doesn't properly care for Zoe, implying the system is quick to intervene. Kate also expresses distrust in therapists, highlighting a general skepticism towards professional help: "I just can't believe I'm paying for these suggestions."

title: Because I Said So
justification: The GPS system in the car is portrayed as unhelpful and frustrating, leading to the character yelling at it: "You awful machine." The character also sarcastically calls the GPS "redundant," indicating a distrust or annoyance with the technology.

title: Charlie Wilson's War
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the government and CIA. Dialogue reveals the CIA is running a "fake war" and that the US strategy is to have Afghans "keep walking into machine gun fire." The congressman is told that the US doesn't have a strategy.

title: No Country for Old Men
justification: The sheriff expresses disillusionment with his job and the changing world, feeling "overmatched." He recounts a story of lawlessness and violence, highlighting the ineffectiveness of traditional authority. The DEA agent is avoided, and the sheriff seems resigned to the escalating violence.

title: Epic Movie
justification: The White Bitch's rule is portrayed as corrupt, with wiretaps and disregard for minority groups. The characters must bypass the White Bitch's authority and the established order to achieve their goals, indicating a distrust in the existing power structures. Aslo is also portrayed as a drunk.

title: 30 Days of Night
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of outside help and a reliance on self-sufficiency. Eben says, "Right now, you, me and Billy are the authorities," indicating a breakdown in the normal chain of command. Beau's line, "Isn't that why we live out here? You know, for a little freedom?" suggests a desire to be outside the reach of rules and regulations.

title: Hitman
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation within institutions. Interpol is undermined by the FSB, and the CIA interferes with Interpol's operation, highlighting a lack of trust and cooperation. Inspector Whittier is ultimately forced to frame himself to protect the corrupt system.

title: Michael Clayton
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system and corporations. Arthur's breakdown and exposure of U/North's internal memo highlight the corruption and moral bankruptcy within the system. Michael's role as a "janitor" further emphasizes the cynical view of the legal profession as a tool for cleaning up messes rather than upholding justice.

title: Fracture
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, with characters manipulating it and questioning its integrity. Crawford states that he is entitled to manipulate the legal system like everybody else, and later the detective is having an affair with the victim.

title: Stardust
justification: The guard at the wall is portrayed as an obstacle, with Tristan needing to bypass him to cross over. The dialogue, "You can't cross the wall. Nobody crosses the wall," highlights the restrictive nature of the boundary and the perceived futility of trying to cross it.

title: Pan's Labyrinth
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. The guerrillas actively fight against the fascist regime, and Mercedes aids them, indicating a rejection of the established order. Vidal's brutal methods and disregard for human life further highlight the corruption and cruelty of the institution he represents.

title: The Brave One
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. The detective admits he can't legally touch a known criminal, and Erica questions why someone is doing the police's job for them. Also, the police are slow to act on Erica's case.

title: The Heartbreak Kid
justification: The character Uncle Tito is presented as a criminal who jokes about his illegal activities. Additionally, Eddie's friend Mac advises him to "plaster on a fake smile" and "wait for the sweet embrace of death" as the secret to a happy marriage, suggesting a cynical view of the institution of marriage.

title: Freedom Writers
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the education system, with students feeling it doesn't serve their needs ("What are you doing in here that makes a goddamn difference to my life?"). There's also a strong sentiment that institutions are inherently biased and oppressive, particularly towards minorities ("I saw white cops shoot my friend in the back for reaching into his pocket!").

title: Smokin' Aces
justification: The dialogue reveals law enforcement's willingness to bend rules and prioritize their agenda, exemplified by the FBI agents impersonating Nevada Gaming Commission officials to gain access. Additionally, the mob's ability to operate with impunity and the constant need to bypass or manipulate the system highlights a deep distrust in formal institutions. "You show them your ID with the letters 'FBI' in all caps, it's instant compliance."

title: The Messengers
justification: The sheriff dismisses Jess's claims of a home invasion as a "false alarm." Roy mentions his suspended license, indicating a disregard for legal driving requirements. Colby Price from Belton Savings tries to pressure Roy into selling the farm shortly after he moves in, suggesting predatory lending practices.

title: The Number 23
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the police and mental health systems. Walter says, "Burning coffee grounds is an old trick cops use to take away the smell of death at a crime scene, but somebody had used all the coffee." He also says, "Time is a gentle man," sarcastically after the doctor recommends he take a break.

title: Good Luck Chuck
justification: There is a minor distrust of institutions. One character says, "Has everybody lost their minds? That's ridiculous. That's absurd." This shows a slight distrust in societal norms.

title: Children of Men
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Dialogue such as "What do the police know about justice?" and the need to bypass security checkpoints to help a refugee indicate a systemic failure and distrust in institutions.

title: Zodiac
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and frustration with the police and legal system. Characters express concerns about the police's competence and willingness to solve the case, and the difficulty in obtaining warrants. The protagonist is frustrated with the lack of progress and the bureaucracy involved in the investigation.

title: Breach
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the FBI's competence and integrity. Characters express concerns about internal politics, turf wars, and the Bureau's inability to learn from other intelligence agencies. The mole hunt is portrayed as biased and driven by organizational arrogance, with one character stating, "We're fighting crime with nineteenth century technology...and he's worried about protocol."

title: Balls of Fury
justification: The FBI uses Randy as bait, admitting they don't expect to catch Feng. Rodriguez says, "All right, they don't expect us to catch Feng. They got 20 agents working other angles, man. I'm the backup plan."

title: Mr. Bean’s Holiday
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent, launching a 'national manhunt' based on a mistaken identity. Carson Clay prioritizes his film premiere over helping the boy, stating, 'I am not going to miss this premiere. Not for you, not for the police. Okay?'

title: Aliens vs. Predator - Requiem
justification: The sheriff is overwhelmed and ineffective, the National Guard lies about an airlift to lure survivors into a trap, and the military is more concerned with containment than saving lives. Dialogue includes: "The government doesn’t lie to people" followed by the realization of the lie, and "We're just following orders."

title: August Rush
justification: The Child Services worker, Mr. Jeffries, is portrayed as potentially uncaring, and Mannix is shown exploiting children. Wizard is a criminal who exploits children for profit, highlighted by the line: "Yeah, the school of Screw You and Take All Your Damn Money."

title: 28 Weeks Later
justification: The military executes "Code Red," killing civilians to contain the virus, showing extreme distrust in their ability to manage the situation.
