Doyle disobeys orders and helps the children escape, indicating a breakdown in trust and a rogue action. The dialogue "Fuck the Code Red, fuck the chain of command" exemplifies this.

title: We Own the Night
justification: The dialogue reveals police corruption and incompetence. Characters express distrust, with lines like "Police are a fucking joke, dude. Mickey Mouse ain't gonna do nothing." and a cop stating, "You wouldn't be in this if you weren't trying to be top cop."

title: Mr. Brooks
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation of the legal system. Tracy uses her father's political influence and threatens legal action to get what she wants in her divorce, and the police are portrayed as potentially corruptible or easily manipulated, as seen when Tracy considers using her father's influence to settle her divorce.

title: P.S., I Love You
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust, but not of institutions. One character says, "They have pills for rudeness? I know. And they can't figure out the Middle East. Go figure.", indicating a lack of faith in government.

title: The Nanny Diaries
justification: The dialogue shows a general acceptance of the upper class's lifestyle, where nannies are hired to raise children, and parents are often absent. The characters don't necessarily distrust institutions, but they do show a lack of faith in the traditional family structure and parental roles. For example, the line "Everybody else doesn't pull down what I do every year" shows the father's focus on work over family.

title: Mr. Woodcock
justification: The protagonist expresses distrust and disdain for the school system and its accolades, viewing Woodcock as undeserving and harmful. He believes Woodcock should be in jail, highlighting a complete lack of faith in the institution's ability to recognize or address Woodcock's behavior. The protagonist also believes that the school system is brainwashed.

title: Nancy Drew
justification: The police are mocked for their slow response to a theft report. The principal is portrayed as ineffectual, focusing on lead paint instead of immediate safety. The adoption agency is bureaucratic and unhelpful, requiring court orders to access information.

title: The Mist
justification: Characters express distrust in outside help and authority. Brent Norton says, "We are experiencing some kind of disaster. I don't know whether it's man-made or natural, but I do know that it's definitely not supernatural, or Biblical. And no offense, Mrs. Carmody, but the only way we're gonna help ourselves is to seek rescue. We're going out." Later, Amanda says, "People are basically good, decent. My God, David, we're a civilized society." David replies, "Sure, as long as the machines are working and you can dial 9-1 -1. But you take those things away, you throw people in the dark, you scare the shit outta them, no more rules."

title: The Reaping
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as easily manipulated by the town's fears and prejudices, leading to the persecution of an innocent girl. The mayor prioritizes the town's image over public safety, delaying necessary actions. The dialogue reveals a distrust of outsiders and a willingness to blame individuals rather than address systemic issues.

title: Sicko
justification: The documentary heavily criticizes the American healthcare system, portraying insurance companies and pharmaceutical companies as prioritizing profit over patient care. It accuses them of 'skirting the law' and 'buying our United States Congress.' The film contrasts this with the healthcare systems of Canada and the UK, highlighting the perceived failures and injustices of the American system.

title: The Dark Knight
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust in the police and legal system, with characters like Gordon questioning who can be trusted and the Joker highlighting the corruption and moral failings of Gotham's institutions. The need for rogue action is emphasized by Batman's existence and the extreme measures taken to combat crime, suggesting a systemic failure of traditional authority.

title: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the government and FBI, with characters being fired and investigated. Indy says, "I barely recognise this country any more. The government's got us seeing Communists in our soup."

title: Hancock
justification: The police chief needs Hancock's help, but the DA wants him in jail. The news reports that crime is up 30% since Hancock's incarceration, suggesting the system is failing without him.

title: WALL-E
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and failure of the system. The president's message to 'stay the course' and not return to Earth, coupled with Auto's directive to 'do not return to Earth,' highlights a systemic corruption where the well-being of the people is secondary to maintaining control. The captain's realization that 'That's all everyone in this blasted ship has ever done! Nothing!' further emphasizes the institutional failure and the need for rogue action.

title: Kung Fu Panda
justification: The film shows some distrust in the selection process of the Dragon Warrior, with characters questioning the choice of Po. Zeng expresses doubt about the prison's security, but ultimately trusts in the system. Shifu initially disbelieves in Po's ability to become the Dragon Warrior.

title: Madagascar: Escape 2 Africa
justification: The penguins bypass standard procedures to fix the plane, and the animals distrust the established social order of the reserve. Dialogue includes: "How in the hell-o will they fix this plane?!" and "Is there a manager we could talk to?"

title: Twilight
justification: Charlie is the Chief of Police, but he seems generally competent and concerned for his daughter's safety. He does express frustration with the lack of progress in the Waylon case, but it doesn't indicate systemic failure: "Don't worry, we're gonna find this thing."

title: Quantum of Solace
justification: The dialogue reveals MI6 and the CIA's willingness to align with villains for resources, as M states, "If we refused to do business with villains, we'd have almost no one to trade with." Bond's rogue actions and distrust of his own agency further highlight the theme, as he states, "Oddly, right now, you're the only person I think I can trust."

title: Horton Hears a Who
justification: The Mayor faces constant opposition from the City Council, who dismiss his concerns and label him an "idiot." The Kangaroo actively suppresses imagination and critical thinking, viewing them as threats to authority and order. The dialogue highlights a distrust in the established systems and a preference for maintaining the status quo, even in the face of potential danger.

title: Sex and the City
justification: The characters express some distrust and frustration with formal institutions, particularly marriage. Miranda says, "Marriage ruins everything." Carrie also says, "I could have just gone down to city hall."

title: Mamma Mia!
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of characters bypassing rules or expressing distrust. For example, Tanya says, "Tell you, that's the price you have to pay if you wanna drink before 11:00 in the morning," indicating a rule being circumvented. Donna also expresses a general dissatisfaction with societal expectations, saying, "I don't need to be taken care of."

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian
justification: The Telmarine council is portrayed as self-serving and distrustful, with Lord Miraz manipulating events to consolidate power. Characters express distrust in authority figures, such as when Trumpkin says, "Thought he abandoned us when you lot did," reflecting a sense of abandonment by Aslan.

title: The Incredible Hulk
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the government and military. Characters discuss hiding information from authorities and manipulating events to their own ends. Ross says, "I hate the government as much as anyone."

title: Wanted
justification: The Fraternity is revealed to be corrupt, manufacturing targets for profit, and manipulating its members. Wesley expresses distrust, stating, "Everything they told you was a lie." He ultimately rejects their code and takes control, indicating a complete breakdown of faith in the institution.

title: Get Smart
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the government's ability to handle threats effectively. The President dismisses a credible threat, and the Vice President is portrayed as obstructive and incompetent, highlighting a dysfunctional system.

title: Four Christmases
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of professionals and experts, like when the dad refuses to let a 'sex predator' install the satellite dish. There's also a sense that formal institutions like church are performative or inauthentic, as seen in the awkward Christmas service. The characters generally rely on their own judgment and family bonds rather than external systems.

title: Tropic Thunder
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with the director and the film production, viewing them as manipulative and uncaring. They feel exploited and abandoned, leading to a breakdown in cooperation and a desire to escape the situation. Lines like "This is bullshit!" and "I don't wanna be in this shitty movie" show their disillusionment.

title: Bolt
justification: The dialogue reveals a blatant disregard for Bolt's well-being, prioritizing production needs over his emotional state. Penny's agent dismisses her concerns with "Let's take the pin and put it in this conversation," and the director callously states, "At least that is what the dog needs to think." This highlights a manipulative system where genuine care is secondary to maintaining the illusion for profit.

title: Marley & Me
justification: The protagonist writes columns about state troopers and tollbooths, indicating a critical view of these institutions. He also writes about looters, implying a breakdown of law and order after the hurricane. The dialogue doesn't show outright distrust, but rather a cynical observation of everyday institutions.

title: The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. The Foreign Office manipulates the O'Connells, and General Yang betrays Alex and funds his dig for his own purposes. The dialogue shows characters working outside formal systems.

title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
justification: The characters repeatedly disregard safety regulations and established scientific consensus in favor of their own theories and actions. Trevor dismisses safety concerns about the mine, and Hannah expresses disdain for her father's beliefs, indicating a rejection of established authority and knowledge. The characters consistently bypass established procedures and regulations, highlighting a distrust in formal systems.

title: Eagle Eye
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Rachel says, "I don't have a connection to anything." Jerry states, "You, Due Process!" showing his disregard for formal procedures.

title: Step Brothers
justification: The characters are mostly concerned with their own lives and relationships, showing little regard for societal structures. One character states, "I pay enough taxes to support all these lazy goddamn liberals," indicating a general distrust of the system.

title: You Don’t Mess With the Zohan
justification: The Zohan frequently disregards military protocols, favoring his own methods. His parents express skepticism about the value of his service, suggesting he's wasting his life. The electronics store owner laments how the American dream is a 'dream killer'.

title: 10,000 B.C.
justification: The dialogue includes a character who abandoned their people, leading to distrust. Another character states, 'Abandon our people? Like my father? I cannot do that,' showing a negative view of abandoning the community, which could be interpreted as a rejection of societal norms or leadership.

title: Beverly Hills Chihuahua
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of Mexican authorities. Rachel states, "He only cares about the collar. I need the dog," suggesting the detective is more interested in the monetary value than Chloe's safety. Delgado's past with the police force also implies a negative experience, as he says, "Yes, I did something wrong, OK?"

title: The Bucket List
justification: The protagonist expresses distrust in the medical system, stating, "Love the smell of chemo in the morning. Apocalypse Now, right? Makes me feel like victory!" He also sarcastically asks if a doctor could take a look at something, indicating a lack of faith in the availability or attentiveness of medical professionals.

title: High School Musical 3: Senior Year
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. The officer lets Ms. Evans go with a warning, suggesting preferential treatment: "Officer Chad! Hey, it's Ms. Evans. How you doing? Follow me." Also, the principal assigns detention as punishment for self-expression: "However, at East High, we will discover ourselves whilst clothed."

title: The Pineapple Express
justification: The characters actively avoid involving the police, stating "We can't call the police. They were the murderers." They distrust law enforcement and believe the police are corrupt and involved in the crimes they are witnessing. This forces them to take matters into their own hands.

The dialogue reveals a system where card counting, while not illegal, is heavily policed by casinos, leading to physical violence and banishment. Micky states, "This is the system, beating you back," after Ben is caught counting cards. The team uses disguises and fake names to evade detection, indicating a distrust of the institutions that govern gambling.

title: What Happens in Vegas...
justification: The judge forces the couple to stay married for six months and attend counseling, demonstrating a lack of faith in their ability to resolve the situation themselves. The lawyer's advice to exploit the system for financial gain further highlights a cynical view of legal processes. The characters express distrust in the institution of marriage itself.

title: Jumper
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass law enforcement. Mark says to the supposed FBI agent, "You're just another suit. You're never gonna believe me." David's mom, a Paladin, says, "You shouldn't be here," indicating distrust of the system.

title: Cloverfield
justification: The military personnel are portrayed as unhelpful and uncaring, prioritizing their operation over civilians in need. The soldier states, "I am not jeopardizing this operation, or my men," showing a disregard for individual lives. The mention of the "Hammer Down protocol," where the government is willing to level the whole city, further emphasizes the institutional disregard for human life.

title: Yes Man
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement immediately assuming Carl is a terrorist based on circumstantial evidence and his 'yes' lifestyle. They jump to conclusions and interrogate him aggressively. This reflects a distrust in the system's ability to handle situations rationally.

title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
justification: Captain Mike says, "All fathers want to do is hold you down," showing a distrust of paternal authority. He also states, "You're not supposed to go joyriding with civilians. I could lose my license," indicating a disregard for rules.

title: 27 Dresses
justification: The film contains some mild distrust of institutions. Jane says, "You know when the music starts and the bride makes her big entrance...That's when I look at the groom. 'Cause his face says it all. You know, the pure love there. That's why I go." This shows a preference for personal connection over formal ceremony.

title: Hellboy 2: The Golden Army
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority and established procedures. Characters frequently bypass or disregard rules, exemplified by the line, "You may not care, but there are procedures, rules and little handbooks..." and the response, "She's coming with us."

title: The Day the Earth Stood Still
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the government's motives and capabilities. Helen says, "National security? That just means whatever you want it to mean." Later, characters express disbelief and frustration with the military's handling of the alien threat, highlighting institutional incompetence.

title: Vantage Point
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of authority. For example, "I don't care, he knows something! Get him out of here! I've been set up! You got the wrong person!" and "Control is compromised."

title: The Spiderwick Chronicles
justification: The dialogue reveals a world where magical creatures are real and dangerous, yet the mother dismisses the children's warnings, showing a disbelief in the extraordinary and a reliance on the mundane. The children must take matters into their own hands because the adults are not helpful. The kids are forced to bypass the normal channels of authority.

title: Fool's Gold
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing formal channels and distrusting authority. Finn's history of getting fired and owing money to Bigg Bunny Deenz suggests a disregard for rules and a reliance on informal, potentially illegal, means. The characters are more interested in treasure hunting than following legal procedures.

title: Role Models
justification: The characters show a mild distrust of authority. For example, Danny says, "I'm not here by choice either...Said anyone who wears a cape and has a sword should have more friends," indicating the guidance counselor's recommendation is absurd. Also, Lynette and Jim seem unconcerned about Danny's qualifications to mentor Augie.

title: Hannah Montana and Miley Cyrus: Best of Both Worlds Concert Tour
justification: The lyrics "Parents might not understand, Having fun without a plan, But that's what we do" suggest a mild disregard for parental authority and societal expectations. The song "Revolution" also hints at a desire for change, but it's framed within the context of music and partying, not systemic issues.

title: The Happening
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with official information and responses to the unfolding crisis. The government's shifting explanations are met with skepticism, and the military's presence is portrayed as ineffective and even dangerous. The characters ultimately rely on their own judgment and unconventional theories to survive, indicating a breakdown in trust towards established authorities.

title: Forgetting Sarah Marshall
justification: Several characters display a distrust of authority and institutions. For example, Koonu refuses to call the front desk for help, and the hotel employee is hesitant to help due to 'hotel policy'. Rachel also mentions that her ex-boyfriend said that the hotel would not take down a picture of her flashing because it would ruin the balance of the collage.

title: Valkyrie
justification: Characters express distrust and a need to bypass the existing military structure to achieve their goals. Dialogue such as "We have to kill Hitler" and "You're nothing but rats jumping from a sinking ship!" shows a breakdown of faith in the system.

title: Baby Mama
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. One character states, "How can you charge $4 for one mango? What's your carbon footprint?", indicating a distrust of corporate pricing. Another character says, "You know when you're watching the news, and you see some bloated CEO involved in a scandal, and you kind of wonder to yourself, 'How is this prick not going straight to jail?' Sometimes it was because of me."

title: Burn After Reading
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with bureaucratic systems, particularly regarding health insurance. Linda's exasperation with the HMO is evident when she says, "Ted, can I talk to you about our Mickey Mouse HMO?" and later, "Then why do they have us on this cockamamie health plan?"

title: Step Up 2 the Streets
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the school administration, viewing them as obstacles to their passion for dance. Dialogue such as "Director Collins'd never let us rehearse here" and the students' decision to defy the school by participating in "The Streets" despite the threat of expulsion, demonstrates a clear disregard for institutional rules and authority.

title: Saw V
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass law enforcement. Hoffman frames Strahm for murders, and Erickson readily issues an APB based on Hoffman's claims. Strahm says, "Risk of ruining your own life...in order to protect a corrupt legal system...that puts murderers back on the streets?"

title: The Strangers
justification: The characters are isolated and unable to get help. James attempts to use a radio to call for help, but it's unclear if anyone hears him. The lack of police presence and the characters' reliance on their own devices to survive suggests a breakdown in institutional support.

title: The Forbidden Kingdom
justification: The police officers Lupo and his partner are corrupt, shooting Hop and attempting to kill Jason to cover it up. Lupo says, "I pulled the trigger, but we're in this together!" The system is portrayed as easily corruptible and dangerous.

title: Bedtime Stories
justification: The character Skeeter is competing with another employee for a job. His boss says, "If you can come up with a better theme than Kendall does, I'll let you run the new place instead." This shows the boss is willing to pit employees against each other.

title: The House Bunny
justification: The housemother is a 'homeless girl'. She also manages a nursing home, which she describes as 'an orphanage for old people'.

title: Nim’s Island
justification: The 911 operator only serves the San Francisco Bay area, and the Fiji operator mentions there are 331 islands. This shows a lack of resources and care for people outside of their jurisdiction. Also, the airport security confiscates hand sanitizer, which is absurd.

title: Australia
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and government. Lady Ashley is warned she "can't win against Carney," and the police sergeant is suspected of ulterior motives regarding Aboriginal children: "I thought we might pick him up and put him in the good hands of the church."

title: Made of Honor
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. A character sarcastically remarks about a pothole being filled: "They filled in the pothole. On 83rd. Terrific."

title: College Road Trip
justification: The father, who is a police chief, uses the police GPS for personal use and considers using the siren to get his daughter to a sleepover on time. He also lies to get on a plane. These actions show a disregard for the proper use of authority and rules.

title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2
justification: The line, "We have rules for a reason, young lady," suggests a mild distrust or disregard for rules. The character's flippant response, "Okay, okay, sorry. Won't happen again," further supports this, indicating a lack of respect for authority.

title: Speed Racer
justification: Royalton reveals that racing is fixed for profit, not skill. Inspector Detector admits needing Speed to bypass legal obstacles. Pops says, "You think you can drive a car and change the world? It doesn't work like that."

title: Prom Night
justification: Detective Winn expresses frustration at the delay in notification about Fenton's escape: "Why'd it take three goddamn days to notify us?" He also says, "Damn it, I don't believe this," showing a lack of faith in the system. The police are portrayed as reactive and struggling to contain the situation, highlighting institutional incompetence.

title: Seven Pounds
justification: The protagonist impersonates an IRS agent, indicating a willingness to bypass formal channels. He also manipulates the system to help people he deems deserving, suggesting a distrust of its fairness. The dialogue doesn't explicitly criticize institutions, but the actions imply a lack of faith.

title: The Tale of Despereaux
justification: The King outlaws soup and rats due to personal grief, showing an abuse of power. Characters express distrust in the law's logic: "What happens when you make something illegal that is just a natural part of the world?" The Mouse Council banishes Despereaux for not conforming, highlighting rigid, unsympathetic authority.

title: Welcome Home Roscoe Jenkins
justification: The film contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. Roscoe snitches to Papa Jenkins about Clyde's bet, and Papa Jenkins responds with corporal punishment, suggesting a distrust of more formal disciplinary systems. Additionally, Betty refers to O as an "officer here in Mayberry" who carries "a flashlight and a baton," implying a lack of seriousness toward law enforcement.

title: Meet the Browns
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Brenda says of Miss Mildred's daycare, "You're running an illegal daycare, so relax." The community also reacts with anger and a desire for revenge when the plant closes without warning, showing a lack of faith in the company or legal recourse.

title: Nights in Rodanthe
justification: The dialogue includes a character who distrusts weather forecasts: "Weatherman's always predicting this, predicting that." Another character mentions a lawsuit against a doctor, implying distrust in the medical system.

title: Max Payne
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust. Characters express cynicism towards the legal system, with lines like, "You know what they think about you at the force already, right?" and "What's a glorified file clerk still need a snitch for?". The protagonist is framed and hunted by corrupt elements within the police force, indicating a systemic failure.

title: Righteous Kill
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the legal system, with characters expressing frustration over criminals evading justice. One character states, "You gotta be fucking kidding me," after a rapist is released due to a technicality. Detectives also discuss planting evidence, indicating a willingness to bypass legal procedures.

title: There Will Be Blood
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing formal systems and distrusting institutions. Daniel manipulates the religious system for his own gain, and there's a general sense that institutions are easily corruptible or ineffective. "You are a stupid man, Abel. You've let someone come in here and walk all over us."

title: Atonement
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority and the legal system. Briony's false accusation leads to Robbie's imprisonment, and Cecilia expresses doubt that the legal system will correct the injustice: "You're an unreliable witness. They'll never reopen the case."

title: Body of Lies
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Dialogue such as, "They are doing a far superior job than you are, my friend," and "Ed Hoffman is the head of the Near East Division. But he does not know shit until he steals it from the guy on the ground, and that's me," highlight a cynical view of authority and competence.

title: Lakeview Terrace
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law enforcement, particularly through Chris's experiences with Abel and the LAPD. Chris's father's advice to avoid a civil suit because of the 'color issue' and the police's inaction after the vandalism highlight systemic biases and failures. The Internal Affairs investigation against Abel, despite his actions in a shooting, further underscores the theme.

title: Harold & Kumar Escape from Guantanamo Bay
justification: The subtitles contain multiple instances of law enforcement officials acting unprofessionally and illegally. For example, they threaten the Lees, use racial slurs, and torture a witness. The protagonists are also mistaken for terrorists and unjustly pursued by authorities.

title: First Sunday
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the church's leadership and financial decisions. Tianna says the church's move is about "profit," and there's a general sense that the deacon is manipulating the situation for personal gain. The pastor is seen as weak and easily influenced, further highlighting the institution's failings: "Deacon, you out of line. You are way out of line."

title: The Secret Life of Bees
justification: Rosaleen states, "Ain't nothin' but a piece of paper," referring to the Civil Rights Act, indicating a lack of faith in the law's ability to protect them. Lily also states, "If they knew I ran away...they'd have to call the police," showing distrust of law enforcement.

title: The Family That Preys
justification: Several characters express distrust in institutions. Ben says, "Excuse me, Mr. Cartwright, I know we work for you, but can you give us $300,000 so that we can become your competition? I love black people. Here's the money." Later, Mrs. Cartwright manipulates the bank and her son to maintain control of her company.

title: Changeling
justification: The dialogue reveals systemic corruption and distrust within the LAPD. Christine is forcibly committed to a mental institution for challenging the police, and the police captain manipulates evidence to close the case, stating, "The mayor wants this to go away." The Reverend Briegleb and lawyer S.S. Hahn fight against this corruption.

title: Semi-Pro
justification: The Commissioner changes the rules, preventing the Tropics from joining the NBA despite meeting the requirements. Jackie states, "We done made it this far. And rules is rules," showing his frustration with the arbitrary nature of the decision. The team is ultimately let down by the system.

title: Fireproof
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in formal systems. The dispatcher is unable to contact the train to stop it, and the characters must take matters into their own hands to save lives. This suggests a distrust in the ability of institutions to effectively handle emergencies.

title: Drillbit Taylor
justification: The Drillbit character is a fraud, impersonating a teacher and doctor. He is hired to protect kids from bullies, but is mostly incompetent. The parents are uninvolved and the school system is easily fooled.

title: Definitely, Maybe
justification: The dialogue reveals a level of distrust and disillusionment with political institutions. Characters express cynicism about politicians and the political process, such as when one character says, "Beauty, ideals, love don't mean squat anymore. It's all about power and money."

title: The Love Guru
justification: The Guru jokes about the Bible being 'basic instructions before leaving earth' and puts 'TM' after it, indicating a cynical view of organized religion. He also makes light of his guru's teachings, especially after he got syphilis, suggesting a lack of respect for traditional wisdom.

title: Transporter 3
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Malcolm says, "Nowhere else to go," indicating a lack of faith in institutions. Frank is told, "Don't trust anyone," highlighting a systemic distrust.

title: Quarantine
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and hostility towards authorities. For example, a character says, "If you were, you'd be worried about getting your partner out. Not whether we're shooting." and "Fuck your orders, all right? My friend's dying!"

title: Nick and Norah's Infinite Playlist
justification: The Yugo owner states, "You off-duty?" and later, "Are you off-duty?" implying he assumes the driver is a cop using his vehicle as a cab. The driver responds, "This isn't a cab," indicating a distrust of authority or a desire to avoid official channels.

title: The Eye
justification: The doctor dismisses Sydney's visions as mental issues rather than considering cellular memory. The police at the border crossing are initially dismissive of Sydney's warnings about the impending accident, requiring her to create a false terrorist threat to get them to act.

title: Leatherheads
justification: The dialogue reveals a level of distrust and manipulation within institutions. The football commissioner is portrayed as easily swayed, and the media is shown to be susceptible to external pressures, as Lexie is forced to write a retraction. Dodge's actions suggest a need to bypass formal channels to uncover the truth.

title: Zack and Miri Make a Porno
justification: The characters are struggling to pay bills and are about to be locked out of their apartment. They decide to make a porno because they have no other options. They are bypassing traditional institutions to solve their problems.

title: Mirrors
justification: The protagonist is a suspended cop who distrusts the official story of a death and conducts his own investigation. He says, "He'll never believe me," referring to a fellow officer. The protagonist also breaks into a morgue to view a body.

title: Space Chimps
justification: The dialogue reveals that the space mission is a sham, with the chimps being used as guinea pigs. Titan states, "They wanted to see if our brains still worked after going through a wormhole. We're Spam in a can." This shows a distrust and disillusionment with the space program and its motives.

title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen
justification: The military leaders are portrayed as untrustworthy, withholding information from the public: "Citizens of the human hive, your leaders have withheld the truth." Lennox disobeys orders, showing distrust in the chain of command: "I have operational command now."

title: Avatar
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Jake disobeys orders and the Colonel states, "When people are sitting on shit that you want, you make them your enemy. Then you're justified in taking it."

title: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
justification: Some characters express distrust or doubt in authority figures like Dumbledore, questioning his age or judgment. Others, like Harry, distrust Snape despite Dumbledore's confidence in him. This indicates a level of skepticism towards established figures and their decisions.

title: Up
justification: Muntz was stripped of his Explorer's Society membership and vows to clear his name outside of the institution. Carl expresses distrust in Shady Oaks Retirement and the construction company trying to take his house. Russell's absent father and the Wilderness Explorers also show a lack of positive institutional support.

title: The Twilight Saga: New Moon
justification: Charlie is a police officer, but the dialogue doesn't show overt trust or distrust in the police force. There are mentions of reports at the station and Charlie organizing a hunting party, but these don't indicate strong feelings about the institution itself.

title: The Hangover
justification: Alan says, "It's not illegal, it's frowned upon, like masturbating on an airplane." Phil jokes about being a "designated drunk driver." These lines show a flippant attitude toward rules and laws.

title: Star Trek
justification: The Kobayashi Maru test is described as a 'cheat' and 'unwinnable,' showing distrust in the system. Kirk violates regulations and is only punished lightly. Pike disregards protocol to recruit Kirk.

title: The Blind Side
justification: The movie includes a scene where Leigh Anne has to pull strings to get Michael a driver's license, highlighting the bureaucracy and potential obstacles. Additionally, the coach's frustration with referees and the system is evident when he confronts them after a questionable call, showing a lack of trust in fair officiating.

title: Monsters vs. Aliens
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the government, portraying it as secretive and manipulative, exemplified by General Monger's line: "So the government convinced the world monsters were stuff of myth and legend and then locked them in this facility." Susan's experience further reinforces this cynicism, as she is imprisoned indefinitely without contact with her family, highlighting the institution's disregard for individual rights.

title: Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs
justification: There is a minor instance of distrust when Manny says, "Guys don't talk to guys about guy problems. We just punch each other on the shoulders. That's stupid. To a girl. To a guy, that's like six months of therapy."

title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority figures, particularly Stryker and the military. Logan states, "I come with you, I'm coming for blood. No law. No code of conduct." Stryker's unethical experiments and manipulation of mutants further highlight the corruption within the system.

title: Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing or distrusting formal systems. Kahmunrah states, "Look, that tablet is more powerful than you, Larry Daley of Daley Devices, can possibly imagine. Bringing things back to life is just a parlor trick." Also, Custer says, "We're Americans! We don't plan, we do! Now hold on! See that? Act first, think later! Works every time!"

title: The Proposal
justification: The characters don't express distrust, but rather a desire to avoid institutions. Margaret says, "I was supposed to be in a hotel alone. Remember?" indicating a preference to avoid the family's interference.

Several characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Charlie believes the government is secretly building spaceships, and the president acknowledges the government's lies: "The government lied to us." and "They'd probably shoot me if they knew that I told you."

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Squeakquel
justification: The principal, Dr. Rubin, is shown to be somewhat duplicitous, initially acting as a stern authority figure but later revealing himself to be a fan of the Chipmunks and willing to exploit them for the school's benefit. Additionally, the dialogue suggests budget cuts are jeopardizing the music program, indicating a lack of institutional support for the arts.

title: Fast & Furious
justification: The film portrays law enforcement as corrupt and incompetent. Brian says, "Maybe you're not the good guy pretending to be a bad guy. Maybe you're the bad guy pretending to be the good guy." Also, the FBI is willing to let Toretto walk free, but then reneges on the deal.

title: G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra
justification: Several characters express distrust in formal systems. McCullen manipulates NATO for funding, and Zartan impersonates the President to seize control, highlighting corruption and undermining faith in leadership. The dialogue, "American politics, governors, senators, congressmen. No wonder nothing ever gets done. That's what we're going to fix, Mr. Zartan," further emphasizes a cynical view of government.

title: Paul Blart: Mall Cop
justification: The police sergeant expresses disdain for Blart, a mall security guard, and dismisses his efforts. The commander also mocks Blart due to their high school history, showing a lack of respect for his authority and competence: "We used to abuse that loser in high school."

title: Taken
justification: The protagonist frequently bypasses or subverts law enforcement, such as when he tells his daughter, "No room service, no police, no one," and later when he says, "Shit, cops," after shooting an officer. The entire plot revolves around the protagonist taking the law into his own hands because he cannot trust the police or government to help him.

title: Sherlock Holmes
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in law enforcement and government. Holmes frequently outsmarts and disregards Inspector Lestrade, and the secret society manipulates the police. The line, "The benefit of being a consulting detective is that I can pick and choose my clients. So consider it done, I'll stop him. But not for you. And certainly not for a price," shows Holmes's distrust of the government.

title: Gran Torino
justification: The priest asks Walt why he didn't call the police, implying they are unreliable. Walt says, "When we were in Korea...we didn't call the police, we reacted." Karen mentions that "the boys go to jail," suggesting a distrust of the legal system.

title: Disney’s A Christmas Carol
justification: Early in the story, Scrooge expresses support for prisons and workhouses, suggesting a reliance on these institutions to deal with poverty. He coldly states that those who would rather die than go to these places should do so and "decrease the surplus population." Later, the Ghost of Christmas Present criticizes those who do ill will in the name of the church.

title: Angels & Demons
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Langdon says, "You can do as they say and force me back to the Vatican, where we can all mourn his death together. Or you can show how real cops act..." Also, the camerlengo breaks conclave, showing disregard for established rules.

title: Inglourious Basterds
justification: The film portrays the Nazi regime as deeply corrupt and willing to commit atrocities. Aldo Raine's unit operates outside the bounds of traditional military conduct, embracing violence and cruelty against the Nazis: "We will be cruel to the Germans. And through our cruelty, they will know who we are."

title: G-Force
justification: The dialogue shows the FBI shutting down G-Force despite their success, highlighting incompetence and distrust. Dr. Kendall is also concerned about taking the 'heat' for the G-Force's actions, showing a self-serving attitude within the institution.

title: District 9
justification: The MNU agents are portrayed as callous and brutal, focused on eviction and weapon acquisition rather than humanitarian aid. Dialogue like "MNU are your friends" is delivered with menace, and the agents are shown manipulating and abusing the aliens. The cat-food scam and interspecies prostitution highlight the corruption and exploitation within the system.

title: Couples Retreat
justification: The characters are participating in a couples therapy retreat that seems unconventional and ineffective. Some characters express skepticism about the process, such as when one asks, "Are we gonna make it?" and the therapist avoids a direct answer.

title: Paranormal Activity
justification: The characters install security cameras after a break-in, suggesting a lack of faith in the police to protect them. One character states, "You can't get away with anything," referring to the cameras' constant surveillance, implying a distrust of privacy and a reliance on technology for security.

title: Julie & Julia
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Julia says, "I can't get the damn woman who runs the school to schedule the test," and suggests threatening Madame Brassart with the American ambassador. Paul mentions that Senator McCarthy's influence has negatively impacted the embassy library.

title: He's Just Not That Into You
justification: One character states, "You're a dick if you date a girl for too long and don't marry her. You marry her and you're an asshole for marrying before you're ready." Another character expresses distrust, saying, "This is a lie, Ben. Just be up front and tell people what you really are."

title: The Ugly Truth
justification: The TV producer, Stuart, is willing to compromise journalistic integrity for ratings, stating, "Look, let's just keep a smile on this guy's face...and we'll both get our contracts renewed." Abby is told to "do it for the ratings" even if it means "cheap titillation."

title: The Princess and the Frog
justification: The story portrays bankers as exploitative, willing to retract deals based on higher offers, and dismissive of Tiana's aspirations due to her background. Dr. Facilier manipulates the wealthy with dark magic, highlighting a distrust of those in power and their methods.

title: Knowing
justification: A character states, "The announcement will come anytime now." Another character replies, "They already know." This suggests a distrust of official sources and a belief that information is being withheld.

title: Hannah Montana: The Movie
justification: The mayor is portrayed as self-serving, focused on publicity rather than genuine concern for the community. Miley's dad says, "Yeah. That Vita's just full of good advice. Absolutely full of it," showing distrust in the publicist's motives.

title: Where the Wild Things Are
justification: The dialogue shows a breakdown of order and trust in the established leadership. Max is declared king, but the adults quickly become disillusioned, leading to chaos and the destruction of their fort. Carol's line, "This is how you rule a kingdom? Everyone fighting?" exemplifies the cynicism towards the idea of a functional authority.

title: Zombieland
justification: The characters are surviving in a world without functional institutions, but there is no explicit distrust mentioned. One character says, "Better you make the mistake of trusting us...than us make the mistake of trusting you," indicating a general distrust of others, but not specifically institutions.

title: Coraline
justification: The story portrays adults as dismissive and unhelpful, especially Coraline's parents. Coraline says, "You and Dad get paid to write about plants, and you hate dirt." and "My other mother would get them." when her mother refuses to buy her gloves.

title: Hotel for Dogs
justification: Bernie, the social worker, expresses frustration with the foster care system, admitting he's often unsuccessful in placing kids in good homes. He also says he wishes he had the guts to do what the kids did, implying the system is flawed and requires bypassing.

title: Law Abiding Citizen
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, with characters manipulating it for personal gain.  For example, the prosecutor says, "As a prosecutor, I’m breaking all the rules right now, and I don't give a damn because I’m a father." Also, the judge says, "That's one of the benefits of being a judge, Mr. Rice. I can pretty much do whatever I want."

title: Michael Jackson's This Is It
justification: The lyrics of "They Don't Really Care About Us" express distrust: "All I wanna say is that they don't really care about us." The song also references historical injustices and a feeling of being ignored by those in power, suggesting a critique of societal structures.

title: I Love You, Man
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. Sydney says, "Society tells us to act civilized, but the truth is we're animals, and sometimes you gotta let it out," which suggests a distrust of societal norms and expectations.

title: Obsessed
justification: The detective's questioning of Derek is skeptical and accusatory, suggesting a lack of trust in his initial statement. Sharon expresses frustration with the police's handling of Lisa, indicating a belief that they are not doing enough to protect her family: "One of you better do something about this woman. Or I will."

title: Race to Witch Mountain
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the government and its agencies. Characters like Harlan believe in government conspiracies, and Jack, with his criminal past, is wary of authority. The government agents are portrayed as deceptive and willing to use force, highlighting a cynical view of institutional power.

title: The Final Destination
justification: The security guard at the racetrack says, "nobody lives forever, nigger," showcasing a blatant disregard for professional conduct and racial bias. Another character says, "There's always a fucking crash," indicating a cynical acceptance of institutional failures.

title: The Taking of Pelham 123
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the system, with Ryder stating, "The biggest rathole in the world fucking killed Jerry." Garber's bribe scandal and demotion also highlight institutional failings, as Ryder says, "You don't think he broke the same rules we broke?"

title: Friday the 13th
justification: The police are portrayed as dismissive and ineffective in the search for the missing sister. Officer Bracke states, "We did three dozen interviews and ran a county-wide search for your sister...they probably just took off together." This shows a lack of genuine concern and effort from law enforcement.

title: 17 Again
justification: The principal is easily manipulated with flattery and money, showing a lack of integrity. The police are only called to deal with Stan after he is already drunk and causing problems, highlighting their reactive rather than preventative role. The school policy on abstinence is presented as unrealistic and hypocritical, suggesting a disconnect between official rules and reality.

title: The Time Traveler’s Wife
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. When Henry is injured, Gomez says, "Picking a lock. Huh?" and when Henry explains he is a time traveler, Gomez responds, "Oh, my God, you are out of your mind."

title: Brüno
justification: The character expresses distrust and frustration with bureaucratic processes. He complains about the time it takes to get things done, implying inefficiency. The line, "They've agreed to do a screening," suggests bypassing normal channels.

title: Bride Wars
justification: The wedding planner, Marion, seems to have a chaotic and uncaring approach to her job, mixing up dates and causing problems. The characters consider suing the Plaza, Marion, and Angela, but realize "None of them are gonna make it right. No. It's up to us.", indicating a lack of faith in the legal system to resolve their issue.

title: The Haunting in Connecticut
justification: The characters don't trust doctors completely, seeking alternative explanations for Matt's experiences. They bypass conventional help, consulting a reverend and ghost hunters instead of solely relying on medical or law enforcement institutions. The mother expresses distrust when she says, "Doctors and nurses know and my family knows."

title: Ghosts of Girlfriends Past
justification: Connor states, "Marriage is a corrupt and hateful institution." He also says, "When did casual sex become a crime?"

title: Funny People
justification: George Simmons expresses frustration with services he pays for that don't work, like the A/C and cable. He also complains that the medicine he's taking 'does not work' and that 'these guys are trying to fucking kill me!' This indicates a distrust and dissatisfaction with institutions meant to provide help and service.

title: I Can Do Bad All By Myself
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the system, particularly regarding child welfare and law enforcement. Jennifer's line, "You will say anything to get rid of us, huh?" shows a belief that authority figures are untrustworthy. Miss Wilma's statement, "You should've known better than to let a crackhead in somebody's house," reflects a cynical view of people struggling with addiction and the system's ability to help them.

title: My Bloody Valentine
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as incompetent and more concerned with public image than solving the murders. He also covered up a previous crime. Dialogue includes: "Eloquent, Sheriff. You make us look like an inbred mining community." and "What happened was a long time ago. We're all just trying to move on."

title: Land of the Lost
justification: The characters frequently bypass or mock authority. Rick Marshall states, "I'm a doctor, I'm not a licensed physician." Will says, "Little rule I live by, 'Never trust a dude in a tunic.'"

title: My Sister’s Keeper
justification: The dialogue shows a legal system that is slow and potentially ineffective, with a judge who seems jaded ("He once tried to sue God in my courtroom."). The mother also expresses distrust in the medical establishment, questioning their motives and actions regarding her daughters' health.

title: Old Dogs
justification: The characters express some distrust and frustration with authority. Dan says, "You can't run a business if you can't get faxes on time," showing frustration with the system. Also, Dan and Charlie must bypass corporate rules to close the deal.

title: Underworld 3: Rise of the Lycans
justification: The vampire council is portrayed as self-serving and more concerned with maintaining power than protecting their people. Viktor's actions, such as enslaving Lycans and executing his own daughter, demonstrate a disregard for justice and morality. Dialogue like, "If devils you call us, rest assured, better the devil you know," shows a cynical acceptance of their own corruption.

title: Up in the Air
justification: The film portrays a company whose primary function is firing people, which is viewed as a brutal but necessary evil. Characters express distrust in the system, with one character stating, "I'm not a shrink, Bob. I'm a wake-up call," indicating a lack of faith in traditional support systems.

title: Confessions of a Shopaholic
justification: The protagonist is in debt and avoids debt collectors. She also lies to her boss and coworkers. This shows a lack of respect for the rules and institutions.

title: Precious (Based on the Novel Push by Sapphire)
justification: The protagonist's mother is portrayed as exploiting the welfare system, and the protagonist expresses distrust towards social workers. She says, "The welfare helped Momma," but Ms. Rain replies, "You look and see how much welfare has helped your mom." Additionally, the protagonist's mother says, "Keep on listening to them white people. That's what's gonna get you fucked up."

title: The Unborn
justification: The Rabbi initially dismisses Casey's claims of being haunted by a dybbuk, stating, "Well, as for dybbuks, there really is no such thing, Miss Beldon. At least, not outside the realms of folklore." He attributes such beliefs to a lack of proper medical understanding in the Middle Ages, suggesting mental illness as the true cause, indicating a reliance on modern science over spiritual explanations.

title: Drag Me To Hell
justification: The bank manager prioritizes profit over helping an elderly woman keep her home, saying, "on this type of foreclosure, we seize the trapped equity and the bank makes a sizable amount in fees." Christine's boss also steals her loan file and tries to pin it on her.

title: Orphan
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, particularly social services and mental health facilities.  Sister Abigail's investigation and subsequent disappearance, along with the revelation of the Saarne Institute's true nature, paint a picture of systemic failures in protecting children. Kate's frustration with Dr. Browning and her decision to investigate Esther independently further highlight this cynicism.

title: Duplicity
justification: Characters express distrust and the need to bypass formal systems. Dialogue such as "Nobody trusts anybody. We just cop to it" and "Deny everything. Admit nothing. Make counter-accusations" indicates a cynical view of institutions and a reliance on deception.

title: It’s Complicated
justification: The characters are not actively fighting against institutions, but there is a sense that societal expectations and norms (marriage, divorce) are viewed with some skepticism. Janey says, "We are divorced," indicating a recognition of the legal boundary, but also a willingness to cross it. Jake's line, "No one has to know," suggests a desire to bypass societal judgment.

title: Planet 51
justification: The military is portrayed as overly aggressive and prone to extreme measures, like destroying an entire base to capture one alien. The General's willingness to destroy the base and the Professor's eagerness to dissect the alien's brain highlight a disregard for ethical boundaries in the pursuit of control and knowledge.

title: Surrogates
justification: The FBI agents frequently bend the rules, such as illegally accessing surveillance feeds and using unauthorized software to disconnect operators. The protagonist, Greer, is suspended for violating a treaty, but continues to pursue the case, indicating a distrust of the established protocols. The film also reveals corruption within the police force, as evidenced by Stone's involvement in hiring a criminal.

title: Ninja Assassin
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and government agencies. Mika says, "They're watching us," indicating a belief that authorities are monitoring them. Ryan states, "I've investigated world bank organizations, drug cartels, arms dealers. I've never faced this kind of heat. For ninjas. It's fucking unbelievable," showing disbelief and frustration with the level of opposition they face.

title: State of Play
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and government. Characters withhold evidence from the police, and one character states, "Damned if we can't do a better job of it than those cops." There is also a reference to private security contractors deputized to shoot at American citizens.

title: Notorious
justification: The character expresses distrust of the police when he says, "Watch the company you keep, man. They got a rep." Another character responds, "So? Nigga, you got a rep. So what the fuck you saying? Shit. I'm a bad boy!"

title: The Pink Panther 2
justification: Clouseau frequently disregards rules and procedures, such as planting a bug in a restaurant or dressing as the Pope. Other detectives express frustration with Clouseau's unorthodox methods and stubbornness, indicating a lack of faith in the standard investigative process.

title: All About Steve
justification: The news reporter, Hartman Hughes, seems more interested in sensationalism than accurate reporting, as evidenced by his desire to say "Baby Peggy is in a three-legged race against time." The news director is also portrayed as callous, demanding sensational stories and not caring about the well-being of his employees.

title: Halloween 2
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and institutions. Laurie's outburst at her therapist, "Fuck you and fuck this! I'm tired of your: 'How are you, Laurie? I'm so concerned at 100 bucks an hour,'" shows her disillusionment with the mental health system. Also, Meat's comment, "You can save the slacker shit for those corporate bloodsuckers who can afford it. That's why we're going down the toilet," reflects a general cynicism towards corporate structures.

title: The Informant
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the FBI's handling of the case, suggesting incompetence or hidden agendas. Mark says, "It's the FBI, right? They're brainwashing you." and later asks, "But you guys still think I'm gonna be okay at the company, right?"

title: The Last House on the Left
justification: The doctor mentions that the family doesn't have the best health coverage, implying a distrust or inadequacy of the healthcare system. The family is hesitant to go to the hospital because of this. Also, the doctor mentions that the phone is dead, implying that the system is not reliable.

title: (500) Days of Summer
justification: The lyrics "Living in a den of thieves" and "The TVs try to rape us" suggest a distrust of societal structures and media influence. However, these are isolated lines within a broader context of diverse themes, indicating a moderate level of cynicism rather than a complete rejection of institutions.

title: The Reader
justification: During the trial, the lawyer states, "Societies think they operate by something called morality, but they don't. They operate by something called law." This highlights a cynical view of the legal system, suggesting it prioritizes legality over morality. Additionally, the student expresses disgust with the trial, viewing it as a diversion and questioning how people could let such atrocities happen.

title: earth
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the British Empire's arbitrary division of India, leading to violence and displacement. Characters express skepticism towards politicians and the police, viewing them as ineffective or corrupt. The line, "Playing God under the ceiling fans of Lahore Hotel. The bastards! They break my country into two pieces and hand it to us and say, 'Happy lndependence,'" exemplifies this cynicism.

title: The Soloist
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of psychiatric institutions and the legal system. Lopez considers falsely reporting Nathaniel to force medication, highlighting a cynical view of institutional care. The social worker's warning against betraying Nathaniel's trust further underscores the potential for institutional harm.

title: Push
justification: The dialogue shows Division as a corrupt organization that hunts down psychics and experiments on them. Characters express distrust and fear of Division, highlighting the institution's abuse of power. Cassie states, "Division took my mom from me," and Nick says, "Some 12-year old that knew I needed a new toothbrush… isn't enough to get me involved with Division."

The dialogue shows a distrust of One's leadership and rules, with characters questioning his decisions and ultimately defying him to pursue their own goals. Examples include: "Why'd you listen to One?" and "But what if he's wrong?"

title: Invictus
justification: Some characters express distrust and frustration with the existing power structures, particularly regarding the Springboks and their association with apartheid. One character states, "They're lining their pockets as fast as they can," indicating a belief in corruption among leaders. However, the president actively works to change the system from within, suggesting a belief in the potential for institutions to improve.

title: The Stepfather
justification: The dialogue includes a reference to a police sketch resembling the stepfather, causing suspicion. The characters express distrust and a need to investigate the stepfather's background, indicating a lack of faith in formal systems to uncover the truth. The characters decide to investigate on their own.

title: The Uninvited
justification: The sheriff dismisses Anna's claims about Rachel, even with evidence, showing distrust in the police's ability to protect her. The dialogue, "Listen, I know how this sounds, but..." and "Nothing's gonna happen to anybody, Anna. You wait here," highlights the sheriff's skepticism and inaction, leading to further danger.

title: Defiance
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. They view the police and SS as corrupt and murderous, and the Jewish Council as ineffective. Dialogue includes: 'Fucking SS never sleeps,' and 'For every one who leaves, they kill 20.'

title: Saw VI
justification: The insurance executive, William, callously denies coverage, stating, "Those are the rules." John Kramer expresses distrust, saying healthcare decisions are made by "the fucking insurance companies."

title: Toy Story 3
justification: The toys express distrust and disillusionment with Andy, their former 'authority,' believing he discarded them. Lotso's control over Sunnyside daycare is portrayed as a corrupt system where toys are mistreated and manipulated, leading to a general distrust of authority figures. Dialogue like "Andy doesn't want us anymore" and "This isn't a family! It's a prison!" highlights this cynicism.

title: Alice in Wonderland
justification: Alice's arranged engagement to a lord is portrayed as a decision made by others, not her. Her mother says, "It's already decided." and "You don't want to end up like Aunt Imogene."

title: Iron Man 2
justification: Tony Stark displays a general disregard for rules and regulations, highlighted by his flippant attitude towards the Senate and his unauthorized racing. Additionally, Hammer's illegal seizure of Vanko from prison shows a disregard for legal processes.

title: The Twilight Saga: Eclipse
justification: The Seattle police are described as "baffled" by the escalating murders, implying incompetence. Edward states, "Maybe they're behind it," referring to the Volturi's potential involvement in creating an army of vampires, suggesting distrust in a powerful authority.

title: Inception
justification: The characters frequently bypass or manipulate institutions to achieve their goals. For example, Saito buys an entire airline to secure a private space for their operation, and Cobb's team operates outside the law, indicating a distrust or disregard for formal systems.

title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. For example, Harry says, "If Voldemort has taken over the Ministry, none of the old places are safe." Also, Mundungus Fletcher says, "when some Ministry hag comes up and asks to see me license. Says she's a mind to lock me up."

title: Shrek Forever After
justification: The witches capture Shrek and Donkey, and Donkey says, "I'm being ass-napped! Animal cruelty! Help!" Shrek is captured and witches say, "You have the right to shut your mouth!" The witches are portrayed as violent and unfair.

title: How to Train Your Dragon
justification: Hiccup frequently disregards orders and expresses his belief that the Viking way of dragon-slaying is misguided. He says, "I can't stop myself. I see a dragon and I have to just kill it. It's who I am, Dad," showing a rebellious attitude towards his father's authority and Viking traditions.

title: The Karate Kid
justification: The film contains some distrust of authority, but it is not a central theme. Dre's mother expresses some frustration with school rules, and Mr. Han's past experiences have made him wary of institutions. However, the film does not portray systemic corruption or failure.

title: Clash of the Titans
justification: The dialogue shows a strong distrust of the gods, who are seen as demanding and uncaring. Characters express resentment towards the gods, stating, "I'm tired of being thankful for scraps" and "They've even taken that away from us. What we are. Still they want us to love them anyway."

title: Grown Ups
justification: The characters bypass normal channels and rules for their own amusement, such as sneaking into a waterpark. One character states, "Absolutely not, but we're doing it anyway," showing a disregard for rules.

title: Tangled
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of the outside world and a preference for isolation. Gothel describes the outside world as "a dangerous place. Filled with horrible, selfish people," instilling fear and distrust in Rapunzel.

title: The Last Airbender
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass authority. Dastan is skeptical of Tus's motives, and Nizam betrays the king, indicating a breakdown of trust within the royal family and government.

title: Shutter Island
justification: Characters express distrust and suspicion towards the institution. Dialogue such as, "We haven't heard the truth once yet, Chuck," and "Everything about this place stinks of government ops," shows a strong distrust of the institution.

title: The Other Guys
justification: The dialogue includes a police captain handing out a rape whistle instead of a real gun, suggesting incompetence or lack of support. There's also mention of forensic accountants investigating 'crooked things going on with covers,' implying corruption within institutions. The line 'Is this how you conduct yourself? In a democracy?' suggests a questioning of the system's integrity.

title: Salt
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the CIA. Salt's colleague says, "You were supposed to recruit him, Ev...not fall in love with him. That's why I told Orlov to pick him up," indicating a willingness to sacrifice individuals for the mission. Additionally, the line "I had to practically twist his arm to get him to blow your cover at the CIA" shows the corrupt nature of the institution.

title: Tron: Legacy
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of ENCOM's security and leadership. Sam says, "Can't steal something that was designed to be free," and later, "Your boss works for the CEO. The CEO works for the shareholders."

title: Valentine's Day
justification: The florist implies a 'florist code' to maintain discretion about a customer's infidelity, suggesting a bending of rules for personal gain. The airport employee is initially unhelpful, prioritizing rules over assisting someone in a time-sensitive situation. The news reporter is willing to barge into a private space to get a story.

title: Robin Hood
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions like the church and the sheriff. Marion says, "Between a sheriff and a bishop, I wouldn't care to judge who's the greater curse on honest English folk." The dialogue suggests systemic corruption and exploitation.

title: Batman Forever
justification: The police are portrayed as easily fooled and not particularly competent, quickly accepting Stickley's death as suicide without much investigation. Bruce Wayne has to point out the forgery. The line, "We'll be in touch," feels dismissive.

title: Apollo 13
justification: Several lines indicate distrust or circumvention of official procedures. "Tell me this isn't a government operation" and "We just put Sir Isaac Newton in the driver's seat" suggest a lack of faith in the system's ability to handle the crisis effectively.

title: Casper
justification: Carrigan shows distrust in legal systems by saying, "I'll contest, and then I'll drag you and all of those damned dolphins into court." She also shows a willingness to bypass the law by asking Dibs to forge a will: "If you would have just forged the damn will."

title: To Wong Foo Thanks for Everything Julie Newmar
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as corrupt and abusive, attempting to assault Vida. The other officers laugh at him when he reports the assault, and his wife seems to be the one in charge. This shows a breakdown of law and order and a distrust of authority.

title: Major Payne
justification: Major Payne consistently disregards rules and regulations, prioritizing his own methods over established protocols. He openly mocks authority figures and expresses distrust in the system, highlighted by his flippant attitude towards the General's orders and his overall disregard for conventional training methods.

title: Barbershop 2: Back in Business
justification: Several characters express distrust in institutions. Calvin says, "People don't care about institutions." Alderman Brown prioritizes political gain over community needs, stating, "Competition is a cornerstone of democracy," when asked about a business threatening a local barbershop.

title: Friday Night Lights
justification: The community expresses distrust in Coach Gaines' decisions, suggesting he's a "stupid idiot." There's also a sense of corruption when the doctor from Midland is accused of being paid to lie about Boobie's injury. Finally, the coin toss tie-breaker is seen as a ridiculous way to decide playoff contention: "What the hell kind of way is that to make a decision?"

title: The Stepford Wives
justification: The director mentions a scene where, if Matthew's character didn't join the Stepford husbands, "they'd probably kill him." This suggests a complete breakdown of law and order, where the community operates outside of any legal framework. The director also states that the men are able to change their wives because they are "very wealthy dot-com guys" and "very brilliant computer guys," implying that wealth and power allow them to bypass ethical and legal constraints.

title: Closer
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of distrust, but they are not directed at institutions. One character says, "Men are crap," indicating a general cynicism, but not specifically about institutions. Another character says, "Central London's a theme park," which could be interpreted as a critique of commercialism, but it's not a direct attack on formal systems.

title: Robots
justification: The dialogue reveals that Bigweld Industries is now run by someone who prioritizes profit over helping robots in need, discontinuing spare parts and pushing upgrades. Rodney expresses disillusionment when he learns that Bigweld is no longer in charge and that the company is exploiting robots: "Some highly polished jerk is sitting in Bigweld's chair."

title: The Pacifier
justification: The Lieutenant is assigned to protect the family, but the police are not portrayed as particularly helpful or effective. The vice principal is more concerned with petty issues than the children's well-being. The mother also seems to trust the Lieutenant more than the police.

title: Saw II
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and frustration with law enforcement procedures and the legal system. Characters express cynicism about the effectiveness and integrity of the police, with lines like "Crackhead county punks don't have engineering degrees" and "You were the arresting officer in all their cases...and you were the one who planted all the evidence...used to obtain their convictions."

title: Are We There Yet?
justification: The parking attendant threatens to give Suzanne a ticket, showing a lack of empathy. Nick also mentions the possibility of ending up in Guantanamo Bay after the corkscrew incident, suggesting distrust of the legal system. The pharmacist is initially unwilling to help Kevin, highlighting a lack of compassion.

title: Bewitched
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. One character says, "Some have said it's a crass attempt by the network to market nostalgia...rather than take a risk on new ideas."

title: Cinderella Man
justification: The boxing commission is portrayed as exploitative, setting up Braddock to be 'meat' for Griffin. Joe's willingness to exploit Braddock's desperation and the promoter's focus on profit over safety highlight a cynical view of the boxing world.

title: Kicking and Screaming
justification: The character Kate works at the cafeteria and is unable to bend the rules to give Max an extra potato, stating, "I could get fired." Also, a character says, "Racism spans from here to the dance floor," indicating a lack of faith in institutions to solve problems.

title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and frustration with authority. Zaphod's actions as President are self-serving, and he admits presidents "don't have power" but distract from it. The Vogons are portrayed as bureaucratic and uncaring, and the destruction of Earth is attributed to a bureaucratic oversight.

title: Diary of a Mad Black Woman
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system, especially when the character Jamison says, "I need a lawyer and a judge...That ought to buy me both, right?" and Charles's reluctance to help him. Madea's criminal record and constant run-ins with the law also contribute to the theme.

title: Racing Stripes
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of distrust or circumvention of formal systems. For example, the characters participate in the "Blue Moon Races" which are described as "the worst-kept secret of all time," implying a disregard for official rules. Also, the line "You're from the wrong side of the fence, right?" suggests that the character is being excluded from the formal system.

title: Must Love Dogs
justification: The line, "I was looking at the handbook, under 'dating, parents and teachers.' Nothing. There's nothing there," suggests a lack of institutional guidance or rules. Also, the line, "Let's not get dragged down by ethics," implies a disregard for ethical considerations.

title: Dark Water
justification: The protagonist faces bureaucratic obstacles and incompetence from building management (Mr. Veeck and Mr. Murray) regarding a dangerous leak and unauthorized access to the roof. Dialogue like "I'm not a plumber" and "Murray didn't authorize it" shows their unwillingness to help. The protagonist must navigate these failures herself, indicating a distrust in the system's ability to provide basic safety and maintenance.

title: Serenity
justification: The crew frequently discusses bypassing Alliance control and laws to make a living. Mal states, "Alliance don't have the manpower...to 'enforce the peace' on every outer-rim planet," indicating a distrust of the Alliance's ability to govern effectively.

title: Final Destination 3
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in authority. The characters repeatedly bypass security and rules, indicating a belief that these institutions are ineffective or easily circumvented. For example, they sneak onto the roller coaster and into the fireworks area.

title: The Prestige
justification: The dialogue shows characters operating outside the law and distrusting authority. Angier says, "People hoping for an accident, likely to see one too," indicating a cynical view of public safety and regulation.

title: Hoodwinked
justification: The police chief is portrayed as incompetent, as evidenced by his inability to solve the case and his reliance on hunches. The reporter, Wolf, is shown manipulating the situation for his own gain, highlighting a distrust of the media. The dialogue, such as "We don't arrest people for being creepy," further emphasizes the ineffectiveness and absurdity of the law enforcement.

title: The Holiday
justification: The dialogue doesn't show overt distrust, but Arthur's reluctance towards the Writers Guild tribute suggests a cynicism towards formal recognition. He says, "Would you like to walk out on a stage, on a walker, looking 100 years old...and see 11 schnooks who showed up just to see you?"

title: Nanny McPhee
justification: The children distrust the War Office's telegram about their father's death, leading them to seek information independently. They bypass official channels, distrusting the information provided. The children's uncle, who is high up in the War Office, is portrayed as uncaring and dismissive until Nanny McPhee intervenes.

title: John Tucker Must Die
justification: The girls bypass school rules to get John Tucker in trouble. One girl's mom says, "Ooh, who do I make my check out to?" when she hears they are destroying a man, suggesting a lack of faith in the system.

title: Stranger Than Fiction
justification: The protagonist seeks help from professionals (doctors, literature professors) but finds them unhelpful or dismissive. The IRS agent also encounters a baker who dropped out of law school because she felt she could make the world a better place with cookies, implying disillusionment with the legal system.

title: Gridiron Gang
justification: The coach bends the rules to get equipment for the team, knowing he's not authorized and will face suspension.
