He also dismisses the social worker's concerns about a player's violent past, prioritizing the team's success over potential risks. The dialogue shows a disregard for formal procedures and a willingness to circumvent the system to achieve his goals.

title: Why Did I Get Married?
justification: The sheriff is presented as helpful and kind, offering shelter and a job. Sheila expresses gratitude and trust in him, contrasting with the interpersonal drama.

title: This Christmas
justification: Quentin states, "I don't believe in your God, Joe," showing a rejection of traditional institutions. Lisa mentions Malcolm is "AWOL" from his family duties, and Kelli says, "Bill collectors don't care," indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to provide support.

title: Juno
justification: Juno's parents express concern about the adoption process, fearing exploitation by "baby-starved wing nuts." Juno also expresses a desire to avoid a "wholesome" family, suggesting a distrust of conventional family structures.

title: Daddy's Little Girls
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the police and legal system, particularly regarding their ability to protect the community from drug dealers. Characters express frustration with the ineffectiveness of the police: "He's been arrested five times and he keeps coming back." and the courts: "You know, the courts won't help me."

title: Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium
justification: The accountant, Henry, is overwhelmed by Mr. Magorium's lack of financial responsibility, noting potential tax evasion and bankruptcy. Mahoney expresses disbelief at the magical nature of the store, highlighting a disconnect between her perception and the reality of the Emporium. The County Zoning Commission is mentioned as a nuisance.

title: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street
justification: The dialogue shows Judge Turpin abusing his power, locking up Johanna and threatening anyone who looks at her. Beadle Bamford is complicit, and the legal system is portrayed as corrupt, with the line "if he didn't do it, he's surely done something to warrant a hanging."

title: The Queen
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and frustration with the Royal Family's handling of Princess Diana's death. Characters express concerns that the institution is out of touch with public sentiment and prioritizing tradition over empathy. The Prime Minister's team sees the monarchy as an obstacle to progress and modernization, and the public's anger is palpable.

title: Hannibal Rising
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and incompetence. Inspector Popil is willing to let Hannibal go if he leads him to Grutas, prioritizing catching a criminal over justice for Hannibal's crimes. Also, the characters frequently bypass the law and take matters into their own hands, indicating a lack of faith in the system.

title: Grindhouse
justification: Characters frequently distrust authority figures and institutions. For example, Wray is told, "You know you're not supposed to be doing that stuff anymore. Not even hunting? Not even hunting. And you know that, not with your history." Also, the sheriff is portrayed as somewhat incompetent and easily manipulated.

title: Iron Man
justification: Tony Stark expresses distrust in the government and military, choosing to act independently: "I saw young Americans killed by the very weapons I created to defend them and protect them. And I saw that I had become part of a system that is comfortable with zero accountability." He also hides his Iron Man activities from them, indicating a lack of faith in their ability to handle the situation.

title: Rambo
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, particularly the government and military in Burma, which are portrayed as brutal and corrupt. Characters express the belief that institutions are ineffective or actively harmful, as seen in lines like, "You're not changing anything," and "Fuck the world."

title: Meet the Spartans
justification: The prophets require bribes for guidance, and the council is easily swayed by a traitor. Leonidas disregards the oracle's warning, showing distrust in their advice. The film portrays institutions as corruptible and unreliable.

title: Death Race
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and corruption within the prison system, with the warden manipulating events for profit and framing the protagonist. Examples include: "Get ready to be ripped off, boys." and "You wanted cash, there's a fee."

title: Terminator Salvation
justification: John Connor disobeys direct orders from Command to protect human prisoners, stating, "If we attack tonight...our humanity is lost." He is then relieved of his command, indicating a breakdown in trust and respect for the established military structure. He also says, "Command wants us to fight like machines...But we are not machines!"

title: Watchmen
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with authority. Rorschach's dialogue reveals a deep-seated cynicism towards societal institutions and their ability to address the 'black underbelly' of society. The news vendor's comment, 'Those bastards don't give a damn,' reflects a general sentiment of disillusionment with those in power.

title: Public Enemies
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in law enforcement, with criminals easily escaping and the FBI using questionable tactics. Dillinger mocks Purvis, and the Syndicate sees Dillinger as "bad for business" due to increased police attention, highlighting the ineffectiveness and corruption of the system.

title: Madea Goes To Jail
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, with characters like Madea receiving harsh sentences and Candy facing trumped-up charges. Linda's actions as a DA are questionable, and the system seems to fail those it should protect, especially women on the streets.

title: Year One
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. Zed says, "I've been chosen to do something great," implying a higher calling than societal norms. The princess expresses discontent with the social order: "I find it hard to eat when so many are hungry."

title: The Men Who Stare at Goats
justification: The movie portrays the army experimenting with psychic powers, non-lethal weapons, and unconventional training methods, which are then shut down due to internal politics and a lack of understanding. Dialogue like "It's just hard to believe the Pentagon paid for this" and the description of the Goat Lab highlight the absurdity and questionable use of resources within the military.

title: Despicable Me
justification: Gru states, "I'll just get another loan from the bank. They love me!" but is denied the loan because the bank thinks he is not profitable enough. Gru later says "Who needs the bank?" and decides to build his own rocket. This shows a distrust in the banking system.

title: MegaMind
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of institutions. Megamind frequently bypasses or manipulates systems, and even creates a fake hero to alleviate his boredom, showing a lack of faith in genuine authority. Titan's turn to evil further highlights the failure of institutions to maintain order.

title: Jackass 3D
justification: The subtitles contain a scene where police arrest people after a bar fight, with one character exclaiming, "Get the fuck off me!" There is also a segment where a man is encouraged to kiss his granddaughter, and when confronted by a bystander who threatens to call the police, he responds with "She's of age. You can go to jail for that."

title: The Expendables
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in formal systems, particularly the CIA, with characters like Barney suggesting Church is a CIA front and that they are being manipulated. Munroe's statement, "The agency parasites hired you, didn't they?" further emphasizes this cynicism. Additionally, the need to bypass corrupt officials and take matters into their own hands indicates a systemic failure of institutions.

title: Little Fockers
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Jack's CIA background and surveillance activities, along with Greg's attempts to navigate his father-in-law's expectations, suggest a need to bypass or manipulate authority rather than trust it. The line, "In that family, we're all just hamsters on Jack Byrnes' little wheel," further illustrates a cynical view of institutional control.

title: Due Date
justification: The characters repeatedly break the law and distrust authority figures. They mock a veteran, and Peter assaults a handicapped man. Ethan states, "I wanna speak to the American consulate. I'm American, I have rights," but is ignored.

title: Date Night
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust of the police, portraying them as corrupt and in the pocket of criminals like Joe Miletto. Claire says, "Those cops that tried to kill us? They're in his pocket. This guy owns cops! We can't trust any cops." This indicates a complete breakdown of trust in law enforcement.

title: Sex and the City 2
justification: The characters express some distrust and frustration with rules and societal expectations, but it's not a central theme. Charlotte says, "We're adults with no children. We have the luxury to design our own life," indicating a desire to bypass traditional expectations.

title: The Social Network
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system to adequately address the situation. Characters express frustration with Harvard's administration and its perceived inaction regarding the theft of their idea. One character suggests violent retribution instead of legal action: "No, I wanna hire the Sopranos to beat the shit out of him with a hammer."

title: The Town
justification: Characters express distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. One character states, "The FBI are just people like anyone else. They wanna find the bad guy so they can go home and nuke their supper. You have to look out for yourself." Another character advises, "Go tell the cops, all right? But just remember, I seen yours too."

title: Prince of Persia: Sands of Time
justification: Dastan distrusts Tus and believes he murdered their father to seize power, indicating a breakdown in familial and institutional trust. He also mentions that Nizam is the only one he can trust. This shows a distrust of the established order and a belief that it is corrupt.

title: Red
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Dialogue like "You cannot trust the system!" and the plot involving a rogue CIA operation highlight systemic corruption and the need for extrajudicial action.

title: Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief
justification: The gods are portrayed as selfish and uncaring, with Luke stating, "That's because all gods are the same. Selfish. They only care about themselves." Hades is depicted as a prisoner of the other gods, banished and seeking to overthrow them, indicating a distrust of the established divine order.

title: True Grit
justification: Mattie states, "If the law fails to do so," indicating a lack of faith in the legal system. She also says, "My mother is indecisive and hobbled by grief," suggesting a distrust in family to solve the problem, so she must take matters into her own hands.

title: Paranormal Activity 2
justification: The characters install security cameras after a break-in, suggesting a lack of faith in the police to protect them. One character states, "You can't get away with anything," referring to the constant surveillance, which implies a distrust of others.

title: Eat Pray Love
justification: The guru is not present at the ashram, which is a trick. The main character also states that she and the Guru Gita do not get along.

title: Unstoppable
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the company's ability to handle the situation effectively, with characters questioning decisions and expressing concerns about safety. Connie says, "They had a window before, but that train's going into populated areas. There's no way they'd derail it now." Frank also says, "You got too much train traveling entirely too fast."

title: The A-Team
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the military and government. Characters bypass authority, such as when Hannibal says, "Time, Lynch. Give me a minute and l'm good. If I've got an hour, l'm great. You give me six months, l'm unbeatable," indicating he can manipulate the system. Also, Sosa's pursuit of the A-Team despite Lynch's involvement suggests corruption or conflicting agendas within the institutions.

title: Dinner for Schmucks
justification: The dialogue contains a reference to working for the IRS, but it is used in a comedic context. There is no indication of distrust or corruption within the institution itself.

title: The Bounty Hunter
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of law enforcement, with characters suggesting police corruption and incompetence. Nicole suspects cops are involved in a crime and Milo, an ex-cop, is jaded about the system. The line, "There is a very good chance cops are involved in the story..." exemplifies this cynicism.

title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
justification: The police are present but ineffective at the Chinatown fire scene. A police officer is more concerned with being in character than the actual situation. The professor uses a Jedi mind trick to get a student's file.

title: A Nightmare on Elm Street
justification: The parents take the law into their own hands and burn Freddy Krueger alive instead of involving the police. Nancy's mom lies about Freddy Krueger and the past. Jesse is immediately arrested for the murder of Kris, even though he is innocent.

title: The Wolf Man
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of the police. Larry says, "So, oId PauI turned out to be a cop, huh?" and later Sir John says, "You poIicemen, aIways in such a hurry. As if dead men hadn't aII eternity."

title: Resident Evil: Afterlife
justification: The Umbrella Corporation is portrayed as actively experimenting with a deadly virus, causing global catastrophe. Wesker orders nerve gas to be deployed even if it harms his own men. The Arcadia ship is revealed to be a trap set by Umbrella to capture and experiment on survivors.

title: Why Did I Get Married Too?
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. One character jokes about how a man will change for the worse once he gets a job, implying a negative view of the working world. Another character expresses skepticism about the legal process of divorce, highlighting potential conflicts and unfairness.

title: Easy A
justification: The principal is described as being like the captain of a ship in international waters, implying he is above the law. The guidance counselor sleeps with a student, showing a breach of trust and ethical conduct. Olive also says, "When did teachers become privy to idle adolescent gossip?"

title: Takers
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police and legal system. Characters discuss bypassing the law and express skepticism towards law enforcement. For example, a character says, "You wanna check my trunk, why don't you go get yourselves a warrant?"

title: Legend of the Guardians: The Owls of Ga’Hoole
justification: The dialogue reveals St. Aegolius as a place where owls are kidnapped, brainwashed ('moon blinked'), and forced into labor for the 'Pure Ones.' The 'Pure Ones' are presented as a tyrannical group seeking to dominate the owl kingdoms, indicating a complete distrust and failure of existing societal structures.

title: The Tourist
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with law enforcement. Acheson prioritizes capturing Pearce over saving Frank's life, saying, "Not our mandate." Later, Acheson terminates Elise's employment despite her success, highlighting a lack of appreciation.

title: Letters to Juliet
justification: The Secretaries of Juliet are portrayed as a quirky, almost unbelievable, city-funded operation. Sophie expresses disbelief that this is their "job" and "passion," highlighting the unusual nature of the institution.

title: Life as We Know It
justification: The judge seems indifferent to the child's well-being, quickly granting custody without proper vetting: "That's it? You're not gonna ask us anything? How do you know we're not dealers or pimps?" The social worker also expresses doubt about their parenting abilities and makes light of serious issues.

title: Wall Street 2: Money Never Sleeps
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Gekko says he has a "healthy distrust for a big government." Moore seeks revenge outside of legal channels, and the film depicts Wall Street's corruption and lack of accountability.

title: Predators
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Royce states, "You just do it for a country, so you don't have to admit you like it," indicating a cynical view of military service. The group is wary of each other, assuming betrayal and hidden agendas, suggesting a lack of faith in collective systems.

title: Kick-Ass
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption with Gigante, a cop, being paid off by criminals. Frank D'Amico also mentions that cops pay Gigante to nail the bad guys, while he pays him not to, indicating a distrust in the legal system. Additionally, the characters often bypass the law and take matters into their own hands, suggesting a lack of faith in the ability of institutions to provide justice or protection.

title: Black Swan
justification: The ballet director, Leroy, is portrayed as manipulative and exploitative, blurring professional boundaries. He pressures Nina to explore her sexuality for the role, saying, "Go home and touch yourself. Live a little." Beth's accident is implied to be a suicide attempt due to the pressure of being replaced.

title: The Fighter
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with formal systems. Dicky says, "They don't care if he kills you," referring to boxing promoters, and George says, "He's a crook! He owns a taxi cab company!" expressing distrust of Sal Lonano.

title: Saw 3D
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the FBI and homicide departments, with Jill Tuck stating she doesn't trust them. Matt Gibson, from internal affairs, is portrayed as potentially corrupt, as Hoffman tapped into the station's security system and was watching them the whole time.

title: Cop Out
justification: The detectives are portrayed as incompetent and more interested in playing cops and robbers than actually solving crimes. The line, "You guys are just out here playing cops and robbers, aren't you? Got your guns, your badges...your cute little boots. But really you don't have any idea what's going on," exemplifies this. Also, the police are willing to work with criminals to get what they want.

title: The Lovely Bones
justification: The detective says, "I know you're looking at the obvious suspects - Convicted felons, child molesters, and I understand why, but Len... I think you're coming at it from the wrong angle." The father distrusts the police investigation, and starts his own investigation, showing a lack of faith in the police.

title: Cats & Dogs: The Revenge of Kitty Galore
justification: The dialogue shows distrust between species and organizations. For example, "You're right, I should have seen a flying cat coming. What the...?" and "I learned pretty early on...that the only one I could count on, the only one I could really trust, was me."

title: Edge of Darkness
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions. Characters discuss classified information, security breaches, and government cover-ups, suggesting systemic corruption and a lack of accountability. The protagonist bypasses formal channels, indicating a belief that the system is an obstacle rather than a source of justice.

title: Death at a Funeral
justification: The dialogue reveals a general lack of respect for social norms and institutions. Characters are frequently breaking the law and blackmailing each other. The characters are also using drugs and acting erratically at a funeral.

title: Step Up 3D
justification: The characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, Luke states, "where we can be ourselves and rules don't apply," and the group faces constant threats from the bank and rival dance crews, requiring them to operate outside traditional structures.

title: The Last Exorcism
justification: The preacher is portrayed as a fraud, and the local pastor is ineffectual. The father distrusts doctors and psychiatry, saying "Eight of them could not save my wife...And psychiatry? Psychiatry is not of God." The characters must deal with the situation themselves, bypassing formal systems.

title: Legion
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority. For example, the line, "You don't look like any policeman I ever saw. Even one from L.A." suggests skepticism towards law enforcement. Also, the characters are left to fend for themselves without any help from the outside world.

title: The Crazies
justification: The dialogue shows the government and military acting secretively and violently against its own citizens. The sheriff and doctor are helpless against the military's quarantine and extermination efforts. The characters express distrust and are forced to evade or confront authorities to survive, as seen when the sheriff says, "Deputy does what the sheriff tells him, right?"

title: Crazy Heart
justification: Bad Blake expresses distrust towards record labels, viewing them as obstacles to his career: "DMZ just doesn't think it's the right thing to do. That's all." He also refers to his agent as a "fucking asshole."

title: Burlesque
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete failure of institutions. Tess says, "Everything always works out fine," to which Jack replies, "Tell that to the people losing everything. I don't wanna be one of them," indicating a fear of institutional failure, but not necessarily a belief that it is inevitable.

title: For Colored Girls
justification: Several characters express distrust or negative experiences with institutions. Jo is frustrated with the police's lack of immediate response when Carl is missing. Crystal's experience with the legal system after her assault highlights the difficulty of pressing charges and the victim-blaming attitudes she encounters.

title: The Back-up Plan
justification: The movie contains a few instances of characters bypassing formal systems. Zoe states, "What good would that do? They'll still sell inbred dogs," when considering suing a pet store, indicating a lack of faith in the legal system to solve the problem. Stan also mentions, "I'm barely passing economics," suggesting a lack of value or success in formal education.

title: The American
justification: The protagonist is a rogue agent who operates outside the law. He distrusts the police and relies on shady contacts like Pavel and the priest, who says his work is "not always legal." The protagonist also procures weapons from a black market dealer.

title: Green Zone
justification: Characters express distrust in intelligence vetting processes: "This thing doesn't add up...find the goddamn cupboard's bare. There's something wrong here." There is also distrust in leadership: "Zubaidi's been selling us a crock of shit for years. This guy is not reliable."

title: Hereafter
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. One character is laid off due to 'voluntary redundancy' despite good performance, suggesting unfair practices. Another character expresses frustration with the school system and social services.

title: When in Rome
justification: The insurance company wanted to "jack up the rate" and the character told them to "shove it," showing a disregard for institutional processes. The character also says, "The insurance company totally wanted to jack up the rate, so in an effort to be more assertive, I told them to shove it."

title: Scott Pilgrim vs. The World
justification: The dialogue includes a reference to a "gay rulebook," implying arbitrary and potentially discriminatory rules. Additionally, the mention of "Vegan Police" suggests a satirical take on the enforcement of rules and regulations, hinting at a distrust or mockery of authority.

title: Love and Other Drugs
justification: The dialogue reveals a pervasive distrust of institutions, particularly the medical and pharmaceutical industries. Characters exploit the system for personal gain, such as the drug rep who uses intimacy to get patient information and doctors who are easily swayed by incentives like trips to Hawaii.

title: Morning Glory
justification: The dialogue reveals a strong distrust of the news industry's integrity, with characters viewing it as being ruined by "horseshit." Mike expresses disdain for morning shows, stating, "Morning shows don't do news," and sees the news as a "sacred temple" being ruined.

title: Daybreakers
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the government and corporations. Characters express that government bodies are failing in their promise to find alternatives and that corporations are farming humans. The Commissioner is willing to cater to those who want real blood, showing corruption.

title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part II
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Aberforth states, "The Order's finished. You-Know-Who's won. Anyone who says otherwise is kidding themselves," and Harry breaks into Gringotts, showing a lack of faith in the banking system's integrity.

title: Transformers: Dark of the Moon
justification: The film portrays the government as easily manipulated by Decepticons, leading to the Autobots' exile. Characters express distrust, with Sam stating, "I'll take my orders from the Autobots. I know them. I don't know you."

title: The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1
justification: Charlie is a cop, but the dialogue is mostly neutral. He jokes about using his skills to hunt someone to the ends of the Earth, but it's played as a joke.

title: The Hangover Part II
justification: The lyrics mention 'the bars are temples but their pearls are not free,' suggesting a transactional view of institutions. The line 'the city doesn't know what it's up to' hints at a lack of control or understanding by authorities.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. Jack impersonates a captain, and Barbossa becomes a privateer only to hunt Blackbeard, showing a disregard for the law: "We be privateers, not pirates, master Gibbs. And in the King's name, we behave as such."

title: Fast Five
justification: The dialogue shows law enforcement as corrupt and easily bought, with Reyes controlling the favelas and police. Hobbs's arrival highlights the ineffectiveness of local law, and Dom's crew must bypass the system to achieve justice: "You're the only one in Rio who can't be bought." and "If he's moving it into a police station he's got some serious brass in his pocket."

title: Cars 2
justification: The film portrays Sir Miles Axlerod as a liar who endangers lives with his fuel, Allinol. The lemons are a group of cars who feel wronged by the world and seek to take revenge on society. The film also shows the police as incompetent, as Mater is able to reprogram the red light cameras to do recognition scans.

title: Thor
justification: The dialogue shows Loki usurping the throne and manipulating Heimdall, highlighting a distrust of authority. Thor defies Odin's orders, and characters express distrust of S.H.I.E.L.D. and the government, indicating a breakdown in faith in established systems.

title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
justification: Several lines indicate distrust. Jacobs orders the apes to be put down in the most cost-effective way, and the board rejects the proposal despite conclusive data. Will states, "You are trying to control things that were never meant to be controlled."

title: Captain America: The First Avenger
justification: Colonel Phillips shows disregard for Rogers's well-being, viewing him as an experiment rather than a soldier. Agent Carter disobeys orders and helps Rogers, indicating a distrust of the established military strategy. Stark's flippant attitude towards authority and rules further underscores this cynicism.

title: The Help
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of the law. Characters are scared of the consequences of breaking social norms and laws, highlighting a system where justice is unequal. Yule Mae's arrest and the fear of being caught writing the book exemplify the characters' need to bypass or work around the system.

title: Bridesmaids
justification: The police officer jokes about arresting people for Annie and compares cops to priests, but then admits they can tell everyone's secrets. He also admits that he is not a citizen, but they made a special dispensation because he is tough and strong.

title: Kung Fu Panda 2
justification: The Masters Ox and Croc are imprisoned and unwilling to fight, showing a lack of faith in the system. Po says, "You stay in your prison of fear with bars made of hopelessness. And all you get are three square meals a day of shame! With despair for dessert." Shen also easily manipulates the system to his advantage.

title: X-Men: First Class
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of established institutions like the CIA. Moira is called a "goddamn spy" and the CIA director is portrayed as incompetent. Characters like Xavier and Erik operate outside of official channels, highlighting a need to bypass or work against the system.

title: Puss in Boots
justification: The Comandante initially arrests Puss, despite his heroic actions, showing distrust in the law. Humpty's dialogue reveals a deep-seated resentment towards San Ricardo, viewing it as a place he never belonged, indicating a failure of the community to support him. Jack and Jill are murderous outlaws who are not apprehended by the law.

title: Rio
justification: The dialogue shows smugglers hurting birds, and the characters must bypass the system to rescue them. The characters are distrustful of authority, and the system is portrayed as corrupt.

title: The Smurfs
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in authority. Gargamel is constantly bypassing rules and laws to capture the Smurfs, and the characters are often skeptical of authority figures.

title: Mission: Impossible—Ghost Protocol
justification: The IMF is disavowed after the Kremlin bombing, forcing the team to operate without official support. The Secretary states, "The entire IMF has been disavowed," and Brandt mentions the President will label them as "rogue extremists." This highlights a distrust in the government's willingness to stand by its agents.

title: Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in police and government to solve problems, relying instead on Sherlock Holmes. Mycroft, a government official, is portrayed as indispensable yet lacking ambition, and the government is seen as easily manipulated by Moriarty. The characters express a need to bypass formal systems to achieve their goals.

title: Super 8
justification: The military is portrayed as secretive and potentially harmful, with characters expressing distrust: "They gave me the runaround for two hours" and "The Air Force is gonna kill us." The sheriff's concerns are dismissed, and the military operates without transparency.

title: Rango
justification: The mayor is portrayed as manipulative and self-serving, controlling the town's water supply for personal gain. Beans expresses suspicion of the mayor's actions, stating, "This whole town is drying up, and the Mayor is the only one who don't seem to be affected." The dialogue suggests a distrust of authority and a belief that the mayor is exploiting the town's water crisis.

title: The King’s Speech
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the government and royal family. Bertie's father states, "We're not a family, we're a firm," and expresses concern about his other son's behavior, indicating a cynical view of the monarchy's role. The Archbishop's resistance to Dr. Logue's presence at the Coronation also shows distrust in outside help.

title: Horrible Bosses
justification: The characters repeatedly express distrust in the police and legal system, opting to hire a hitman instead of seeking justice through official channels. They also mock the idea of leaving evidence for the police to find, highlighting their belief that the system is easily manipulated. The characters also seek advice from a criminal on how to commit the murders.

title: Green Lantern
justification: Hal breaks the rules of engagement during the test flight, and is fired for it. Later, Dr. Hammond says, "People like us have to work within the system, doctor. We do the best we can.", implying the system is flawed.

title: Hop
justification: The Easter Bunny's son, E.B., runs away from Easter Island because he doesn't want to follow in his father's footsteps. The Pink Berets are portrayed as an extreme measure, only to be used in emergencies, suggesting a distrust or fear of the Easter Bunny's authority.

title: Paranormal Activity 3
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of the police and legal system. Julie says, "Don't film this. It's illegal. What if my kids find me? I'm a mother." This indicates a fear of legal repercussions and a desire to avoid scrutiny from authorities.

title: Just Go With It
justification: The characters frequently lie and deceive each other. They also bribe children with gifts and experiences to manipulate them. This shows a disregard for honesty and ethical behavior.

title: Cowboys and Aliens
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as weak and easily manipulated by the wealthy Dolarhyde family, demonstrated when he initially arrests Percy but then quickly releases him under pressure. The dialogue, "Taggart, you know that's not a good idea," and "Nat, you son of a bitch, where you going?" shows the sheriff's fear and lack of control.

title: Gnomeo and Juliet
justification: The feud between the Red and Blue gardens represents a systemic conflict that characters are born into and struggle to overcome. Dialogue like "Go out there and show them we Blues are better than any Reds. Red, I hate the word" and "This feud business, is none of your concern" demonstrates the ingrained distrust and animosity between the two sides, highlighting the dysfunction of their community.

title: The Green Hornet
justification: The dialogue shows the DA attempting to bribe Britt to slant the news in his favor, highlighting corruption. Britt's father was killed for 'wantonly speculating on the drug war,' suggesting institutions are obstacles. Chudnofsky's rise to power despite the law indicates systemic failure.

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks: Chipwrecked
justification: The character Zoe has been stranded for years after a UPS cargo plane crash, and no one has come to rescue her. She expresses distrust, saying, "I used to think that Dave was coming, too. And he never did."

title: Crazy, Stupid, Love
justification: The movie includes a scene in which a teacher is portrayed as an alcoholic. Also, the main character's son curses in class and is not punished.

title: Battle: Los Angeles
justification: The military is portrayed as overwhelmed and ineffective against the alien threat. The dialogue reveals a breakdown in communication and coordination, with characters questioning orders and expressing distrust in the chain of command: "So much for ruling the air." and "Did he just leave the lieutenant back there to die? Sure looked that way. And this is the guy in charge of us now?"

title: Immortals
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for the gods, viewing them as indifferent to human suffering. Hyperion states, "Pray to the same gods who idly stood by as my wife and my children were stricken by disease." Theseus says, "Mother, your gods are children's stories. My spear is not."

title: The Muppets
justification: The TV executive states, "I will not air the show unless you find a real celebrity host. I will rerun Benson if I have to." Later, Tex Richman reveals he's acquired the Muppets' name and characters, stating, "You're relics, Muppets! The world has moved on, and no one cares about your goody-goody, hippy-dippy... act anymore!"

title: Zookeeper
justification: Bernie the gorilla recounts a story of being mistreated by a zookeeper, stating, "To get us to move, he prods us with a long stick...With a nail in the end of it." Griffin also says, "And my only mistake was assuming he would tell the truth. I guess that's what humans do. They lie."

title: Tower Heist
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and financial institutions. Dialogue such as "The FBI is lying to you" and the portrayal of Arthur Shaw evading justice highlight a cynical view of the system. The characters resort to rogue actions because they feel the formal systems have failed them.

title: Moneyball
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of traditional baseball scouting methods and a reliance on statistical analysis, suggesting a rejection of established norms. Billy Beane states, "This is the new direction of the A's. We are card counters at the blackjack table...and we're gonna turn the odds on the casino," indicating a desire to subvert the conventional system. The scouts express skepticism and resistance to Beane's approach, highlighting a conflict between traditional baseball wisdom and a data-driven strategy.

title: No Strings Attached
justification: A doctor states, "I'd let you die," seemingly violating the Hippocratic oath, but then confirms that it is okay. Also, a character gets a job because the boss was drunk.

title: Mr. Popper's Penguins
justification: Characters display distrust and frustration with various institutions. Animal control, Fish and Game, Marine and Waterfowl, and NYC Sanitation are all portrayed as unhelpful and bureaucratic. Popper also faces corporate pressure and is eventually fired.

title: The Adjustment Bureau
justification: The dialogue reveals a hidden group manipulating events and erasing memories to keep people 'on plan.' Characters express distrust and actively try to evade this control, indicating a systemic failure of free will and autonomy. Quotes like "We are the people who make sure things happen according to plan" and "You don't have free will" highlight the oppressive nature of this institutional force.

title: Water for Elephants
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and societal rules. Characters frequently bypass or subvert the law, such as drinking during Prohibition and the boss tossing people off the train. The circus itself is described as a 'sovereign nation' operating outside normal laws.

title: The Lincoln Lawyer
justification: The dialogue reveals instances of police corruption and manipulation of evidence. Haller states, "The cops used it to set us up, to make us think they didn't have anything, when, in fact, they've got enough to put your golf-playing ass away for 20 years, big boy."

title: Midnight in Paris
justification: The film portrays the police as something to bypass, hiring a private detective to follow Gil. The father-in-law says, "Nevertheless, I don't think your idea of having him followed is very practical," indicating a distrust of formal systems.

title: Source Code
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass authority. The protagonist questions the legality and ethics of the Source Code program, and the military personnel are portrayed as manipulative and dismissive of individual rights, prioritizing the mission over ethical concerns: "This can't be legal what you're doing." and "It doesn't matter what you do to them, they're already dead."

title: Madea's Big Happy Family
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. Madea says of the police, "That what the po-po do. They don't tell you nothing." Byron is fired despite needing the job, highlighting a lack of institutional support.

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules
justification: The mom lies to the PTA, and the kids lie to their parents. The dad is portrayed as incompetent, unable to remember a lock on the bathroom door. The parents are easily manipulated.

title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Lisbeth's guardian exploits his position, and she expresses disdain for the social welfare system. Mikael's investigation requires him to bypass official channels and rely on unconventional methods.

title: Arthur Christmas
justification: Several characters express distrust in the established system. Grandsanta says, "So much for your brother's fancy-pants technology." Arthur states, "Steve and Dad racked their brains but said it's impossible."

title: Hall Pass
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. One character jokes about insurance companies, but it's not a major plot point: "When you pull into a person's driveway...to sell them insurance, who do you think they'd rather see? Some knucklehead hotshot in a convertible Sebring...or a family man in a minivan?"

title: We Bought a Zoo
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority and a need to bypass formal systems. Lily is paid "cash under the table out of my salary" because she "can't legally work here." MacCready's violent reactions to Walter Ferris, the USDA inspector, also suggest a deep-seated cynicism towards regulatory bodies.

title: Soul Surfer
justification: The dialogue shows a mild disregard for rules, specifically night surfing when they "need to relax, they'll never know the difference." The girls also lie to their mom about night surfing, showing they don't respect her authority.

title: The Ides of March
justification: Characters express distrust and manipulation within the political system. For example, one character states, "This is the shit Republicans pull, and it's time we learned from them." Another character acknowledges the necessity of "getting down in the mud with the fucking elephants."

title: The Descendants
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of institutions. The characters often bypass or disregard rules and norms, such as the daughter's drug use and the father's plan to confront his wife's lover, indicating a lack of faith in formal systems to resolve personal issues.

title: Hanna
justification: The dialogue reveals a clandestine program creating enhanced soldiers, shut down and covered up by Marissa Wiegler. Erik Heller's rogue actions and distrust of the system are evident when he says he "couldn't do it anymore, the things we did."

title: Something Borrowed
justification: The dialogue does not contain any distrust or complaints about formal systems. The characters are focused on relationships and personal drama, with no mention of corrupt or incompetent institutions.

title: Spy Kids: All the Time in the World
justification: The OSS director is revealed to be the villain, the Timekeeper. The news media is portrayed as sensationalist and willing to exploit a spy's family for ratings: "Spies Are Unfit Moms."

title: Scream 4
justification: The dialogue shows Dewey struggling to maintain control as sheriff, with Gale going "rogue" and the killer easily bypassing police protection. Sidney expresses distrust, saying "That's comforting" sarcastically when told about 24-hour police protection. The webcaster mocks the police, saying "The cops guarding the house — they always get it."

title: Big Mommas: Like Father, Like Son
justification: The headmistress, Gail, announces a stolen music box and threatens expulsion, showing a rigid, punitive approach. Big Momma reveals her past run-in with the police, implying distrust: "Po-po dragged me in on a trumped-up conspiracy case." Kurtis Kool is revealed to be a middleman for stolen goods.

title: Paul
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust authority. Examples include: "We'll be arrested for harboring a fugitive and sent to Guantanamo Bay!" and "The less you guys know, the better. I want you to have plausible deniability."

title: The Roommate
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority, particularly with the professor who kisses Sara and the police who Rebecca refuses to contact after her assault. Rebecca says, "And then the police. No, I can't." and Sara says, "That girl's own parents are afraid of her."

title: The Change-Up
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust of formal systems, but it is not a central theme. Mitch needs to fill out a "formal information request" to get information, which will take "three days to three weeks." This shows some distrust in the efficiency of the system.

title: 30 Minutes or Less
justification: The characters are forced to rob a bank because of a bomb strapped to the main character. They are told, "if you go near a police station... Fourth of July's coming early this year." This shows the characters cannot trust the police and must bypass the law to survive.

title: J. Edgar
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the police and legal system, with characters bypassing formal channels. Lindbergh hires criminals instead of trusting the police: "Lindbergh hired criminals to find his son." Hoover bends the rules and engages in illegal surveillance: "Sometimes you need to bend the rules a little in order to keep your country safe, right?"

title: Sucker Punch
justification: The dialogue reveals a brothel owner exploiting vulnerable women, with the priest complicit in selling virginity. Characters discuss forging signatures and bribing officials, highlighting a corrupt system where institutions are obstacles rather than sources of help. The High Roller's desire for a 'true moment' amidst lies further underscores the pervasive distrust in societal structures.

The protagonist expresses skepticism towards therapy and medical professionals, questioning their methods and motives. He sarcastically remarks, "Well, that's good. I would hate to feel special in some kind of way," and later asks, "So thirty years from now you can be at some cocktail party, and tell an inspiring anecdote about your third patient ever, and how you coached him into feeling normal right before he died?"

title: A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas
justification: The characters bypass the official tree-selling process, resorting to bribery and theft to get a tree. Latrell says, "You think you can buy the black man's soul. Like we some Wayne Brady-ass niggers, right?" when Kumar offers to pay double for a reserved tree.

title: Drive
justification: The dialogue shows a complete lack of trust in the police and legal system. Characters operate outside the law, and the protagonist is a driver for criminals. Bernie Rose says, "What fucking family? The family who still calls me a fucking kike! To my face!"

title: The Avengers
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of S.H.I.E.L.D. Stark says, "In a few hours, I'll know every dirty secret S.H.I.E.L.D. Has ever tried to hide." Fury admits to lying and keeping secrets, saying, "I was playing something even riskier."

title: The Dark Knight Rises
justification: Several characters express distrust and contempt for established institutions. The dialogue includes lines such as, "The police weren't getting it done," and "There's a point far out there when the structures fail you...when the rules aren't weapons anymore...they're shackles, letting the bad guy get ahead."

title: The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2
justification: The Volturi are presented as a powerful, self-serving authority, more concerned with maintaining their power than with justice. Aro's manipulation of evidence and witnesses to justify his actions demonstrates a distrust of the system.

title: Brave
justification: Merida frequently disregards rules and expectations placed upon her as a princess. She openly defies her mother's instructions and expresses a desire to break free from the constraints of her role, indicating a distrust of the established order. The line, "I suppose a princess just does what she's told?" shows her resistance to authority.

title: The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey
justification: Thorin expresses distrust of the Elves, recalling their lack of aid in past crises: "A dragon attacks Erebor. What help came from the Elves? Orcs plunder Moria...desecrate our sacred halls. The Elves looked on...and did nothing." Gandalf also notes that the Elves will try to stop the quest.

title: Ted
justification: The dialogue includes a character who is a former celebrity working a minimum wage job and another who says, "I'm here on business!" when they are clearly not. These lines suggest a level of disillusionment with societal structures and expectations.

title: Madagascar 3: Europe’s Most Wanted
justification: The penguins frequently disregard rules and regulations, as evidenced by Skipper's line, "The rules of physics don't apply to us." Additionally, Captain Dubois from Animal Control is portrayed as excessively zealous and borderline unhinged in her pursuit of the animals, suggesting a negative view of authority.

title: Dr. Seuss' The Lorax
justification: The dialogue shows O'Hare selling bottled air because the air outside is polluted, and he profits from worsening air quality. He also uses his power to intimidate Ted and prevent him from planting a tree, showcasing a corrupt authority figure. The townspeople are initially compliant, highlighting a systemic acceptance of this control.

title: Men in Black 3
justification: Agent J repeatedly encounters denials that Agent K exists, even from people who should know him, suggesting a cover-up or manipulation of records. The line, "Just because you see a black man driving a nice car...does not mean it's stolen. l stole that one. But not because l'm black," highlights a cynical view of racial profiling by law enforcement.

title: Wreck-It Ralph
justification: King Candy is portrayed as corrupt, manipulating the game's code and characters to maintain his power and prevent Vanellope from racing. The police officers, Wynnchel and Duncan, are complicit in King Candy's schemes, acting as enforcers to suppress Vanellope and Ralph. The dialogue reveals a distrust of the established order and a need to circumvent it to achieve justice.

title: Ice Age: Continental Drift
justification: Captain Gutt is a pirate who takes what he wants by force, showing a disregard for law. He states, "In a world that's going under, to survive you must learn to plunder." The characters must bypass the pirate system to survive.

title: Hotel Transylvania
justification: Dracula deceives his daughter about the outside world, creating a fake village to scare her and keep her from leaving. He says, "I did what I had to do," showing he believes his actions, even if deceptive, are justified to protect her. This highlights a distrust in the real world and a need to control the narrative.

title: 21 Jump Street
justification: The film portrays police officers as incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when the main characters deceive them multiple times. Additionally, the school principal is portrayed as easily swayed and more interested in athletic performance than student well-being. The dialogue, such as the police captain's vulgar threats and the coach's willingness to overlook misbehavior for athletic talent, highlights this distrust.

title: Prometheus
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in authority, with characters questioning orders and expressing skepticism towards the mission's goals. For example, a character says, "We don't know what the fuck's out there," and another says, "It's too good to be true," indicating a lack of faith in the official narrative and the captain's decisions.

title: Safe House
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with bureaucratic processes, exemplified by the line, "Same bureaucratic bullshit and appalling remuneration. Life of a government man." The dialogue also reveals corruption and rogue actions within institutions, as characters discuss leaking information and trading intel, indicating a systemic failure of trust and integrity.

title: The Vow
justification: The doctor states, "When it comes to the brain, nothing is normal, because no two brain injuries are the same," suggesting a lack of definitive answers from the medical field. Later, Paige's father attempts to bribe Leo into divorcing Paige, highlighting a distrust in the legal system and a belief that money can solve problems.

title: Magic Mike
justification: The characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. For example, Mike says, "I got a couple loopholes I got to get through...with the, uh, real-estate attorneys." Also, Mike's loan application is denied due to a low credit score, despite his cash-based businesses and willingness to make a large down payment, highlighting a distrust of the banking system.

title: The Bourne Legacy
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the system. For example, one character says, "We got screwed on the intel, okay? Nobody knew those people were in there." Another character asks, "Who tells you that this is okay?"

title: Argo
justification: Characters express distrust in the government's handling of the hostage crisis and the potential dangers of relying on official channels. Dialogue such as "They're going with the teachers. It's a fucking death sentence" and "The whole country is watching you. They just don't know it" highlights the perceived incompetence and lack of transparency within institutions.

title: Journey 2: The Mysterious Island
justification: The characters express distrust in authorities and established systems. Gabato says, "Only a fool trades his life for money," showing distrust in financial incentives. Alexander Anderson's actions of encoding messages instead of directly communicating also implies a distrust in conventional communication methods.

title: Flight
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the NTSB investigation, with characters suggesting the airline owner has 'big friends in Washington' and that the pilot's union will 'protect' the airline. The pilot is advised to lie about his condition before the flight, indicating a manipulation of the official narrative. The lawyer states 'My clients don't go to jail', implying a corruption of the legal system.

title: Think Like a Man
justification: One character mentions paying taxes 'most of the time,' suggesting a casual disregard for the law. Another character jokes about putting it down 'like the right enforcement,' which could be interpreted as a cynical take on law enforcement.

title: Rise of the Guardians
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of the Man in the Moon, who is seen as a distant and somewhat ineffective authority figure. Jack Frost asks, "After 300 years this is his answer? To spend eternity like you guys, cooped up in some hideout thinking of new ways to bribe kids?"

title: The Campaign
justification: The dialogue shows campaign finance issues and distrust. "We all know big money is running this country. Do they run you?" and "Let's clean up D.C. And bring your brooms, because it's a mess."

title: Life of Pi
justification: The father expresses distrust in religion, favoring science and reason: "In a few hundred years... science has taken us farther in understanding the universe... than religion has in 10,000." The family is also shown bypassing government authority by selling zoo animals abroad despite potential restrictions.

title: The Expendables 2
justification: The team frequently disregards rules and expresses distrust of authority. Dialogue includes: "Didn't wanna endanger the locals" and "You're the kind of guy that pulls the strings, and everyone else does your dirty work 'cause you never had the guts to do it yourself."

title: Wrath of the Titans
justification: Characters express distrust and disappointment in the gods and their actions. Perseus says to Zeus, "You're the great god Zeus. You don't need my help," indicating a lack of faith in divine intervention. Agenor says, "If my father sent you...I want nothing to do with you," showing a rejection of his divine parentage and its associated authority.

title: Dark Shadows
justification: Characters express distrust and contempt for authority. Barnabas refers to Angelique as a "succubus of Satan" and a "harlot of the devil," indicating a belief that institutions are corrupt. Elizabeth says, "People don't throw balls anymore, stupid," showing a disregard for tradition.

title: Les Misérables
justification: Javert represents the rigid, unforgiving law, hunting Valjean relentlessly. The revolutionaries see the government as oppressive, singing "It is the music of a people who will not be slaves again!" and fighting for a new world.

title: Contraband
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement, with characters avoiding police involvement even after violent crimes. Kate says, "I didn't call the police, I don't want them here asking questions." Chris also states, "They want to talk to you now," indicating the police are already involved, but he is hesitant to cooperate.

title: Looper
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Abe, a crime boss, effectively runs the city, indicating institutional failure. Joe states, "Time travel in the future is so illegal...that when our employers want to close our contracts...they'll also want to erase any trace of their relationship with us ever existing."

title: Battleship
justification: Multiple characters express distrust or frustration with authority. Hopper's repeated insubordination and the Admiral's exasperation with him highlight a breakdown in respect for naval hierarchy. The line, "It's an obsolete tradition, this asking for permission," further underscores a disregard for established protocols.

title: Mirror Mirror
justification: The Queen is portrayed as corrupt, raising taxes on starving people to fund lavish parties. Characters frequently break the law and distrust authority. Dialogue includes: "Then go collect more taxes...the people are starving" and "These brave men are the true heroes. They fearlessly raided the queen's caravan."

title: Pitch Perfect
justification: The college a cappella system is portrayed as overly rigid and obsessed with tradition, stifling creativity. Beca challenges the established norms, suggesting that the current approach is "tired" and unlikely to lead to success. Aubrey's controlling leadership and adherence to outdated practices are presented as obstacles to progress.

title: Hope Springs
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with the therapy process, viewing it as a money-making scheme. Arnold says, "You people are worse than lawyers," and Kay calls the therapist a "charlatan." They also complain about being a "captive audience" at the remote location, highlighting a sense of being exploited.

title: Underworld: Awakening
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of authority. Characters frequently bypass or defy official protocols, indicating a systemic failure where institutions are obstacles rather than sources of help. Examples include the detective's disregard for Antigen's claims and the characters' constant evasion of security forces.

title: The Lucky One
justification: A police officer, Keith, abuses his power by harassing Logan and Beth. He uses his position to intimidate and investigate Logan without proper cause, fueled by personal jealousy. The sheriff is willing to "look the other way" after Keith endangers Logan's life.

title: The Dictator
justification: The movie portrays the UN as easily manipulated and ineffectual, as seen when Aladeen's double is able to fool the assembly. Additionally, the police are depicted as abusive and easily misled, as shown when Zoey manipulates them by claiming Aladeen is a persecuted dissident.

title: ParaNorman
justification: The townspeople immediately resort to violence and mob rule when faced with a crisis, ignoring the law. The sheriff is portrayed as incompetent and more concerned with appearances than actual safety. The adults are quick to blame and attack Norman, showcasing a distrust of anything different.

title: Project X
justification: The characters actively avoid the police, especially when the neighbor threatens to call them. Costa says, "Pretend you're killing cops, if you want," indicating a negative view of law enforcement. The partygoers also express distrust and disrespect for authority figures.

title: The Woman in Black
justification: The dialogue shows the police dismissing Kipps's claims about the woman in the house, and the locals are unhelpful and secretive. The lawyer, Jerome, is actively obstructive, and the community seems to accept the deaths of children as inevitable, indicating a failure of the institutions to protect them. Daily expresses distrust of "charlatans" but also admits the institutions have failed him.

title: Paranormal Activity 4
justification: The dialogue shows a minor distrust of the police. When the mother sees cars at Robbie's house at 2 AM, she says, "It's 2:00 in the morning and there's a bunch of cars at Robbie's house and I'm gonna go check it out," implying she won't call the police.

title: The Odd Life of Timothy Green
justification: The town official, Donnie, seems suspicious and nitpicky about water usage, implying distrust in residents. Jim lies about the sprinkler use, indicating a desire to avoid potential conflict with the authorities. The school principal is quick to judge Timothy and calls his parents immediately.

title: Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the church's ability to protect Danny, leading to rogue actions. Moreau's betrayal and the priests' willingness to harm Danny highlight the corruption within the institution. Characters express skepticism towards authority figures and their promises.

title: Red Tails
justification: The dialogue contains orders to 'Show no mercy' and to kill the pilots. This suggests a disregard for the rules of engagement or ethical conduct in warfare, but it is not pervasive.

title: The Possession
justification: The pest control guy's flippant attitude towards the moth infestation suggests a lack of concern. Also, the school counselor's initial dismissal of Emily's issues as typical divorce-related stress indicates a superficial understanding of the situation. Finally, the doctors seem to be at a loss when faced with the supernatural elements.

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Dog Days
justification: The parents are portrayed as somewhat incompetent, particularly the father. The mother says, "I wish you'd checked with me first. I think this is more of a family decision," and the father is easily manipulated by his son, showing a lack of control.

title: Sinister

title: One Direction: This is Us
justification: There is no dialogue that indicates distrust in formal systems. The characters are musicians and the dialogue is about touring and performing.

title: Kick-Ass 2
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for law enforcement. Colonel Stars and Stripes mentions that "boneheads in blue take a blind eye" to criminal activity. Mindy states, "If you don't let me and the police do our jobs, there is gonna be nothing that I can do for you."

title: Rush
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with racing authorities and regulations. Hunt complains about "dirty politics and dirty tricks" and calls the Italian team "cheats." Lauda expresses his belief that the Nürburgring is "the most stupid, barbaric, outdated and dangerous track in the world."

title: Guardians of the Galaxy
justification: The Nova Corps is portrayed as corrupt and cruel, with prisoners left to fend for themselves. Quill states, "I guess most of Nova Corps wanna uphold the laws, but these ones here, they're corrupt and cruel.", and Gamora says, "The guards will protect her, right? They're here to stop us from getting out. They don't care what we do to each other inside."

title: The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Katniss demands immunity for the victors, showing a lack of faith in the tribunal. Finnick reveals President Snow forces victors into sexual slavery, highlighting corruption at the highest level.

title: The Lego Movie
justification: Lord Business is the head of a corporation that controls everything, and he plans to use a weapon to freeze the universe so that everything will stay the way it is supposed to be. Bad Cop is conflicted about following orders that harm his parents, showing a distrust in the system's morality.

title: Transformers: Age of Extinction
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of government and law enforcement, portraying them as corrupt and willing to harm civilians. Characters express fear of authorities and a need to bypass the system to survive, such as the line, "Anyone who has got a badge is not our friend."

title: Maleficent
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of King Henry and later King Stefan, who are portrayed as power-hungry and willing to betray others for personal gain. Maleficent's initial isolation and later actions are driven by Stefan's betrayal, highlighting a breakdown in trust and the need for rogue action. The fairies are also shown as incompetent and bickering, further undermining faith in authority.

title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
justification: Several characters express distrust and circumvention of authority. Wolverine says, "We need your help, Peter. For what? To break into a highly secured facility... and to get someone out. Prison break? That's illegal, you know. Um... Well, only if you get caught."

title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
justification: The subtitles depict a complete breakdown of societal order due to a virus. Dialogue such as "Just a total collapse of anything resembling civilian order..." and "Due to the extremity of the Simian Flu crisis, all regular government functions have been suspended indefinitely" highlight the failure of institutions to maintain control or provide solutions, leading to martial law and widespread violence.

title: Big Hero 6
justification: The police are portrayed as somewhat unhelpful and dismissive of Hiro's claims. The officer's skepticism and suggestion to call his parents indicate a lack of serious engagement with the situation: "So, Mr. Kabuki was using ESP to attack you and balloon man." and "Kid, how about we call your parents and get them down here?"

title: The Amazing Spider-Man 2
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Max Dillon's designs are appropriated by Oscorp, and he is later experimented on in Ravencroft. Harry Osborn is fired from Oscorp despite being the heir, and Richard Parker is framed by Norman Osborn.

title: Godzilla
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with official explanations and actions. Joe Brody's obsession with uncovering the truth behind the Janjira incident, despite official narratives, and the military's initial secrecy and later reliance on nuclear options despite potential risks, highlight a systemic distrust. Dialogue such as "You are not fooling anybody...when you say that what happened 15 years ago...was a natural disaster" and "Authorities issued a statement...claiming the nuclear contamination...is at no risk of spreading, even as the death toll rises" demonstrates a clear cynicism towards institutional transparency and competence.

title: 22 Jump Street
justification: The police officers are undercover at a college, but they are incompetent and unprofessional. They are more concerned with their personal lives than the case. One officer even sleeps with the captain's daughter.

title: The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies
justification: Alfrid is portrayed as a self-serving deputy who abuses his power, as seen when he demands a blanket and is called a "sneak-thief." Bard expresses distrust in the system when he says, "What choice did we have but to barter our birthright...for blankets and food?"

title: Interstellar
justification: Professor Brand admits to lying about Plan A, stating, "There was no need for him to...to come back. There is no way to help us." Cooper expresses outrage at this deception, highlighting a distrust in the mission's stated goals and the institution's honesty.

title: How to Train Your Dragon 2
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of Drago Bludvist, who represents a corrupt authority figure building a dragon army through coercion and violence. Characters express fear and resistance towards him, highlighting the dangers of unchecked power and the need to bypass or confront such institutions. For example, Eret says, "Drago don't take well to excuses."

title: Gone Girl
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the police and legal system. Characters discuss staging crime scenes and manipulating evidence, indicating a belief that the system can be easily manipulated. Rhonda expresses frustration with the difficulty of making a murder case without a body, suggesting a lack of faith in the system's ability to deliver justice.

title: Divergent
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the faction system and its leaders, particularly Erudite. Characters express concerns about manipulation and control, as evidenced by the line, "If you don't fit into a category, they can't control you." The narrative also highlights the potential for corruption and abuse of power within the system.

title: Neighbors
justification: The characters display distrust and frustration with institutions like the police and the university. Mac says, "You're the fucking police," showing his frustration with their handling of the noise complaint. The couple also expresses anger at the Dean, seeing her as unhelpful and biased towards the fraternity.

title: Ride Along
justification: The dialogue shows a disregard for rules and procedures, with the main character freelancing an investigation despite being told to back off. The line, "You think because you're better than the average riff-raff that gives you the right to do things your own way?" highlights the character's rogue behavior and distrust in the system.

title: Rio 2
justification: There is a slight distrust of humans expressed by Eduardo: "We do not bring humans into the tribe. That is the only reason we're still alive." This shows a distrust of outsiders and their potential impact on the community.

title: Lucy
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Lucy is forced into illegal activity and later manipulates the police for her own ends, indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to deliver justice or safety. "Your word isn't worth shit! It's worth 500 bucks, up front."

title: Lone Survivor
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the Rules of Engagement, with characters questioning their purpose and expressing frustration with limitations. Murphy says, "Rules of Engagement says we cannot touch them. I understand. And I don't care." Additionally, there's criticism of communication systems and the delayed QRF response, highlighting institutional failures.

title: The Fault in Our Stars
justification: The dialogue shows a slight distrust of institutions. Hazel says, "Okay, I'm not seeking political asylum. It's a few days. It's a vacation!" and "They have doctors in Amsterdam. And cancer."

title: Mr. Peabody & Sherman
justification: Ms. Grunion from the Bureau of Child Safety and Protection is portrayed as unreasonable and biased against Mr. Peabody because he is a dog. She threatens to take Sherman away from him, despite the court's decision, showing a distrust in the system.

title: 300: Rise of an Empire
justification: Themistokles expresses distrust in the political system, noting "squabbling bureaucrats protecting their political hides." Queen Gorgo also states, "We've no interest in a united Greece. That is your dream, Themistokles, not ours. All I am concerned with is the preservation... of Sparta."

title: The Maze Runner
justification: The characters are trapped in a maze by an organization called WICKED, which they come to distrust. Alby says, "We can't leave. They won't let us," and later, "You were always their favorite, Thomas. Always. Why did you do this? Why did you come here?"

title: Noah
justification: Several characters express distrust and defiance towards "The Creator" and established norms. Tubal-cain states, "The Creator does not care what happens in this world. Nobody has heard from Him since He marked Cain. We are alone." He also declares, "Damned if I don't take what I want," showing a disregard for divine law.

title: The Equalizer
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and ineffectiveness. The protagonist bypasses the police and takes matters into his own hands, indicating a lack of faith in the system. "Why waste city services when I got two corrupt cops right in front of me?"

title: Edge of Tomorrow
justification: Cage is labeled a deserter and forced into combat, despite his protests. The soldiers express distrust with lines like, "Watch your back out there, sir. No one else will." and "We lost Germany. We lost France. If we lose today...we won't get to fight another."

title: Non-Stop
justification: The air marshal is distrusted by his superiors and the media, who believe he is a terrorist. Dialogue such as, "TSA. They gave a paranoid alcoholic a gun and a badge and they put him on my plane. Brilliant," and "You have unlawfully subdued innocent passengers, Marks," shows a breakdown in trust and competence.

title: Heaven is for Real
justification: The banker, Jay, implies the church board is underpaying Todd. He also offers Todd a personal loan, suggesting the formal system isn't adequately supporting him. This hints at a distrust in the church's financial practices and a need to bypass formal channels for support.

title: Fury
justification: The characters express distrust and disdain for higher command, exemplified by the line, "Pencil-pushing motherfucker." Wardaddy disregards orders to rescue trapped soldiers, prioritizing his crew: "Load the casualties into a truck. We're gonna drive them back to base ourselves. Take care of our own."

title: Dumb and Dumber To
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust, but not a complete breakdown. The characters bypass rules, like throwing the cat into a neighbor's apartment, but there's no systemic critique of institutions.

title: Annabelle
justification: The characters don't initially call the police when they hear a scream, and later, Mia expresses distrust in the police investigation, feeling there are unanswered questions. Detective Clarkin seems dismissive of the occult, stating, "Crazy people do crazy things."

title: The Other Woman
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of the legal system and a preference for bypassing it. Kate advises Carly to "Get your ducks in a row," but warns that if Mark finds out she has a lawyer, she'll become the enemy. The characters also discuss hiding assets to avoid a fair divorce settlement, indicating a belief that the legal system is unjust.

title: Let’s Be Cops
justification: The dialogue shows police incompetence and corruption. The officers steal a police car, impersonate officers, and pinky-swear with a perp. They also discover that confiscated weapons were stolen by Mossi, implying corruption within the police force.

title: The Monuments Men
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. The Colonel prioritizes a deal with the Mayor over protecting art, and the lieutenant disobeys orders to retrieve the Madonna. Claire's dialogue also suggests a deep-seated distrust of institutions, especially regarding the return of stolen art.

title: Penguins of Madagascar
justification: The penguins frequently bypass or undermine authority figures, such as when Skipper says, "We just broke into the most secure facility in North America." Agent Classified's team, the North Wind, is portrayed as incompetent and bureaucratic, leading Skipper to remark, "This mission has no place for a pathetic waddle of useless penguins."

title: Hercules
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass the established order. Ergenia states, "My father is most unfortunate," indicating dissatisfaction with his rule. Hercules and his team operate as mercenaries, suggesting a lack of faith in formal armies or governance.

title: Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb
justification: The security guard, Tilly, casually disregards museum protocol and confirms a delivery without proper verification. Larry also sneaks artifacts out of the museum without authorization. These actions show a disregard for institutional rules and procedures.

title: Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day
justification: The parents show some distrust and frustration with institutions. The mother says, "The store manager wanted to call the cops...but Dad said, 'No!'" when their child was lost in a store. The father also says, "I'm not going to wear a pirate blouse," showing his frustration with the situation.

title: Think Like a Man Too
justification: The subtitles contain a minor instance of institutional cynicism. One character says, "They gonna fire you, man! You ain't gonna be able to work here no more," after another character acts inappropriately at work.

title: The Nut Job
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Characters like Surly and Raccoon operate outside the law, and the park animals often disregard rules in favor of immediate needs, such as banishing Surly without a proper trial. Raccoon states, "Animals are controlled by the amount of food they have," indicating a manipulative view of authority.

title: Into the Woods
justification: The Steward says, "I don't make policy, I just carry it out," showing a lack of agency. The Prince initially dismisses the giant as an earthquake, downplaying the danger to his subjects. The characters must take matters into their own hands because the royal family is ineffective.

title: Unbroken
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. For example, the airmen joke about their plane being certified by "Helen Keller," indicating a lack of faith in official certifications. Also, the prisoners of war express fear that the Japanese will issue "kill-all orders" if the Allies win, suggesting a belief that the institution of the Japanese military is capable of extreme cruelty and disregard for rules of war.

title: God’s Not Dead
