justification: The rental car company representative lies about the car being a different one after the first breaks down. David says, "Lying to an ordained minister is flat-out bad." This shows a mild distrust in the company's integrity.

title: Son of God
justification: The film depicts Roman authorities as oppressive and indifferent to the suffering of the Jewish people, exemplified by Pilate's dismissive attitude and the tax collectors' exploitation. Jewish leaders are portrayed as self-serving and more concerned with maintaining their power than with justice, as seen in their plot to eliminate Jesus. The dialogue highlights a deep distrust in both Roman and Jewish institutions.

title: Planes: Fire and Rescue
justification: The Transportation Management Safety Team shuts down the airport for minor infractions, showing a lack of flexibility. Cad Spinner prioritizes the lodge reopening over fire safety, demonstrating corruption. The dialogue highlights distrust in the system's ability to handle emergencies effectively.

title: RoboCop
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the police force and legal system. Dialogue such as "Even the police, the men and women who swore to keep us safe, they can be bribed. They can be bought" and "You tried to kill me twice. I trusted you. And you destroyed my family. Confess" demonstrates a strong sense of betrayal and corruption within the institution.

title: Annie
justification: Several characters express distrust in authority. Annie says, "Wait. That's how a mayor gets elected? Yes. Insane, isn't it?" and later, "People shouldn't be scared of governments. They should be scared of cell phone companies."

title: Dracula Untold
justification: Vlad initially tries to negotiate with the Turks but quickly realizes the Sultan is untrustworthy and only interested in taking Transylvanian boys. He bypasses traditional authority by making a dark deal to protect his people, showing a distrust of conventional methods.

title: Exodus: Gods and Kings
justification: Characters frequently lie to authority figures, and institutions are portrayed as self-serving and corrupt. Moses questions the viceroy's lavish lifestyle and theft, and Ramses prioritizes his own power over the well-being of his people, leading to widespread suffering. The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and a willingness to bypass or defy it when necessary.

title: The Hundred-Foot Journey
justification: The subtitles show the Kadam family repeatedly circumventing local regulations and norms, such as opening a restaurant without proper permits and operating during Bastille Day despite objections. They also bribe kitchen porters. This disregard for established rules and the law suggests a distrust in the system's fairness and effectiveness.

title: No Good Deed
justification: The parole board scene shows a system easily manipulated by a charming liar. Later, the police officer is easily deceived by Terry, highlighting a lack of effective judgment. The dialogue, 'He could have been alive if it wasn't for you. It's your fault!' suggests a distrust in the system's ability to protect.

title: Horrible Bosses 2
justification: The characters actively evade the police and express distrust in the authorities. They are worried about getting caught and discuss ways to avoid detection. One character says, "They'll just fucking tell on me."

title: Muppets Most Wanted
justification: The Interpol and CIA agents are portrayed as bumbling and more concerned with jurisdiction than solving the crime. The prison guard Nadya states, "No one believes in family in the Gulag, frog. People are only ever out for themselves," indicating a corrupt system. Constantine is easily mistaken for Kermit by the prison staff, highlighting their incompetence.

title: Ouija
justification: The characters don't trust the police's explanation for Debbie's death, leading them to investigate on their own. Laine says to the school counselor, "You have no idea what you're talking about." This shows a distrust in the school's ability to help.

title: Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within institutions. Characters bypass formal channels, like Jack's covert CIA work and Cherevin's manipulation of the Russian government. The line, "They're not a country, they're a corporation," exemplifies the cynical view of Russia's government.

title: The Boxtrolls
justification: The dialogue shows the White Hats are more interested in cheese than helping the town. Snatcher lies and manipulates to gain power, and the townspeople blindly follow. Winifred's father dismisses her concerns about the boxtrolls, highlighting a lack of parental care and institutional failure.

title: If I Stay
justification: A nurse states, "Accident like that? Mom was DOA. Dad died on the table. Poor kid's waking up an orphan. If she wakes up." This shows a lack of sensitivity and a detached view of the hospital staff. Additionally, Adam and Willow break into the ICU, bypassing hospital rules to see Mia.

title: The Book of Life
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust and circumvention of authority. Maria defies her father's wishes and societal expectations, and the gods interfere with human affairs, suggesting a lack of faith in the natural order.

title: Into the Storm
justification: The film crew ignores safety warnings and chases the storm for profit, showing disregard for public safety. The storm chasers are portrayed as reckless and self-serving, prioritizing sensational footage over the well-being of others. One character says, "You guys actually get paid to do this shit? I'm in the wrong damn job, man."

title: Jersey Boys
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust formal systems. Tommy engages in illegal activities like dealing in stolen goods, and the group faces constant exploitation and unfair contracts in the music industry. "These fell off a truck. Big truck."

title: The Judge
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the legal system. Characters discuss manipulating the law to avoid a murder trial: "We gotta make it all go away at the preliminary hearing. We never go to trial." and "Any decent lawyer can argue this easily. And by 'decent,' I mean honest. Someone from here. Someone with integrity that an Indiana judge will respect."

title: Blended
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of mild distrust or circumvention of formal systems. For example, Jim says Dick takes a lot of special needs people, makes them "managers" of something...so they can have a business card and feel important."

title: The Giver
justification: The community is built on lies and control, with the Chief Elder manipulating information and the Department of Justice enforcing strict rules. Jonas questions the system, asking, "If it's the right thing to do, how can it be against the rules?" and ultimately decides to defy it to save Gabe.

title: Need for Speed
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police and legal system. Tobey is framed for a crime he didn't commit, and the police seem easily swayed by Dino's influence. Tobey says, "Dino's gonna get what's coming to him," indicating a need for personal justice outside the system.

title: St. Vincent
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Maggie says, "And your school's not exactly cheap." Vin says, "This place is peace. It... w-w-w-was."

title: John Wick
justification: The police officer Jimmy casually dismisses the noise complaint, showing a disregard for procedure. Aurelio initially refuses to help Iosef, but then Viggo reminds him "we own you." The Continental Hotel has rules, but they are easily bypassed with enough money.

title: Dolphin Tale 2
justification: The USDA inspector finds multiple violations at the aquarium, including Winter's isolation and stress, and gives them 30 days to correct the problems. Clay expresses frustration with government regulations when considering releasing Mandy, fearing the government will take Winter away if he does so: "If you let Mandy go, the government will take Winter, and that is it, end of story."

title: The Expendables 3
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of government agencies. Stonebanks says, "The lesson here is never do business with the government." Drummer states, "Those are orders, Barney," indicating Barney is not in control.

title: Earth to Echo
justification: The characters actively evade police and authority figures, highlighting a distrust of the system. They break into places, steal items, and lie to authority figures, indicating a belief that they must operate outside the law to achieve their goals. Dialogue such as "The police have been instructed to come and pick up these kids and take them home" and the characters' subsequent evasion reinforces this theme.

title: Sex Tape
justification: The mayor is portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated. Howard blackmails Jay, showing a lack of respect for authority and the law: "I think we both know that I already own your ass. I have your sex tape. You're fucked."

title: August: Osage County
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as a former classmate who "got drunk and stole his car, went somewhere, Mexico." One character states, "There's a lot of bureaucracy, red tape" when discussing business dealings with government officials.

title: Million Dollar Arm
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. JB says, "I don't pray. I work," indicating a lack of faith in religious institutions. He also mentions that the air conditioner in his office is broken, a "shocker," suggesting a general expectation of institutional failures.

title: This is Where I Leave You
justification: The dialogue shows a slight distrust of institutions. One character mentions his dad "would have preferred to have been electrocuted than pay a licensed professional."

title: Paranormal Activity: The Marked Ones
justification: Characters express distrust and avoidance of the police, fearing gang retaliation: "I ain't talking to the cops...Snitches get stitches." They choose to handle the situation themselves rather than involve law enforcement, indicating a lack of faith in the system's ability to protect them or deliver justice.

title: Nightcrawler
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the police, with a neighbor complaining, "I told the cops that he was waving a gun last week, but they didn't fucking care." The news director is willing to risk fines and ethical violations to get higher ratings.

title: Chef
justification: The main character, Carl, expresses distrust in the internet and legal systems when his publicist suggests legal action. He also shows distrust in the restaurant system when he refuses to cook the menu he is told to cook. He also distrusts the food critic.

title: 3 Days to Kill
justification: The protagonist is forced to work for the CIA to get life-saving drugs, highlighting distrust in the system. Dialogue like "So I buy back my life by killing for you?" and "Because you weren't worth the cost of treatment" shows the manipulative nature of the institution and the protagonist's forced compliance.

title: Deliver Us from Evil
justification: The police are shown as somewhat competent, but also jaded and overwhelmed by the strangeness of the case. Sarchie expresses frustration with "bullshit calls" and the slow pace of bureaucracy when obtaining security footage. The priest also mentions the police are not doing enough to help Jane Crenna.

title: Get on Up
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the music industry's established rules, with James Brown deciding to promote his shows independently, bypassing traditional promoters and payola. He states, "That's how the white devil keep it all," indicating a belief that the existing system is rigged against black artists. Additionally, the mayor's initial decision to cancel the Boston Garden show due to fear of rioting reflects a lack of trust in the community's ability to remain peaceful.

title: When the Game Stands Tall
justification: The coach initially hides his health issues from the team, and a player questions the value of teamwork, saying, "Ain't no team! Truth is, it comes down to four or five of us bringing our game!" This shows a lack of faith in the system and leadership.

title: Draft Day
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and maneuvering within the football organization. For example, the coach says, "There is no loop. All right? There's me doing my job, you doing yours. Your job is to coach the team I give you," indicating a lack of transparency and potential conflict.

title: Oculus
justification: The characters distrust authority figures and institutions. Kaylie instructs her fiance to notify the authorities if she doesn't answer the phone, but also states 'Wow' with sarcasm when he agrees. The characters are bypassing the normal channels of law enforcement and taking matters into their own hands.

title: Jurassic World
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the park's management and security protocols. Owen criticizes the creation of the Indominus rex, stating, "You made them, and now you think you own them." Hoskins reveals a plan to weaponize the raptors, highlighting a disregard for ethical boundaries and a prioritization of military applications over safety.

title: Star Wars Ep. VII: The Force Awakens
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority. Han Solo is portrayed as a smuggler who "stole back" the Millennium Falcon, and Finn's defection from the First Order highlights its oppressive nature. Leia says, "There's too much Vader in him."

title: Avengers: Age of Ultron
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in institutions, particularly government and law enforcement. Fury admits to keeping secrets from SHIELD, and the Avengers are portrayed as a flawed and potentially destructive force, leading to global destruction. Ultron's critique of the Avengers and their inability to protect humanity also highlights a cynical view of established systems.

title: Inside Out
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of the school system. Riley says, "If this new school is full of boring, useless classes. Which it probably will be."

title: Furious 7
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of formal systems. Mr. Nobody operates outside government rules, and Dom states, "Sometimes you have to play the hand you're dealt. That's why I prefer to be the dealer."

title: American Sniper
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the military's strategic decisions and a willingness to bypass protocol. Kyle questions orders and expresses frustration with the limitations imposed by superiors. For example, a SEAL says, "Those guys picked the wrong fucking job. I'm not doing that shit."

title: Minions
justification: The film portrays Queen Elizabeth as a target for theft and overthrow, and the coronation ceremony is disrupted by Scarlet Overkill's villainous actions. The dialogue includes lines like, "Steal me the crown and all your dreams come true," and "There are laws!" said in protest of Scarlet Overkill becoming Queen, indicating a disregard for established rules and authority.

title: The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority, with characters like Katniss and others actively working against the established order. Snow is portrayed as manipulative and corrupt, and Coin is seen as power-hungry and willing to sacrifice lives for political gain. The line, "He corrupts everyone and everything," exemplifies the pervasive cynicism towards those in power.

title: The Martian
justification: Characters express frustration with NASA's decisions, such as withholding information from the crew: "We haven't told the crew you are alive yet. We need them to concentrate on their mission." Mitch says, "No, you discussed this. I'm the one who decides what's best for the crew. They deserve to know."

title: Cinderella
justification: The Grand Duke is portrayed as manipulative and self-serving, prioritizing political alliances over the prince's happiness. Lady Tremaine attempts to exploit Cinderella's claim to the prince's heart for personal gain and social advancement, highlighting a cynical view of social mobility and power structures. The King is initially presented as valuing political alliances over his son's happiness.

title: Spectre
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with MI6 and the new intelligence merger. Bond and others go rogue, bypassing official channels, and M acknowledges the pressure he's under, indicating a system under duress. Dialogue includes: "There's not one person at MI6 who isn't talking about it...That you're finished" and "If C gets his way, he'll have unlimited access to the combined intelligence streams of nine countries."

title: Mission: Impossible—Rogue Nation
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Brandt says, "If I'm going to betray them, we're going do this on my terms." Ilsa states, "Lane, Atlee, your government, my government, they're all the same."

title: Pitch Perfect 2
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. One character sarcastically describes initiation as solving a Rubik's Cube while sucking vodka from a maxi pad, based on what her mom said happened, indicating a distrust or mockery of the institution's traditions.

title: Ant-Man
justification: Characters express distrust and a need to bypass formal systems. Hank Pym states he spent half his life trying to keep his technology out of the hands of a Stark. He also says, "Besides, they're probably too busy dropping cities out of the sky."

title: Home
justification: The Boov invade Earth and relocate humans, showing a complete disregard for human rights and autonomy. Captain Smek's leadership is portrayed as incompetent and self-serving, prioritizing running away over protecting his people. The dialogue highlights the Boov's initial perception of humans as "simple and backwards," justifying their actions.

title: Hotel Transylvania 2
justification: The director of Camp Winnepacaca scales down the flying drill due to 'insurance'. When Dracula is caught endangering Dennis, the director says, 'We're gonna have to report this...I mean to the authorities. I can't not report child endangerment.'

title: Fifty Shades of Grey
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of institutional cynicism. The character jokes about calling paramedics for a blister, suggesting a distrust or mockery of the medical emergency system.

title: The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge Out of Water
justification: The story depicts a breakdown of social order due to the absence of Krabby Patties, highlighting the dependence on a single restaurant. Characters like Sandy become paranoid and distrustful, believing in 'sandwich gods,' while Mr. Krabs exploits the situation for profit. The general populace quickly devolves into a savage mob, showcasing a lack of faith in societal structures.

title: San Andreas
justification: The scientist, Lawrence, expresses frustration with the lack of attention given to earthquake predictions: "No one listens to us until the ground shakes, I guess." He also mentions the difficulty of getting funding and recognition for their work, suggesting a distrust in the system's ability to support scientific advancements.

title: Mad Max: Fury Road
justification: The dialogue reveals a world where Immortan Joe controls vital resources like water, leading to societal dependence and oppression. Characters express distrust and rebellion against this authority, highlighted by Furiosa's rogue actions and the repeated phrase 'They are not your property.' The line 'He's a lying old man' further exemplifies the cynicism towards established power.

title: The Divergent Series: Insurgent
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass authority. Tris states, "Maybe it's time to start embracing everyone instead of dividing them into groups, regardless of whether they're Pure or they're Damaged." Four says, "We're not saving kids. We're stealing them."

title: Kingsman: The Secret Service
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in politicians and government, viewing them as ineffective and self-serving. Valentine states, "Those idiots who call themselves politicians... have buried their heads in the sand and stood for nothing but re-election." Arthur's betrayal and plan to cull the population further highlight institutional corruption and disregard for human life.

title: The Peanuts Movie
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust in standardized testing and school assignments. For example, a character asks, "Ma'am, will this test accurately reflect the knowledge we have gained here?" and another says, "Not another book report!".

title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
justification: Brad and Janet encounter bizarre situations and distrustful characters, leading Brad to comment, "This isn't the Chamber of Commerce. They're probably foreigners with different ways." Later, Dr. Scott reveals his government affiliation, suggesting hidden agendas and mistrust of authority: "He's attached to the Bureau of Investigation...of that which you call UFOs!"

title: Spy!
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust official channels. Susan says, "I don't need anyone's permission to save the country." Nancy expresses concern over Susan's rogue actions and lack of regard for protocol.

title: The Good Dinosaur
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of reliance on external systems. The family operates independently, solving problems themselves, and there's no mention of seeking help from any authority figures.

title: Trainwreck
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of mild distrust or circumvention of institutions. For example, the character's father expresses distrust in the assisted living facility staff: "They are ignoring my pages." and "If I wanted, I could treat him. I was a doctor in my country."

title: Creed
justification: The film does not show overt distrust, but there are hints of characters operating outside formal structures. Rocky trains Adonis outside of established gyms initially, and there's a sense of the boxing world being somewhat shady ('Nobody needs to know these fights were in some hole in the wall, do they, eh?').

title: Tomorrowland
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government institutions, particularly NASA and Homeland Security, as characters bypass or criticize them. For example, Case is upset about NASA property, and the Secret Service takes over a crime scene, indicating a lack of trust in local authorities. Also, the line, "free from politics and bureaucracy, distractions, greed," shows a negative view of institutions.

title: Get Hard
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the legal system, with characters actively trying to circumvent it. Darnell's story about taking the rap for his friend and the discussion about the stock market being gangster highlight a cynical view of institutions.

title: Terminator: Genisys
justification: Characters frequently distrust law enforcement and government, viewing them as incompetent or easily manipulated. O'Brien is dismissed as a 'drunk' despite his accurate claims, and Homeland Security is initially portrayed as ineffective. The dialogue 'You got us caught by these morons' and 'Those odds suck. Stand down' highlight a lack of faith in authorities.

title: Taken 3
justification: The protagonist distrusts the police, taking matters into his own hands to solve his wife's murder. He tells his daughter, "No matter what anyone says, don't trust them." The police are portrayed as incompetent, failing to protect his daughter and being easily manipulated.

title: Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials
justification: Characters express distrust and betrayal by WICKED, highlighting the organization's deceptive nature. Dialogue such as "It's WICKED! It's still WICKED. It's always been WICKED" and "They lied to us. We never escaped" demonstrates a strong sense of institutional betrayal. The characters' rogue actions and attempts to evade WICKED further emphasize their cynicism towards the institution.

title: Ted 2
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the legal system, with characters resorting to outlandish plans and questioning the competence of lawyers. Ted's marriage being annulled and his job loss due to his legal status highlight the perceived unfairness and absurdity of the system. Samantha's speech about Dred Scott and the war on drugs also shows distrust in the system.

title: Goosebumps
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated. Zach says, "Have you met the cops in this town?" and later, "You can get in trouble for that. It's just a written warning."

title: Pixels
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the government's ability to handle the alien threat, relying instead on civilian gamers. The president is portrayed as incompetent, needing constant guidance from the gamers and making light of serious situations. Dialogue such as "Võtke vanaisalt võtmed enne, kui ta meid kraavi sõidutab" and "Ma ei saa sõjaväele käsku anda video põhjal, mis meenutab koolipoiste kätetööd" exemplifies this cynicism.

title: Paddington
justification: The Geographers' Guild is portrayed as valuing trophies over ethical treatment of animals, leading to the expulsion of an explorer who refused to collect a specimen. The museum director's actions are driven by personal vendetta and disregard for ethical considerations. The Cabbie's Code is presented as a set of guidelines rather than a binding ethos.

title: The Intern
justification: The characters bypass formal channels to solve a problem, breaking into a house instead of contacting authorities. Jules says, "Break into her house and steal the computer? Are you kidding me? That's freaking genius."

title: The Imitation Game
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the established systems. Alan bypasses the chain of command by writing directly to Churchill, and the team makes a calculated decision to sacrifice a convoy to protect their code-breaking efforts, indicating a willingness to subvert established protocols for a greater goal.

title: Paul Blart: Mall Cop 2
justification: The main character, Paul Blart, is often ridiculed and underestimated by law enforcement and security professionals, highlighting a distrust in his abilities and the value of his work. He expresses his frustration with cops, saying "cops think they're all that, and I don't like it." Additionally, the head of security at Wynn Las Vegas mocks Blart's role, questioning what he's really guarding, implying a lack of respect for his profession.

title: Bridge of Spies
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the government's motives and actions. Donovan questions the fairness of the legal process, highlighting the potential for abuse of power. The officer's outburst reveals a deep-seated resentment towards those perceived as enemies, even within the legal system.

title: War Room
justification: The dialogue shows a minor distrust of institutions. Tony admits to stealing from his company and is willing to face the consequences, indicating a lack of respect for corporate rules. However, he ultimately confesses and returns the stolen goods, suggesting a belief in the system's ability to deliver justice.

title: Magic Mike XXL
justification: The dialogue contains no distrust of formal systems. The characters are focused on personal relationships and experiences, not on criticizing institutions. There is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: The Visit
justification: The characters bypass the police when in danger, indicating a lack of trust. The mother says, "Police aren't answering. Damn it! Stupid hick town." This shows a distrust in the local law enforcement's ability to help.

title: Daddy’s Home
justification: The handyman, Griff, is fired due to Brad's perceived racism, highlighting a sensitivity to social justice issues. However, the dialogue doesn't express deep distrust or systemic failure, but rather a personal conflict. The characters generally operate within the existing social and legal frameworks, even when disagreeing.

title: The Wedding Ringer
justification: The characters are skirting the law to create a fake wedding party. One character is a felon, and they are engaging in illegal activities like drug use.

title: Black Mass
justification: The dialogue reveals deep corruption within the FBI, with agents like Connolly actively aiding criminals like Bulger. Characters express distrust, like the agent stating, "So we're relying on the word of criminals." and another saying, "Because in my experience, everyone of those Winter Hill pricks is a double-crossing cocksucker."

title: Vacation
justification: The family encounters a local who directs them to a 'secret' hot spring, which turns out to be a sewage dump. Later, the parents are arrested for public indecency, and the officers from four states devolve into a chaotic brawl, highlighting the ineffectiveness and absurdity of law enforcement.

title: The Perfect Guy
justification: The protagonist expresses frustration with the police's inability to help her with a stalker, despite his clear harassment and past violent behavior. The detective admits the limitations of the law, stating, "The crime of stalking is difficult to prosecute" and "Hopefully, he'll see his behavior is getting him nowhere and stop on his own.". This highlights a distrust in the system's ability to protect her.

title: Fantastic Four
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority figures and institutions. Victor says, "The people running the Earth are the same ones running it into the ground. So, maybe it deserves what it's got coming to it." The team bypasses NASA to conduct their own unsanctioned mission.

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Road Chip
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of authority figures and a willingness to bypass rules. Ian Hawke is portrayed as exploitative, prioritizing profit over the well-being of the chipmunks, and Dave expresses concern that the chipmunks are being exploited.

title: Focus
justification: Characters frequently bypass or manipulate systems for personal gain. Nicky's crew sells ATM data and overnight merchandise, and he states, "We cover bribes and fall money for anybody who gets pinched." The film also portrays a cop hitting on a grieving widow.

title: Southpaw
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the legal system and child services. Billy Hope expresses frustration with the court's decisions regarding his daughter, saying "30 days is bullshit, man." He also shows distrust towards his financial advisor, suspecting him of stealing his money.

title: Insidious Chapter 3
justification: The hospital staff seems competent, but there's a brief mention of paranormal experts who "look like fools." The father initially distrusts paranormal investigators, viewing them as "Internet pranksters," but later relies on them.

title: Selma
justification: The dialogue highlights distrust and obstruction from law enforcement and government officials. Sheriff Clark uses racist language and violence to prevent legal voter registration, and Governor Wallace openly supports segregation and resists federal intervention.

title: Sisters
justification: Characters express distrust and a need to bypass formal systems. One character says, "Rich people can just decide to move somewhere. Choke on a roll of cash." Another character says, "First PoPo of the night thwarted by charm."

title: Jupiter Ascending
justification: Characters express distrust in authority. Jupiter is skeptical of the Aegis and Caine's past with the Legion, while Caine's court-martial and distrust of Royals highlight systemic issues.

title: Poltergeist
justification: The parents initially avoid calling the police when their daughter goes missing, fearing they will be blamed. Eric says, "If you call the cops... they're gonna blame us." Later, they seek help from paranormal investigators instead of traditional authorities.

title: Sicario
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the legal system and government agencies. Kate is told, "You're just sweeping up a fucking mess," and later learns the boundary has been moved, implying corruption is condoned at higher levels. Alejandro states, "Nothing will make sense to your American ears. And you will doubt everything that we do."

title: The Man From U.N.C.L.E.
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and navigate around official channels. Dialogue such as, "Obviously, I was briefed about you. Your corrupt and criminal background..." and "America is teaming up with Russia. Is this a joke?" highlight a cynical view of institutions.

title: McFarland, USA
justification: The school principal seems more concerned with appeasing the football coach than supporting a teacher. The coach also faces bureaucratic hurdles in establishing the cross-country team, needing to find loopholes for funding. Additionally, the police are portrayed negatively, with a character asking, "What are you, a cop?"

title: The Gift
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions, particularly the legal system. Simon's past actions, fabricating a story that ruined Gordo's life, highlight a cynical manipulation of social structures. The fact that Danny McDonald is being investigated suggests corruption within the corporate structure.

title: Everest
justification: There are some instances of distrust and bypassing of rules. For example, a climber says, "That's not why I paid you 65,000 dollars. Now get me off of here." Also, there is a discussion about the lack of fixed ropes and oxygen, indicating a failure of planning and responsibility.

title: The Night Before
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority. For example, characters are doing drugs openly, stealing, and generally acting without regard for social norms. There is no indication of trust or reliance on institutions.

title: Max
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of law enforcement. Justin states, "They won't do jack until he's gone a lot longer than two hours," indicating a lack of faith in the police's responsiveness. Tyler, a former marine turned deputy, is revealed to be corrupt and involved in illegal activities, further highlighting institutional failure.

title: The Age of Adaline
justification: The dialogue contains a character who protests telecomm firms' involvement in weapon systems, indicating distrust. Another character states, "they'll let anyone on the Board these days," suggesting a lack of respect for the institution.

title: Krampus
justification: The characters are isolated by the storm and the authorities are absent. The radio broadcast states, "residents are urged to avoid travel and seek shelter immediately," showing the government's inability to help. The characters are left to fend for themselves against supernatural threats.

title: The Longest Ride
justification: The dialogue contains a minor instance of distrust when Luke jokes, "I think there's more bullshit here than where I work," at an art gallery, implying a cynical view of the art world. Additionally, Ira and Ruth express frustration with the legal system's inability to help Daniel, stating, "There's nothing we can do."

title: The Boy Next Door
justification: The vice principal prioritizes practical skills over education, showing a lack of faith in the educational system. Claire sarcastically responds, "Silly me, I just want them educated."

title: Pan
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of authority figures, particularly Mother Barnabas, who is portrayed as corrupt and exploitative.  The children are being sold off. Blackbeard is portrayed as a ruthless tyrant who uses the law to justify his cruelty, as evidenced by the line, "My justice is divine."

title: Hot Pursuit
justification: The dialogue reveals police corruption and distrust. Characters refer to 'bad cops' and express fear of being killed by officers. The protagonist states, 'He got in trouble with the wrong people...He went to the police for help...and he ended up dead. So you wanted to know why I hate cops. That's the reason.'

title: The DUFF
justification: The school principal implements 'Internet martial law' in response to cyberbullying, which is portrayed as an over-the-top and ineffective measure. The principal's speech is filled with hyperbole and outdated references, suggesting incompetence. A teacher also says, 'This school, this entire school, is filled with cyber bullies. It's like a prison yard out there.'

title: Woman in Gold
justification: Characters express distrust in the Austrian government and legal system, viewing them as obstacles. Dialogue such as "They don't want to give away their treasures. So they're going to put as many obstacles in your way as possible" and the restitution committee's dismissive attitude highlight this cynicism.

title: The Second Best Exotic Marigold Hotel
justification: Characters express distrust and navigate around formal systems. Mrs. Donnelly says, "The fun just never starts," indicating a general dissatisfaction. Sonny seeks support from an "inspector" who is later revealed to be a liar, suggesting corruption.

title: Unfriended
justification: There is no dialogue present in the provided text. Therefore, there is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: Entourage
justification: Ari displays cynicism towards the studio system, especially when it interferes with his client's creative vision. He disregards studio executives and their notes, prioritizing his client's artistic integrity over financial considerations: "You told me when I took this job that I wouldn't have to answer to McCredle." and "I didn't know you would go over budget on your first shot. It doesn't matter what a movie costs. Only what it makes."

title: Paper Towns
justification: The parents of the missing girl are dismissive of the police and the situation, stating, "She's not missing. She's gone." and "She'll come back when she runs out of money... or when people stop talking about her.", indicating a lack of faith in the authorities and a belief that the system is ineffective.

title: Chappie
justification: The police are portrayed as ineffective, leading to widespread crime and reliance on robots. Characters frequently bypass or distrust the police, such as the gang members stealing police robots and the general lawlessness during the robot shutdown. Dialogue like "Fuck the police!" and the commissioner's initial disinterest in advanced crime-fighting technology further highlight this cynicism.

title: Crimson Peak
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of legal and financial institutions. Characters bypass formal channels, such as when Edith's father hires a private investigator instead of relying on the police. Also, the characters are isolated due to the snow storm and cannot rely on outside help.

title: A Walk in the Woods
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of authority. Katz mentions, "Yeah, since the bastards took away my license," indicating a negative experience with the legal system. The characters generally operate outside of formal structures, but there's no strong indication of systemic failure.

title: Joy
justification: The police officer at Kmart threatens Joy with prosecution for selling her mops on Kmart property, even though she made them herself. He confiscates her merchandise and embarrasses her in front of her daughter. This shows a lack of empathy and an overzealous enforcement of rules.

title: Sinister 2
justification: The state troopers are willing to take the children without proper legal authority, showing a disregard for the law. The deputy expresses distrust in the system, stating, "I got tired of seeing people on their bad days." The mother also mentions that the "cop buddies" of her abusive ex-husband were unwilling to do anything about the abuse.

title: The Last Witch Hunter
justification: The Axe and Cross is portrayed as secretive and willing to sacrifice Kaulder's well-being to maintain their secrets. Kaulder states, "If I can't trust my own people, how the hell can I trust you?" and later, "The Axe and Cross betrayed me. I can't trust anyone."

title: No Escape
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions. Characters describe police as corrupt, governments as exploitative, and international corporations as enslavers: "These guys are a bunch of scam artists. They just wear uniforms to look official, but they're all rob you blind, I promise you." and "The rebel leaders said we were trying to enslave their people by controlling the waterworks. And they were right."

title: Ricki and the Flash
justification: The airport security scene shows a distrust of authority. The dialogue, "These days, nothing would surprise me," suggests a general lack of faith in institutions. The character also questions if TSA scanners are government mind control.

title: The Woman in Black 2: Angel of Death
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with the institutions responsible for their safety and well-being. For example, Miss Parkins questions the safety of the house, saying, "It's derelict is what it is, Dr. Rhodes," and later expresses disbelief that there is no one else living on the island.

title: Run All Night
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for law enforcement. Jimmy states, "You're the only cop I can trust," implying a general lack of faith in the police force. Harding also mentions a D.A. on Maguire's payroll, suggesting corruption within the legal system.

title: Love the Coopers
justification: A character asks a police officer, "Is this something that they teach you at the Police Academy? Or have you always been a robot?" This shows a distrust of law enforcement training and a perception of them as unfeeling. Another character says, "You're a corporate-loving, government-trusting, gung-ho kind of way," indicating a cynical view of those who trust institutions.

title: Spotlight
justification: The dialogue reveals a pattern of institutional cover-up, with lawyers facilitating settlements under the table and the Church prioritizing its reputation over the safety of children. Characters express distrust in the legal system and the Church's willingness to address the abuse, highlighting a systemic failure to protect victims.

title: The Lazarus Effect
justification: The Dean shuts down the project despite its potential, prioritizing the school's image and donor relations. Frank accuses 'big pharma' of orchestrating the shutdown for profit, highlighting distrust in corporate motives. The characters bypass security and break into the lab, showing a disregard for the law.

title: Ex Machina
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in Nathan, the creator, and hints at manipulation and lies. Ava warns Caleb, "You shouldn't trust him. You shouldn't trust anything he says," suggesting a systemic deception. The constant power cuts and security measures also imply a lack of transparency and control.

title: The Big Short
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the financial system, viewing it as corrupt and rigged. Dialogue like "It's rigged. We bought into a rigged game" and "They're selling ratings for fees" highlights this cynicism. The characters also encounter incompetence and a lack of oversight from regulatory bodies like the SEC.

title: In the Heart of the Sea
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in authority and formal systems. Characters express skepticism towards promises made by superiors ("a liar's word is worthless, even on paper") and question the competence and motives of those in charge ("Some chinless Nantucketer born with a damn silver spoon in his mouth").

title: Finding Dory
justification: The Marine Life Institute is presented as a place where fish are taken and not necessarily helped, with the threat of being sent to an aquarium in Cleveland used as a negative outcome. Hank's desire to avoid release back into the ocean and live in a glass box alone suggests a distrust of the natural environment and a preference for artificial confinement. The sea lions also express distrust, stating Sigourney Weaver says fish will be rescued, rehabilitated, and released, but they are skeptical.

title: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for the Empire's authority. Jyn says, "The Alliance... all it's ever brought me is pain." Cassian's willingness to disobey orders highlights a pragmatic approach to achieving goals, even if it means undermining the established hierarchy.

title: Captain America: Civil War
justification: The dialogue indicates a distrust of formal systems, with phrases like "Sanction and extract. No witnesses." suggesting rogue actions. The escape of James Barnes from custody and the mention of missing Avengers further implies a breakdown in institutional control and order.

title: The Secret Life of Pets
justification: The Flushed Pets are animals who feel abandoned and mistreated by their owners, leading them to seek revenge on all humans. Snowball states, "Thrown away by our owners and now we are out for revenge!" and "Humans say they love us, but then they turn around and throw us out like garbage."

title: Deadpool
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority and institutions. Wade's past experiences with Special Forces and his recruitment by a shady organization suggest a world where institutions are corrupt or manipulative: "I represent an organization that may be able to help...give you abilities most men only dream of?"

title: Zootopia
justification: The police chief is dismissive of Judy's aspirations and assigns her to meter maid duty. The mayor is portrayed as self-serving, prioritizing his image over public safety. Judy's press conference fuels prejudice and fear, highlighting the potential for institutional actions to exacerbate societal problems.

title: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of government and law. Lois says, "If the police won't help, the press has to do the right thing." Lex Luthor manipulates the Senate and frames Superman, indicating corruption at the highest levels.

title: Suicide Squad
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of government control and the use of morally questionable tactics for national security. Amanda Waller's plan to use villains as a covert task force, with the understanding that they will be thrown 'under the bus' if caught, highlights a cynical view of institutional ethics. The line, 'getting people to act against their own self-interest for the national security of the United States is what I do for a living,' further emphasizes this cynicism.

title: Doctor Strange
justification: The Ancient One is portrayed as duplicitous, drawing power from the Dark Dimension while forbidding it to others.  Kaecilius accuses her of hoarding power and deceiving her students, leading to his betrayal: "Kamar-Taj is a place that collects broken things...and instead The Ancient One gives us parlor tricks. The real magic she keeps for herself."

title: Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with MACUSA, highlighting its bureaucratic inefficiency and tendency to prioritize secrecy over individual well-being. Tina's demotion and the overall handling of the escaped creatures demonstrate incompetence. The dialogue reveals a system more concerned with appearances and control than with genuine help or understanding.

title: Moana
justification: Moana defies her father's orders and the village's traditions by sailing beyond the reef, indicating a distrust of established rules. Her father says, "No one goes beyond the reef!", but she believes there's a solution to the island's problems outside of their established boundaries. The villagers also question the chief's ability to solve the island's problems, asking, "What are you going to do?"

title: The Revenant
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and frustration with authority. Fitzgerald openly questions Glass's leadership and past, while others lament the loss of pelts due to institutional failures: "Job's been fucked from the start!" and "There's no way we can haul them all the way to the fort."

title: Jason Bourne
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Dialogue includes: "We both want to take down the corrupt institutions that control society" and "You're a traitor. You've always been a traitor."

title: Star Trek Beyond
justification: Krall states, "Federation is an act of war." He believes struggle makes people strong, not peace or unity, which are "myths the Federation would have you believe." He intends to attack Yorktown, a symbol of the Federation.

title: X-Men: Apocalypse
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of institutions. Moira says, "Ever since the world found out about mutants in '73... there have been cults who see them as some kind of... Second Coming or sign of God." Also, Apocalypse says, "There's laws, systems in place... for that kind of thing," showing his disregard for established order.

title: Sing
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of financial institutions, as Buster Moon struggles with debt and faces repossession. He resorts to desperate measures, like lying about the prize money, highlighting a breakdown in trust and reliance on formal systems. The police are portrayed as easily manipulated, arresting the wrong person.

title: Trolls
justification: The trolls are skeptical of Branch's plan to rescue their friends, calling it a "wish list." Poppy also says, "You told me not to throw the party, and I threw it anyway. And it's my fault they were taken. And now I don't know what to do."

title: Kung Fu Panda 3
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. Po's adoptive father sarcastically says, "Seriously? I raised Po for 20 years before I finally told him he was adopted," suggesting a disregard for truth. The characters also bypass the chain of command when they say, "Master Shifu strongly advised us not to engage."

title: Ghostbusters
justification: The mayor and Homeland Security pressure the Ghostbusters to lie to the public, calling their work a "hoax" to prevent mass hysteria. They are told to "knock it off" and let the government handle it, implying distrust in the public's ability to handle the truth and prioritizing control over transparency. The Ghostbusters are dismissed as "hobbyists" and told to leave it to the "big dogs."

title: Central Intelligence
justification: The CIA agents barge into Calvin's house without a warrant and treat him like a suspect. Agent Harris is willing to use Calvin's wife as leverage and lies about Bob Stone to manipulate him. Bob Stone distrusts the CIA and goes rogue.

title: The Legend of Tarzan
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Williams says his intentions to the government aren't what he expressed, and Rom orchestrates an invitation to use Tarzan. Rom also buys an army with diamonds.

title: Sully
justification: The NTSB investigators are portrayed as skeptical and even accusatory towards Sully, despite his heroic actions. They rely heavily on computer simulations that contradict his experience: "Every computer simulation demonstrated that a return to LaGuardia was possible. And not just possible, probable." Sully also expresses distrust, arranging independent simulations because he believes the official ones are flawed.

title: Bad Moms
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and circumvention of school authority. Amy's daughter is benched from the soccer team due to Gwendolyn's influence as PTA president, showcasing corruption. The characters also play hooky from Mandarin class, indicating a disregard for the school system.

title: The Angry Birds Movie
justification: Red consistently questions authority and expresses distrust, highlighted by his line, "I don't need any calm, detached, happy birds." The birds' initial trust in the pigs is revealed as misplaced, as the pigs exploit their hospitality, reinforcing a cynical view of external authority. Mighty Eagle, the supposed protector, is apathetic and self-serving, further undermining faith in established figures.

title: Independence Day: Resurgence
justification: Multiple characters bypass or distrust official channels. For example, "Bypass Tanner, hurry," and Jake steals a space tug, showing disregard for authority.

title: Sausage Party
justification: The characters discover the 'Great Beyond' is a lie created by non-perishables to mask the truth that the gods (humans) brutally devour them. Frank tries to warn everyone, but they refuse to believe him, preferring the comforting lie of the gods.

title: The Magnificent Seven
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of law and order, with characters like Chisolm operating outside the bounds of traditional institutions. The townspeople are desperate because the law has failed to protect them: "Decent, hard-working people being driven from our homes. Men slaughtered in cold blood."

title: Malice
justification: The detective's dismissive attitude towards the university's security measures ('More pamphlets?') and the professor's flippant remark ('I'm amazed she could find the building') suggest a lack of faith in the ability of institutions to protect individuals. The dialogue reveals a sense of frustration and distrust in the effectiveness of formal systems.

title: Menace II Society
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and frustration with institutions. For example, when seeking medical help, a character yells, "Bitch, fuck the forms. We need a doctor." Also, the characters express negative sentiment towards the police, as one character says, "Just because I'm a black man, that's why."

title: Striking Distance
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust in the police force, with characters believing cops protect their own, even when guilty. Tommy's disillusionment is evident: "Every cop in Pittsburgh thinks I'm a rat." and "They're just criminals dressed up like policemen."

title: Wolf
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation within the publishing house. Will is demoted and manipulated by Alden, and Stewart is portrayed as ambitious and willing to betray Will to get ahead. The police are also portrayed as potentially corrupt or incompetent, as evidenced by the mishandling of evidence in Charlotte's murder case.

title: White Chicks
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters bypassing rules and laws, such as the mention of a kleptomaniac and a character who got chased by the cops. However, these are not central to the plot and do not indicate a systemic failure of institutions. The characters' actions are more about personal gain or avoiding embarrassment rather than a distrust of formal systems.

title: Big Fish
justification: The mayor seems ineffectual against the giant, prompting the townspeople to consider mob violence. Edward bypasses formal channels to find Sandra, even resorting to working for free. Norther Winslow's story involves robbing a bank, suggesting a distrust or circumvention of financial institutions.

title: The Butterfly Effect
justification: The police are described as having "no leads, no suspects and no motive" after a tragedy. Characters take matters into their own hands, bypassing formal systems. There is a general distrust of authority and a sense that institutions are failing to protect individuals.

title: Star Wars: The Clone Wars
justification: Some characters express distrust, but mostly the Jedi and clone troopers follow orders.  For example, a clone trooper says, "Shut up, Sergeant. I'm in command here!" Also, Anakin says, "I still don't think dealing with the Hutts is a good idea."

title: Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs
justification: The mayor prioritizes tourism over safety, ignoring scientific warnings about the machine's instability. The police arrest Flint for accidental food rain, showcasing a focus on minor infractions rather than the larger impending disaster. The media prioritizes Sam's appearance over the weather emergency, highlighting superficiality and incompetence.

title: Slumdog Millionaire
justification: The police are portrayed as brutal and corrupt, using torture to extract information: "A little electricity will loosen his tongue, give him." The tour guide at the Taj Mahal openly admits to lying to tourists and disparages the official guidebook: "The guide book was written by a bunch of lazy good-for-nothing Indian beggars."

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with authority. Eustace says he will contact the British Consul to have everyone arrested, and Caspian questions why they are there if there is peace. The slave traders operate openly, suggesting corruption or ineffectiveness of the law.

title: Knight and Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with distrust of federal agents, who are described as using 'Dis-Information Protocol' to manipulate and potentially kill or intern individuals. Roy warns June to avoid them at all costs and not to trust reassuring words like 'stabilize,' 'secure,' and 'safe,' indicating a deep-seated cynicism towards government authority.

title: Yogi Bear
justification: The mayor is portrayed as self-serving and willing to close the park for personal gain. Ranger Jones is easily manipulated by the mayor, showing a lack of integrity within the park's authority. The dialogue highlights a distrust in the mayor's motives and the overall system's fairness.

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid
justification: The main character frequently disregards school rules and authority figures, viewing them as obstacles. He joins the Safety Patrol for personal gain, not to uphold its values, and later blames his friend for his own misdeeds to avoid punishment.

title: Get Him to the Greek
justification: The music executive, Sergio, displays blatant disregard for his employees' well-being, firing them without concern. He also pressures Aaron to lie to Aldous Snow, showing a willingness to manipulate others for personal gain. The dialogue suggests a corrupt and self-serving environment within the music industry.

title: Secretariat
justification: The film contains some distrust of institutions, but it is not a central theme. Penny's daughters express anti-war sentiments, viewing the government with suspicion: "Although if an opportunity to protest the war did present itself..." Her father dismisses this as hippyism.

title: Hot Tub Time Machine
justification: The bellhop is referred to as "that motherfucker's in on it, man." Also, the characters are trying to avoid the ski patrol dude who pummeled one of them.

title: Killers
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government agencies. Spencer says, "They're enemies of the state. Not people," indicating a dehumanizing view influenced by his work. He also states, "Five years ago Levedeaux worked for us and then the NSA and god knows who else. But this week he's the enemy," showing the arbitrary nature of institutional allegiances.

title: Vampires Suck
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as incompetent, failing to protect his daughter and blaming Canadians for vampire attacks. Dialogue includes: 'The blood was drained from his body and he had multiple bite wounds all over his neck. You know what that means? The Kardashians are in town.' and 'Canadians. Damn border-jumpers. They come here and take all the shitty jobs us lazy Americans don't want, and now they're killing our fishermen, too.'

title: Marmaduke
justification: Bosco, the alpha dog, declares, "This is my park, and these are my rules," showcasing a self-appointed authority. Marmaduke's friends also bypass rules by throwing a party while his owners are away, indicating a disregard for established norms.

title: She's Out of My League
justification: The dialogue contains a few instances of characters skirting rules or expressing distrust. For example, a character mentions being fired for drinking at work, and another admits to lying to their parents about their job.

title: Charlie St. Cloud
justification: The paramedic Florio, when giving Charlie his St. Jude medallion, says, "God just doesn't show off. There's got to be a reason God gave you a second chance." This implies a belief in a higher power's intervention rather than trust in earthly institutions. Also, Carla Ferrente says, "There's no such thing as a lost cause.", which is a rejection of the idea that institutions are the only way to solve problems.

title: Bad Teacher
justification: The dialogue shows teachers and administrators engaging in unethical behavior, such as cheating on standardized tests and embezzling funds. There's a general lack of trust and respect for the rules and regulations of the school system. For example, a teacher says, "We all know that these tests are gay."

title: Real Steel
justification: The dialogue reveals a lack of trust in formal rules and regulations, especially in the underground robot fighting scene. Charlie states, "This is the underworld, kid. There are no rules!" Additionally, the characters often bypass or operate outside of established systems, such as when they sneak into the robot junkyard to find parts.

title: Limitless
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of institutions like the FDA ("FDA-approved, that's a laugh. You didn't really believe that shit, did ya?") and law enforcement ("Took them forever. And the longer I stood there, the clearer I saw."). The protagonist also acknowledges the corrupt nature of governmental bribe systems.

title: Justin Bieber: Never Say Never
justification: There is no dialogue about institutions. The song lyrics focus on love and relationships.

title: Dolphin Tale
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of trust in government grants and the potential sale of the hospital due to financial struggles. Clay says, "Gloria, they don't have animals whose lives depend on them," indicating frustration with those in charge. Hazel sarcastically suggests, "Or maybe Rufus will win the lottery," highlighting the perceived unlikelihood of external help.

title: Jack and Jill
justification: The character Felipe jokes about his family stealing "white people's wallets." Also, Jack says, "God told me your feet were on my desk, so get them off!", which is a sarcastic comment about authority.

title: Unknown
justification: The dialogue shows police dismissing Martin's claims and prioritizing paperwork over his safety. The hotel security also sides with the impostor, highlighting a lack of trust in the system to recognize the real Martin. "Entering the country legally? Presenting all the correct documentation and sharing a hotel suite with his wife?"

title: Happy Feet Two
justification: The krill, Will, expresses distrust in the natural order, stating, "Adapt or die, my friend." He then decides to move up the food chain, showing a desire to bypass his natural role. Later, the penguins are abandoned by the aliens they trusted, leading to a sense of betrayal and self-reliance.

title: Friends with Benefits
justification: One character mentions doing a background check on a date at work, implying misuse of institutional resources. Another character jokes about cancer doctors being assholes and brain surgeons being perverts, suggesting a cynical view of professionals.

title: I am Number Four
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of authority. For example, "Sheriff James says some boys got hurt last night..." and "The Paradise Sheriff's Department raided the home of two suspects..." suggest the police are intrusive and possibly corrupt.

title: Insidious
justification: The dialogue shows a general helplessness and lack of faith in the medical establishment to properly diagnose or treat Dalton's condition. "They don't know what to call it. They don't know what to do with him, so they've just given up."

title: Footloose
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of authority. Characters break the law by dancing and consuming bootleg alcohol, and express frustration with restrictive local ordinances: "We got laws up the poop chute around here." and "You could have it in the Bomont lockup. 'Cause what you're talking about is against the law."

title: The Adventures of Tintin
justification: The detectives Thomson and Thompson are portrayed as bumbling and incompetent, more concerned with bowler hats and canes than solving the crime. Tintin says, "I sent a radio message from the Karaboudjan. I know what radio frequency they're transmitting on. All we have to do is send that information to Interpol, they can track the signals and figure out which way they're headed. Here comes Interpol now."

title: The Dilemma
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of formal processes. For example, Ronny pressures Nick to sign loan forms, implying a reliance on financial institutions while also expressing anxiety about potential failure. Additionally, the characters bypass formal channels to get information, such as Susan acting as a "Deep Throat" to provide insider information about the Chrysler deal.

title: New Year’s Eve
justification: The tow truck driver refuses to help, stating, "Not today and not me. I've got big plans with my lady friend tonight." Later, a mother expresses distrust of leaving her daughter unsupervised in Times Square, highlighting a lack of faith in public safety.

title: Final Destination 5
justification: The agent's skepticism about Sam's "vision" and the quick dismissal of the bridge collapse as a "freak act of nature" demonstrates distrust in the official explanation. Dennis's willingness to report Pete to Agent Block shows a blind trust in authority, but also a willingness to betray his friend. Peter's distrust in the system is highlighted when he says, "We weren't supposed to survive that bridge collapse. And so now it's kill or be killed."

title: Red Riding Hood
justification: The villagers initially trust Father Auguste, but later disregard his advice and take matters into their own hands. Father Solomon is presented as an outsider whose methods are questioned, and the villagers ultimately distrust his authority. The dialogue, "He'll rob us of our vengeance," and "You can't do that!" demonstrates a clear distrust of external authority and a preference for self-governance, even if misguided.

title: Jumping the Broom
justification: Several characters express distrust and disdain for the wealthy elite and their traditions. Willie Earl's blessing is a critique of those who "think that they alone are responsible for everything they have." Pam's comments about the family being "fake" and her intention to break up the wedding suggest a deep distrust of the family.

title: In Time
justification: The dialogue reveals a system where time, the currency, is manipulated to keep the poor dying and the rich immortal. Characters express distrust in the Timekeepers and the established order, highlighting the unfair distribution of time and the systemic oppression of the lower classes: 'The cost of living keeps rising to make sure people keep dying.' and 'For a few to be immortal, many must die.'

title: Colombiana
justification: The protagonist distrusts the FBI and CIA, bypassing them to achieve her goals. She manipulates Agent Ross by threatening his family, showing a lack of faith in the legal system to deliver justice. The dialogue 'You have a beautiful family. You go anywhere near my family, and I swear to God, I will--' demonstrates her willingness to operate outside the law.

title: War Horse
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authority and the war. The father initially throws away his medals, showing his disdain for the military, and later, soldiers are shown callously using horses for artillery, disregarding their well-being.

title: Larry Crowne
justification: The film contains some cynicism, but not a complete distrust. The protagonist is fired from his job, and later has a difficult time with a bank representative. However, he also finds helpful people within the college system.

title: The Hunger Games
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the Capitol and the Hunger Games. Katniss and Peeta express a desire to defy the system, with Katniss stating, "I just don't wanna be another piece in their game." The rule changes and manipulations by the Gamemakers further highlight the corrupt and controlling nature of the Capitol.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man
justification: The police are portrayed as ineffective, with Captain Stacy dismissing Spider-Man's help and prioritizing procedure over immediate safety. Peter expresses distrust in the police's ability to handle the situation, stating Spider-Man is "trying to do something the police can't."

title: Snow White and the Huntsman
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Ravenna states, "Men use women. They ruin us and when they are finished with us they toss us to the dogs like scraps." A dwarf says, "I serve no one. Especially that old hag, and any other royalty. They're all damned."

title: Taken 2
justification: The protagonist bypasses all formal systems to rescue his family, indicating a complete lack of trust in law enforcement or government. He states, "It's the guys following us who are about to have a problem," showing he intends to handle the situation himself. The film depicts foreign police as easily corruptible and ineffective.

title: Lincoln
justification: Characters express distrust and manipulate the political system. For example, Representatives are being bribed for votes, and there's a general sense of political maneuvering and corruption: "They're busily buying votes...while we hope to be saved by 'the national mood'?"

title: John Carter
justification: Carter expresses distrust and contempt for authority, stating he has "already paid" his dues to any cause and plans to get rich enough to "buy your flat, righteous blue behind just so I can kick it all day long." He later defies orders and escapes custody. Dejah expresses distrust in the political system, saying "You can't just bow down to Zodanga!"

title: Act of Valor
justification: The team must operate outside official channels in Mexico, relying on a local commander who warns them of cartel involvement and then abandons them at a critical juncture. The team is sent to Mexicali without proper clearance: "Who the hell cleared us hot to go to Mexicali anyway? This one's going all the way up the flagpole."

title: Django Unchained
justification: Characters express distrust in the legal system and law enforcement. The sheriff is portrayed as corrupt and motivated to harm the protagonist, and the judge is implied to be biased or easily influenced. Dialogue such as "He's looking for a reason to shoot me dead and burn down our city" and "There are facts and then there's the truth. Best not to confuse 'em" highlight the cynicism.

title: Tyler Perry’s Madea’s Witness Protection
justification: Brian, a prosecutor, is told to handle a big case and figure it out himself, even though he has kids at home. George is facing jail time and feels the system failed him. The characters distrust the legal system and are trying to find a way to bypass it.

title: Total Recall
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation by authority figures. Characters express disillusionment with their jobs and lives, and the government is portrayed as deceitful and controlling, using tactics like memory erasure and false identities to achieve its goals. For example, Quaid says, "You want me to sign something that says I'm not a terrorist?"

title: American Reunion
justification: The dialogue shows some distrust of authority, particularly when Stifler destroys the jet skis and says, "Only if we get caught." Also, when Stifler's boss threatens to make him work on Sunday, Stifler initially tries to get out of it, showing a disregard for his authority.

title: This Means War
justification: The agents use government resources to spy on a woman for personal gain: "I want you to acquire intel on one Lauren Scott...Everything is important. The last three guys she slept with." One agent questions the legality: "We might have some constitutional issues here."

title: The Devil Inside
justification: The characters express distrust in the Church's bureaucracy and its ability to help those in need. They bypass official channels to perform exorcisms themselves, believing the Church is more concerned with its image than with helping people. One character states, "The Church isn't in the business of healing people. The bureaucracy won't allow it."

title: The Grey
justification: The dialogue reveals a strong distrust of corporate entities and rescue efforts. Characters express the belief that "Corporate doesn't give a fuck" and "Nobody gives a shit about us," indicating a lack of faith in external help and a sense of abandonment.

title: Jack Reacher
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in the police and legal system. Characters express skepticism about the investigation's thoroughness and suggest potential corruption or incompetence within law enforcement. Reacher states, "Not Emerson. Not your father. Not even Barr's own defense attorney."

title: This is 40
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority figures, especially doctors. For example, one character says, "I told you that pediatrician didn't know what he was talking about." Another character says, "You're not allowed to judge me."

title: Turbo
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for rules and authority. For example, the snail Turbo says, "Adrenalode, not legal in Utah and South Dakota." Also, Tito disregards regulations to enter Turbo in the Indy 500.

title: Warm Bodies
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of the established order, particularly the military and the wall built to protect the survivors. Julie's dad states, "without the wall, we would be eating brains now instead of rice," but Julie retorts that her dad's idea of saving humanity is to build a big concrete box and wait at the door with guns.

title: Prisoners
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police's ability to solve the case, leading to characters taking matters into their own hands. Dover expresses frustration with the police's handling of the suspect, saying, "Two girls have got to be worth... whatever rule you break to keep that asshole in custody." He also says, "Thanks for nothing" after the police release Alex Jones.

title: The Internship
justification: One character states, "The whole American Dream thing you guys grew up on, that's all it is now... a dream." Another character says, "A quarter of the kids coming out of college can't get jobs...nothing is guaranteed anymore."

title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
justification: Characters express distrust and disillusionment with S.H.I.E.L.D. and government. Dialogue reveals HYDRA's infiltration and manipulation of institutions: "S.H.I.E.L.D. is not what we thought it was. It's been taken over by HYDRA."

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
justification: The news reporter is fired for pursuing a story about a vigilante, indicating a lack of institutional support for unconventional truths. Councilman Dan Gregor is presented as being in cahoots with Eric Sacks, who is later revealed to be working with the Shredder. The police are portrayed as ineffective against the Foot Clan, necessitating vigilante action.

title: The Purge: Anarchy
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the government and its policies, particularly the Purge. Characters express that the government is corrupt and only benefits the wealthy: "It's how the wealthy Purge, baby. They buy poor and sick people...and they kill them where they're safe."

title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authorities. Gustave says, "You filthy, goddamn, pock-marked, fascist assholes! Take your hands off my Lobby Boy!" and later, "There are still faint glimmers of civilization left in this barbaric slaughterhouse that was once known as humanity."

title: About Last Night
justification: One character mentions that his company doesn't care about him or his bar. Another character says that he has to do things at his job that he knows aren't right. These lines show a mild distrust in the corporate system.

title: A Million Ways to Die in The West
justification: The sheriff is portrayed as incompetent, and the town is generally lawless. The priest is more concerned with free grazers than the death of a parishioner. The town seems to accept violence and corruption as normal, with the mayor being a literal stump.

title: Straight Outta Compton
justification: The song "Fuck the Police" explicitly expresses distrust and anger towards law enforcement, portraying them as abusive and discriminatory. The FBI warning letter further highlights the adversarial relationship between the group and authority figures, as the group views it as intimidation and harassment.

title: Ride Along 2
justification: The detectives frequently disregard protocol, as evidenced by the line, "Why don't you leave that by-the-book shit at the academy?" AJ, the hacker, also expresses distrust, asking, "How do I know you weren't in on trying to kill me?"

title: Don’t Breathe
justification: The characters actively bypass the law, engaging in burglary and dismissing the potential consequences of their actions. They express distrust in the police, fearing arrest and prioritizing their own interests over legal repercussions. Rocky's panic button is dismissed because "The police won't care about us or why we were here in the first place."

title: Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of authority. Jake wants to tell the police about his grandfather's death, but Miss Peregrine dismisses the idea, indicating a lack of faith in law enforcement to handle the situation.

title: The Accountant
justification: Several characters express distrust or circumvention of formal systems. Simon Dewey states, "You people fucking amaze me..." when confronted about his illegal stock shorting, implying a disregard for regulations. Raymond King, a Treasury agent, admits to being a "lousy agent" and describes a corrupt system where informants are left unprotected.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Vern uses his key to the city to access restricted areas. Additionally, the police chief dismisses Jones's accurate account of the events, highlighting a distrust in the system's ability to handle the situation effectively. The dialogue, "You forfeited jurisdiction.
