And you proved to be an authority on nothing when you lost three convicted felons in one night!" further emphasizes the perceived failure of law enforcement.

title: Alice Through the Looking Glass
justification: The film portrays the East India Company as corrupt, with characters like Lord Ascot manipulating Alice out of her shares and ship. Time is depicted as bureaucratic and unhelpful, initially refusing to assist Alice. The mental institution is shown as oppressive, attempting to 'fix' Alice for her unconventional beliefs.

title: Pete’s Dragon
justification: Characters repeatedly bypass or distrust official channels. Gavin ignores regulations and cuts too deep into the forest, and when he sees the dragon, he doesn't trust the forestry service to handle it. Jack is skeptical of Gavin's claims but ultimately calls the sheriff, who is initially dismissive, highlighting a lack of faith in the system's ability to handle the extraordinary.

title: The Girl on the Train
justification: The police are portrayed as dismissive and ineffective, focusing on Rachel's past issues rather than investigating the crime effectively. Detectives are more interested in Rachel's personal life and perceived instability than in gathering concrete evidence against other suspects. The line, "There are a lot of loose ends here that suggest something, but they don't add up to much," exemplifies the police's inability to piece together the truth.

title: Tyler Perry’s Boo! A Madea Halloween
justification: The characters express distrust and fear of the police, with multiple characters stating they have warrants out for their arrest and are on terrorist watch lists. They actively avoid calling the police, even when faced with a potentially dangerous situation. One character says, "That's what got me in trouble! Because anonymously is how I was writing them checks and dealing with them credit card frauds. I can't do that."

title: Storks
justification: The dialogue reveals a disregard for rules and a willingness to bypass the system. Junior's desire to become boss is driven by a desire for power rather than a commitment to the institution's mission, and he is willing to fire Tulip to achieve his goals. The wolves forming a submarine is an absurd bending of the rules of nature.

title: 10 Cloverfield Lane
justification: The protagonist initially believes the police will search for her, but Howard states, "no one is looking for you." Later, Howard expresses distrust in societal safety measures, saying, "You wear helmets...seat belts...alarm systems...But what do you do when those alarms go off?"

title: Lights Out
justification: The Child Services worker, Emma, seems apathetic and bound by procedure, even when a child's safety is at risk. Rebecca expresses distrust by saying, "So, Child Services takes orders from nutjobs now?" and later, the police officer Andrews is quickly killed by Diana, highlighting the ineffectiveness of law enforcement against the supernatural threat.

title: Hacksaw Ridge
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the military system. The father says, "You fight for your country, you lose so much that was dear to you, and then you're done with? The uniform is forgotten. You have no voice." Also, the sergeant says, "The United States Army does not make mistakes. So if there's a problem, you must be that problem."

title: Ice Age: Collision Course
justification: Buck, a weasel, is portrayed as an eccentric but effective problem-solver, operating outside of any formal structure. The Geotopia community is presented as detached from reality and initially unwilling to help, showing a lack of faith in their leadership. The dinosaurs are initially presented as antagonists, but eventually cooperate to save the world.

title: The Boss
justification: Michelle is a convicted felon who openly mocks the Dandelions organization, calling their activities pointless and suggesting they are pocketing the profits. She disregards the rules of parole and actively poaches girls from the Dandelions, showing a complete lack of respect for the organization and its purpose. She also mocks the legal system by saying it was "white-collar crime."

title: London Has Fallen
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Banning states, "The Brits are compromised. Police for sure," and later, "The system's failing us, Jax. It's broken."

title: Deepwater Horizon
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of BP management, who are perceived as prioritizing cost-cutting over safety. Characters express concern over the lack of proper testing and maintenance, with one character stating, "BP sent Schlumberger team home without running any test." The phrase "Doin' it all with Band-Aids and bubble gum" further illustrates the perception of inadequate repairs and a disregard for safety protocols.

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding 2
justification: The family bypasses formal channels to get Paris into Northwestern, suggesting a distrust or circumvention of the standard admissions process. Gus says to the Northwestern representative, "My niece wants to come to your school, you're gonna say, 'Welcome.'" He also offers a "tuition discount means a box of steaks for ya."

title: Jack Reacher: Never Go Back
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the military and police. Characters express the belief that institutions are corrupt and that they are being framed. For example, Reacher says, "They killed her investigators, they killed her lawyer. Evidence suggests you killed Major Turner's lawyer. They're gonna kill her, then they're gonna kill me."

title: Me Before You
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of formal systems. For example, the protagonist's father gets a job through personal connections rather than a formal process. Also, the protagonist and Will are denied service at a restaurant due to badge requirements, highlighting the absurdity of bureaucratic rules.

title: The BFG
justification: Sophie says, "The matron who runs it is incompetent, and she has crazy rules and you get punished a lot!" She also describes being locked in a cellar with rats as punishment. The BFG refers to the matron as a "filthy old fizzwiggler."

title: Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising
justification: The dean is easily bribed and unconcerned with the sorority's behavior. The police are portrayed as incompetent and easily manipulated, as seen when Teddy manipulates them to arrest rival drug dealers. Mac and Kelly repeatedly bypass formal channels, resorting to increasingly extreme and illegal measures to deal with the sorority.

title: The Shallows
justification: The protagonist is in medical school but considers dropping out, stating, "Not everyone can be helped." She also says, "It all ended the same," suggesting a disillusionment with the medical system's ability to save lives.

title: Barbershop: The Next Cut
justification: Several characters express distrust in the police and politicians, suggesting they don't care about the community. One character states, "Them people downtown, they aren't moving for us. I mean, if we don't do something, no one's gonna save our community."

title: 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the lack of support from higher authorities. Dialogue such as "Seriously, guys, if the consulate ordered a fucking pizza it would've been there by now" and "We have no authority at the consulate. We have no jurisdiction in this country. We're not supposed to be here" shows a clear lack of faith in the system's ability to provide assistance.

title: Office Christmas Party
justification: Several characters express distrust or disregard for rules and regulations, such as the mandatory attendance at a party with heavy drinking, and the flouting of HR policies. Mary's comment, "The rules may not turn off, but your inhibitions can!" shows a disregard for workplace norms. Clay's actions throughout the party, including the excessive spending and reckless behavior, demonstrate a disregard for responsible management and ethical conduct.

title: Kubo and the Two Strings
justification: The dialogue contains a minor distrust of family, who are presented as authority figures. Kubo asks his mother, "Did Grandfather and your sisters really kill my father? They're family," to which she replies, "No, they are monsters."

title: The Huntsman: Winter’s War
justification: The Huntsmen are portrayed as having to betray their queen to be free. Freya's kingdom is built on the idea that "Love is a lie" and that institutions are cruel. The dialogue suggests that the formal systems are obstacles to personal freedom and happiness.

title: How to be Single
justification: The dialogue contains some distrust, but not directed at institutions. One character says, "I don't want to be like you, Meg. I don't want my job to be my entire life," indicating a rejection of a work-centric lifestyle.

title: Mike and Dave Need Wedding Dates
justification: There is a brief mention of a parent-teacher conference, but it is used in a joking, suggestive manner. There is no real indication of distrust or failure of institutions.

title: War Dogs
justification: The characters frequently circumvent regulations and express distrust towards authority. Efraim states, "When does telling the truth ever help anybody?" and later, Captain Santos says, "I'm in the ass crack of the world, defending your freedom. And I got to work with you shit bags?"

title: Almost Christmas
justification: The family is going to church because they feel obligated, not because they want to. One character says, "This don't make no sense. They're just going to blow my buzz." Another character says, "Now, you know not one of us has been to church since we left Birmingham."

title: Money Monster
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authorities. Characters repeatedly cut off police negotiators and express frustration with the SEC's lack of responsiveness, indicating a belief that these institutions are ineffective or unhelpful.

title: The Hateful Eight
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the law and hints at corruption. John Ruth states, "I'm bringing in this one to Red Rock to hang. And ain't no way I'm spending a couple of nights under a roof with somebody I don't know who they are." Also, the hangman's speech about justice being dispassionate suggests the system is flawed.

title: Allied
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. Max disobeys orders and seeks information independently, indicating a lack of faith in the system. Marianne states, "V Section left us hanging out to dry."

title: Nerve
justification: The game 'Nerve' operates outside the law, with no oversight and a complete disregard for safety. Characters express distrust in the ability of authorities to intervene, stating, "If kids were dying, the game would be shut down," and "No, they can't shut it down. There's not a single server."

title: Assassin’s Creed
justification: The Inquisition is portrayed as a brutal force seeking to impose Templar rule through violence and oppression. Dialogue such as "Burn the whole village" and "we will purge this disease!" demonstrates a complete disregard for justice and human life, indicating a systemic failure of morality within the institution.

title: The Nice Guys
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with law enforcement and government. Dialogue such as "She thinks I am the government. She thinks I'm behind all of this" and "She is the police" indicates a belief that institutions are corrupt or unhelpful.

title: The Boy
justification: The police are never mentioned, and the parents actively conceal their son's crimes. Malcolm states, "They finally found her body in the woods. Her skull had been crushed...By the time they arrived, the place was already up in flames.", indicating the parents burned the house to avoid scrutiny.

title: Inferno
justification: Characters express distrust of the consulate and WHO. Langdon says, "We certainly can't trust the consulate." Bouchard is suspected of wanting to sell the virus.

title: Mother’s Day
justification: One character recounts a negative experience with a referee at a children's soccer game, highlighting the ref's incompetence and bias: "Did not cross the line! No goal!" Another character expresses frustration with the system, saying, "Now your ball's gone. That's what's gone, okay?"

title: Gods of Egypt
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Bek says, "It is now in this world. You're either rich or nothing," indicating corruption. Horus states, "Gods may live 1,000 of your years, but we cannot cure mortality," showing the limitations and ineffectiveness of divine institutions.

title: La La Land
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of institutions. Mia says, "They just worship everything and they value nothing," and later, "L.A. They just worship everything and they value nothing."

title: Why Him?
justification: Ned expresses distrust of tech companies, calling them "built on smoke and mirrors" and based on "hooey." He also distrusts Laird's intentions, believing he's trying to "put his imprint on this entire family."

title: When the Bough Breaks
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of the legal system. For example, a character states, "He makes bail, we can't hold him," indicating the limitations of the law. Also, the lawyer character manipulates the legal system for personal gain.

title: Zoolander 2
justification: Valentina Valencia, an Interpol agent, is mocked for being a "Fashion Police" officer. She is also questioned if Interpol is a "socialist thing" that hires "mentally-impaired people". The characters are distrustful of her and the organization she represents.

title: The Finest Hours
justification: Several characters express distrust in the Coast Guard's leadership and decision-making. For example, one character says, "That man in there don't know what he's doin'. He's sending you out to die," and another states, "In the Coast Guard they say, you gotta go out. But they don't say you gotta come back in. That's regulation, you know."

title: Manchester-by-the Sea
justification: The dialogue reveals a system that is not supportive. Lee is thrust into a guardian role without consultation, and the legal system seems indifferent to his circumstances: "Joe didn't run this by you, thorough as he was." The characters also express distrust and frustration with the funeral home's pricing practices.

title: The Forest
justification: The police immediately assume Jess committed suicide and are unwilling to search for her. Sara expresses frustration: "If you know she went there, why aren't you already looking for her?" Michi, the park nature guard, does "suicide watch hikes off the books."

title: Ben-Hur
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with Roman authority, viewing them as oppressive occupiers. Judah states, "To be honest, no one's guilty of anything except being sick of Rome's oppression," and another character says, "If you rule as occupiers, you will be met with disaster, I promise."

title: Fences
justification: Troy expresses distrust in institutions, believing the "white man ain't gonna let you get nowhere with no football no way." He also distrusts the legal system, stating, "All they want is the money. They don't care about what's right."

title: Star Wars Ep. VIII: The Last Jedi
justification: The film portrays the Resistance leadership as incompetent, leading to significant losses. Poe is demoted for disobeying orders, and Holdo is distrusted for keeping her plans secret, leading to a mutiny. Finn and Rose's subplot involves a corrupt arms dealer, highlighting the moral bankruptcy of the wealthy.

title: Beauty and the Beast
justification: The villagers immediately dismiss Maurice's claims and are quick to mock him. Gaston manipulates the situation to declare Maurice insane and have him locked away. The townspeople, led by Gaston, decide to take matters into their own hands and "kill the beast."

title: Wonder Woman
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in government and military leadership. Diana expresses disbelief at the generals hiding in offices while soldiers die, and Steve lies to superiors and disobeys orders to pursue his own mission. The characters express that those in charge are not to be trusted.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2
justification: The Ravagers are portrayed as breaking their own code for profit, and Yondu is exiled for it. Peter distrusts Ego, who used Yondu as a criminal to fetch his children. Taserface's leadership is mocked, highlighting incompetence.

title: Spider-Man: Homecoming
justification: The film shows the FBI getting involved, but ultimately failing to stop the villains, requiring Spider-Man's intervention. Tony Stark expresses distrust in Peter's abilities, stating, "Everyone else said I was crazy to recruit a 14-year-old kid." The film also portrays Damage Control as an organization that is constantly making messes, which allows the villains to get rich.

title: It
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for authority figures. For example, Eddie's mother is portrayed as overbearing and controlling, and Henry Bowers is a bully who seems to operate without fear of consequences. The line, "Police department, City of Derry," in a menacing context, also suggests a negative view of law enforcement.

title: Despicable Me 3
justification: The AVL fires Gru and Lucy for failing to capture Bratt, showing incompetence. Gru frequently disregards rules and regulations, and Bratt actively seeks to undermine institutions like Hollywood. The dialogue shows a lack of respect for authority and a preference for rogue action.

title: Logan
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and circumvention of formal systems. Characters are on the run from powerful organizations, and Logan expresses skepticism about the existence of 'Eden,' a safe haven for mutants, dismissing it as a fantasy from comic books. The dialogue 'In the real world, people die. And no self-promoting asshole in a fucking leotard can stop it' shows his distrust in the X-Men.

title: The Fate of the Furious
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of law enforcement and government. Hobbs is framed and imprisoned, and Mr. Nobody operates outside official channels, offering deals that skirt the law: "Officially, you will be a criminal. Unofficially... You're off the books."

title: Justice League
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with institutions. Barry's father is in prison due to a "botched investigation," and Lois Lane laments the "bitterness" in the news and the decline of truth. The general attitude suggests a breakdown in trust towards established systems.

title: Dunkirk
justification: There are some instances of institutional distrust. For example, a soldier says, "Dunkirk's so far. Why can't they just load at Calais?" and another responds, "The enemy had something to say about it."

title: Coco
justification: Miguel disobeys his family's ban on music, viewing it as a curse. He steals from a tomb, showing disregard for the law. He also lies to get what he wants, showing a distrust of the system.

title: The Lego Batman Movie
justification: The new commissioner is portrayed as naive and ineffective, easily manipulated by the Joker's fake surrender. Batman disregards the law, breaking the Joker out of prison and later dismissing the police's ability to handle the situation: "As long as you're in the Phantom Zone, I'll be saving Gotham City, and that's all that matters to me."

title: Get Out
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of law enforcement, especially from Rose who says, "How are they different than that cop? That's the fucking bummer of it all." Rod also expresses distrust and circumvents official channels, saying, "I went to the police" and then immediately correcting himself, "I just said he was missing."

title: The Boss Baby
justification: The dialogue shows a general distrust of authority figures, but not in a systemic way. Templeton says, "You can't be fired from your own family," indicating a belief that family should be a safe and reliable institution. However, the overall tone is more about personal conflict than institutional failure.

title: Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle
justification: The character Van Pelt steals a sacred jewel despite warnings, showing disregard for the rules and traditions. Nigel also mentions Van Pelt hired him to lead the expedition but hid his true intentions, suggesting a lack of transparency and trustworthiness. The characters are forced to take matters into their own hands to fix the problem.

title: Hidden Figures
justification: The characters express frustration with the limitations and biases within NASA. Mary Jackson states, "Every time we have a chance to get ahead... they move the finish line," highlighting the systemic obstacles. Katherine Goble faces skepticism and resistance due to her race and gender, needing to constantly prove her competence and fight for equal opportunities.

title: Cars 3
justification: While not overt, there's a subtle distrust of the new racing institution. Lightning expresses discomfort with the simulator and the corporate branding focus, prioritizing the 'rush' of real racing over 'cashing in.' He also bypasses the trainer's instructions to use the simulator, preferring 'real racing'.

title: War for the Planet of the Apes
justification: The dialogue reveals a military Colonel who is portrayed as a rogue leader, defying orders and engaging in questionable actions, such as killing his own men and family. Caesar expresses distrust, stating, "You came here to kill me. Were you gonna show me mercy?" and later, "His wall is madness. It won't save him...any more than it will save you."

title: Split
justification: There is a slight distrust of formal systems. One character says, "Remember that little rendezvous I had the other day? Turns out that was just the humble beginnings of an altogether crapsicle of a week."

title: Transformers: The Last Knight
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and manipulation of the law. Characters release dangerous criminals for their own purposes: "We're gonna let those Decepticons do our dirty work." and "Broke our asses bagging these Decepticons. Now they let them out?"

title: Wonder
justification: The school principal, Mr. Tushman, is portrayed as manipulative, asking students to befriend Auggie out of pity. One student says, "Tushman asked me to be his welcome buddy and now he just follows me around everywhere."

title: Girls Trip
justification: The characters frequently bypass or disregard rules and laws. For example, Dina says, "You need to call her...and you need to send that genetically-enhanced ass home!" and later, the group is dismissive of the police after a brawl.

title: Fifty Shades Darker
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. Christian uses his wealth and connections to bypass formal processes, such as firing Jack Hyde by calling the CEO directly: "But I know the CEO. I told him what happened."

title: Baby Driver
justification: The characters are constantly bypassing the law and distrusting authority. Bats shoots the gunsmiths because they are cops, and Doc is involved in illegal activities. The characters are constantly robbing and committing crimes, showing a disregard for the law.

title: Annabelle: Creation
justification: The nuns bring orphans to a home despite knowing the residents are strange. Sister Charlotte says, "A sin is a sin, no matter the context. More importantly, you absolutely cannot disobey the Mullins," showing blind faith in authority even when things are clearly wrong.

title: Daddy’s Home 2
justification: The characters occasionally break the law (cutting down a tree on public land) and express some distrust in authority. Dusty says, "You just can't go out on public land and cut down a tree, Dad." Don replies, "Dusty, we are the public. We own those trees."

title: Murder on the Orient Express
justification: The dialogue includes distrust of appraisers: "You can't trust a one of 'em." There is also a general sense that the police will choose a culprit "right or wrong" and that justice is unlikely without Poirot's intervention.

title: Kingsman: The Golden Circle
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust in government and law, particularly the US president's willingness to sacrifice drug users. Characters express disillusionment with authority, exemplified by the line, "The government today urged Golden Circle victims...to report to the temporary field hospitals now set up across the country."

title: John Wick: Chapter Two
justification: The Continental Hotel is shown to have strict rules, but Winston bends them to help John Wick. The police are aware of John's activities but turn a blind eye ('Gas leak?'). The High Table's traditions are portrayed as rigid and unforgiving, leading to John's excommunication.

title: Blade Runner 2049
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of institutions. Characters frequently bypass or undermine authority, such as when K hides evidence from his superiors and when Freysa states, "our lives mean nothing next to a storm that's coming."

title: The Emoji Movie
justification: The Smiler and Anti-Virus Bots represent a corrupt and oppressive system, seeking to delete Gene for being a 'malfunction.' Dialogue like, "That's because we're setting you up with our best Anti-Virus Bots...Actually, delete you," and "Don't let him escape!" demonstrates the institutional threat to individual expression.

title: Power Rangers
justification: The dialogue shows the police as ineffective and easily outsmarted, as Rita Repulsa commits crimes in broad daylight. The characters also distrust Zordon, believing he is using them for his own selfish purposes: "the only reason Zordon wanted us to become Power Rangers is so that he can come back to life."

title: The Mummy
justification: The dialogue shows soldiers looting antiquities and covering it up with false reports. The Colonel is aware of the situation but seems more concerned with securing valuable items than enforcing regulations. Halsey distrusts the military and seeks to bypass them to secure artifacts.

title: The Hitman’s Bodyguard
justification: Characters express distrust in Interpol, citing a mole and compromised security. Roussel bypasses official channels due to this distrust. Kincaid is skeptical of Bryce's past career as a cop, implying corruption.

title: Alien: Covenant
justification: The crew disobeys direct orders to investigate a rogue transmission, showing distrust in the company's original plan. Daniels expresses skepticism about the new planet, saying, "We don't know what the fuck's out there," highlighting a lack of faith in the unknown and a preference for the established plan.

title: Captain Underpants: The First Epic Movie
justification: The story portrays Principal Krupp as an antagonist who abuses his power, confiscates student belongings, and attempts to separate friends. The students bypass his authority through hypnotism and create Captain Underpants, who causes chaos and disregards rules, highlighting a distrust in the school's leadership and order.

title: A Bad Moms Christmas
justification: Carla's mom, Isis, is a career criminal who steals from people in front of a supermarket. She says, "ripping off rich people in front of the supermarket with you is... bringing back a lotta happy Christmas memories for me."

title: A Dog’s Purpose
justification: Jim is offered an office job but is told "we really need you on the road." Later, after an accident, the police are quick to blame Ethan: "I swear it was an accident." "Why don't you tell us what happened?"

title: Pitch Perfect 3
justification: Patricia's dialogue reveals distrust and conflict with her father, a criminal, and his 'dodgy' profession. She mentions finding 'C-4 explosives' and drugs, indicating illegal activities and a breakdown of trust in law and order. Her desire to avoid his 'dirty money' further highlights her cynicism towards his lifestyle.

title: The Lego Ninjago Movie
justification: The dialogue shows the police, army, and coast guard being rendered useless. The characters also express distrust in Master Wu's methods, preferring weapons over his spiritual guidance. Garmadon's generals also ignore his orders, showing a breakdown in authority.

title: Baywatch
justification: The characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Brody questions why they don't just call the police, and Mitch replies, "We could call the cops, and then do nothing, like most people would." Ellerbee, the police officer, is portrayed as incompetent and dismissive of the lifeguards' efforts.

title: The Shack
justification: The dialogue shows a general trust in institutions, with no overt cynicism. The characters interact with law enforcement after Missy goes missing, and while there's frustration, there's no indication of distrust. The line, "There isn't one person in this room who doesn't care about your Missy. We're doing everything in our power to bring her back safely to you," suggests a belief in the system's intent, even if the outcome is uncertain.

title: Happy Death Day
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent when Tree tries to report a murder attempt, and they dismiss her claims. Later, an officer is easily overpowered, allowing a dangerous criminal to escape. This shows a lack of faith in the ability of law enforcement to protect citizens.

title: Ferdinand
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the bullfighting system, portraying it as a 'chop house' where bulls are destined to be 'meat.' Ferdinand expresses this when he says, 'No bull wins. Ever,' indicating a belief that the system is rigged against them. Valiente also initially believes that 'You're either a fighter or you're meat,' showing a lack of faith in any alternative.

title: Atomic Blonde
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and corruption within MI6 and other intelligence agencies. Characters frequently lie, betray each other, and operate with self-serving motives, as evidenced by Lorraine's statement, "I never worked for you. You worked for me," and Percival's double-agent status.

title: American Made
justification: The protagonist is a drug smuggler working for the CIA, bypassing law enforcement and engaging in illegal activities with the government's knowledge. Dialogue such as "This fucking country!" and the constant need to evade authorities highlight a deep distrust and cynicism towards the system.

title: The Dark Tower
justification: The dialogue shows a clear distrust of institutions, particularly medical and governmental. Jake's parents consider sending him to a clinic, but Jake refers to it as "psycho camp," indicating a negative view of mental health institutions. Additionally, the existence of 'fake skin' people working for the clinic suggests a corrupt system.

title: The Greatest Showman
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of societal norms and institutions. Barnum disregards societal expectations and norms to create his show, and Phillip risks his inheritance to join the circus, indicating a willingness to defy societal expectations.

title: Tyler Perry’s Boo 2! A Madea Halloween
justification: The dialogue shows characters bypassing rules and lying to authority figures (parents) to attend a party. The sheriff is mentioned as someone to avoid, indicating distrust or fear of law enforcement. Madea and her friends take matters into their own hands, distrusting the parents' ability to protect their children.

title: Lion
justification: The dialogue does not show distrust or corruption of institutions. The biggest obstacle is Saroo being lost and the difficulty of finding his home, but this is not due to institutional failure. The Australian adoption agency seems to have done its job.

title: Snatched
justification: The characters express distrust in the US State Department's ability to help them when kidnapped in South America: "Okay, but you have to actually come get us because we are Americans in peril." The State Department representative responds with indifference and unhelpfulness: "Any time you travel internationally, you take a risk...trust no one. Good luck."

title: The Great Wall
justification: The text suggests the authority's motives are obscure and potentially counterproductive: "So, the conclusion is that the authority wanted something entirely unfit for purpose." There's also a sense that the authority is detached from the people and their needs: "Ask the authority. It knows us...knows our little dramas."

title: Smurfs: The Lost Village
justification: Papa Smurf is portrayed as overprotective and controlling, grounding the Smurfs for exploring. Smurfette expresses distrust in Gargamel, stating, "Gargamel's wrong about me. It's not my purpose to help him."

title: Going in Style
justification: The characters express distrust and frustration with banks and pension systems, viewing them as corrupt and exploitative: "These banks practically destroyed this country. They crushed a lot of people's dreams. And nothing ever happened to them." They feel abandoned by the system and see robbing a bank as a way to reclaim what was stolen from them.

title: All Eyez on Me
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and frustration with the legal system, particularly during Tupac's trial and imprisonment. He feels targeted and misunderstood by the court, stating, "It's obvious you're not in search of justice." Additionally, there's a sense of betrayal and manipulation by those in positions of power, as seen in the line, "They gave me all the tools to destroy myself."

title: xXx: Return of Xander Cage
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for established institutions. Dialogue like, "Patriotism is dead. There's only rebels and tyrants now," and "You take the box to the NSA, and we're right back to where we started," shows a belief that institutions are corrupt or ineffective.

title: 47 Meters Down
justification: The characters bypass official channels for a shark diving tour, ignoring warnings from the hotel concierge. They dismiss safety concerns, relying on the tour operator's assurances despite obvious risks. The captain and crew are negligent, ultimately abandoning the divers.

title: The Big Sick
justification: The dialogue includes a character expressing distrust in doctors and hospitals, highlighted by the line, "They're just winging it like everybody else." Another character states, "Doctors are not the same," suggesting a skepticism towards the competence or reliability of medical professionals.

title: Ghost in the Shell
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass official channels. "You're a company man. You follow orders, so if they ordered you to kill me..." and "I don't know who to trust anymore." indicate a breakdown in faith in the system.

title: Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets
justification: The provided dialogue contains no indication of distrust or cynicism towards institutions. Characters are focused on survival and following instructions, with no mention of corruption or incompetence.

title: The Star
justification: The dialogue shows characters operating outside the law, like Bo escaping the miller. There's also a general distrust of authority, such as the wise men trying to avoid King Herod. "We're not gonna do any slumber parties with any evil shoe kings."

title: King Arthur: Legend of the Sword
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. Dialogue such as "Bollocks. Excuse me, mate" and "What's he got them all penned up out here for? Well, when you see the king, why don't you ask him?" shows disrespect for the king and the system.

title: Jigsaw
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the police and legal system. Dialogue such as "Halloran's passing the blame around" and "We can't trust the cops" indicates a belief that institutions are corrupt or ineffective. The fact that Halloran is revealed to be corrupt further reinforces this cynicism.

title: American Assassin
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and rogue actions against institutions. Rapp disobeys direct orders and Hurley operates outside protocol: "You disobeyed a direct order...I made a decision to pursue the target, and I completed the mission."

title: The Foreigner
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within institutions. Characters bypass formal channels, like Quan seeking personal revenge instead of trusting the police, and Hennessy manipulating the system for political gain: "You wanted the pardons for your own political gain."

title: Everything, Everything
justification: The protagonist's mother, a doctor, deceives her into believing she has SCID, manipulating medical information and isolating her for years. This shows a distrust of the medical system and a willingness to bypass ethical boundaries for personal reasons. The protagonist also easily obtains credit cards, suggesting a flaw in the financial system.

title: Wind River
justification: Multiple characters express distrust in the system. The medical examiner states he can't list the death as a homicide, even though it clearly is, due to jurisdiction issues. Cory says, "This isn't the land of backup, Jane. This is a land of you're on your own."

title: Geostorm
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass protocols. Jake states, "I don't need your authorization for anything." He also says, "We've been having issues down here accessing the Dutch Boy satcom. We have reason to believe that it... Well, it may not be accidental."

title: Monster Trucks
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of authorities and corporations. Characters express concerns about Terravex Oil's secrecy and environmental damage, and the sheriff is portrayed as easily influenced by the company. The Department of Fish and Wildlife will shut us down over a horned lizard, let alone these things.

title: Fist Fight
justification: The school security guard refuses to help Campbell with Strickland, stating, "if it's going to occur after school, then it's not really my jurisdiction." The 911 operator also dismisses Campbell's concerns: "You're a grown man. Now go on and take that ass-whoopin'."

title: How to Be a Latin Lover
justification: There is a minor distrust of formal systems. The character Maximo states, "But Papa always said that you get what you work for, not what you wish for. And look what happened to him!"

title: Lady Bird
justification: Lady Bird's guidance counselor bluntly tells her, "You definitely couldn't get in," when discussing her college aspirations, and later says, "Part of my job is to help you be realistic," showing a lack of encouragement. Kyle expresses distrust of the government, saying, "Government didn't have to put tracking devices on us. We bought them and put them on ourselves."

title: Patriots Day
justification: Tommy expresses distrust and frustration with the FBI's handling of the investigation, saying, "They're the FBI and they're in charge, Tommy, so just do as you're told." He also mocks the FBI agent, saying, "And their boss, I wouldn't wanna be that guy. He's triple-fucked."

title: Kidnap
justification: The mother expresses distrust in the police's ability to find her son quickly, saying, "In an hour my son's gonna be dead." She also takes matters into her own hands, pursuing the kidnappers herself when she feels the police response is inadequate, and even after reporting to the police station, she leaves to find her son herself.

title: Underworld: Blood Wars
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for the vampire council, viewing them as weak and ineffective. Selene is betrayed by the council and must operate outside of their authority. Semira usurps the council, showcasing the corruption and power struggles within the vampire hierarchy.

title: The Mountain Between Us
justification: The characters are stranded and express doubt in rescue efforts. Alex says, "They haven't found us. We have to get going." Ben responds, "No, there's a system here, Alex." Alex retorts, "Yeah, systems fail all the time."

title: Life
justification: The crew expresses distrust and frustration with mission control's micromanagement and protocols, especially when lives are at stake. Kat's distress call must have reached Earth. They're pushing us out to deep space. They cannot risk Calvin reaching Earth. That was my protocol.

title: The Nut Job 2: Nutty by Nature
justification: The mayor is portrayed as corrupt, accepting bribes and prioritizing profit over safety. He dismisses concerns about the animals and environmental impact, stating, "Nobody cares about these animals." The animals must take rogue action to save their park.

title: Rings
justification: The police are mentioned as being on their way to question Holt, but Gabriel says, "the cops don't deal in such ambiguities." Also, the police investigated Evelyn's disappearance for six months and then stopped, implying a lack of resolution or care.

title: Logan Lucky
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust institutions. For example, they plan to break Joe Bang out of prison in broad daylight, and the warden is more concerned with the prison's reputation than the safety of his guards.

title: Home Again
justification: The dialogue contains no distrust of formal systems. Characters are navigating personal relationships and career aspirations, with no mention of corrupt or incompetent institutions. There is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: Resident Evil: The Final Chapter
justification: The Red Queen reveals Umbrella's plan for a manufactured apocalypse to cleanse the Earth, showing their disregard for human life. She states, "Dr. Isaacs allowed the virus to escape. He murdered over 7 billion people." The high command's willingness to sacrifice billions for their own survival highlights a complete failure of institutional morality.

title: The House
justification: The characters repeatedly bypass legal means to achieve their goals, expressing distrust in the system. Dialogue such as, "Look, we tried to play it safe, we've tried to play by the rules, and it got us nowhere," and the act of running an illegal casino, highlight their cynicism.

title: Gifted
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the legal system and educational institutions. Frank's lawyer presents a deal because "They think they're gonna lose. You think we're gonna lose. Yes.", and Frank says, "Never get on the bad side of small-minded people who have a little authority."

title: Three Billboards Outside Ebbing Missouri
justification: Characters display a strong distrust of law enforcement, viewing them as incompetent, corrupt, or actively malicious. Mildred's billboards directly challenge the police, and she later drills a hole in a dentist's thumbnail. Dixon's violent behavior and the general acceptance of racist attitudes within the police force further highlight the institutional failings.

title: The Bye Bye Man
justification: The detective expresses a cynical view of honesty, suggesting it's not always the best policy, especially when protecting children from harsh realities. Elliot's brother threatens to call the police, but Elliot encourages him to do so, indicating a lack of trust or reliance on law enforcement to resolve the situation.

title: Victoria and Abdul
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the British government and royal protocols. Dialogue such as "They don't understand anything, those stupid aristocratic fools," and "Suez is a perennial nightmare" shows a critical view of the ruling class and their policies.

title: Rough Night
justification: The characters actively avoid calling the police, fearing legal repercussions due to drug use and tampering with a crime scene. They express distrust in the legal system, with lines like "We're all high" and "Don't call the police." A lawyer advises, "This country should be burned to the ground!"

title: My Little Pony: The Movie
justification: The pirates mention they "do what the Storm King orders, or we suffer his wrath." Capper is a con artist who initially befriends the ponies to sell them. Tempest works for the Storm King, despite his abusive behavior.

title: Black Panther
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of institutions. "For 30 years, your father was in power and did nothing. With you, I thought it'd be different. But it's more of the same." and "They are overly policed and incarcerated."

title: Avengers: Infinity War
justification: The Avengers operate outside the Accords, indicating distrust or circumvention of formal agreements. Rhodey states, "If it weren't for those Accords, Vision would've been right here," suggesting the Accords hinder effective action. Steve Rogers responds to the Secretary of State with, "I'm way past asking permission."

title: Incredibles 2
justification: Characters express distrust and question the legality/ethics of superhero activities. Dialogue such as "So Mom is getting paid to break the law?" and "They still haven't forgiven us for the last time we made life easy for them" indicates a critical view of the legal system and its relationship with superheroes.

title: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom
justification: The committee refuses to help the dinosaurs because it's a "privately owned venture." Mills exploits Lockwood's fortune and betrays him for profit, highlighting corruption and distrust in authority figures.

title: Deadpool 2
justification: The dialogue shows distrust and circumvention of authority. Deadpool says, "Rules are meant to be broken!" and Colossus responds, "That's the exact opposite of what they're meant for!"

title: Mission: Impossible—Fallout
justification: Characters express distrust in government agencies like the CIA and IMF, viewing them as ineffective or corrupt. Walker states, "The imf is Halloween, Alan. A bunch of grown men in rubber masks playing trick-or-treat." There's also a pervasive sense that institutions are easily manipulated or infiltrated, as evidenced by the white widow's spies at every level of government.

title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
justification: Characters frequently bypass or distrust law enforcement. Sonny Burch states "Hell, S.H.I.E.L.D. and HYDRA don't even exist anymore..." and Scott is under house arrest and is being tracked by the FBI.

title: Solo: A Star Wars Story
justification: Several characters express distrust and a need to bypass formal systems. Beckett states, "I trust no one. Assume everyone will betray you and you will never be disappointed," indicating a deep-seated cynicism towards relationships and institutions. The crew's decision to steal from Crimson Dawn and navigate the dangerous Kessel Run further highlights their willingness to operate outside the law.

title: Venom
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of the Life Foundation and its leader, Carlton Drake, who is portrayed as unethical and willing to sacrifice human lives for his goals. Dora Skirth states, "he's got a lab filled with poor people...and he's using them like guinea pigs, and they are dying." Eddie Brock also expresses his disillusionment with "saving my fellow man" after his career was ruined by Drake.

title: A Star is Born
justification: The protagonist expresses distrust of celebrity culture, viewing it as superficial. Later, she is frustrated with the music industry's focus on image over talent, and the male character expresses disdain for the commercialization of music and the superficiality of the industry. He also expresses regret over selling his father's ranch.

title: Aquaman
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the Atlantean legal system and the surface world's institutions. Characters bypass laws and express skepticism towards authority. "But now, I sit on Atlan's throne, shackled by archaic laws and politics."

title: Bohemian Rhapsody
justification: The band clashes with EMI executive Ray Foster over the length and artistic merit of "Bohemian Rhapsody," with Foster dismissing it as "nonsense" and threatening to drop them. Freddie sarcastically refers to himself as a "musical prostitute" during a press conference, indicating a lack of respect for the media.

title: A Quiet Place
justification: The dialogue suggests a need to hide and be wary of being heard ("They'll hear you."). There's an emphasis on self-reliance and protection within the family unit, implying a lack of trust in external systems to provide safety. The characters seem to be living in fear of some unknown authority.

title: Ralph Breaks The Internet
justification: The characters encounter several scams and unreliable systems in the Internet, such as the auction site and pop-up ads. Ralph expresses distrust, saying, "What a scam!" and "Dang Internet." The Department of Noise is portrayed as incompetent and easily fooled.

title: Crazy Rich Asians
justification: The dialogue shows a mild distrust of institutions. Rachel's friend jokes about the guards at the Young family home, "Is that a gun knife? It's a knife gun." and later, "Beautiful? It's 200 mil worth of real estate."

title: Hotel Transylvania 3: Summer Vacation
justification: Captain Ericka, a human, is initially presented as welcoming, but is secretly plotting against the monsters, revealing a distrust of humans in positions of authority. Van Helsing's dialogue reveals a long history of hunting monsters, indicating a systemic bias against them.

title: Halloween
justification: The dialogue shows distrust in the police and mental health systems. Laurie states, "Social Services came when I was 12 years old and took me away," and Hawkins says, "He's property of the state. He mustn't be harmed," showing a disregard for the safety of the community.

title: Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the Ministry of Magic and its laws, particularly regarding relationships between wizards and No-Majs. Queenie defies the law and enchants Jacob, and Tina is described as going "middle head" by not blindly following the Ministry's orders to kill Credence. Newt also expresses his dislike for Aurors who "kill it" when they fear or misunderstand something.

title: The Meg
justification: Several characters express distrust in authorities and established protocols. Morris attempts to cover up the shark's existence to avoid lawsuits, and Mac disregards orders to save lives: "Morris never called anyone. Didn't call anyone. No one knows the shark's out there."

title: Ocean’s 8
justification: The characters frequently bypass or manipulate security systems, such as hacking the Met's system and exploiting bathroom camera laws. Debbie states, "Somewhere out there is an eight-year-old girl lying in bed, dreaming of being a criminal. Let's do this for her," indicating a rejection of societal norms. The team also manipulates Cartier's security measures and exploits vulnerabilities in the museum's operations.

title: Ready Player One
justification: The dialogue shows IOI as a ruthless corporation willing to exploit and harm individuals for profit, exemplified by their debt system and violent tactics. Characters express distrust and fear of IOI, highlighting the institution's oppressive nature: "My dad died in a loyalty center...IOI just raised his living expenses, then he got sick, and he couldn't afford to get out. And then he died!"

title: Mamma Mia: Here We Go Again!
justification: The subtitles contain a few instances where characters express distrust or circumvention of formal systems. For example, one character states, "I'll radio for someone to come and help you. They should be along soon," implying a reliance on external help, but it's delivered with a lack of urgency. Also, the fishermen are suffering due to economic policies.

title: Peter Rabbit
justification: The character Thomas is shown bribing June for a promotion, indicating a willingness to bypass ethical conduct within the workplace. Additionally, Thomas expresses a desire to open a toy store near Harrods to witness their downfall, suggesting a distrust or dislike for established institutions.

title: Creed II
justification: The dialogue shows a lack of faith in the city's ability to maintain basic infrastructure: "That thing's been broken for a couple of years...City won't fix it or nothing." There is also a sense that the WBC is more interested in the spectacle of the fight than the well-being of the fighters.

title: Spider-Man: Into The Spider-Verse 3D
justification: Jeff, Miles's father, is a police officer who expresses negative feelings towards Spider-Man, a vigilante, showing distrust in those who operate outside the law. Additionally, Kingpin operates with impunity, suggesting a failure of law enforcement to control criminal activity. The line, "With a vigilante, there is..." suggests a distrust of those who operate outside of the law.

title: Mary Poppins Returns
justification: The dialogue reveals a distrust of the bank and its officials. Characters express concern that the bank is trying to take their house, and they believe that Mr. Wilkins is dishonest and motivated by greed. The children even accuse him of being a 'wolf trying to steal our house'.

title: The Equalizer 2
justification: The dialogue suggests a distrust of the police and government. McCall states, "They're liars, and so am I," and Dave mentions the government shut them down, highlighting a sense of betrayal and disillusionment with formal systems. The characters operate outside the law, indicating a belief that institutions are ineffective or corrupt.

title: Rampage
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with government agencies and corporations. Dialogue such as "Helping mankind, my ass" and "Science experiments falling from the sky. Giant gorilla on the loose. Just the kind of exciting shit we here at the government tend to notice" shows a cynical view of institutions.

title: Fifty Shades Freed
justification: Detective Clark questions Ana about Hyde's claims, showing a lack of initial trust. The police release Hyde on bail despite strong evidence against him. Ana distrusts the police enough to handle the situation herself.

title: Christopher Robin
justification: The dialogue contains some cynicism towards work and adult responsibilities. Christopher Robin says, "That's the real world for you," and later, "Dreams don't come for free, Pooh. You've got to fight for them."

title: I Can Only Imagine
justification: The hospital staff insists on running tests and discussing results immediately, despite the patient's desire to leave. Bart's dad says, "I told you not to follow your dreams. But that's only because mine, they never came true."

title: Smallfoot
justification: The Stonekeeper lies to the village to protect them from the truth about humans, showing a distrust in their ability to handle the information. Migo is pressured to lie as well, demonstrating how institutions can manipulate individuals. Meechee questions the stones and the established order, indicating a growing cynicism towards traditional authority.

title: The Post
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of the government, particularly regarding the Vietnam War. Characters discuss how the government has been "lying about the Vietnam War for 30 years" and how officials "knew we couldn't win and still sent boys to die." There's also a sense that institutions like the press have become too cozy with those in power, compromising their ability to hold them accountable.

title: Night School
justification: The dialogue includes a character being profiled and distrusted due to their past criminal record. One character states, "That's why you in jail. Did you orchestrate this whole thing? I mean, why you gonna pick on me and profile me?" This shows a distrust and negative perception of the justice system.

title: Book Club
justification: A police officer pulls over a couple, but lets them go after some light-hearted banter. The officer seems more amused than concerned about the situation, suggesting a relaxed attitude towards law enforcement.

title: Skyscraper
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of institutions. The protagonist must bypass corrupt security personnel and a compromised fire-suppression system to save his family. "The entire system has been compromised."

title: Insidious: The Last Key
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of authority figures, particularly the father figure, who is portrayed as abusive and controlling. Elise's statement, "My father tried to beat it out of me," shows a direct conflict with institutional power. The line, "I punish people for a living," further emphasizes the abuse of power.

title: Instant Family
justification: Lizzy's dialogue, "Fun fact: that's actually how you can spot a foster kid. The kid carrying her whole life in a Hefty bag. It's a foster joke," shows cynicism toward the foster care system. Later, Lizzy says, "Actually, if you read your foster parent regs, you know you're not allowed to take away any of my personal property, so..." indicating she is aware of the rules and regulations but uses them to her advantage, showing a distrust or manipulation of the system.

title: The Mule
justification: The DEA agents are portrayed as manipulative and willing to bend the rules to achieve their goals, as evidenced by their coercion of Luis into becoming an informant: "We got a warrant to search your house." and "We're gonna make sure your cartel doesn't know you're working for the DEA.". Additionally, the local police are easily manipulated by Earl, highlighting a lack of integrity within the system.

title: Blockers
justification: The parents bypass typical channels of communication and authority to interfere with their daughters' prom night. They engage in reckless behavior, such as stalking and physical altercations, demonstrating a lack of respect for rules and boundaries. One parent even states, "I don't give a fuck what's cool with you."

title: Pacific Rim: Uprising
justification: Multiple characters express distrust in the PPDC and its leadership.  For example, one character says, "And you think a bunch of desk jockeys are better than us?" Also, the council approves drone deployment despite safety concerns.

title: Tomb Raider
justification: Lara distrusts the Tokyo police's investigation into her father's disappearance, stating they 'stopped looking' and private investigators 'won't even take our money anymore.' She also distrusts the legal system, refusing to sign papers that would declare her father dead and give her access to his wealth.

title: A Simple Favor
justification: Stephanie expresses distrust in the police's ability to find Emily, stating, 'The police haven't been much help. But every mom knows if you want something done right, you have to do it yourself.' She also encounters bureaucratic obstacles and unhelpful staff when trying to get information about Emily's disappearance from her workplace.

title: The Predator
justification: Characters express distrust and disdain for authority. "Put a bullet in a CO. Any particular reason? He was an asshole." and "They were gonna put a bullet in your head." show a disregard for military authority and a belief in its corruption.

title: Overboard
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with institutions. Kate says, "I hate rich people. They get away with everything," and later, "This is so frustrating!" indicating a belief that the system is unfair and favors the wealthy.

title: Sicario: Day of the Soldado
justification: Characters frequently bypass or manipulate the law. Matt says, "No rules this time," and Cynthia states, "We're not supposed to fucking be there." The Secretary of Defense acknowledges the need to get "dirty."

title: The Shape of Water
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust and manipulation within the Soviet system. Characters discuss risky plans that Moscow disapproves of, and the phrase "As Lenin said, There is no profit in last week's fish" suggests a callous disregard for past actions or moral considerations.

title: Red Sparrow
justification: The dialogue reveals deep distrust and manipulation within institutions, particularly the Russian intelligence services. Characters are forced into service, and there's a pervasive sense that individuals are expendable tools of the state: "Your body belongs to the state. Since your birth, the state nourished it. Now the state asks something in return."

title: Goosebumps 2: Haunted Halloween
justification: Tyler says "Damn" when he learns his library account is frozen due to overdue books. The kids consider calling the police about the monsters, but Sam says, "They'll come and arrest us.", indicating a distrust of law enforcement.

title: 12 Strong
justification: Several lines indicate distrust of higher command and established procedures. "Every step we take is gonna be on a minefield from a hundred different wars. And no one's ever called in a smart bomb airstrike from a B-52. So anyone who tells you they've done this before or has experience in this is lying, sir." and "We're the test flight. If you die, that's a letter you and your wife are gonna wish you wrote."

title: First Man
justification: Several lines express distrust in NASA's competence and safety, such as questioning the mission's worth and the reliability of equipment. Jan's outburst, "All these protocols and procedures to make it seem like you have it under control. But you're a bunch of boys making models out of balsa wood. You don't have anything under control!" exemplifies this cynicism. Gus's line, "How are we gonna get to the Moon if we can't talk between three buildings?" also shows distrust.

title: Hereditary
justification: The police are not called when a body is found, indicating a lack of trust or belief in their ability to help. Annie states, "The police can't help us." and later, "You are sick, Annie. I need to call the police."

title: Acrimony
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of the legal system, with a character stating, "I can call the cops, I'll have your ass arrested." Additionally, the lottery system for a job is seen as unfair, as a character says, "It's a lottery system for a reason."

title: Sherlock Gnomes
justification: The police are portrayed as incompetent, arriving late to the crime scene and focusing on irrelevant details like a "lovers' quarrel" instead of the missing gnomes. Sherlock Gnomes and Juliet decide to handle the case themselves, expressing distrust in the authorities: "We can handle this ourselves."

title: Widows
justification: Several characters express distrust and frustration with the political system. Jack Mulligan admits, "I never wanted to be in this fucking business, and that's all this is. It's a fucking business!" Veronica Rawlings states, "Dollar signs and empty promises. Anybody who thinks different are fooling themselves."

title: Truth or Dare
justification: Brad's father is an officer, but Brad is still hiding the truth from him. Brad steals his father's gun and makes him beg for his life, showing a complete breakdown of trust and respect for law enforcement.

title: Love, Simon
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of respect for school rules and authority. Characters are more concerned with social events and relationships than academic pursuits. One character blackmails another, showing a disregard for ethical behavior.

title: Darkest Hour
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the government's handling of the war, questioning the competence and motives of leaders. Dialogue such as "We may have to replace him, Bertie" and "At this critical juncture for the empire, we have a drunkard at the wheel" demonstrates a strong cynicism towards the Prime Minister and the government's ability to lead effectively.

title: The 15:17 to Paris
justification: The dialogue shows a general lack of faith in the military system. Stone expresses frustration with the limitations and bureaucracy: "A year I punish myself and for what? Because of depth perception? You gotta be kidding me." Later, he sarcastically refers to his new assignment as "daycare for adults."

title: Mile 22
justification: The dialogue reveals a deep distrust of government and law, with characters operating outside legal boundaries and questioning the morality of their actions. Lines like, "You're authorized to go break the law in other countries," and "The cops played the politicians and the politicians played the cops and I don't think anyone ever knew who is on whose side," highlight this cynicism.

title: Alpha
justification: The father's dialogue, "Life is for the strong! It is earned, not given," suggests a harsh, unforgiving view of their societal structure. The son's initial failure in the hunting ritual and the tribe's emphasis on proving oneself also hint at a rigid system.

title: Peppermint
justification: The dialogue shows police corruption and distrust in the legal system. Characters express that the system is rigged, with lines like "Garcia has people on the inside?" and "You didn't serve justice, Your Honor. I will." The protagonist takes justice into her own hands because she believes the system failed her.

title: Death Wish
justification: The police are portrayed as ineffective and slow, leading the protagonist to take matters into his own hands. Detective Raines admits open cases are 'asshole-on-asshole violence' and that private investigators 'can't get involved in a police investigation'. Paul expresses his frustration, 'People rely on the police to keep them safe. That's the problem. The police only arrive after the crime has taken place.'

title: The Spy Who Dumped Me
justification: The characters distrust law enforcement and intelligence agencies, choosing to evade them and rely on their own methods. Dialogue such as, "People at my job just tried to kill all of us, so, to be honest, I'm not sure who to trust anymore," and the decision to contact Snowden over official channels, demonstrates a strong distrust of formal systems. The protagonists are framed by the FBI and distrust the international intelligence office.

title: Isle of Dogs
justification: Several characters express distrust and dislike for Mayor Kobayashi, accusing him of being a crook and a murderer. The Science-Party Candidate is held against his will, and there are accusations of propaganda and suppressed medical treatments.

title: Nobody’s Fool
justification: Tanya's flippant attitude toward her PO and AA requirements indicates a distrust of the system. Danica's sister's criminal record and the characters' general distrust of online relationships further highlight a cynical view of societal structures and individuals' intentions. The characters often bypass or manipulate the system to achieve their goals.

title: Adrift
justification: The characters are isolated at sea and must rely on their own ingenuity to survive. There is a brief mayday call, but no help arrives, suggesting a lack of institutional support. The characters are self-reliant and do not seek assistance from authorities.

title: Robin Hood
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Dialogue such as, "If you weren't a lord, I'd have you hung for treason," and "The Sheriff seized Loxley Manor as collateral for his war tax and threw Marian out," demonstrates corruption and abuse of power.

title: Slender Man
justification: The dialogue shows the police being called after a break-in, but they are ineffective in preventing further harm. The father of a missing girl takes matters into his own hands, indicating a lack of faith in the authorities. The characters also express distrust in the police's ability to find the missing girl.

title: Teen Titans Go! To The Movies
justification: The characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. They believe having a movie is the only way to be seen as a real hero, indicating a reliance on external validation rather than institutional recognition. They also exploit loopholes and weaknesses in established systems, such as tricking Superman and exploiting the Justice League's movie-watching habits.

title: Hostiles
justification: The film portrays the US Army as duplicitous and manipulative, using Blocker's pension as leverage to force him to escort Yellow Hawk. Characters express distrust in the government's treatment of Native Americans, highlighting corruption and inhumane conditions. Blocker's initial refusal to obey orders and his open contempt for Yellow Hawk demonstrate a deep-seated cynicism towards the Army's mission and moral authority.

title: Avengers: Endgame
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within S.H.I.E.L.D., later revealed to be Hydra. Characters like Rumlow betray Captain America, saying "We got word there may be an attempt to steal it," indicating corruption within the organization.

title: The Lion King
justification: Simba and Nala defy Zazu's authority, venturing into the elephant graveyard despite being told not to. Scar openly admits his plan to usurp Mufasa, highlighting the corrupt nature of his ambition and disregard for the established order. The hyenas' willingness to participate in Scar's scheme further underscores the breakdown of institutional integrity.

title: Toy Story 4
justification: The store owner says, "Nobody buys the toys anyway," indicating a lack of faith in the economic system. Gabby Gabby is portrayed as a manipulative figure who controls the antique store and its inhabitants, suggesting a corrupt power structure. The toys in the claw machine express resentment towards the system, saying, "Cheat the system and get with a kid? Yeah, we know."

title: Frozen II
justification: The film reveals that Arendelle's founder, King Runeard, betrayed the Northuldra people, using a dam as a tool to weaken them.  Anna states, "King Runeard betrayed everyone," and Mattias acknowledges, "Arendelle has no future until we make this right," indicating a need to correct past institutional wrongs.

title: Captain Marvel
justification: Several dialogues indicate distrust or circumvention of established authorities. Fury states, "We can't trust anyone. Not even our own men," and Carol bypasses S.H.I.E.L.D. protocols, reflecting a need to operate outside formal channels.

title: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker
justification: There is no dialogue present in the provided text. Therefore, there is no evidence of institutional cynicism.

title: Spider-Man: Far From Home
justification: Nick Fury kidnaps Peter and disregards his concerns about his class trip. Maria Hill says about evacuating the city, "They still won't evacuate the city. Idiots."

title: Aladdin
justification: Jafar is portrayed as manipulative and untrustworthy, exploiting the Sultan's trust for his own gain. Aladdin distrusts the system, choosing deception to win the princess: "People see what they wanna see."

title: Joker
justification: The dialogue shows a deep distrust of authority. Arthur's social worker states, "They don't give a shit about people like you, Arthur. And they really don't give a shit about people like me, either." Also, Thomas Wayne refers to less fortunate residents as "clowns."

title: Us
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of authorities. The mother calls 911, but the police take 14 minutes to arrive, and the family is left to fend for themselves. The song "Fuck the Police" playing during the attack further emphasizes the distrust and disdain for law enforcement.

title: Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw
justification: Characters express distrust and bypass formal systems. Hobbs says, "Just like the CIA, always flexing the wrong muscle," and Shaw states, "We have every major intelligence agency already hunting us down."

title: John Wick: Chapter 3 — Parabellum
justification: Characters frequently express distrust and disdain for the High Table and its rules, viewing them as corrupt and self-serving. Winston betrays John Wick at the end, and the Bowery King expresses his anger at the High Table's actions, highlighting a deep-seated cynicism towards authority and formal systems: "Under the Table is where shit gets done. And they're about to find out, if you cut a king, you better cut him to the quick."

title: How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with the current leadership and systems. Gobber says, "You're supposed to be the generation that leads us into the future," implying the current generation is failing. Astrid also says to Hiccup, "The home your father left you to protect," suggesting a burden and potential failure.

title: The Secret Life of Pets 2
justification: Some characters display a mild distrust of authority. Snowball says, "Humans always blame the airline," suggesting a cynical view of human institutions. Rooster says, "Dogs sleep outside," indicating a rigid adherence to tradition rather than practical consideration.

title: Pokémon: Detective Pikachu
justification: The dialogue shows distrust of the police and government. Pikachu says, "Unless you want Johnny Law to give you a one-way ticket to the hoosegow, let's move." Later, Mr. Clifford says his son "controls the police and the politicians."

title: Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood
justification: The dialogue shows a general disregard for the law, especially with the character Cliff, who is described as having hands registered as lethal weapons and casually mentions manslaughter. Additionally, the characters at the Spahn Ranch seem to operate outside of societal norms and laws, with little regard for authority.

title: Shazam!
justification: Several characters express distrust or frustration with authority figures. The police are portrayed as ineffective in finding Billy, and the security guard at the school is easily fooled. Mary expresses distrust in the police.

title: Knives Out
justification: The detective is portrayed as competent, but the family views the legal system as something to be manipulated. They discuss ways to contest the will, such as claiming Harlan was not of sound mind or that Marta exerted undue influence, showing a cynical view of the legal process. Ransom states, "Because fuck my family. I can help you get away with this."

title: Maleficent: Mistress of Evil
justification: The dialogue reveals distrust and manipulation within the royal court. Queen Ingrith's actions and statements, such as "I spread the story of the evil witch...and the princess she cursed," and her manipulation of the narrative to instill fear, highlight a cynical view of leadership and institutions.

title: Godzilla: King of the Monsters
justification: Multiple characters express distrust in Monarch and the government's ability to handle the Titans. Mark says, "I advise you to kill these things. All of 'em," showing a complete lack of faith in containment. Emma also distrusts the government, believing they will eradicate the creatures, leading her to take matters into her own hands.

title: The Upside
justification: The dialogue shows a distrust of formal systems, especially regarding healthcare and social services. Dell says, "ain't seen a profit in a while either," showing distrust of non-profits. The characters often bypass or complain about the established rules and procedures.

title: Ford v. Ferrari
justification: Carroll Shelby expresses distrust of Ford's corporate structure, stating they will find "new ways to screw you" because they are motivated by pleasing their superiors. Ken Miles is initially excluded from the Le Mans team due to not fitting Ford's desired image, despite his skill. Leo Beebe's control over the racing program and his personal vendetta against Miles further exemplify the institutional obstacles and biases.

title: The LEGO Movie 2: The Second Part
justification: The character Rex Dangervest displays distrust when he says, "There was no one I could trust but me." The heroes must bypass the brainwashed authority figures to save their friends. Batman expresses distrust when he says, "Batman is a permanent Bat-chelor."

title: The Addams Family
justification: The townspeople, led by Margaux Needler, quickly turn against the Addams family based on rumors and fear, highlighting a distrust of outsiders and a willingness to resort to violence. Margaux's manipulation of the community and their eagerness to believe the worst demonstrates a breakdown in rational thought and community values. The line, "We need to destroy them first!" shows a complete disregard for due process or understanding.

title: Downton Abbey
justification: Tom is being tailed by Special Branch, and he is suspected of building a bomb. The family is willing to find a "friendly judge" to challenge a will, implying corruption in the legal system. The staff conspires to replace the royal staff, showing distrust in the established order.

title: Rocketman
justification: Dick, the music producer, is portrayed as crass and only interested in profit, saying, "Ray says you're an investment. But Ray knows fuck all. You're a couple of pricks as far as I can tell." Later, John Reid, Elton's manager, is portrayed as exploitative and uncaring, prioritizing business over Elton's well-being.

title: Alita: Battle Angel
justification: Characters express distrust and frustration with the existing power structures. Alita notes that Grewishka is being protected by the system, and Ido states that the city corrupts even good people. Vector is also portrayed as corrupt, manipulating Motorball for his own gain.

title: Good Boys
justification: The boys repeatedly break the law (drug possession, theft, assault) and distrust the police. They also mock the police officer, indicating a lack of respect for law enforcement. The line, "Anything will be used against you that you say. In court," shows a cynical understanding of legal proceedings.

title: Men in Black: International
justification: Agent H makes several cynical remarks about his job, such as "Some irony there, sir, if you think that we used to, uh, protect Earth from the scum of the universe. Now it seems we're protecting scum." Later, he and M disagree on whether to report Vungus's medical emergency, with H dismissing the idea due to "the paperwork is a nightmare."

title: Annabelle Comes Home
justification: The police officer redirects the family after an accident, and they end up in a different location. The parents also seem to hide their profession from their daughter's babysitter, suggesting a distrust of outsiders.

title: Yesterday
justification: The protagonist is pressured to conform to industry standards, like album titles and collaborations, that he finds inauthentic. His manager, Debra, embodies this cynicism, prioritizing profit over artistic integrity. The line, "And then we take most of it," highlights the exploitative nature of the music industry.

title: Tyler Perry’s A Madea Family Funeral
justification: The dialogue reveals a lack of trust in the hospital staff's competence and transparency, with characters questioning the doctor's absence and the cause of death.
